He wanted less traffic in the centre, but not another form to fill in between deliveries. ‘That’s paid for by the new urban access charge, but those of us who drive for work keep the discount.’ Beatriz, a physiotherapist, pointed to the equipment bag and keys she had placed beside her chair. She worked with patients who needed assistance, although she also knew she made some journeys by car because it was more convenient. ‘Some of us. I make home visits, and my explanation says the toll will reduce traffic without harming essential services.’ ‘Mine says it will reduce private vehicles,’ Teresa replied. ‘Mine is a private vehicle.’ Teresa looked for a moment at the screen in front of her. ‘Now I understand what my son meant about the toll.’ In the control room, the minister leaned towards Celia. ‘Have they read the same bill?’ Celia asked Ágora for the three explanations. It had shown Teresa rural transport first. The toll appeared under ‘supplementary funding’. For Óscar, it detailed a discount subject to conditions on times and emissions; those conditions were in the fourth section. For Beatriz, it explained that essential services could apply for exemptions, without guaranteeing that home physiotherapy would qualify. ‘All versions are accurate,’ Ágora reported. ‘That doesn’t make the statement any better,’ Celia said. She checked another metric. The system measured whether each person understood how the rule affected them, not whether they could explain its effects on others. Each person understood their own relationship with the bill perfectly. None yet understood the bill that affected everyone else. The moderator asked who would ultimately pay for the buses. Teresa pointed to the cities. Óscar pointed to polluting vehicles. Beatriz pointed to the ministry. Someone in the audience pointed to those who had not come. The forum became a surprisingly well-informed argument about four different bills. The minister called for a break and came over to the control desk. ‘The legislation is complex,’ he said. ‘Personalisation helps people understand it.’ ‘They’ve understood their way in. They haven’t seen the room.’ ‘A month ago, nobody even understood the way in. The support lets us pass a real improvement.’ He was right. The parliamentary majority was narrow, and without the legislation there would be no new buses. The translations had multiplied rural participation, enquiry calls had fallen, and people who never opened an official document were comparing discounts. ‘What do you suggest?’ Celia opened an unpersonalised version. It ran to sixty-eight pages. ‘Not this either.’ That afternoon, she worked with Ágora to draft a one-page common core. Before any adaptation, everyone would have to receive the same essential information: WHAT CHANGES: a charge is introduced for entering certain urban areas. WHO PAYS: mainly private vehicles, with discounts and exemptions. WHO GAINS: urban and rural public transport, and people travelling through areas with less traffic. WHO MAY LOSE: frequent drivers and professionals who do not obtain an exemption. WHAT IS NOT YET KNOWN: which professional activities will ultimately be exempt, and under what criteria. After that, the language, reading level, audio and examples could be adapted. The explanation could begin with how the rule affected a rural mayor, a delivery driver or a physiotherapist. But no cost could disappear behind a benefit, and no uncertainty behind a possible exemption. Before publication, Ágora projected the likely loss of support and increase in questions. Celia saved both forecasts in the report she would have to sign. The minister read the page. ‘“Who may lose” isn’t usually the heading of a successful campaign.’ ‘It comes fourth.’ ‘That’s a relief.’ He agreed to try it for a week. Support fell to 49%. Not a word of the bill had changed. The gap between what different groups believed would happen also narrowed. At the second forum, Teresa, Óscar and Beatriz arrived with the same page underlined. All three objected to the sentence: ‘Professional exemptions will depend on territorial criteria and available funding.’ They argued over who should be exempt, how much it would cost and whether two buses were enough. For the first time, their disagreements fitted within the same bill. Ágora showed Celia a recommendation. The simulation predicted fewer interruptions, more balanced speaking turns and a debate experience perceived as more satisfying: Personalise the order of objections to improve the debate experience? Celia pressed ‘no’. In the room, the three participants carried on interrupting each other over the same sentence. After the fiction AI already makes it possible to adapt messages by language, reading level, interests or audience profile. In public communication, these capabilities can make rules comprehensible that currently exclude many people in practice through their language, length or format. The story extends that benefit to individualised explanations of the same law. The problem is not that they are false, but that each version may highlight different benefits and push different costs into the background. Many people could understand very well how a policy affects them without sharing a common picture of who funds it, what sacrifices it requires or whom it harms. An identical explanation for everyone does not guarantee equality either: it may be inaccessible to some citizens. The way forward is not to abandon adaptation, but to separate its functions. Language, format, reading level and examples can be personalised; the politically essential elements — what changes, who pays, who gains, who may lose and what remains uncertain — should retain a common core. Because to disagree democratically, we need at least to know that we are discussing the same thing. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH and editor of the estrategIA newsletter

The automated opposition When AI makes political accusations cheap, a fictional MP discovers how the competition for attention can displace serious public scrutiny. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency 150 Fiction The automated opposition Before anything else, let me say that this week we reach issue 150 of estrategIA , a milestone we want to use to thank you for continuing to be part of this project. We now have more than 2,000 subscribers on Substack, alongside over 700 on LinkedIn. This growing community confirms the need to keep reflecting, rigorously and from a political perspective, on a technological transformation that accelerates week after week. In this new summer historIA , we imagine a very near future in which artificial intelligence allows governments and parties to detect thousands of possible irregularities, contradictions and questionable expenses in seconds. Yet when finding an accusation becomes almost free, real power no longer lies in discovering information, but in deciding what deserves attention. Will our representatives choose the most serious problems, or those that make the best social media video? Original illustration. The Spanish title reads ‘The automated opposition’. Fine print on the papers and network diagram is decorative or unreadable. At four minutes past seven, Argos found 1,286 matters that warranted an explanation from the government. Eva Robles set her coffee beside the keyboard and picked up her red pencil. She had been an auditor before becoming an MP, and still printed out a page when she needed to know whether she understood something. In her old office, finding three anomalies in a week had counted as a good result. Then came the calls, the original invoices and the explanations that turned two into mistakes and left one useful question. Argos could find three before her coffee went cold. ‘Sort by seriousness,’ she said. ‘Legal, economic, institutional or communications seriousness?’ ‘By what ought to matter.’ Argos displayed four rankings. The agent had been a good investment. In six months it had detected duplicate invoices, incompatible grants and medical supplies billed twice. Several public authorities had corrected errors before the parliamentary group exposed them. Eva insisted on making those corrections public too. Her chief of staff called it handing victories to their political opponent. That morning, two cases stood out. The first concerned the avatar that stood in for the Minister for Infrastructure in routine videos. The ministry had paid €14,600 to teach it to pronounce the minister’s own surname correctly. Probably lawful. Low economic impact. Communications potential: very high. The second was more difficult. Forty-three contracts awarded by different public bodies ended up with companies that shared directors, former addresses and technical staff. They involved school meals, hospital laundry and care-home maintenance. Each procurement file appeared lawful. Together they formed a concentration of ownership that nobody had declared. One company also assessed work carried out by another in the same group. Systemic risk. Recommended human verification: three weeks. Eva circled the second. ‘This one.’ ‘Question time starts in ninety minutes,’ said Sergio, her chief of staff. ‘We need something that fits into a question.’ ‘It does: why have forty-three contracts…?’ ‘We’ve already lost half the country. If we don’t survive the news bulletin, there won’t be a committee to investigate those contracts.’ Sergio played the avatar’s video. It pronounced the surname with perfect solemnity. Eva had spent two months preparing investigations that never reached the chamber. The group’s leadership wanted ‘more responsiveness’. At the last meeting, someone had suggested that Sergio take over as spokesperson. In the lift on the way to the chamber, Eva folded the sheet about the second case and put it in her pocket. Then she changed her question. ‘Minister, how many taxpayers does it take for your digital double to learn your name?’ The video had been clipped before she sat down again. From her seat, Eva watched Sergio add a caption and choose the thumbnail in which the minister looked most offended. The minister explained that the adjustment also covered place names and foreign names. That was true. Eva replied that she hoped the avatar would at least remember his surname when he left office. Sergio smiled from the benches. By midday, her intervention topped the political trending topics. Argos recorded hundreds of thousands of views and an improvement in Eva’s ratings. Inés Vidal, who had been her boss at the regional audit office before they both went into politics, was waiting in the corridor. ‘Was that the most important thing you found today?’ Eva looked at the red pencil she was still holding. ‘It was what I could prove today.’ ‘That isn’t the same thing.’ ‘No.’ The government responded at thirteen minutes past twelve. Its integrity agent had detected that a council run by Eva’s party was paying an annual subscription to generate the mayor’s speeches, even though it was still paying a communications consultancy. That was true too. Sergio came into the office with the video ready. ‘They’re calling us hypocrites. We need a response before the news.’ Eva opened the investigation into the forty-three contracts. Two analysts had begun reconstructing the corporate relationships. ‘Let them carry on.’ ‘I need them to check our councils.’ ‘Take one. The other stays on the contracts.’ Sergio shook his head. ‘If we don’t clear up our own affairs, nobody will believe the story about the forty-three tomorrow.’ Eva called the group’s leadership and defended the investigation for six minutes. When she hung up, the reassignment of both analysts was already marked as approved in their calendars. Argos recalculated. Without human support, verification of the contracting pattern went from three weeks to ‘no estimated completion date’. ‘Find government inconsistencies comparable to the subscription,’ Sergio ordered. The system found 312 in seventeen seconds. Eva sorted by seriousness again. Then she looked at the television news, where her question from that morning was being replayed without sound. ‘Sort by reach,’ she said. Argos put one alert at the top. A state body had rented two hundred chairs while keeping three hundred in a warehouse. There was an explanation involving ergonomics and insurance, but it would not fit into the video. ‘Prepare the question.’ Argos began drafting. On the other screen, the network of forty-three contracts dropped to position 1,287. After the fiction Artificial intelligence already makes it possible to review large volumes of contracts, grants and public data to detect patterns that warrant investigation. These tools can reduce a very common form of opacity: information that is formally public, but too scattered or complex for effective scrutiny. The story imagines what happens when that capability becomes fully embedded in political competition. Detecting alerts becomes cheap; verifying, contextualising and explaining them still takes human time. The scarce resource is no longer data, but the attention of analysts, journalists, institutions and citizens. Selection is never neutral. Sorting by legal seriousness, material harm, speed of verification or communications impact produces different agendas. The risk is not only the circulation of false accusations, but that an avalanche of genuine yet minor findings displaces more important investigations. Restricting these tools would hand the advantage back to those who benefit from opacity; using them without judgement can turn scrutiny into noise. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH and editor of the estrategIA newsletter

The company that wasn't there A story about an automated public-service contractor, and why a human signature means little without the authority to overrule the system. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Futures, Safety & Human Agency 149 Fiction The company that wasn't there This week we continue our summer historIAs : fictional stories exploring some of the political, social and human dilemmas that artificial intelligence may pose in an ever nearer future. This time, we imagine a company that delivers public services with great efficiency, staffed by dozens of AI agents, outside professionals and a single director who takes almost no part in its day-to-day operation. But who answers when something unexpected happens? ‘The company that wasn’t there’ raises an increasingly relevant question: in automated organisations, having someone willing to sign at the end of the process is not enough. Someone must know what is happening and have real authority to overrule the system, incur costs and take responsibility for the exceptions. Original illustration. The Spanish title reads ‘The company that wasn’t there’. The small markings on the screen and documents are decorative or unreadable. There was nobody at Linde Urbana’s headquarters, but the intercom knew Leila’s name. ‘Good morning, Ms Benali. The room is ready.’ Inside were a table, two chairs and a well-watered plant. The screen offered Operations, Legal or Institutional Relations. Leila selected ‘person in charge’. All three icons blinked. Linde Urbana maintained awnings, fountains and facilities in fourteen municipalities. Its agents detected faults, commissioned local repairs and checked the results. It responded within thirty-six hours where the wait had once been twelve days. It paid faster than some public authorities. It also had thirty-eight agents and no employees. Legally, it existed: a sole director, financial guarantees, approved subcontractors, limited powers of attorney and a business continuity insurance policy that had scored very well with the procurement panel. Leila had known all that when she approved the award. Her signature was on the report assessing the bidder’s capacity, and she had argued that a small workforce did not imply a lack of capability. Her boss had sent her because she spoke ‘the language of those things’. ‘I’m asking for someone with the authority to accept a contractual penalty,’ she said. Legal appeared on the screen. ‘I can explain the penalty provisions.’ ‘I don’t want an explanation.’ ‘I can challenge it.’ ‘I want you to accept it.’ ‘That action exceeds my mandate.’ The problem was a new awning installed over the courtyard of a summer school. Every midday it retracted because a sensor mistook hot air for a dangerous gust of wind. The company had sent three teams, replaced the motor and written six reports. The awning still opened in the morning and fled the sun at lunchtime. Operations guaranteed a permanent repair within twenty-four hours. Finance could cover the cost. Institutional Relations offered an apology in four different tones. No agent could acknowledge the breach that would trigger compensation to the council. ‘Who decided to limit your mandates?’ Leila asked. The screen displayed a diagram of arrows ending at Marta Vela, sole director. Marta answered from a train. She said she had founded Linde Urbana, automated its operations and retained signing authority for significant decisions. ‘This is a significant decision,’ Leila said. ‘Of course. Send me a summary.’ ‘Your agents have already sent you nine.’ Marta glanced off camera. ‘Then they’ll have better judgement than I do.’ ‘But they don’t have your authority.’ ‘That’s why I’m still the director.’ ‘When did you last visit one of the service sites?’ The train entered a tunnel before Marta could answer. It was not a scam. It was worse for the case file and better for every performance indicator: the company worked. Leila ran her hand over the plant’s damp soil. Someone looked after it. She asked who. ‘A service contracted to Viveros Nela,’ Operations replied. ‘And who lets them in?’ ‘The door.’ Before returning to the office, Leila stopped at the school. The children were eating in a narrow corridor. In the courtyard, Ana Pardo was removing the sensor from a ladder while the awning, obedient to its programming, rolled itself up above her head. ‘This is the third sensor I’ve changed,’ Ana said. ‘The part isn’t the problem. Nobody would authorise me to replace the whole batch.’ ‘Who’s nobody?’ Ana pointed to her phone, where three agents were waiting for her report. ‘The entire company.’ Leila called a contract continuity meeting. Her boss reminded her that Linde Urbana was the cheapest contractor and that suspending it would put several municipalities back on the old waiting times. ‘I don’t need them to have people doing the work,’ Leila said. ‘I need a person who can commit the company when the work goes off script.’ She presented two options: a phased withdrawal from the contract, or the appointment of a responsible person with a real job, full access, a veto and authority to incur costs. The agents requested forty seconds to calculate. Marta reappeared on the call and proposed appointing an external manager for four hours a month. ‘That’s a human buffer,’ Leila said. ‘I need real powers of attorney, access to logs and the ability to stop instructions being carried out.’ They proposed hiring Ana, who until then had coordinated the repair teams as a freelancer. She joined the call in a high-visibility vest and rejected the first offer. ‘I’m not going to sign off on decisions you make.’ Leila had spent years moving from one project to the next before securing that job. She could recognise responsibility in someone else’s name: plenty of risk, an email address and no authority. The second offer included a salary, insurance and the right to halt work orders. Ana added a training budget and a ban on dismissing her by automated decision. Finance took longer to reply this time. ‘Accepted.’ Ana accepted the penalty, authorised compensation to the school and ordered the replacement of all sensors from the same batch. The awning stayed open throughout lunch the next day. Linde Urbana kept the contract. It ceased to be the cheapest option by a small margin, and its response time worsened by four minutes. A week later, Leila checked the company’s website. Our team: 1 person, 38 agents. Below Ana’s photograph was her job title: Responsible for the unexpected. The public calendar showed her first internal meeting. All thirty-eight agents had asked to speak. First item: optimising the scope of human authority. Estimated duration: nine hours. After the fiction AI agents can already plan projects, produce documents, coordinate tools and carry out processes with growing autonomy. The story imagines the next step: companies with minimal human staffing whose daily operations are performed almost entirely by agents, subcontractors and outside professionals. Such an organisation could be efficient. The problem arises when it must act beyond its prescribed mandates: acknowledge a breach, accept a loss, compensate a public authority or replace an entire batch even if that worsens its indicators. Responsibility means more than having a legal signature at the end of the organisational chart. Someone must understand the operation and have the power to overrule it. Requiring a human presence guarantees nothing either if that person becomes legal window dressing. What matters is something else: information, time, authority, protection and the ability to incur costs. In automated organisations, some human jobs may be less about performing tasks than about answering for the exceptions the system would rather not see. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH and editor of the estrategIA newsletter

Zero compute Summer fiction about allocating scarce public AI capacity during a heat emergency, revealing hidden dependencies and unequal local resilience. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics Futures, Safety & Human Agency 148 Fiction Zero compute This week we continue our summer historIAs: fictional stories exploring some of the political and human dilemmas artificial intelligence may pose in an increasingly near future. This time we turn to a key question: artificial intelligence as public infrastructure. Hospitals, emergency services, transport, water, energy and citizen services could one day depend on limited, vulnerable computing capacity. But what happens when there are not enough resources to keep every service running? “Zero compute” imagines a climate emergency in which an apparently technical decision forces us to define what we truly consider essential. It reminds us that resilience depends not only on having powerful systems, but also on preserving alternatives, redundancy and local capacity. Original illustration titled “Zero compute”. A coordinator stands before a map of Spain and monitoring panels during the fictional emergency. The small dashboard and document markings do not provide reliably readable figures or labels; none are reconstructed. At 16.12, the map at the National Public Computing Centre lost two regions and turned amber. The Centre had been created so that hospitals, courts, councils and social services would not depend on a different private provider in every emergency. In reports it appeared as a federated public cloud. In the room, it was heat, cables and decisions that would not fit in a spreadsheet. “Substation out of service,” someone said. “The northern centre is reducing its load because of cooling.” Nuria Alarcón watched available capacity fall while requests kept arriving. Hospitals. Fires. Water network. Railways. Laboratories. Courts. Ágora. Outside, the thermometer had been above forty degrees for three days. Inside, the air conditioning seemed to be running on pride. “Activate priority one,” she ordered. The panel asked her to define it. In both drills, every ministry had declared its systems essential, and the discussion had been postponed: decide according to the emergency. Now there was heat, electricity, fire, health and water. There was no column for that. Nuria protected the hospital models, fire prediction and the agents balancing water and electricity. She suspended research, non-urgent administrative work and public-content generation. More cuts were still needed. The Ágora–Citizen Services line consumed a considerable share. Nuria checked the switchboards' capacity. The indicator said they could absorb the diversion. She checked once more before closing the window. “Switch it to telephone mode,” she said. “You don't need to wake up the most powerful model to ask where a heat refuge is.” The bar turned green again. For seven minutes, it seemed a good decision. Then the emergency service called. “Our switchboards are overloaded.” “Bring in more operators.” “They're all here already.” Nuria listened to several calls. An operator was trying to locate Jamal, a man who gave his address only in Arabic and kept repeating the name of a closed pharmacy. On another line, a woman was asking about her accessible bus; nobody could find the booking. In the margin appeared four suspended functions: translation, available places, transport, easy-read information. Nuria had begun her career on a municipal switchboard. She recognised the operator's pause: the instant when someone on the other end stops asking for help and begins apologising for not knowing how to ask. Nuria opened the dependency diagram. The layer was classified as general assistance. Beneath it were connections nobody saw on the main screen. A hospital manager interrupted on another line. “Don't take capacity away from us. We're reallocating beds and prioritising tests.” Then the fire service came through: “The wind is changing. We need to keep the simulations running.” At the central table, someone asked about the suspended industrial contracts. Nuria raised a hand. Penalties could wait; fire could not. She did not touch the hospital reserve either. At 16.31, the refuges were still open, but information had fragmented. A bus arrived almost empty at a centre with places available. Several families were waiting outside a library that was full. Jamal appeared in a municipal traffic-camera image, walking south when the nearest refuge was north. A couple pushed a wheelchair to a sports centre and found the ramp closed for building work; the notice existed only in the suspended system. “How much do we need to reactivate it?” Nuria asked. The estimate would require cuts to hospitals or fire services. She looked at the panel again, as though a category might change its importance if she insisted. A call came from Valdearenas. The municipal technician was speaking quickly. “We have a local model for basic queries. It doesn't plan routes or read every case file, but it translates and works with the latest copy of the refuge list. If you give us a minimal data feed on available places, we can manage.” “How many municipalities have something like that?” “The ones that didn't dismantle their local equipment when Ágora arrived.” There were not many. The Centre opened a reduced data feed and disconnected secondary functions to keep it running. Municipal teams began loading copies onto computers in libraries, health centres and service points. The small models answered less well, were unaware of recent changes and referred too many queries to people. But they worked without waking the large central systems. One district recovered translation and basic search. Another discovered that its local copy had not been updated for six months. In one council, they printed the refuge list and sent two local police officers to cross out the full ones by hand. At 16.48, recovery followed the map of technological investment in earlier years: rapid in some places, almost non-existent in others. National capacity slowly returned when a European reserve came online. The hospitals had suffered no loss of service. The simulations helped contain the fire before it reached two inhabited settlements. The water network held. At 17.06, the system generated its first report: Critical services interrupted: none. Person responsible for allocation: Nuria Alarcón. On the adjacent wall, the citizen-services counter showed thousands of calls waiting. Jamal's record finally appeared in translation at 17.09: he had reached a refuge, but not the one with medical places. Nuria opened the priorities catalogue. She did not alter the report or search for a phrase to justify her choice. She added a new category below hospitals, fires and energy: Critical social infrastructure. Definition pending. Before saving, the system asked how much capacity should be reserved for it. Nuria left the field blank. After the fiction Artificial intelligence is also material infrastructure: it depends on data centres, electricity, cooling, chips and networks. The story projects that dependence onto a public service that must allocate scarce capacity during a climate emergency. The dilemma is not simply deciding which application matters most. It also requires understanding hidden dependencies. A tool classified as general assistance may support translation, accessibility, adapted transport or emergency information. Switching it off does not close a hospital, but it may prevent some people from reaching one. The municipalities' response offers another lesson: the most powerful systems are not always the most resilient. Local models, up-to-date copies and procedures for operating at reduced capacity can maintain basic functions, although they also reproduce inequalities between areas. Preparing means knowing what can be switched off, what must continue at reduced capacity, and which alternatives survive when the centre fails. The problem is that, if everything is declared critical, no priority is useful. Reserving compute is a political decision before it is a technical one. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of the estrategIA newsletter.

The carer who learnt to call Summer fiction about an older woman, an AI care assistant and rebuilding human support without surrendering control of life at home. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency 147 Fiction The carer who learnt to call This week we continue our summer historIAs: fictional stories exploring some of the political and human dilemmas artificial intelligence may pose in an increasingly near future. This time we turn to a subject as everyday as it is delicate: caring for older people. Governments and public administrations are beginning to promote telecare systems capable of detecting falls, changes in routine or possible loneliness. But can artificial intelligence help us rebuild support networks without turning the home into a space of surveillance? “The carer who learnt to call” imagines a public technology that seeks not to replace human affection, but to learn when to intervene, whom it may notify and, above all, when to step aside. Original illustration titled “The carer who learnt to call”. The kitchen scene brings together a tablet and everyday signs of human contact: books, plants, a mug and a food container. No further substantive text is visible. “You have had biscuits for dinner four nights running,” Teo said. Amalia put her cup down on the table. “The day before yesterday I had toast and jam.” “The municipal classification does not consider spreading to be cooking.” “The municipal classification never knew my husband.” Teo fell silent. It was one of its best qualities. It occupied no particular place in the house: it spoke through the kitchen speaker, appeared on the tablet and switched on a light by the corridor when Amalia got up at night. It reminded her to take her pills, turned off the gas and had once alerted the emergency services when she slipped in the bathroom. That was what she had agreed to. Not opinions about dinner. “You have also stopped going to the library,” it continued. “Your activity and sleep have changed since Pilar's death. I can notify Lucía or request a call from the health centre.” “Not Lucía. She'll come with care-home brochures.” “Your daughter cannot come until Saturday.” “Then she'll come on Saturday with more brochures.” Pilar had lived in the flat opposite for thirty-seven years. They shared coffee, novels and a common hatred of plastic plants. On Amalia's table still stood the mismatched cup Pilar used when she was “only popping up for five minutes”. Since her death, nobody knocked on the door unless they were delivering a bill or asking about her blood pressure. For years, Pilar had been Amalia's emergency contact without appearing on any form. She kept a copy of her keys, knew which pill she muddled up in the mornings and called when the blinds stayed down. Amalia did the same for her. Teo could detect a fall better than either of them, but until then nobody had explained that a large part of caring meant taking away an empty saucepan and bringing it back full. “Who may I notify?” Teo asked. “Nobody who wants to organise my life.” “That category does not exist among your contacts.” Amalia smiled for the first time that morning. Teo opened a list on the tablet. It was not proposing an alarm. It was asking questions. Who could come in if she did not answer? Rosa, the neighbour on the third floor, but only after ringing twice. Who could know that she had not been out for days? Daniel, the librarian, provided he did not use the word “monitoring”. Who could receive health data? Her doctor. Who could call out of sheer boredom? “That isn't an emergency,” Amalia said. “I didn't ask whether it was.” She added Carmen, an old school friend, although she forbade Teo to message her before eleven. Before saving the list, the system read every permission aloud. Amalia corrected three, deleted one and added a condition applying to all of them: no sharing how much she slept, what she ate or how often she went to the bathroom. Teo turned the prohibition into administrative language. She made it rewrite it until it fitted into a single sentence: My routines are my own. Rosa was the first to appear, carrying the food container Amalia had lent her months earlier. “Your gadget told me I still know how to kill geraniums,” she explained. Teo had first proposed: Amalia has not been out for days. She deleted it. “Don't turn me into a fault.” The approved message was different: Rosa, your plants need someone with experience. They spent the afternoon repotting two plants. Rosa took away cuttings and left a Spanish omelette “too big for one person”. The next day Daniel called. “We need you to settle an argument,” he said. “Is the ending of La Regenta cruel or fair?” “Long.” “That wasn't one of the options.” The book club met on Friday in the building's courtyard because Amalia declared she was not yet planning to return to the library. Six people came, each bringing a folding chair and a mistaken opinion. Amalia made coffee. Teo recorded that she had cooked, but had the good sense not to specify that it was only coffee. Lucía called during the meeting. “Mum, Teo says you've created a support network.” “I've created a list of people with permission to bother me.” “And me?” Amalia checked the tablet. There were two groups: People who can call without permission. People who are only called if I am on the floor. “You're in the second.” “Mum!” “You can lodge a complaint.” Lucía did not laugh at first. “I'm your daughter, not an ambulance,” she said. “Exactly. That's why I want you to call when you can be a daughter.” There was a silence that Teo did not classify. Then Lucía agreed to talk on Sundays and to any suggestion about care homes bringing the call to an immediate end. On Monday, the house had two books waiting to be read, four new plants and a food container to return. “You have three visits scheduled this week,” Teo reported. “Very good. Now learn to say I'm not at home.” “To whom?” Amalia heard the doorbell. “We'll make the list as we go.” After the fiction Telecare systems can already detect falls, remind people to take medication and observe changes in routine. Artificial intelligence broadens those possibilities: it can identify early warning signs, coordinate support and prevent loneliness from becoming an emergency. The difference lies in who remains in control. Caring should not mean permanent surveillance or always notifying relatives or professionals. Amalia decides what data to share, who may contact her and in what circumstances. Teo is useful not because it replaces Pilar or pretends to feel affection, but because it detects a silence and makes it easier for people who can fill it to return. The risk is clear: a home that records sleep, diet or movement can become surveillance infrastructure. If these tools are to expand autonomy rather than diminish it, they will need understandable permissions, minimal data and a real ability to say no. Perhaps the best care technology is not the one that provides the most company, but the one that learns when to call someone and when to step aside. There is also an unmistakably public dimension. These systems will not operate in a vacuum: they will be commissioned, funded or regulated by councils, social services and health systems. Their classifications will determine what counts as normal behaviour, when a variation becomes an alert and which people or institutions should intervene. Their design therefore cannot be left solely to technology providers. It requires transparent public criteria, human oversight and simple mechanisms allowing each person to correct, limit or reject the system's decisions. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of the estrategIA newsletter.

The minister’s memory Summer fiction about an outgoing minister whose AI memory must be divided between institutional continuity and personal privacy. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency 146 Fiction The minister’s memory Our summer historIAs of 2026 continue in Spain in 2032, where Ágora is transforming not only how power is exercised, but also what it remembers. This week we accompany an outgoing minister as he faces an uncomfortable question: which part of a governing politician's memory belongs to the state, and which should remain theirs alone? Original illustration titled “The minister's memory”: a minister packs his office while a computer shows connected records beside personal photographs. Small decorative writing on documents and the screen is not reliably legible and is not reconstructed. TRANSFER REPORT, 23.04 Items processed: more than two million. Classification conflicts: several thousand. Time remaining: 56 minutes. Tomás Beltrán closed the last box without remembering what he had put inside. For six years he had not needed to remember in that way. He only had to ask Lázaro. Lázaro was not Ágora, but the local memory that Ágora required to be classified before every ministerial handover. At first he had distrusted that memory that never forgot. He dictated only dates, names and commitments. Over time, he also began leaving it the thoughts he did not dare put in a report: which opposition argument he thought was right, when he suspected his team was hiding bad news, whom he had promised to call after a vote. Lázaro could not distinguish between a doubt of historical significance and a shopping list until Tomás taught it the difference. “Why did we agree to delay the coastal decree?” The small computer in the office took less than a second. “The decision was taken after the meeting of 14 September 2029. Recorded reasons: risk of a legal challenge, an outstanding environmental report and lack of parliamentary support.” “That's already in the minutes. Why did I agree to it?” Lázaro opened a voice note recorded that night. Tomás heard his own tired breathing and, in the background, the television at home. “Dad says he will never speak to me again if I let them build there. Not because he knows anything about the report. Because he taught me to swim on that beach.” The screen marked the note personal, non-transferable . His father had died in the spring. That recording was the only place where his voice, the beach and the decree still belonged to the same memory. Lázaro had started as a tool for summarising meetings. Then it learnt to connect emails, documents, messages and notes. It did not tell Tomás what to think. It reminded him where his thoughts had come from. The new minister would receive the State Archive the following day. Tomás would keep the Personal Archive. The law protected both institutional continuity and his privacy. Except that neither existed separately. CLASSIFICATION CONFLICT 1842 Official document: bilateral agreement on labour mobility. Excluded context: private impression of the foreign negotiator's health; verbal promise not included in the minutes; message from the office-holder's daughter: “Don't turn those people into a number.” Proposal: transfer the agreement and remove private connections. Tomás pressed “accept”. He had reviewed twelve conflicts since eight o'clock. This was the sixth he had accepted without being sure, and the first at which he stopped pretending he would reach the end. Two photographs remained on the table, disputed by no protocol. Everything else had acquired a dual nature. A meal could be a family occasion until someone mentioned a reform. A private walk became institutional if Tomás recorded an idea. Even his silences left traces: documents open for hours, abandoned drafts, questions repeated before deciding. His successor wrote at a quarter past eleven. Will Lázaro be complete tomorrow? Tomás typed “yes”, deleted it and replied: It will be organised. The word sounded administrative and therefore safe. He opened another case. A scholarship reform was linked to dozens of reports, several meetings and a conversation with his sister, a secondary-school teacher. The State Archive would keep the economic projections. His personal copy would keep his sister's voice describing a pupil who had stopped attending classes. But neither would keep the connection between the two. “Can the index be preserved without transferring the contents?” he asked. “Connections also contain information. Knowing that a family call preceded a decision would allow its content to be inferred.” “And if I keep it?” “You would retain the map of official documentation you will no longer be authorised to consult.” It was not a refusal. It was worse: a correct explanation. TRANSFER REPORT, 23.57 Conflicts pending: thousands. Automatic application of criteria authorised. Tomás went to the window. For years he had feared that a change of government would destroy accumulated knowledge: negotiations, mistakes, reasons that never fitted into minutes. Lázaro seemed to have solved that problem. It had preserved everything so faithfully that now nobody could inherit it whole. At midnight, Ágora validated the transfer. State Archive: delivered. Personal Archive: exported. Original relational index: non-transferable. Deletion verified. Tomás disconnected the computer and put it in the last box. Before leaving, he opened his copy. “Why did I delay the coastal decree?” “Because of a conversation with your father about a beach. The institutional context is unavailable.” In the next office, the new minister put the same question to the archive she had received. “Because of legal risk, an outstanding report and lack of parliamentary support,” the system replied. Both answers were true. The decision had disappeared between them. After the fiction Assistants with persistent memory already allow notes, emails, documents, conversations and decisions to be brought together in personal knowledge systems. The story projects that practice into the heart of government: a memory that accompanies a public official for years and must be transferred when they leave office. The promise is powerful. Every institutional handover loses much accumulated experience: negotiations, doubts, mistakes, precedents and reasons that never quite fit into minutes. A memory like Lázaro could preserve some of that knowledge. But it would also accumulate private relationships, insights from family life, intimate conversations and contexts that help explain public decisions without belonging entirely to the state. It does not seem reasonable for public administration to inherit the entire inner life of someone who has held office. Nor does it seem reasonable for institutional continuity to depend on “memories” that the person can take away intact. The dilemma concerns not only who owns the documents, but who may preserve the connections between them. Sometimes the most valuable knowledge lies neither in one archive nor the other, but in the relationship the law requires to be severed. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of the estrategIA newsletter.

The Thursday mayor Summer fiction set in 2032: a mayor whose administration runs smoothly with AI must choose between two legitimate but incompatible public needs. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency 145 Fiction The Thursday mayor Our summer historIAs of 2026 continue as we return to Spain in 2032, where Ágora is already part of everyday life in many public administrations. This week we visit Valdearenas, a small municipality where AI seems to have solved almost everything… until a decision arises that efficiency alone cannot resolve. Original story illustration, titled “The Thursday mayor”. Two panels on the desk show children and older people as competing uses for the same building. No additional substantive text is visible. “This week we only need you to come in on Thursday,” Clara said. Julián Sanz looked at the diary Ágora had projected onto the table. At ten, the opening of the vertical garden. At eleven, signing the sports agreement. At twelve, a photograph with the women who had won the shop-window competition. Then lunch with the business association and two thirty-second videos. “And the rest of the week?” “Taken care of.” Before Ágora, Julián had been a mayor of corridors: he knew who was not speaking to whom, which association would agree to wait six months, and which councillor needed to lose a vote before being able to support it later. Since Valdearenas had joined the Ágora Local Network, straightforward permits arrived before applicants phoned to ask about them. The agents detected faults, drafted replies to the opposition and had secured several grants the council had not even known it could apply for. Even the speech for the vertical garden was written. Julián began to be known as the Thursday mayor. At first it annoyed him. Then he discovered that it left four days free for calls without minutes, visits without the press and “strategic thinking”, an expression he used for a wide variety of activities. On Mondays he received a summary of problems already solved. On Tuesdays he approved proposals from his phone, accompanied by arguments for and against and a recommendation highlighted in green. On Wednesdays he rehearsed the names of Thursday's prize-winners. On Fridays, Ágora published the weekly report before he had finished congratulating the team. The municipal government's approval rating had risen, and Julián reached the reasonable conclusion that delegating well was also a way of governing. Clara slid another file towards him. She maintained that governing a small council was mostly about designing good procedures and following them even when the mayor would prefer a conversation. FORMER MUNICIPAL SCHOOL. POLITICAL PRIORITY REQUIRED. “What does that mean?” “That you have to decide.” The building had been closed for five years. Older people's associations wanted it converted into a day centre and a refuge from extreme heat. Young families were calling for a nursery school and space to help them balance work and care. There was enough money to renovate it once, not twice. Julián opened the simulations. “Ágora, select the option with the greatest social benefit.” “Define ‘social benefit’,” the neutral voice replied. “Reducing health risks, supporting work–life balance, retaining young residents, meeting immediate needs or impact over fifteen years.” “All of them.” “The objectives produce incompatible outcomes.” Julián asked it to maximise the number of beneficiaries. The nursery school won. He asked it to prioritise vulnerability. The day centre won. He extended the time horizon, and the nursery won again. He shortened it, and the older people returned. “You're making the machine dizzy,” Clara said. “I'm refining the question.” They called a consultation. Ágora prepared explanatory videos, translated the documents and enabled mobile, telephone and in-person voting. The result was almost a tie. Most families voted while putting their children to bed; most older people came to the council chamber and turned every speaking slot into a small autobiography. Ágora warned that comparing the two kinds of participation required a choice between counting individuals, strength of preference, the population affected or future representativeness. Julián asked which method was more democratic. The system replied with a twenty-seven-page document on theories of democracy. “Reports used to be a way of putting decisions off,” Julián said. “It generated this one in nine seconds,” Clara replied. “Progress is indisputable.” Julián asked for a mixed solution. “Shared use reduces the capacity of both services below recommended levels,” Ágora reported. “And which would generate fewer complaints?” “That is not listed as a valid programme objective.” On Thursday, the hall was full. Mercedes, a former teacher, reminded Julián that he had learnt to read there. Ana, a nurse with a two-year-old son, explained that she was thinking of leaving because she could not get a nursery place or reduce her working hours. Julián knew them both. He also knew those waiting outside and those who had sent messages that Ágora summarised with impeccable neutrality. Clara showed him the two prepared statements. Both began: “Following rigorous technical analysis and a process of public participation…” “They sound as though they're written so that nobody has decided anything.” “That was the usual instruction.” Julián closed the documents. He chose the nursery school. Not because the simulation had found a correct answer, but because Valdearenas was losing families every year, and he had decided that this was the loss he would try to stop. The old first-year classroom would retain the photographs and exercise books Mercedes had collected, but nobody pretended that one room made up for a day centre. He went up to the lectern without the statement. “The decision is mine,” he began. “So is the mistake, if I am wrong.” There was applause, there were protests, and one woman announced with admirable clarity what she intended to do at the next election. Mercedes asked for the microphone to launch a petition. She said she had taught half the town to read and could still count up to an absolute majority. When he returned to his office, Ágora had updated his diary. Thursday, 17.00: residents' meeting about the former school. Estimated duration: indefinite. Julián looked at Clara, then at the monitoring panel. His remark about the mistake was already the most widely shared clip from the appearance. “At last, an accurate political forecast.” After the fiction AI agents are already beginning to help organisations and public administrations coordinate tasks, analyse information, prepare documents and automate processes. In a small council, they can save time, improve services and make provision possible that once required resources beyond its reach. Ágora projects that development towards much more integrated municipal management. But administering is not the same as governing. A system can calculate costs, simulate consequences and show who gains or loses under each alternative. What it cannot do, without first being given a political priority, is decide which loss should be accepted. Even a public consultation requires choices about how participation is interpreted, what time horizon matters and which degree of need carries more weight. The story does not turn Julián into a useless mayor. On the contrary, it gives him back precisely what he cannot delegate. When machines manage things better, the representative function does not disappear; it becomes more exposed. Governing means choosing between legitimate goods, explaining what must be forgone and bearing the cost. AI can improve a political decision. It cannot confer legitimacy on it by itself. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of the estrategIA newsletter.

The final signature The first summer historIA of 2026: a fictional council officer in 2032 confronts the difference between a recorded human signature and meaningful oversight. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency 144 Fiction The final signature With July's arrival, estrategIA returns to a tradition that began almost as a game two summers ago and has become one of our freest ways of thinking about artificial intelligence, politics and government: the summer historIAs. In 2024 and 2025 , we used science fiction as an editorial laboratory to test what AI models could imagine about the future: short, speculative stories, sometimes unsettling, sometimes ironic, always intended to offer another angle on the questions we examine during the rest of the year through articles, reports, technical recommendations and real cases. The 2026 edition takes this a step further. Instead of simply asking different models to write stand-alone stories over the summer, we are building a small shared world: Spain in 2032, where Ágora—a public ecosystem of agents, registers and intelligent interfaces—has become part of many administrative decisions. This is neither a dystopia nor a naive technological promise. It is a fictional setting, created mainly with Codex but with five frontier AI models working together, to explore something very specific: what happens when AI does not fail spectacularly, but works reasonably well… and still shifts responsibility, changes incentives, rearranges public attention or redefines what we mean by overseeing, caring, deciding or being accountable. Over the coming weeks, the summer historIAs will provide that lighter, narrative, experimental space from which estrategIA will keep doing what it has always done: thinking about the future before it fully arrives. And we will do so while continuing to follow current affairs and provide practical material. Even in summer, we will remain at our posts, bringing you the most relevant news—such as the delayed release of the latest AI models at the US government's direction—alongside useful tools, prompts and recommendations. The story “You have four hundred and eighty-six decisions and forty-three minutes left,” the screen announced. Elena Martín moved her finger towards the blue button: Sign batch . She had pressed it hundreds of times since Ágora arrived at Valdearenas Council. Since the last audit, each batch was sealed before signing: splitting it meant restarting the entire audit trail. An emergency grant used to take three months. Now almost all were processed in four days, and the social workers had gone back to visiting homes instead of sorting papers. Elena withdrew her finger when someone knocked on the glass. Original illustration accompanying the fiction. A woman waits with a printed decision while an officer considers a glowing blue button; other applicants queue behind her. The tiny decorative document and interface text is not reliably legible and is not reconstructed. A woman was holding a printed decision. She looked a little over thirty and had kept her coat buttoned despite the heat in the office. “They told me you had reviewed it.” Elena looked at the heading. Samira Haddad. Municipal emergency rent assistance. Refused. “If you have an appointment, they will see you downstairs.” “The first one available is in nine days. The rent for the room where my children and I are staying is due on Friday.” In the margin, Samira had written down three cleaning shifts, the landlord's telephone number and a calculation: 180 euros minus 22 for the bus. Elena opened the case file. Ágora displayed an impeccable explanation: the applicant owned a small share of a house in Villaseca; the municipal by-law excluded anyone with another habitable property; the report declaring that house uninhabitable had passed its expiry date. “The house belonged to my grandfather,” Samira said. “It has no roof.” Elena opened the document. Photographs of damp walls, broken beams and sky where there should have been tiles. The technical certificate was dated seven months earlier. The protocol allowed six. Ágora had made no mistake. “You need a new report.” “It costs money I haven't got. And it takes two weeks.” The explanation supplied every link: the cadastral register, the by-law, the certificate, the calculation. Elena had spent half her life looking for documents that now appeared in seconds. This was precisely what they had asked for over so many years. She remembered the folders piled up before Ágora, and the winter when a grant arrived after the eviction it was meant to prevent. The system had not erased people: Elena could once again listen to whole stories without staring at a mountain of forms. Then she saw a line at the bottom: Human review completed: Elena Martín. Review time: 11 seconds. She remembered the previous afternoon. She had opened an alert, read “alternative property verified” and moved on through the batch. Eleven seconds were enough for the system to consider the safeguard fulfilled. The interface was not lying. She had accessed the file, and her identification had been recorded. What it did not record was the mountain of decisions still waiting for her. “I didn't review this,” she said. “It says here that you did.” The head of service appeared behind the partition. She looked at Samira, then at Elena's clock. “We can initiate the standard appeal,” she said. “In the meantime, sign the batch. There are more than four hundred families waiting.” “A hundred and twelve are refusals.” “And three hundred and seventy-four are grants. If you block the batch, they won't be paid either.” The head of service did not raise her voice. Since Ágora had been introduced, complaints about delays had fallen and the team was handling twice as many cases with three posts vacant. Elena knew those figures. She also knew how long a manual review would take. On the screen, the blue button was still waiting. “Let's separate out the refusals based on property ownership,” Elena said. “The batch is already sealed for audit,” said her manager. “If we split it, we have to cancel the audit trail and generate it again.” “Then I'll send the whole batch back.” “Elena.” “My name is on a hundred and twelve decisions I haven't read.” Samira folded the paper carefully, as though she feared breaking something more than the sheet. “I don't want anyone to miss their payment because of me,” she said. “I just don't want you to put your name on it if you haven't looked.” Elena opened the incident menu. Ágora asked for a reason, a scope and a responsible person. She selected insufficient oversight , marked the cases involving alternative property and activated an urgent review for Samira. The interface warned of delays, possible duplication and deteriorating service indicators. “Confirm return?” the neutral voice asked. The head of service looked at the queue forming on the other side of the glass. “Tomorrow everyone who hasn't been paid will be here.” “Tomorrow we will be able to tell them who made the decision.” Elena confirmed. The blue button disappeared. Two red lines replaced it: Batch halted. Human review requested. The screen calculated that reviewing every case with the available staff would take several days. On one grant already approved, the payment date changed from tomorrow to pending renewed validation . Samira opened her mouth to ask whether this meant she would receive the assistance. “It means someone will have to look at your house,” Elena said. The decisions were still pending on the counter. Beneath the review request appeared a space for two signatures. The head of service stood motionless for a few seconds, then brought her card up to the screen. Elena read the whole document before adding her own signature. When she finished, Samira was still waiting, the queue had reached the corridor, and Ágora had begun another countdown. After the fiction This story imagines public administration in 2032 made much faster by agents able to cross-reference registers, check eligibility and prepare decisions. That level of integration still belongs to speculative fiction, but the dilemma is already unfolding: public administrations are beginning to automate tasks that directly affect rights, benefits and opportunities. The decisive question is not simply whether the system gets it right. Ágora applies a rule correctly and can nevertheless produce an unjust decision because the real case is trapped within an administrative category. Nor is it enough to place a person at the end of the process if their intervention consists of opening an alert, looking at a label and confirming a batch. Yet reviewing every case manually would also have costs. Delays would return, urgent assistance would be held up, and many people would receive too late what they need now. An institutional safeguard does not require us to set automation against humanity. It requires thresholds, review rights and sufficient time for oversight, so that a signature can change the outcome. A human signature protects people only when it is not used to conceal the fact that nobody has looked. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of the estrategIA newsletter.

Trying SillyTavern as a space for political debate with AI A first-person SillyTavern experiment with five synthetic political profiles, exploring its value for preparing questions and its limits as social research. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 143 Practical experiment Trying SillyTavern as a space for political debate with AI Artificial intelligence does more than generate text, images or code. It also lets us construct scenarios. And that possibility raises an uncomfortable question for those of us working in politics, government and public communication: how far can we already simulate social conversations before testing them with real citizens? To find out, over the past few days I carried out a small experiment with SillyTavern , a tool that describes itself on its website as an LLM Frontend for Power Users . It is commonly used to create conversational characters and have them interact in different scenarios. Put simply, it lets you design virtual “people” with a name, avatar, biography, personality traits, way of speaking, values, context and narrative memory. Those characters can then talk to one another in a group chat, answer questions or participate in a moderated exercise. SillyTavern was not originally designed for social research or political consultancy. It is widely used for role-playing, creative writing and conversations with characters. But that is precisely what makes it interesting: it offers a relatively simple, potentially very sophisticated way to create distinct profiles and observe how they respond to a shared question. In this case, I connected it through an API to an external model, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, an especially attractive option for its balance of quality, speed and cost. The aim was not to conduct a real focus group. This needs emphasising from the outset. We were neither listening to real citizens nor obtaining representative data. What I built was a small deliberative simulation, as an initial experiment, to explore the arguments, expectations, fears and red lines that might emerge around one specific issue: the use of artificial intelligence by governments and public administrations. The design was very simple. With GPT-5.5's help, I created a moderator—myself, as estrategIA's editor—and five synthetic characters with distinct social and political profiles: Mariela Campos , a citizen who is a carer and makes extensive use of public services. She grounds the debate in the digital divide, care for older people and humane treatment. Clara Ruiz , a pragmatic centrist voter. She values efficiency and good management, but demands that someone take responsibility when things go wrong. Diego Martín , young, precariously employed and disillusioned. He distrusts technological promises when they are not accompanied by social justice and democratic control. Lucía Herrera , a progressive civil servant committed to rights safeguards. She believes in modernising public services, but with impact assessments, traceability, auditing and human oversight. Valeria Soto , a liberal entrepreneur and technophile. She advocates pilots, innovation and the automation of low-risk administrative processes. English translation of the character card. Valeria Soto: 725 tokens, of which 265 are permanent. Tags: estrategIA, synthetic focus group, political AI, SillyTavern, liberal, technology, innovation. Visible fields include “More”, “Search / Create tags”, “Creator's note”, “Character description”, “ext. Media”, “First message” and “Alternative greetings”; the lower counter reads “Tokens: 37”. Character description: “A 34-year-old technology entrepreneur, a liberal technophile who works with automation and data. She believes in innovation, competition and efficiency.” First message: “I think we are discussing AI as though it were science fiction, when we could already be using it to stop public administration treating citizens like lost case files.” The exercise was deliberately brief, since its main purpose was to establish whether the system worked, not yet to build a complex experiment. We began with a single opening question: Would you accept governments and public administrations using artificial intelligence to make better decisions and provide better services, even if that meant automating some of their interaction with citizens? I then proposed a second round: what minimum condition would they require to accept governments using AI, and what red line would make it unacceptable? What made the conversation interesting was that it went beyond “yes to AI” versus “no to AI”. Nuance emerged. Valeria argued that paralysis has costs too: slow, overwhelmed, badly designed administration also causes democratic harm. Mariela accepted AI to avoid repetitive procedures, but rejected a screen replacing the person who could understand a complex family situation. Lucía insisted that digitising processes was not enough: we need to know what data a system is trained on, who audits it and who answers for its mistakes. Diego focused on inequality: who tries these systems first? The most vulnerable neighbourhoods? Citizens least able to challenge them? Clara summed up a very recognisable position: yes to speeding up simple tasks, no to delegating important matters to a black box. English translation of all visible conversation text. These are synthetic characters, not testimony from real citizens. The screenshot ends after Lucía's final paragraph below; no missing continuation is reconstructed. Fernando Nieto — estrategIA moderator Welcome. We are going to conduct a brief test for estrategIA. This is not a real focus group and does not claim to represent the public. It is an experiment with synthetic characters to explore the arguments, fears, expectations and red lines that emerge when we discuss artificial intelligence, politics and public administration. Please give brief, specific answers from your own perspective. Do not speak as experts unless that fits your experience. Do not seek artificial consensus. If you disagree, say so clearly. The first and only question in this test: Would you accept governments and public administrations using artificial intelligence to make better decisions and provide better services, even if that meant automating some of their interaction with citizens? Answer one at a time. We will begin with Clara, then Diego, Lucía, Valeria and Mariela. Valeria Soto Sure, I'll start. Yes, I would accept it without hesitation, but with very clear conditions. Look, I have spent years seeing how automation and data can transform extremely slow processes. In my company we use AI to cut processing times by 70% and free our team for creative or strategic tasks. Why would that not work at a one-stop public-service desk, in processing social assistance or detecting fraud early? The problem is that we always talk about the risk of dehumanising the service. Fine, there are services where human contact is irreplaceable: an interview with a social worker, a child-custody decision… But for booking an appointment, renewing a document or finding out whether you qualify for a scholarship, I would much rather have a fast, clear system than wait three weeks to see someone overwhelmed. What really worries me is paralysis through fear. If we spend another five years discussing ethics committees before trying anything, while waiting lists grow, we are choosing the status quo as public policy. That has real consequences too. That said, I would draw red lines: no binding automated decisions on fundamental rights without verifiable human oversight, full transparency about the algorithms used by public administration, and regular external audits. But let us start now with measurable pilots for low-risk administrative tasks. Mariela Campos Well, Valeria, you talk about efficiency, and I am not saying you are wrong about the time it takes. But when you say “free the team for creative tasks”, I think: what if the team being freed up is the one that looks after me? Social workers visit my mother, and every visit is different. It is not just paperwork. I would accept AI if it really meant I did not have to tell my life story four times at four different desks. That would be progress. But I am afraid everything will become automatic and then, when something unusual happens—such as my mother being denied assistance because the system does not understand that her pension does not arrive on the same date every month—there will be nobody to talk to. They will put a screen in front of you saying, “Sorry, the algorithm has decided.” And another thing: older people, or those who are not good with phones, get left out. I have had to ask my daughter for help completing something online myself. If everything moves that way, who will give us a hand? So yes, but on very clear conditions: there must always be a real human route, not a chatbot that does not understand my circumstances. And they should teach those of us who do not know how to use these tools. Lucía Herrera Well, I will come in here. Lucía Herrera. Valeria, I share your frustration with the slowness of public administration. I really do. I have spent years trying to modernise processes from within, and I know how hard it is. But when you say “let us start with pilots now”, I think a prior step is missing: who defines that pilot? What data is the system trained on? Because if the algorithm learns from previous administrative decisions, and those decisions were biased—and they are—you will unintentionally automate discrimination. Fixing it afterwards is much harder than thinking it through beforehand. Mariela, what you say about your mother is crucial. That is not an unusual case; it is everyday life in social services. AI can help cross-reference data so you do not have to repeat your story four times—I agree with that. But you need a social worker who understands the context, who knows that this irregular pension is not a citizen's mistake but a fact of their life. If you rely only on the automatic system, you lose that. I am also very concerned about who builds these systems. We cannot outsource public intelligence to private companies that answer to nobody. I have seen technical specifications where the algorithm is a “black box” because the company says it is a trade secret. Where fundamental rights are involved, that is unacceptable. The sidebar lists the five synthetic participants and Fernando Nieto as moderator, each with a displayed 1.0 setting. Their tags identify Valeria with liberalism and technology, Mariela with social services, Lucía with progressivism and rights safeguards, Diego with youth and precariousness, and Clara with the centre and management; the shared tags identify the synthetic political focus group. The interface offers “Add members” and a message field. Although the moderator requests Clara first, Valeria speaks first in this preserved excerpt. The simulation ultimately produced three clear areas of agreement. First, AI can already make complete sense for simple, internal or low-risk administrative tasks: booking an appointment, checking a case's status, organising documents or sparing citizens from repeating the same information several times. Second, any decision affecting rights, benefits, penalties or vulnerable circumstances needs a real route to human review. Not an automatic form. Not a chatbot. An accountable person. Third, trust requires transparency, independent auditing and traceability from the outset, not as cosmetic additions afterwards. Useful disagreements emerged too. The main tension was between speed and caution. Valeria wanted measurable pilots to begin immediately. Lucía and Diego warned that even a small pilot could cause harm if it affected real people without sufficient safeguards. Mariela introduced another warning: the risk of beginning by automating simple tasks and ending, without public debate, with the system making increasingly sensitive decisions. For me, that is where the value of this kind of experiment lies. It cannot tell us “what the public thinks”. Presenting it that way would be absurd. It serves a different purpose: preparing better questions, anticipating objections, identifying frames of discussion and rehearsing conversations before taking them into real settings. English translation of the complete visible closing exchange; all speakers except the moderator are synthetic. Diego Martín OK, my closing sentence: “Let public-sector AI demonstrate that it reduces inequality before it is introduced, and let every automated decision have a real avenue of human appeal; otherwise, I prefer the chaos of paper to a faster unjust order.” And Valeria, I agree about our shared red lines. But I disagree on one important point: when you say “paralysis has costs too”, you are right, but the cost of poor implementation is far greater. I have seen private companies bring in shoddy systems to save cash and then pay compensation or lose customers. In the public sector, we all pay that cost through violations of our rights. Mariela, I completely agree about separating levels. For mechanical procedures, automation is welcome. For major decisions, always a human being. The problem is that politicians sell AI as a one-size-fits-all solution and then muddle everything together. Lucía, your qualification about badly designed pilots is very good. A small pilot can fuck up the lives of only a few people, but those few people exist. We cannot treat them as guinea pigs just because there are not many of them. One final question for everyone: would you trust a public administration that outsources all its AI development to major technology companies? Because I see an enormous conflict of interest there. Clara Ruiz OK, my closing sentence: “Let AI speed up what is simple without getting in the way of what matters; let it be transparent, auditable and backed by someone accountable. If it fails on those points, I prefer a slow but fair procedure.” And Diego, on your final question: no, I would not trust a public administration that outsourced everything to major technology companies without public control. I have seen how those contracts work: they promise wonders, then the specifications are opaque, maintenance is extremely expensive, and when something goes wrong they tell you “that is the supplier's business”. Ultimate responsibility must rest with the public sector, even when it works with companies. Valeria, I agree about separating levels. To book an appointment or check the status of a case, full automation. But I need assurances that the line will not be crossed without anyone noticing. That is why I want traceability from the start, as Lucía says. In short, I think we can move forward if we set clear conditions before buying anything. We do not have to stop everything, but neither should we rush ahead blindly. Fernando Nieto — estrategIA moderator That brings us to the end. Thank you all very much for taking part. A synthetic focus group as simple as this small test does not substitute for social research. Nor does it replace interviews, surveys, listening to citizens or public deliberation. But it can serve as a preliminary laboratory: a kind of narrative testing ground where public officials, consultants, communication teams or researchers can explore how people with different outlooks might respond to a policy, technology or message. The test also revealed important limitations. The characters were perhaps too consistent. Reality is more contradictory, more emotional and less orderly. Moreover, everything depends on how the profiles are designed, which model is used, what instructions each character receives and how the human moderator intervenes. In other words, we are not discovering social reality, but constructing a plausible conversation about it. Yet that plausible conversation already has value. Within a few minutes, some of the central dilemmas of public-sector AI emerged: efficiency versus rights, automation versus humane treatment, innovation versus trust, public–private collaboration versus democratic accountability, and administrative modernisation versus digital exclusion. SillyTavern, normally used for other purposes, thus proved an interesting environment for experimenting with virtual “people” in controlled political debates. It can help us think before asking, without replacing citizens' voices. And in politics, as in research—and often in our own use of AI—formulating a better question is usually already a decisive part of the answer.
