A minister, a Raspberry Pi and Claude: why Singapore’s second brain matters for politics Singapore's foreign minister and a personal AI memory system: technical competence, institutional learning and the political value of showing the code. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services AI in Practice 136 Analysis A minister, a Raspberry Pi and Claude: why Singapore’s second brain matters for politics Archive note: roles, ages, product capabilities and relative dates are preserved as reported on 6 May 2026. The Facebook quotation is transcribed from the English visible in the original image; the translated X post and other quotations are translated from the Spanish source, without claiming to recover their original English wording. I came across it by chance last week, in my X timeline. A tweet by Gavriel Cohen — the developer of NanoClaw himself — announced, with considerable astonishment, that Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, had just published the complete architecture of his “ second brain for a diplomat ” . The tweet, reproduced below in translation, pointed to the Facebook post in which Balakrishnan announced his invention. I clicked on the GitHub gist expecting, at most, a personal note a few paragraphs long. English translation of the Spanish-rendered post by Gavriel Cohen (@Gavriel_Cohen) shown in the screenshot. The image itself says “Translated from English”; this is a retranslation, not a verified transcription of his original wording. Truncated links are not reconstructed. Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs published the architecture for his “second brain for a diplomat” yesterday. Architecture diagrams, design rationale, the whole package. A developer-style write-up of his own system. It runs on a Raspberry Pi. It connects to his WhatsApp and Gmail, transcribes voice notes locally, ingests speeches and articles, and builds a knowledge graph over time. It answers questions, drafts speeches and condenses information. He says he does not dare switch it off. What @VivianBala built is one of a kind. There is no other setup like it. But the things he built it from are not. It combined four open-source pieces: @NanoClaw_AI, the agent framework: github.com/qwibitai/nanoc… Mnemon, the persistent memory layer: github.com/mnemon-dev/mne… OneCLI, the credential proxy that keeps API keys outside containers: github.com/onecli/onecli Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Wiki pattern, the synthesis approach: x.com/karpathy/statu… None of them is his. The composition is. Then he published the composition: gist.github.com/VivianBalakris… He did not keep it in-house as an advantage for Singapore. He did not turn it into a product. He did not hoard it. He wrote it up and put it on GitHub. Tens of thousands of doctors, lawyers, researchers, investors and operators are building unique setups for themselves right now. Some simpler than Vivian’s, others more elaborate. The impulse will be to keep it to yourself. Treat it as your advantage. Think about what product or company you could build from it. Resist that impulse. Vivian put it directly: “The diplomat who learns to work with AI will have a significant advantage. I think that advantage is now.” Transcription of the original English Facebook post visible in the image, by Vivian Balakrishnan. The interface shows “2h”, not an absolute publication date. AI agents have crossed a threshold I didn’t expect so soon. Not just impressive demos — but practical tools for daily use. I’ve been tinkering with what I think of as a ‘second brain’ for a diplomat, using two open-source building blocks: NanoClaw by Gavriel Cohen (github.com/qwibitai/nanoclaw) — a self-hosted Claude assistant that connects to messaging channels and runs locally on a Raspberry Pi — and the LLM Wiki pattern by Andrej Karpathy, which compiles a compounding knowledge graph from speeches and articles over time. It answers every question, researches topics, provides daily updates, drafts speeches and condenses information. It has become invaluable — I don’t dare switch it off! The diplomat who learns to work with AI will have a meaningful edge. I think that edge is now. Technical write-up: https://gist.github.com/VivianBalakrishnan/a7d4eec3833baee4971a0ee54b08f322 What I found was something else entirely. It was a technical document several thousand words long, with diagrams, explanations of design decisions and links to the source code. I had seen documentation like that before, of course, but on GitHub, written by developers, not by a serving foreign minister . And here is a brief confession: I myself have spent several weeks exploring the idea of a personal “second brain” — with Obsidian connected to a Claude Cowork workflow and to Codex, and some earlier experimentation with OpenClaw and Telegram — and I can say quite clearly that, unfortunately for me, I am light years away from what Balakrishnan describes. That is precisely what makes this case interesting. Not because it is beyond reach, but because it establishes a horizon that many professionals — politicians, consultants and communicators — should start taking seriously. The minister who codes It is worth putting the man in context, because the first temptation would be to dismiss this as an individual eccentricity. It is not, despite how exceptional the case is at present. Vivian Balakrishnan, 65, an ophthalmologist by training , studied medicine at the National University of Singapore after receiving the President’s Scholarship, and went on to run Singapore General Hospital before entering politics in 2001. He has been Minister for Foreign Affairs since 2015 , but between 2014 and 2021 he also led Singapore’s Smart Nation Initiative, the broad strategic framework under which the country built its national digital identity, integrated public services, interoperable payments system and national artificial intelligence strategy. Then there is the telling detail. In 2015, when Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong published a Sudoku solver written in C++ as a hobby project, Balakrishnan responded by translating it into another programming language and commenting wryly on the technical difficulties involved. This is not a minister who discovered ChatGPT in 2025: he is a public official with more than a decade of practical experience in the state’s digital transformation, who also writes code for pleasure. That completely changes how we should read what he has published. NanoClaw, explained for everyone Let us strip away the technical layers and focus on what matters. The infographic further down will probably make it even clearer and easier to understand if you do not have a technical background. NanoClaw is a personal AI assistant — similar to OpenClaw , but minimalist in design and more focused on security — which the minister runs on a Raspberry Pi , a low-cost mini-computer that fits in the palm of your hand, in his own local environment. It is built on Claude, Anthropic’s model, but the important detail is not the model: it is the plumbing around it. That plumbing does three things that no “standard ChatGPT” yet does . First, it connects to his actual communication channels — WhatsApp, Gmail and a small website — transcribes his voice notes on the device itself, without the audio ever going out onto the internet, and processes images. Second, it runs scheduled tasks: daily summaries, alerts and ingestion of articles the minister saves from his phone using Obsidian’s Web Clipper. Third — and this is what is really interesting — it accumulates knowledge over time . The difference between accumulating knowledge and simply “searching documents” is not trivial. Most of today’s AI assistants do the latter: they index files and retrieve snippets of text when you ask a question. Useful, but superficial. What Balakrishnan has built does the former: a system that distils discrete facts from every speech, article or conversation it ingests, organises them into a kind of knowledge map — entities, concepts and timelines — and then synthesises them into wiki-style pages that he can read and correct himself in Obsidian. It is the practical implementation of an idea popularised by Andrej Karpathy — co-founder of OpenAI, former head of AI at Tesla and now one of the sector’s leading voices — under the name LLM Wiki : the idea that a useful assistant should do more than search text; it should build a body of synthesised knowledge that becomes more valuable the more you use it . Conceptually, it is the difference between having a search engine and having a notebook in which someone records, on your behalf, what matters about everything you read. For readers with a more technical background, all the code and documentation are openly published: the main gist and the NanoClaw repository . For everyone else, this mental picture will do: a Raspberry Pi on a desk, connected to WhatsApp, reading speeches and articles, building over months a map of what its boss knows and needs to remember. Following what we learnt in last week’s issue, we asked ChatGPT Images to create an infographic explaining the system’s operation in a very simple, stripped-down way, so that anyone could understand it. Here is the visual summary, which should make the process and system even easier to grasp. English transcription of the generated infographic: “How the Singapore foreign minister’s ‘second brain’ works”. A personal AI assistant that reads, listens, remembers and helps with decisions. The graphic’s claims about local processing are reproduced as its simplified explanation; they should not be read as proof that all model inference happens locally. 1. Inputs — information arriving each day: WhatsApp messages; Gmail emails; voice notes with local transcription; articles and websites clipped from a phone; documents, speeches and reports; images. 2. The system — NanoClaw: runs on a Raspberry Pi in the local environment. Transcribes and processes locally: voice notes become text without going out onto the internet. Processes images and files: extracts useful information from documents and images. Scheduled tasks: daily summaries, alerts, automatic content ingestion and so on. AI with context, Claude: understands, reasons and generates useful, personalised responses. 3. Outputs — what the minister receives: personalised summaries; alerts and reminders; answers and support in real time; wiki-style pages in Obsidian; maps, timelines and relationships; information ready for decision-making. 4. Structured memory — the real “brain”: turns scattered information into useful knowledge that grows over time. It extracts key facts from every message, article or document; organises them into a knowledge graph of entities, concepts, dates, places and relationships; generates wiki pages in Obsidian by topic, person, organisation and event; knowledge becomes connected, updated and more valuable every day. How it works in practice: 1. New information arrives through the connected channels. 2. The system processes it locally and extracts what matters. 3. AI understands it, relates it to what it already knows and saves it. 4. Ready-to-use summaries, alerts and wiki pages are generated. 5. The minister reviews, corrects and adds his judgement. 6. The system learns and improves with each cycle. Key principles: privacy — sensitive data are processed locally; structured memory, not just text search; transparency — code and architecture published; human review at all times; designed to help him decide, not to decide for him. Closing text: “In a few words: it is not a chatbot. It is a personal infrastructure for memory and knowledge that helps a diplomat understand better, remember more and decide more clearly.” Three strategic lessons from this case 1. Radical transparency is beginning to be a source of credibility, not a risk The natural reflex in any government office would be to hide a system like this or dress it up in an empty press release. Balakrishnan does the opposite: he publishes the architecture, design decisions, security criteria and link to NanoClaw’s open repository. He even explains mechanisms for keeping API usage down, such as preliminary scripts that avoid waking the agent when an automated check is enough. In doing so, he turns the tool into a political message: he conveys technical competence and a willingness to be held accountable. Recent European “counterexamples” are telling. Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, acknowledged last August that he used ChatGPT for “second opinions” and immediately faced a media crisis: “You were elected by the voters, not ChatGPT.” In the United Kingdom, minister Peter Kyle’s prompts were published following a citizen’s freedom-of-information request. The lesson: using AI quietly and explaining it poorly becomes a scandal. Publishing it with sound judgement neutralises the scandal before it exists. 2. The difference between searching documents and building memory is the difference between an organisation that reacts and one that learns In any public administration — and any professional practice or organisation, including our own — useful knowledge is scattered across emails, reports, meetings, notes and personal memory. Every change of cycle destroys a large part of that knowledge. A structured-memory system such as Balakrishnan’s is neither a search engine nor a chatbot: it is infrastructure for preserving continuity. In diplomacy, where every precedent and nuance carries weight, that capability is a pure competitive advantage. But the lesson applies equally to any consultant, teacher or communication professional whose livelihood depends on accumulated intellectual work. 3. A missing layer is neither fascination nor regulation: it is operational understanding Much of the public debate about AI in the West swings between two extremes: superficial enthusiasm for the latest fashionable tool and abstract regulatory fear. What is missing — and where Singapore is several years ahead — is the middle ground: knowing exactly what an agent is, what giving it memory entails, why it matters that certain processes run locally, and when to automate and when not to. Without that layer, laws are written blind, public projects are contracted to consultancies that sell them as black boxes, and people who make their living in communication or political consultancy are excluded from the conversation that matters because they do not understand it. Why all this matters There is a line from Balakrishnan himself, at the end of his post, that is worth reading slowly: “The diplomat who learns to work with AI will have a meaningful edge. I think that edge is now.” The important thing is not the sentence. The important thing is that, when it came with a public repository containing the entire architecture, it ceased to be a declaration and became evidence that he knows what he is talking about . That is probably the new rule of the game for political communication about AI: it is not about speaking eloquently about the future. Increasingly, it is about “showing the code”. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH and editor of the estrategIA newsletter

Just a few days ago, on 21 April, OpenAI introduced ChatGPT Images 2.0 , its new image generation and editing model integrated into ChatGPT . The tool can already be used within the conversation itself, including on free accounts, although with usage limits and some advanced functions reserved for paid plans. As usually happens with these launches, it is wise to keep a little distance from the initial enthusiasm, but our first tests point to a clear improvement : greater visual coherence, a better understanding of complex instructions, more orderly composition and, above all, an increasingly reliable ability to integrate legible text into images, which makes a real difference for many uses. The first comparisons by Artificial Analysis and Arena AI also place it at the top of image generation, ahead of GPT Image 1.5 (the previous model), Nano Banana 2 and Nano Banana Pro (Google’s models), by a considerable margin . Hour 2: consultation with official sources. Hour 3: response decision. Hour 4: publication of a clarification. Hour 5: impact monitoring. Hour 6: report and learning. Add three side columns: responsible people; critical decisions; mistakes to avoid. Style: serious, institutional, realistic and modern, with the appearance of an operational protocol for a government office. Perfectly legible Spanish text. The fifteen swatches include cream, beige, tan, ochre-brown, dark brown, olive tones, green, teal, navy, plum and warm reds/oranges. Less flattering colours: portraits in pale pink, lilac, pale blue and grey; swatches in pale pink, lilac, blue-grey, pale blue, grey, muted blues, charcoal and black. Ideal neutrals: cream, beige, taupe, brown and dark blue-grey. Metallics: gold and copper. Recommended patterns: leopard, paisley and houndstooth. Combinations that work: dark green/beige/ochre; navy/olive/cream; rust/cream/brown; teal/brown/ochre. Avoid very cool or neon outfits: the crossed-out combinations are neon pink/blue/yellow-green; pale aqua/lilac/pink; and pale grey/slate blue/navy. As these examples show, ChatGPT Images 2.0 represents a significant leap in AI’s visual generation and editing capabilities; the leap is functional, not aesthetic. It still has limitations — for example, it still fails to depict certain Salamanca monuments accurately or place them correctly on a map — but it opens up a very promising field of experimentation for public, political and institutional communication. The underlying consequence is clear: the ability to produce high-quality visual communication ceases to be a bottleneck for small institutions, which may help balance communication against major political actors. The decisive question is no longer simply what the model can generate, but what responsible, clear and strategic uses we can design with it. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH and editor of the estrategIA newsletter

How councils can lead the transformation of local government through artificial intelligence without leaving anyone behind Román Robles Valades sets out how municipalities can adopt AI responsibly, connecting staff development, data sovereignty and better public services. Román Robles Valades Government & Public Services Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics AI in Practice 134 Analysis How councils can lead the transformation of local government through artificial intelligence without leaving anyone behind This issue's main article is by Román Robles Valades , Deputy Mayor of Galapagar and an AI and big data specialist. Drawing on practical experience, he considers how municipalities can lead the transformation of local government through artificial intelligence with sound judgement, responsibility and without leaving anyone behind. Román initiated MUNICIP-IA , the event on AI in the public sector held in Galapagar in March, in which Institución Educativa ALEPH took part. We find his contribution particularly interesting because very few people combine technical knowledge in these fields with the political responsibility of running a municipality. There are two ways to approach a conversation about artificial intelligence in public administration: with fear or with sound judgement. We have spent too long choosing the first. The time has come to choose the second, and councils have a historic opportunity to lead that change. When I talk about artificial intelligence in a municipal context, I am not talking about science fiction or a distant future. I am talking about today: chatbots answering residents' questions at three in the morning, algorithms optimising waste-collection routes, systems detecting anomalies in public spending before they become real problems. The technology already exists. The question is whether we want to use it well. Spanish municipalities handle enormous quantities of data every day: municipal population registers, building permits, social services case files, revenue collection and urban mobility. For decades, that asset has lain dormant on servers, on paper and in information silos that did not communicate with one another. AI is, in essence, the tool that allows us to turn all that accumulated knowledge into real intelligence serving citizens. The myth of the job destroyer The most widespread — and, in the short term, most mistaken — narrative about AI in the public sector is that it will immediately eliminate jobs. It is understandable that this fear exists: automation has always created uncertainty. But we should distinguish the short term from the medium and long term, because the dynamics differ. In the short term, AI eliminates repetitive, low-value tasks rather than jobs: manual document management, sorting applications and answering frequently asked questions. What it frees up is time: a social worker's time to give vulnerable families real attention instead of filling in forms; a planning officer's time to resolve complex enquiries rather than searching for case files in physical archives. In the medium and long term, however, greater caution is needed. AI can transform organisational structures, professional roles and the very architecture of public services far more profoundly. Uncertainty increases the further ahead we look, and denying that would be naive. What we can say is that the ultimate impact will be determined by the decisions we make today, rather than by the technology: how we design the transition, how much we invest in training, how we support staff as duties are reassigned, and what governance we build around these systems. Moreover, AI's arrival in the public sector is creating professional roles that barely exist in municipal organisation charts today: public data managers, algorithm auditors, digital sovereignty officers and specialists in technological ethics. If the transition is managed well, its net effect on public-sector employment need not be negative. But that outcome is not guaranteed by default: it will depend on organisational design, investment in human capital and the political will to preserve quality public-sector employment. Galapagar: a laboratory for local innovation Galapagar is a municipality of around 38,000 people in the hills north-west of Madrid. It is not a great metropolis; it has neither Barcelona City Council's budget nor the size of the city of Madrid. That is precisely why it is a relevant example: what a medium-sized municipality can do with sound technological judgement disproves the argument that digital innovation is “a big-city affair”. Since 2023, with the arrival of a governing team committed to modernisation, the council has embarked on a roadmap towards intelligent administration. This commitment to technology is a matter of conviction, not a whim: more efficient management frees resources for what truly matters — the residents who need them most. The digital transformation of a council such as Galapagar does not necessarily require extraordinary budgets or a decade-long horizon, but it does require investment proportionate to each administration's starting point. The scope, depth and pace of change will depend on organisational design, available resources, existing digital maturity and each municipality's particular context. What all successful cases share is a combination of three ingredients: sustained political will, trained professionals and a clear framework of priorities. We must also understand that digitising an obsolete process merely produces a faster obsolete process, and that AI should be applied to structures already put in good order, with quality data. Real applications of AI in municipalities such as Galapagar include: Citizen services around the clock: conversational assistants that complete procedures without the need to travel or book an appointment. Managing the local area: predictive models for infrastructure maintenance and the early detection of incidents. Intelligent social services: data analysis identifying vulnerability before it becomes more severe. Resource optimisation: cleaning routes, adaptive lighting and efficient management of the water cycle. Transparency and spending oversight: detecting budget anomalies through automated analysis. Citizen participation: systems that analyse residents' proposals and group together the area's real needs. Three conditions for getting it right AI in public administration can be a powerful tool or a major source of problems, depending on how it is implemented. In my experience, both technical and political, there are three conditions without which a project is doomed to fail — or, worse, to cause harm. The first is the regulatory framework. The European Artificial Intelligence Act establishes obligations and prohibitions that councils must know and comply with. Some public-sector AI systems — such as those making decisions that affect citizens' rights — are high-risk and require audits, records and effective human oversight. It is not optional. It is the law. Municipalities that get ahead in complying with it will avoid penalties and, above all, avoid making mistakes that affect real people. The second condition is data sovereignty. Data in municipal population registers, social services files and planning permits are public-sector data that residents entrust to their councils. Who safeguards them, where they are stored and under what conditions they are processed are not technical questions: they are political questions of the first importance. Councils cannot outsource their digital sovereignty to large technology corporations without guaranteeing that these data remain under public control, with the strongest privacy safeguards. The third condition is effective control of bias. Algorithms learn from historical data, and historical data contain the biases of the societies that generated them. An AI system trained on data from past years can perpetuate — and even amplify — existing inequalities: in access to social services, resource allocation, and the attention given to certain neighbourhoods or groups. Auditing the algorithms used by public administration is a democratic safeguard, not a bureaucratic burden. AI as a tool for fiscal fairness One argument deserves more attention than it usually receives in debates about AI and public administration: efficiency is not a neoliberal value; it is a value of equity. When a council reduces the cost of handling a case file through intelligent automation, that saving can be reinvested: in a new social worker post, extracurricular activities in schools or better municipal sports facilities. Whether those savings actually translate into more and better services, rather than simple cuts, is a political decision. Applied well and with the right priorities, AI does not shrink the state: it expands it, enabling it to reach places it could not reach before. With resources limited — a reality Spanish councils know well — every euro saved on bureaucratic inefficiency is a euro that can be invested in real public policies. This is not techno-utopianism. It is straightforward arithmetic, provided the political will is there. The time to act is now The window of opportunity will not remain open indefinitely. Municipalities that lead the responsible adoption of AI over the next two or three years will be better placed to benefit from European digital transformation funding, attract technology talent into the public sector and offer their residents a quality of service that still seems aspirational today. The transition to intelligent local government is not a project for a single term of office. It is a generational project. But the first steps — auditing existing data, training staff and defining a strategy for algorithmic governance — can and must begin now. Councils are not businesses. They cannot and should not compete in the market. But they can be the area's best employers for technology talent, the most rigorous in handling residents' data and the most demanding about the ethical standards of the systems they implement. That is their competitive advantage: trust. And in the age of data, trust is the scarcest and most valuable asset there is. Román Robles Valades Deputy Mayor, Galapagar Town Council. Three possible futures for artificial intelligence in 2030 Three alternative AI futures for 2030 — plateau, sustained ascent and rapid take-off — and why strategic preparation must work across all three. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency Government & Public Services Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 133 Analysis Three possible futures for artificial intelligence in 2030 Archive note: these scenarios and judgements retain the perspective of 15 April 2026. Time horizons such as “the next two or three years” refer to that publication date. What will the world of artificial intelligence look like in four years' time? Nobody knows for certain, but the question matters too much for us simply to shrug. What we now call artificial intelligence is no longer the friendly chatbot that surprised us at the end of 2022. It has become a force that reorganises industries, transforms professions and redefines the balance of power between countries. Anticipating where it is heading is no academic exercise: it is a practical necessity for anyone who wants to make informed decisions about their career, their business or their country. Over recent weeks, for several important projects, I have carried out intensive foresight work, cross-referencing technical, economic and geopolitical sources to try to map the most likely scenarios between now and 2030. We want to share the essentials of that exercise in a very condensed form. Rather than betting on a single forecast — the familiar categorical prediction that rarely comes true — we have followed the OECD's recommendation to work with several plausible scenarios at once . The result is three possible futures. Three worlds with logics of their own, representing branching paths rather than an inevitable staircase. Plateau — AI as electricity: everywhere, but no better at thinking The first scenario — probably the least plausible in the light of recent advances — envisages no major qualitative leap in artificial intelligence between now and 2030, but its becoming ubiquitous. Models will not be radically more intelligent than today's, but they will be vastly cheaper and embedded in almost everything: from the software we use at work to public administration procedures and the management of a small or medium-sized business. Think of how electricity changed factories in the early twentieth century. Production was revolutionised not by a new invention, but by energy becoming so cheap and ubiquitous that it reorganised everything else. The same could happen with AI: it does not need to become smarter to change the world profoundly; becoming cheaper and easier to use would be enough. The subtler risk in this scenario would be complacency: believing that, because no superintelligence has arrived, there is no urgency. Meanwhile, whoever controls the infrastructure — data centres, chips and platforms — will capture most of the value others generate. As we have been reporting in estrategIA, this is already happening. Ascent — the machine that sustains work: more intelligent, more autonomous, more disruptive The second scenario — the one we consider most likely — is considerably more unsettling. Here, AI improves substantially and cumulatively in reasoning, the ability to act independently and mastery of multiple formats. The arrival of the much-discussed AGI — artificial intelligence capable of matching human beings in everything — is not declared before 2030, but the automation of intellectual work becomes broad and deep. The crucial change is that systems move from assisting with tasks lasting minutes to sustaining complete workflows for days or weeks with little human supervision. The question stops being “Can AI write a good report?” and becomes “Can it carry out an entire audit, a legal process or the complete development of a computer program?” Regular readers know this is one of the issues that concerns us most: the growing pressure on entry-level positions in professions such as law, finance, consultancy and programming. The routine tasks that historically helped train younger people are precisely the first to be automated. In this scenario, the risk is not mass unemployment overnight, but something more insidious: an economy that produces more with fewer people, in which wealth is concentrated among those who own the models and infrastructure, while the traditional mechanisms that distribute prosperity today — employment, wages and social security contributions — erode without anyone having replaced them. As we said in our requests at the beginning of the year, politicians cannot keep governing for the next election when we face a technology that will transform the world for the next generations. Take-off — the unexpected leap: AGI and superintelligence before 2030 The third scenario is perhaps less likely than the second, but it also has the most profound consequences. We are not talking here about AI improving AI research: as several major laboratories have already reported, that is beginning to happen. We are talking about something qualitatively different: artificial intelligence at or above human level in practically every relevant field — known as AGI — emerging before 2030, and that capability rapidly developing into artificial superintelligence, or ASI, far surpassing human beings. A large part of the scientific community believes this will happen in the coming decades, but not so soon: not within the next three or four years. This scenario branches into two very different paths. If the technology is developed with effective controls and international governance, we could witness an era of unprecedented scientific abundance: accelerated advances in medicine, energy and new materials. But if, as many of us fear, competition between companies and powers drives the deployment of increasingly powerful systems without the necessary safeguards, with policymakers taking the wrong measures towards a technology they do not understand, the consequences could be serious and unpredictable. Shortages of advanced chips and limits on electricity generation currently act as natural brakes. Yet we should not place too much faith in their continuing to be enough to slow a technology whose principal distinguishing feature is its ability to improve itself. Preparing for uncertainty Our analysis leads to a clear conclusion: the likeliest outcome is neither that the world comes to a halt nor that it becomes unrecognisable, but that, in the short term, we enter an era of uneven acceleration. Some countries, companies and individuals will advance far faster than others. That gap will depend not only on the technology, but on who has the infrastructure, energy, education and strategic vision to make use of it. The window for taking the decisions that will define our position is narrow: the next two or three years will be critical. The task is not to guess which of these three worlds we will inhabit, but to develop the capacity to act effectively in any of them. The real risk is not choosing the wrong scenario, but preparing for only one — or not preparing at all. AI is not taking our work away. It is freeing us from it. If technology can separate income from employment, the political task is to share its gains—and the freedom they could make possible. Fernando Nieto Lobato Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Futures, Safety & Human Agency 132 Opinion AI is not taking our work away. It is freeing us from it. Translation note: the quotations attributed to Eugen Richter and Bismarck, and the wording of Genesis 3:19, are translated from the Spanish article. They are not presented as independently verified English quotations or as text from a specified English Bible edition. This week's main article deliberately adopts a different frame from the prevailing one. It does not deny the risks of automation. It questions whether we should continue treating human employment as an end in itself when technology may begin to make it possible to separate work, income and dignity. The fact that some people find a deep vocation in their profession—I am fortunate to be among them—does not make that experience universal. Nor does it justify organising all of social life around the obligation to work in order to survive, when technology may offer new alternatives in the coming years. The fundamental question is not whether AI will transform work, but whether we will distribute fairly the material freedom it could create. The dominant framing of artificial intelligence, which fills the press with catastrophic headlines , uncritically repeats a dogma: if AI destroys jobs, we face a catastrophe. That framing confuses a means with an end. For centuries, paid work has been the main route to an income. It does not follow that it must remain the organising principle of human life when machines are taking on a growing share of the tasks that once demanded our effort. The question is not how to defend employment at any cost, but how to protect people when employment is no longer necessary. That is the discussion we should be having as the next wave approaches. The illusion of the happy worker The panic about automation runs up against an uncomfortable reality. Gallup's State of the Global Workplace 2025 report, based on surveys in more than 160 countries, finds that only 21% of workers worldwide are engaged at work. Some 62% are not engaged—popularly labelled “quiet quitting”—and 17% are actively disengaged. That disconnection cost $438 billion in lost productivity in 2024 alone. Europe's figures are worse: just 13% engagement , the lowest of any region, alongside 73% of workers who are not engaged and 15% who are actively disengaged. Engagement stands at 8% in France, 9% in Spain and 10% in Italy . This does not prove that most people hate their jobs, but it does show that a huge proportion experience work with detachment, resignation or exhaustion. Add to this the fact that 56% of Spanish employees report ending their working day with high levels of stress, according to ManpowerGroup's 2025 Talent Barometer , and the conclusion is clear: a very substantial proportion of people tolerate their work out of economic necessity, not as a vocation. Defending the preservation of those tasks at all costs is not defending workers; it is defending a structure that no longer works for the majority. We have already left the fields behind It is worth recalling something elementary. In Spain, 42% of the population worked in agriculture in 1960 ; today, barely 4% do. In the United States, the share fell from 60% in 1850 to 2% today , while total output multiplied. We do not call that process a catastrophe; we call it structural transformation. It brought displacement and social pain, but nobody would wish to return to a world in which most people spent their lives bent over from dawn to dusk. And that transition took place without any safety net comparable to what we could design today. We do not mourn the loss of back-breaking labour; we debate how its benefits were shared. That is precisely the question AI raises again: not whether machines will do work, but who receives the dividends from that work. Retirement as a window onto the future The usual counterargument, beyond economics, is that without employment people lose their purpose. Research on retirement substantially qualifies that claim. In the United States, the MassMutual Retirement Happiness Study (2024) found that 67% of retirees reported being happier since they stopped working. A 2025 European meta-analysis covering 32 studies confirmed a significant positive effect of retirement on well-being, and another review involving more than 557,000 people concluded that retirement reduces the risk of depression by around 20%. The crucial distinction is voluntary versus forced : when people choose and their income is secure, most redefine their sense of purpose beyond the obligation to work. This is not conclusive evidence about a future post-work society, but it does undermine the intuition that the absence of paid employment necessarily brings emptiness. It is no accident that the Spanish word for retirement, jubilación , comes from the Latin iubilare : to shout for joy. Of course, some people do not want to retire and find an irreplaceable source of purpose in their profession. The argument is not to ban work or insist that it should disappear, but to make it optional, now that a powerful new technology, together with robotics, is beginning to lay the foundations for that possibility. That is precisely why the key is not to eliminate work, but to guarantee income. What retirement shows is that, with financial stability, most people do not lapse into inertia: they reorganise their lives meaningfully. For several decades, moreover, a significant share of jobs will still have to be done by humans, from care work to the supervision of complex systems. They will be taken on mainly by people who find a vocation in them or want a higher income. That is exactly the hypothesis being explored by basic income pilots. The problem is distribution, not technology We should remember that every major system of social protection met with the same scepticism. When Bismarck introduced Germany's first retirement pensions in the 1880s, much of the liberal opposition denounced them as a step towards dependence on the state. The economist and parliamentarian Eugen Richter went so far as to describe the development as “not socialist, but communist”. Bismarck himself answered such criticism with a mixture of pragmatism and disdain: “Call it socialism or whatever you like; it makes no difference to me.” Decades later, Franklin Roosevelt faced very similar accusations when establishing Social Security in the United States. Today, nobody seriously questions the right to a pension. Basic income now occupies the same uncomfortable position that pensions occupied 140 years ago: an idea that seems impossible until it no longer does. It is true that AI will also create jobs we cannot currently imagine, as every previous technological revolution has done. But there is a crucial distinction: unlike the loom or the internal combustion engine, AI is the first technology capable of improving its own capabilities. That means the productivity gains it enables will be cumulative rather than one-off. In many sectors, the amount of human work needed to sustain production will fall faster than consumption can absorb—perhaps with the exception of areas such as healthcare and care work, where unmet demand is enormous. In that context, mechanisms such as basic income are not only a matter of justice. They are also a way to sustain demand and prevent the economic system itself from contracting for lack of consumers with spending power. This does not mean the transition will be immediate or linear, but it does require us to reconsider the foundations of the present system. Denying that AI could have a painful impact on employment would be naive. But the central issue is not slowing automation; it is capturing and redistributing its productivity gains. Universal basic income pilots—albeit conducted in a very different context from the one we will face in the coming years—confirm this with evidence rather than theory. In Finland (2017–2018), recipients experienced better mental health without leaving the labour market. The large US study by OpenResearch revealed a crucial nuance: recipients of guaranteed income worked somewhat less on average, but were 10% more likely to look for work and showed a stronger preference for meaningful jobs. Material security did not remove agency; it reduced desperation and expanded people's ability to choose. Ireland's recent basic income programme for artists completed the picture: more time devoted to creative work, less anxiety and an estimated social return of €1.39 for every euro invested. How could we finance the transition? Two approaches are already being seriously considered, and a third is beginning to gain ground. The first is to tax the exceptional gains from automation: the robot tax that Bill Gates proposed in 2017 , complex to design but difficult to dismiss as a principle of distributive justice. The second is to capture rents from AI's energy and data infrastructure. The International Energy Agency projects that data centres' electricity consumption will double to around 945 TWh in 2030, from 415 TWh in 2024. If the new economy rests on shared, finite resources, it makes sense for some of that value to return to society. The third approach, still lacking mature mechanisms, may be the most powerful in terms of justice: a data dividend. Large AI models were not trained in a vacuum. They were fed millions of articles, blogs, photographs, forum posts and lines of code produced by ordinary people over decades. That content was used on a vast scale without a clear compensation scheme. A data dividend would not be a state handout, but something closer to overdue royalties on the collective intellectual capital we have all contributed. California explicitly put forward the idea in 2019 , inspired by the Alaska Permanent Fund, and Jaron Lanier has spent a decade arguing that data is unpaid labour. Implementation is complex, but the principle is difficult to dispute. A renaissance of vocation Consider a translator of Chinese trapped today in the monotony of translating technical manuals for vacuum cleaners and other technology products into Spanish to make ends meet. With their needs met and AI handling the mechanical part, that person could choose to translate classical Chinese poetry, teach or start a business. The point is not that everyone will become an artist. The argument is both more modest and more powerful: a society rich in automation can allow many more people to organise their lives around vocations, care or projects of their own, rather than solely around whatever the market urgently pays for. There is another effect that the discourse of fear entirely overlooks: separating survival from employment could unleash the largest wave of entrepreneurship in history. Today, most people do not start businesses because the cost of failure is unbearable. Without a material cushion, innovation is a privilege for those who already have wealth or networks. A sufficient guaranteed income, combined with increasingly affordable AI tools, would open the door to thousands of people who would use that same artificial intelligence to build businesses, solve problems and create wealth from creativity rather than desperation. Real economic freedom is not only the ability to consume; it is also the ability to take risks without putting survival at stake. The biblical phrase “you shall earn your bread by the sweat of your brow” (Genesis 3:19) is not an eternal commandment about vocation: it was conceived as a consequence of original sin, not as a model of a fulfilled life. Classical thought understood this perfectly well. For the Stoic tradition and thinkers such as Seneca, the true human tragedy was not the absence of work, but the squandering of our scarce lifetime on empty occupations that distance us from self-mastery. Otium —time for personal cultivation, reason and civic virtue—was the natural condition of the free citizen, while negotium —business, literally the negation of leisure—was barely tolerated as a necessary servitude. It was much later that history took a perverse turn. Max Weber masterfully documented how the Protestant ethic and emerging industrial capitalism turned that consequence into the highest social virtue. Suddenly, productive exhaustion—something those of us who are rather addicted to work know quite a bit about—became a moral imperative. Bertrand Russell had already rebelled against this deception in 1932. In calling for a four-hour working day, he lucidly denounced the veneration of unceasing work as, at bottom, the morality of slaves. For two centuries, that moral inversion held because technology still required human labour on a massive scale. Today, for the first time in history, we are beginning to have the technological capacity to reverse that anomaly and make our liberation real —although the pace at which AI takes over tasks remains uncertain and will depend on political choices as well as technical advances. The only thing we still lack is the institutional architecture to ensure that the immense dividends of automation reach society as a whole, rather than only the companies developing the technology. The question that will define our time is not whether artificial intelligence will take our work away. The real crossroads is much deeper: if AI, together with robotics, removes the need for compulsory human effort over the coming years and decades, will we use that achievement to expand freedom for the majority, or entrench ourselves in defending jobs that no longer add value while wealth becomes even more concentrated? An algorithm will not decide the difference between a dystopia of exclusion and the rebirth of a free society. We will. The new watchdogs of power: how AI is democratising public scrutiny AI is lowering the barriers to public scrutiny. The question is how democratic institutions will respond to these new civic capabilities. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Government & Public Services 131 Analysis The new watchdogs of power: how AI is democratising public scrutiny Regular readers of estrategIA will know that we have been following closely—both in these pages and through our lists on X and other channels—the emergence of initiatives that use artificial intelligence to scrutinise the public sector. A few days ago, technology analyst and Error500 founder Antonio Ortiz published an interesting article, Watchdogs of power with artificial intelligence , bringing together some of the most promising current examples. Reading it was the perfect prompt to explore this phenomenon in this week's estrategIA: one that has expanded rapidly in recent months as AI capabilities have advanced. The information imbalance between the state and the citizen has always had a quiet ally: opacity in practice. For years, public administrations have complied with the letter of the law by publishing millions of data points, often burying them in endless PDFs, impenetrable official bulletins or labyrinthine platforms. The explosion of generative AI and the phenomenon of vibe coding —developing software by describing what you want it to do in ordinary language—which we discussed recently , are changing the rules. A citizen equipped with language models can now compress work that once took months into a few hours. One point needs to be clear from the outset: these tools do not, by themselves, “prove” corruption. What they do is different, and perhaps more valuable: reduce the operational opacity of the state and quickly indicate where to look for possible offences or malpractice. AI is removing the friction that prevents public information from being genuinely open to scrutiny. Data activism and civic scrutiny are hardly new. Over the past decade, we saw admirable civic tools emerge, from platforms for submitting freedom of information requests to projects that painstakingly extracted data— scraping —from official bulletins. But developing them required teams of programmers, months of work and extensive technical knowledge. The real shift introduced by AI is the dramatic lowering of the barrier to entry. What was once the preserve of civic hackers and experienced developers is now within reach of citizens with no formal computing background, who can build their own transparency projects simply by talking to a machine. Spain's new civic wave Spain's ecosystem offers the best example of this second generation of civic tools. Projects are flourishing, driven by individuals or very small teams who use generative AI to build in days what once took months: Contratación Abierta : developed by engineer David Fernández, this platform allows users to scrutinise small-value public contracts awarded by thousands of public bodies. Its Red Flags Monitor applies more than 30 statistical analysis techniques to identify patterns that deserve closer examination, such as amounts suspiciously close to the legal threshold above which a contract must be put out to tender. Menjòmetre : created by the anonymous collective Segell Fosc and developed entirely with AI. This observatory cross-references grants and contracts in Catalonia to produce a statistical index of concentration, recurrence and relative position. Its strength lies in methodological transparency: the team publishes its code openly and makes clear that its score reflects recurring statistical patterns, not a moral judgement. Larenta.es : Pau March, a marketing professional without a conventional software development background, used AI tools to create an assistant that analyses more than 370 regional and national deductions from Spain's personal income tax, IRPF. In two minutes, it translates tax jargon into language citizens can understand. From data to algorithms: we should not forget the groundwork that made this possible, led by outstanding individual campaigners such as Jaime Gómez-Obregón and pioneering organisations such as Civio . I can speak from experience here: I have been a supporting member for years. Last year, Civio secured a Supreme Court ruling recognising its right to access the source code of BOSCO, the software used to determine eligibility for Spain's social electricity discount. That milestone takes the debate into a new dimension: from data transparency to algorithmic transparency. If the state makes decisions through software, public scrutiny requires that code to be opened up. Latin America: from the pioneers to generative AI Latin America offers a fascinating perspective because it reveals the phenomenon's full lineage: from the major early projects that established its methods to the latest conversational tools. The pioneers in journalism and civil society: before the ChatGPT boom, projects such as Operação Serenata de Amor in Brazil were already automating the detection of suspicious parliamentary expenses through their robot, Rosie. Along similar lines, the Funes algorithm, created by the Peruvian outlet OjoPúblico after 15 months of multidisciplinary development, established a methodological gold standard for cross-referencing databases and detecting risks of collusion. These are the giants on whose shoulders the new wave stands. Living infrastructure: Brazil's ecosystem has also produced Querido Diário , which uses AI to centralise, open up and make searchable the official gazettes of thousands of municipalities. It is not the latest generative AI, but it tackles the fundamental bottleneck: turning unmanageable PDFs into structured data on which conversational models can subsequently operate. The new AI-native generation: the shift towards agile, conversational tools is already visible. In March 2026, Argentina saw the launch of OpenArg , a platform with a multi-agent architecture that queries 32 public data portals in real time to answer citizens' questions with charts and direct sources. Institutional automation: the Chilean state, meanwhile, shows that public administrations are taking notice too. ChileCompra has expanded automated monitoring to 100% of the procurement processes published on Mercado Público, applies 15 control rules and has already issued alerts about potential conflicts of interest. It has also announced plans to introduce language models during 2026 to review tender specifications, administrative decisions and technical annexes automatically. Decentralising scrutiny The lesson of this new wave of tools is clear: effective transparency is about making data intelligible, not simply publishing more of it. The capacity for scrutiny is becoming radically decentralised. It no longer depends exclusively on large newsrooms, oversight bodies or specialist technical teams. We are no longer talking simply about cheaper software production, but about code ceasing to be a barrier to entry. With the frontier AI already in our hands, any ordinary citizen with no prior computing knowledge can sit down at a screen, describe an instance of opacity that angers them and build their own public scrutiny project from scratch. In this new landscape, where the monopoly on civic oversight is breaking open in favour of ordinary people, the fundamental question is no longer simply whether society can hold power to account more effectively. The real challenge is whether democratic institutions themselves can absorb and respond to these civic capabilities without stripping them of independence, traceability and public control—and while developing initiatives of their own that rise to the same standard. Artificial intelligence and electoral disinformation: lessons from Chile and Argentina for democratic governance in Latin America Eight Fundación Botín programme participants examine AI-amplified electoral disinformation in Chile and Argentina and the institutional responses Latin America needs. Martín Telleria; María Fernanda Pech Novelo; Steeven Johannes Flor Pio; Genesis Dejaneyra Cadenasso Correa; Maria Antônia de Medeiros Dantas Costa; Valentina Silva Schmidt; Katherine Lizeth Bernal Santos; Samuel José Vega Martínez Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Government & Public Services 130 Analysis Artificial intelligence and electoral disinformation: lessons from Chile and Argentina for democratic governance in Latin America Today's issue is rather special. By a considerable margin, it brings together more authors than any we have published so far. It is written by a group of Fundación Botín participants who stood out in the government simulation run by ALEPH Educational Institution as part of the Programme for Strengthening the Public Service in Latin America . Since 2010, this initiative has brought together 30 young Ibero-Americans in each edition, preparing them to help strengthen the region's institutions in the near future. It is a particularly interesting programme which, for readers who may be interested, has just opened applications for its next edition. In recent years, working closely with the programme's academic director, Ignacio Verón , ALEPH Educational Institution has provided practical training and supported participants in developing their final projects. We thought it would be valuable to give them the opportunity to research artificial intelligence in Latin America and share what they learnt in the following estrategIA article. AI enters the campaign—and changes the rules Technological innovation is moving rapidly and is already part of political and democratic processes. In Latin America, electoral integrity is determined not only at physical ballot boxes, but also in an increasingly influential digital environment. AI did not create disinformation, but it has intensified its reach. False content can now be generated automatically, messages personalised at scale and manipulated material, such as deepfakes, produced with unprecedented sophistication. The underlying problem is substantial: electoral disinformation is becoming more frequent, more sophisticated and harder to control, especially where regulatory systems still follow analogue-era assumptions. Growing dependence on digital platforms and the opacity of the algorithms organising the information we see compound the problem. English reading of the original infographic, “AI and disinformation in electoral campaigns: lessons from Chile and Argentina for democratic governance in Latin America”: Regional context and vulnerability: informational vulnerability, dependence on social media, algorithmic power, echo chambers, institutional weakness and regulatory gaps. The image links the circulation of false content with eroding trust, referring to UNESCO and Elaine Ford. The underlying problem: AI intensifies disinformation through automated false content, messages personalised at scale and manipulated material or deepfakes. Control becomes difficult as deliberate strategies confront traditional methods. The image also labels echo-related and emotional prioritisation, referring to the OECD. Chile and Argentina: manipulated videos, electoral-fraud narratives, smear campaigns and information taken out of context. A hybrid structure combines politicised users, networks of automated accounts and recommendation algorithms. Responses and limitations: monitoring and verification exist, but responses remain reactive. A small parenthetical line beneath “Reactive responses” is malformed in the original and is not reconstructed. Lessons for democratic governance: comprehensive preventive strategies, adaptive regulation, algorithm oversight, coordination between authorities and platforms, and sustained media-literacy policies. The closing message calls for stronger institutional capacity to manage automated information environments. Disinformation is also not accidental. It involves deliberate strategies to weaken political opponents or reinforce particular narratives. Chile and Argentina are especially relevant cases: they are advanced in digitalisation, but also exposed to these dynamics. Moreover, many digital platforms operate business models centred on capturing users' attention. This can encourage polarisation, radicalisation and social fragmentation, weakening democratic consensus. Why is Latin America particularly vulnerable? AI's impact on elections cannot be understood without considering the regional context. In Latin America, the problem becomes critical through the convergence of three factors: informational vulnerability, institutional weakness and regulatory gaps. First, there is heavy reliance on social media as a primary source of political information. According to UNESCO , the circulation of false content during elections can alter public perceptions and erode democratic trust. Second, as Elaine Ford (2019), a Peruvian political scientist and director of the NGO Democracia Digital, argues, digital platforms are not neutral spaces. They are environments mediated by algorithms that influence public deliberation. In politically polarised contexts, this amplifies “echo chambers”, where people consume only information aligned with their beliefs. Added to this is what Francisco Balaguer Callejón (2022), Professor of Constitutional Law at the University of Granada, calls “algorithmic power”: a form of influence operating without direct democratic control. Opaque criteria for prioritising content create inequalities that current regulatory frameworks cannot effectively oversee. The challenge, therefore, is not solely technological. It requires stronger institutions, updated regulation and digital literacy. Otherwise, AI will continue to amplify structural problems such as institutional distrust and polarisation. Chile and Argentina: what is happening in practice? Recent developments in Chile and Argentina reveal common patterns in disinformation during electoral campaigns. The principal types of content detected include: Manipulated or altered videos. Unfounded narratives of electoral fraud. Smear campaigns against candidates. True information presented out of context. AI has also enabled automated production of false content and highly precise targeting of political messages. The problem concerns not only production, but circulation. Various studies show that this material spreads more readily through ideologically homogeneous networks, reinforcing existing beliefs; see Calvo and Aruguete, 2020 . Nor does that spread occur spontaneously. The actors involved are not isolated. They form a hybrid structure combining: Highly politicised users. Coordinated networks of automated accounts. Digital platforms with recommendation algorithms. Those algorithms prioritise engagement, often favouring emotional or polarising content irrespective of its truthfulness; see OECD, 2023 . Institutional responses have also emerged. In Chile, the Electoral Service has promoted monitoring and digital civic-education strategies. Argentina's National Electoral Chamber has followed a similar approach. Independent initiatives such as FastCheck.cl and Chequeado have likewise played a key role in verification. Evidence suggests that corrections can reduce the persistence of false beliefs if circulated in time; see Guess et al., 2020 . Despite these advances, a problem remains: many responses are still reactive, taking effect only after disinformation has gone viral. What Latin America can learn These cases suggest several lessons for the region. First, AI-amplified disinformation should not be understood simply as a technical problem. Above all, it is a challenge of democratic governance affecting institutional trust, public deliberation and electoral legitimacy. Second, comprehensive preventive strategies are needed, including: Adaptive regulatory frameworks. Effective oversight of algorithms. Coordination between authorities and digital platforms. Sustained media-literacy policies. Finally, Latin America's challenge is clear: strengthen institutional capacity to manage increasingly automated information environments. Electoral integrity depends no longer solely on traditional procedures, but also on how the digital ecosystem is regulated and governed. Further reading To explore some of the concepts discussed here: On algorithmic power's impact on democracy: Balaguer Callejón, F. (2022), La Constitución del algoritmo [The Constitution of the Algorithm], Fundación Manuel Giménez Abad. On digital platforms' role in public deliberation: Ford, E. (2019), El reto de la democracia digital: hacia una ciudadanía interconectada [The Challenge of Digital Democracy: Towards an Interconnected Citizenry]. On strategies to counter electoral disinformation: UNESCO (2023), Cómo contrarrestar la desinformación electoral: guía práctica para organizaciones y cuerpos electorales [How to Counter Electoral Disinformation: A Practical Guide for Electoral Organisations and Bodies].
