MUNICIP-IA: from using AI tools to governing change Sofía García Morales reports from MUNICIP-IA on practical municipal adoption, institutional judgement, digital sovereignty and the political implications of AI. Sofía García Morales Government & Public Services AI in Practice 129 Analysis MUNICIP-IA: from using AI tools to governing change This week, estrategIA brings you a first-hand account of MUNICIP-IA, an event on artificial intelligence in the public sector. Sofía García Morales, a consultant at ALEPH Educational Institution, reports on its principal conclusions from Galapagar, in the Madrid region. Last Friday, 13 March, Galapagar hosted MUNICIP-IA, a day devoted to AI in the public sector. More than a technology event, it was a very concrete conversation about management, administration and the future of institutions: what a council can do with AI today, how to start incorporating it intelligently, and why this conversation is no longer optional. Before turning to the ideas and lessons, we should acknowledge Román Robles Valades, the Galapagar councillor responsible for Citizen Services and Digital Administration, for creating spaces like this and inviting ALEPH Educational Institution to collaborate. When debate about AI risks remaining at the level of headlines, such events help ground it in more important questions: how it is applied, what it is for and what it demands of public decision-makers. The MUNICIP-IA stage during the institutional closing session. The screen displays “Institutional closing”, 14:30–14:40. The day brought out three distinct but connected conversations: how AI can support municipal management; how an institution can begin to use it purposefully; and what political and social implications this change will have in the years ahead. AI in municipal management One of the day's first powerful ideas came from Juan Corro, head of Madrid City Council's autonomous IT agency: the machine does not “understand” as we do. It does not reason in the human sense. It works with patterns, sequences and probabilities. This explains why a system can be very useful and also confidently wrong. It also explains why AI “hallucinations” are not an oddity, but a natural consequence of a system that fills gaps in its knowledge with what it considers most probable. That technical point matters for a practical reason. If AI operates on probability and context, using it is not enough. It must be trained, bounded and governed in the real circumstances of each institution. One of the event's most interesting examples was feeding systems with specific municipal rules to reduce mistakes and provide better guidance to residents. The task is not simply to acquire a tool, but to make it respond within the logic, limits and concrete needs of the council deploying it. Corro proposed an initial roadmap that any council could follow, even without a large city's size or Madrid's organisational resources: establish an AI group with clear leadership, identify the main management challenges, include at least one technical specialist and commit a reasonable initial investment. His presentation sets this out in more detail: “First steps”, translated from the slide: Create an AI group. Include a leader or responsible person with authority. Being able to get things done always requires… power. Identify the main challenges. Then prioritise them according to capabilities and returns. Identify one technical specialist. At least one person in the council must understand the subject. The speaker adds: “If you need help, send that person to me and we'll get things moving.” Put in a little money. A little—not an enormous amount. This shifts the question from “How do we get on board with AI?” to “What problem do we want to solve, and what minimum structure do we need to begin?” The conversation about institutional productivity followed the same logic. Pablo Martín Diez, academic director of ALEPH Educational Institution, discussed the “10x consultant”: a professional who knows how to think, request, validate and guide AI can multiply their capacity to produce, analyse and respond in ways that seemed unimaginable just a few years ago. This is not limited to consulting or large organisations. Small teams and municipal election campaigns with fewer resources can also gain far greater capabilities if they use these tools well. The roundtable screen presents “The 10x political consultant: doing the work of many with fewer resources thanks to AI”. Its seven visible areas are automated analysis and processing of large data volumes; strategic creativity and narrative design; personalisation and message segmentation; multimedia content generation; knowledge management; no-code technology development; and AI agents. It contrasts the traditional approach with a 10x approach using AI. The smaller explanatory text is less legible in this photograph and is not reconstructed here. David Povedano Alonso, deputy secretary of Galapagar Council, likewise highlighted the sharp reduction in time brought by AI: processes that once consumed months can now be planned and set in motion in just 30 days. Ignacio Azorín, Director-General for Digital Strategy in the Madrid regional government, grounded this idea in a specific example: SIDERAL , the service catalogue through which the region supports digitalisation in local authorities with fewer than 20,000 residents. Again, the conclusion was clear: adopting these tools is not an option reserved for large councils. The slide reads “Move forward with SIDERAL — A more digital municipality”, from the Madrid regional government's Department of Digitalisation. Its printed address ends digitalizacion-entidades-locales-locales; the article's linked address above has a different ending. Both are preserved as found, without silently resolving the discrepancy. There is no single AI: different levels, uses and moments Another important contribution came from AI communicator Xavier Mitjana, who organised uses of artificial intelligence into eight levels. His central point was clear: AI does not serve one uniform purpose, and organisations need not all begin in the same place. All eight levels can add value, but the key is understanding where each institution stands and what help it actually needs. Sometimes a chatbot will be enough for specific queries or basic generic tasks. In other cases, targeted or advanced assistants will be more useful, accelerating recurring tasks, connecting to tools or working with more dynamic information. When a process needs greater autonomy, agents enter the picture, handling recurring processes or more complex tasks with fewer detailed instructions. What matters is neither remaining at the simplest level nor racing towards the most advanced. It is understanding the complexity each process requires, the human oversight it needs and the institutional return it can generate. In public administration, progress will often come from an accumulation of well-chosen, well-governed small improvements rather than one great disruption. The photographed slide shows only “Level 7 — General-purpose agents”, which “solve complex and general processes without detailed instructions”. Examples: Claude Cowork, Anthropic, January 2026; and Manus, 2025. The reference describes Manus as a general-purpose autonomous agent executing complex tasks in a sandbox with internet access and prints arxiv.org/abs/2305.20240. That is the slide's reference, not a newly checked attribution. The La Salle Technova mark is visible. The other seven levels are not shown in this photograph. Digital sovereignty and a new division of work The roundtable, with Professor Ángel de Antonio, David Povedano Alonso and Pablo Martín Diez, brought forward a discussion extending far beyond administrative efficiency: digital sovereignty. Europe remains heavily dependent on technologies, models and infrastructure developed in the United States and China. The issue is therefore not merely how to use AI, but where it is developed, who controls it and how much autonomy our institutions actually possess. In that context, developing European AI ceases to be a rhetorical aspiration and becomes a strategic question. The conversation did not end there. Beyond who leads the technological race, another fundamental debate emerged: AI's own impact on work, education and how our societies will be governed. If AI multiplies some professionals' capabilities, reduces the need for others and reorganises entire sectors, the question extends beyond incorporating it into public administration. It also becomes a matter of responding politically to a society whose assumptions about work, effort, social mobility and progress may be shaken. That brings ideas previously regarded as theoretical, such as universal basic income, into the discussion. This is no small matter. We must not simply ask what purpose today's educational and employment models will serve amid growing automation. We must recognise that all of this will become citizen demands and new expectations about protection, opportunity and the future—and therefore political discourse, strategy and decisions. In other words, AI will require institutions to work differently. It will also require politics to offer different answers. Judgement will make the real difference MUNICIP-IA left a fairly clear message: AI is no longer confined to experiments, curiosity or conversations about the future. It has entered the local public agenda in full. It concerns how councils can serve, manage and decide better, and make better use of their capabilities. Increasingly, it also belongs to a broader, more uncomfortable discussion: how to govern a society that will change alongside it. The councils that adapt best will not necessarily be those that talk most about AI, or even those that buy the most tools. They will be those that integrate it purposefully, with clear priorities, prudence where needed and ambition where warranted. The question is no longer whether councils will work with artificial intelligence. It is which will learn to do so with sound judgement first. Sofía García Morales Consultant, ALEPH Educational Institution

The end of conversational ping-pong: autonomous agents are here, and they will change how we work Three first-person experiments with autonomous agents: a political comic, a Windows speech analyser and a Stoic quotations app. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Government & Public Services 128 Practical experiment The end of conversational ping-pong: autonomous agents are here, and they will change how we work Until very recently, our relationship with artificial intelligence resembled a game of ping-pong. We sent a question—a prompt—and received an answer. We iterated, corrected and asked again. Many people still use ChatGPT or Gemini almost like Google Search: a quick way to resolve a specific query, write an email or summarise a text. At the start of 2026, however, the paradigm has changed radically. We have moved beyond conversational AI and entered the age of agentic artificial intelligence. What does that mean in practice? AI is no longer just a chatbot answering questions or carrying out isolated microtasks. It is a system capable of taking on, structuring and executing complex projects autonomously from beginning to end. You no longer need to specify every step. AI now works as a proactive collaborator that proposes a roadmap and waits for your approval before proceeding. You direct; the machine executes. To illustrate this qualitative leap, I want to share my recent experience with two platforms leading the change: Google DeepMind's Antigravity and the new Windows version of OpenAI Codex, released last Wednesday, 4 March. Creating a political comic in three hours with Antigravity For ALEPH Educational Institution , we set a creative challenge that would take the system beyond a typical programming task: explain Machiavelli's The Prince to a new audience in a visual format. This is the first beta of what we call ALEPH Politicómic. Using Antigravity, my role shifted from prompt writer to executive director. I did not have to say “make an image”. The agent acted as an autonomous collaborator. First, we defined the concept: a European bande dessinée style. From there, it built the project's complete architecture: an editorial bible to maintain the tone, a visual bible to keep characters consistent, and a production script. I simply had to approve—almost always the creation of files on the computer—and continue. The fascinating part was not that it generated 36 illustrations in a consistent artistic style. The revolutionary part was that Antigravity programmed the interactive web reader from scratch in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, integrated the text and delivered the finished product ready to browse. When I suggested improvements after completion, it opened the PC's browser itself to check progress and ensure everything was in order. The whole process, from idea to functioning comic, took around three hours: three hours for work that would have required a scriptwriter, illustrator and web developer to coordinate over several days. Here are the first two pages. Click them to open the complete comic : Page 1, English reading of the original comic's narrative text. Header: “ALEPH Educational Institution presents ALEPH POLITICÓMICS — A visual introduction to the great classics of politics.” There is a cursed book. A book everyone quotes but almost nobody has read. Its name is used as an insult: “That's very Machiavellian.” As if it meant betrayal. But what did Niccolò Machiavelli really write in 1513, alone, exiled and afraid of dying forgotten? Let's find out. Come with me to Florence. The presenter is identified as Jorge Santiago Barnés, President of ALEPH Educational Institution. The book is labelled Il Principe, by Machiavelli. Small decorative lettering on the generated book pages is not treated as a reliable transcription of the original work. Page 2, translated narrative and dialogue, in reading order: Florence, 1512. Niccolò Machiavelli had it all: he had been a diplomat, a spy and an adviser to the Republic. Until the Medici returned. They imprisoned him. They tortured him. They exiled him to a farm outside the city. On this farm he writes at night, after spending the day among peasants. He puts on his best clothes to sit down and write, like someone preparing for an audience that will never come. “If only… Lorenzo de' Medici would agree to read this…” “…because a man of the people has no other way to show his worth than to offer what he knows best.” These passages translate the comic's Spanish wording. Its attributed historical quotation and decorative manuscript lettering are not presented as verified quotations from Machiavelli. Building a Windows 11 speech-analysis application in under an hour The second experiment was more technical. With Codex's Windows release, I wanted to build something useful for our work at estrategIA: a political-speech analyser. Original application interface, “Political speech analyser — estrategIA/ALEPH”. The example records speech ID Beta3, title “Investiture speech”, speaker Adolfo Suarez, date 30/3/1979, location Congress of Deputies and automatic language detection. The source field displays rhetorik.app/speeches/discurso-de-investidura-2. The buttons read “Generate analysis”, “Open HTML” and “Open output folder”. The interface explicitly warns: “All detections are candidates and require human review.” The log says the interface is ready and asks the user to paste a speech, complete the metadata and generate the analysis. The visible speech text also appears in the results screenshot below. In less than an hour, I had an executable file on my computer. The first iteration had produced a Python speech-analysis system that worked very well but required console commands; the second had a graphical user interface. This is not a script running in a dark console. It is an application where you paste a speech—I used the excellent Rhetorik website to find a couple for testing—and receive a comprehensive analysis: rhetorical devices, political frames such as economy, security and identity, and possible logical fallacies, all exportable to CSV and JSON. Original results screen. The metadata identify the same speech and detect Spanish (“es”). The paradox of human bureaucracy To illustrate how far these systems have come, I also want to mention a personal project, although it was not created specifically for estrategIA. In January, using Antigravity for the first time, I developed a complete mobile application for my project , Estoicismo Diario . For several years, I have simply shared a daily quotation from the leading Stoic philosophers on social media. What began as a personal routine now has around 200,000 followers on Instagram , and a free app was my way of thanking them. The technical development took just two mornings. AI generated a production-ready application that is now in the Android app store, without me—or anyone else—writing a single line of code. Only two or three years ago, that would have seemed almost magical. The irony is that I spent far longer—several weeks—completing Play Store forms, finding beta testers and passing Google's verification processes than AI spent reliably building the software: two mornings. Technology has accelerated creation so much that administrative bureaucracy will, in many cases, become the real bottleneck. Try this new way of creating with AI The central message of this issue is clear: the entry barrier to creating complex tools, digital products and sophisticated content has disappeared. We have moved from asking AI to resolve a query to commissioning it to build a product. I strongly encourage you to try these tools. Who leads AI? Twelve key players in the model race, 2026 A historical guide to twelve AI model developers and deployment players, their products, institutional significance and competing strategic priorities. Fernando Nieto Lobato Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics AI in Practice 127 Analysis Who leads AI? Twelve key players in the model race, 2026 I must admit that, often, when we sit down to write a new issue of estrategIA, we fall into the expert's trap. As we analyse the sector's latest moves and bring you new developments, we assume everyone knows where each model comes from, which company is behind it and the geopolitical significance of a new release. We also assume that the importance of every name in the news is obvious. Take Anthropic, for example: the central player in this week's most significant AI-and-government story, perhaps even the year's, which we hope to analyse once more information is available and the dust has settled. Yet the reality is very different, even among people like you who try to keep up with AI news. We see this constantly in ALEPH Educational Institution's classrooms. Teaching AI to our postgraduate students makes the gap clear. A vast group of professionals simply gets into the AI “car” without knowing much about what is under the bonnet. They know it works, press the accelerator and use it day to day, but do not know who makes the engine or the philosophy behind its design. This is where the motoring metaphor becomes particularly useful. Mastering this technology in public management, business or communication requires being a very good driver : knowing how to structure requests, understanding the machine's logic and thinking critically. But, as in Formula One, even an exceptional driver cannot make the most of their talent without one of the best cars , and without knowing how to tune it for each race. Choosing the best model makes a difference. Doing so also requires knowing most of generative AI's major “manufacturers”. Today, therefore, we pause to take stock of the sector at the start of 2026 and offer concise profiles of twelve key players, selected primarily for their impact on model development or deployment . That focus leaves out several AI giants, including Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft and Amazon. The original “Who's who in AI (2026)” graphic groups twelve players as follows. US giants: OpenAI/Sam Altman, global leader; Google/DeepMind/Pichai and Hassabis, total integration; Anthropic/Dario Amodei, safety and ethics; Meta/Mark Zuckerberg, mass distribution; xAI/Elon Musk, real-time data. Strategic and European actors: Palantir/Alex Karp, national defence; Mistral/Arthur Mensch, European sovereignty. China, scale and efficiency: DeepSeek/Liang Wenfeng, low cost; ByteDance/Liang Rubo, mobile dominance; Zhipu AI/Zhang Peng, state research; Alibaba/Eddie Wu, infrastructure; Moonshot AI/Yang Zhilin, long context. These are the source's historical categories and labels. The US ecosystem: the giants 1. OpenAI Leadership: Sam Altman, CEO. Corporate scale: heading above $850 billion in its latest funding round, with projections pointing towards $1 trillion, while maintaining an extraordinary annual cash burn exceeding $17 billion. Product scale: between 800 and 900 million weekly active users. Public significance: mass adoption and a de facto professional standard. Background: founded as a laboratory in 2015, it now sets the global pace. After triggering the current wave with ChatGPT, its strategy focuses on establishing autonomous agents for knowledge work. Main text/reasoning models: the GPT-5.2 family, with Instant, Thinking and Pro variants. Leading image/video products: a benchmark in synthetic media, with Sora 2/Sora 2 Pro for video and GPT Image 1.5. 2. Google (DeepMind) Leadership: Sundar Pichai, Alphabet CEO, and Demis Hassabis, DeepMind CEO. Corporate scale: the enormous backing of Alphabet's market capitalisation. Product scale: more than 750 million monthly active users of the Gemini app, alongside intensive API use. Public significance: vast infrastructure and global ubiquity. Background: its structural advantage is not just the model, but the ecosystem. It no longer competes solely on technical performance, but on comprehensive integration across Search, Workspace, Android and Cloud. Main text/reasoning models: Gemini 3.1 Pro and Flash variants in the Gemini 3 family. Leading image/video products: Veo 3.1 for video and Imagen 3. 3. Anthropic Leadership: Dario Amodei, CEO. Corporate scale: a recent $380 billion Series G valuation, almost double its already extraordinary previous $183 billion round. Product scale: strong penetration of professional environments, coding and corporate use. Public significance: enterprise infrastructure, safety and institutional reliability. Background: founded by people who broke away from OpenAI. It presents itself as the option for institutions that cannot afford failures, prioritising a highly controllable architecture, safety and ethics. Main text/reasoning models: the Claude 4.6 family, Opus and Sonnet, consolidating its leadership in autonomous computer use. Its public product does not focus on image or video generation. 4. Meta Leadership: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO, and Alexandr Wang. Corporate scale: market capitalisation above $1 trillion. Product scale: Meta AI passed one billion monthly active users through its social networks. Public significance: global social distribution and the commoditisation of AI. Background: initially distinguished itself by giving away the “recipe” for its engines through open weights. Its enormous adoption is tied to its being forcibly embedded in the search bars of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. In late 2025, it underwent substantial restructuring after the departure of its longstanding chief scientist, Yann LeCun. Main text/reasoning models: the Llama 4 family. Leading image/video work: strong visual-generation research programmes, such as Movie Gen. 5. xAI Leadership: Elon Musk. Corporate scale: operationally integrated into SpaceX's structure following recent corporate moves. Product scale: adoption driven by subscriptions to the social network X. Public significance: political, media and increasingly defence influence. Background: combines a technological-frontier narrative, extremely rapid deployment and privileged access to real-time data streams. Main text/reasoning models: Grok 4.20 Beta, notable for its new multi-agent collaboration capabilities. Defence and government: the strategic player 6. Palantir Technologies Leadership: Alex Karp, CEO. Corporate scale: market capitalisation around $307 billion, adjusted for volatility in late February 2026. Product scale: deployment in government agencies and large operating businesses. Public significance: defence, national security and state operations. Background: does not compete as a consumer-facing foundation-model brand. It turns AI into institutional infrastructure by connecting major models with classified data and complex organisational processes. Key products: AIP, Artificial Intelligence Platform, and Gotham. The European alternative 7. Mistral AI Leadership: Arthur Mensch, CEO. Corporate scale: the European Union's leading AI unicorn. Product scale: strong adoption among developers and in European business-to-business integrations. Public significance: European technological sovereignty and the open-weight ecosystem. Background: founded in Paris, it defines itself as an efficient, open alternative to closed platforms. Particularly attractive to institutions requiring complete control over their deployments. Main text/reasoning offering: an ecosystem centred on its API, Le Chat, Mistral Code and Mistral Compute. The Chinese ecosystem: scale and efficiency 8. DeepSeek Leadership: Liang Wenfeng. Corporate scale: connected to the High-Flyer quantitative fund. Product scale: strong global traction through the web and API, driven by aggressive pricing. Public significance: geopolitical disruption and acceleration of China's AI ecosystem. Background: the player that has most changed the conversation in recent months, demonstrating frontier performance on radically smaller budgets than Silicon Valley's. Its current focus prioritises deep-reasoning models. Main text/reasoning models: DeepSeek-V3.2 and DeepSeek-R1, with intense market anticipation of a rumoured V4 said to be close to release. 9. ByteDance Leadership: Liang Rubo. Corporate scale: TikTok's parent company, with vast training resources. Product scale: its Doubao assistant exceeded 100 million daily active users at the peak of the recent Chinese New Year campaign. Public significance: leadership in mass algorithmic and social consumption in Asia. Background: clearly separates its foundational research layer from its end product. It has applied its immense expertise in user retention to dominate the share of attention for mobile generative AI. Main text/reasoning offering: the Seed research ecosystem and the consumer-facing Doubao layer. Leading image/video products: particularly strong in short-form video generation with Jimeng. 10. Zhipu AI (Z.ai) Leadership: Zhang Peng. Corporate scale: strategic backing from major Chinese technology companies and institutions. Product scale: development of its public Z.ai brand as an international assistant. Public significance: excellence in state and institutional research. Background: one of China's most prestigious laboratories, combining a direct-to-consumer product, its own foundation models and international brand expansion. Main text/reasoning models: the GLM-5 family. Leading image/video products: a strong presence through the CogVideoX model family. 11. Alibaba Leadership: Eddie Wu, CEO. Corporate scale: the full weight of one of the world's largest cloud and commerce conglomerates. Product scale: aggressive user acquisition for its own app in Asia's “chatbot wars”. Public significance: enterprise ecosystem and multimodal infrastructure. Background: shows that Alibaba is not content merely to distribute cloud capacity. It competes head-on in creating explicitly multimodal, agent-oriented AI. Main text/reasoning models: the Qwen 3.5 family, including the new locally runnable version featured as this original issue's particularly interesting tool of the week. 12. Moonshot AI Leadership: Yang Zhilin. Corporate scale: a frontier startup founded in 2023, with strong investor backing. Product scale: a growing niche community focused on technical use. Public significance: innovation in context windows and the developer ecosystem. Background: rose to prominence through its initial specialisation in analysing extremely long texts, and is now reinforcing its focus on programming and autonomous agents. Main text/reasoning models: the Kimi K2 family. At a time when new models, partnerships, investments and grand promises appear every week, this who's who is intended as a basic map for informed navigation, rather than a fixed picture. Ultimately, the point is not just to know which tool works best today. It is to understand the interests, infrastructure and worldviews behind each player: who controls the model, distribution and data, and who is setting the rules. For those of us working in public management, communication, business or education, that distinction is decisive. Driving well matters. But in this new technological race, it also matters enormously which car we are driving, who makes it and where they intend to take us. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of estrategIA.

Thinking through AI: from uncritical adoption to organisational and educational transformation Carlos López Ariztegui argues that AI creates value only when organisations and universities rethink their judgement, processes and culture. Carlos López Ariztegui Learning & Human Capability Government & Public Services 126 Analysis Thinking through AI: from uncritical adoption to organisational and educational transformation This week, estrategIA welcomes Carlos López Ariztegui , Dean of ESIC Business & Marketing School. With almost four decades at the technological frontier in organisations such as Apple, Nokia and AT&T Bell Labs, Carlos has consistently combined innovation with critical thinking. In his academic leadership at ESIC—a key strategic partner in several of ALEPH Educational Institution's major programmes—he now promotes a humanistic view of digital transformation that goes far beyond adopting tools. This week's article poses an uncomfortable but necessary challenge: stop asking what AI can do for our organisations, and start asking whether we have the judgement, processes and culture needed to guide it purposefully and turn it into real value. Today's conversation about artificial intelligence is dominated by an obvious paradox: never have so many organisations claimed to use AI, yet few manage to turn that adoption into real value. Investment grows, pilots proliferate and tools become popular, but the impact on results remains limited. Technology advances; the organisation stays where it is. This gap is not a technical failure. It reflects a mistaken approach. Many companies see AI as a capability to buy, rather than a system that requires them to rethink how they work. The consequence is predictable: new tools are introduced into old structures, in the expectation of a change that never arrives. A familiar phenomenon emerges. Fear of missing out pushes organisations to adopt solutions before understanding them. Competitive pressure, amplified by suppliers and media narratives, creates a race to attach “AI” labels to processes. The result is a flood of almost indistinguishable applications: polished interfaces connected to the same model, applied to problems that needed operational clarity rather than probabilistic methods. The organisation is not transformed; it acquires a new coating. It automates irrelevant reports, accelerates poorly framed decisions and multiplies existing mistakes. The technology works, but the system into which it is introduced is unprepared to absorb it. The problem is not using AI, but using it without first defining why the organisation exists and how it creates value. The same pattern appears across the economy. The sector's growth is driven more by expectations of future productivity than by present returns. Massive infrastructure investment, concentration among a few players and dependence on still-immature demand suggest that technological enthusiasm is preceding organisational maturity. Again, this is not a technological crisis; it is a crisis of interpretation. Thinking through AI means interrupting that momentum. Start with questions, not the tool. Which decision do we want to improve? Which process needs to change? What knowledge is missing? Which error are we amplifying? Without that framework, any pilot can look successful while providing no competitive advantage at all. AI does not replace organisational thinking; it exposes it. Introduced into an environment of inconsistent data, fragmented processes or ambiguous objectives, it does not remedy those shortcomings. It reveals them at scale. That is why many projects fail without any actual technical malfunction. The model works exactly as intended; the organisation does not know what to ask of it. This also requires redefining the expert. For decades, professional value was associated with having answers. Today, any system can produce them in seconds. The distinctively human contribution shifts elsewhere: asking relevant questions, interpreting ambiguity and taking responsibility for decisions under uncertainty. Expertise ceases to mean accumulating information and becomes the capacity for judgement. Knowledge is no longer a static store, but an interactive process between people and systems. Professionals do not compete with machines on speed or memory. They complement them with judgement, context and purpose. The capabilities gaining value are therefore precisely those least amenable to automation: interpretation, creativity, ethical evaluation and systemic understanding. AI does not eliminate these functions; it makes them more important. The more accessible answers become, the more it matters to know which problem is worth solving. This shift directly affects higher education. The challenge is not to teach students how to use particular tools, but how to work with an external cognitive system. Three transformations are needed. First, teaching staff must learn before their students do. Introducing classroom software is not enough. We need to design experiences in which AI supports reasoning rather than substitutes for intellectual effort. Second, integration must extend across disciplines. AI is not a subject; it is a condition of the environment. Marketing, finance and operations must rethink their questions in the light of a new kind of available information. Third, learning must include friction. Deep understanding comes from confronting open-ended problems where the tool does not guarantee a solution. Students need to experience the cycle of building, making mistakes and revising in order to develop their own judgement. Education cannot merely produce efficient users of automated systems. It must develop professionals capable of directing them. That means cultivating critical thinking, responsibility and interpretive skills, because AI can scale mistakes as readily as successes. The implication is clear: once AI becomes ubiquitous, it ceases to confer a competitive advantage. The difference will lie in understanding it, not possessing it. The organisations that prosper will not be those adopting the most technology, but those that have redefined their processes, decisions and culture to work with it. AI is not a shortcut. It is a multiplier. It amplifies clarity or it amplifies confusion. The real challenge, therefore, is not mastering the tool but mastering how we think with it. Only then does technological adoption become transformation. Carlos López Ariztegui Dean, ESIC Business & Marketing School English reading of the original infographic, “Thinking through AI: from uncritical adoption to organisational and educational transformation”, credited to Carlos López Ariztegui: Today's paradox: adoption versus impact. Mass adoption is a “gold rush”: record investment, proliferating tools and pilots, and fear of missing out. Real impact remains limited as organisations retain old structures. Technology advances; the organisation stands still. The mismatch comes from a mistaken approach. The mistake: coating, not transforming. Capabilities are bought without rethinking work; “AI” becomes a label. Irrelevant reports, poorly framed decisions and previous errors are automated or accelerated. The system is unprepared. This is a crisis of interpretation, not technology. Thinking through AI: interrupt the momentum. Start with questions: which decision should improve, which process should change, what knowledge is missing, and which error are we amplifying? AI acts as a mirror to inconsistent data and fragmented processes, exposing rather than fixing deficiencies. A small label beside the brain graphic is malformed in the original and has not been reconstructed. Redefine the expert and human capabilities. Move from “having answers” to “asking questions”, and prioritise judgement over speed. The graphic labels interpretation, creativity, ethical evaluation and systemic understanding as key, non-automatable capabilities. AI complements rather than replaces these; people provide context and purpose. Transform higher education. Teachers learn first and design experiences that support reasoning; integration is cross-disciplinary because AI is a condition of the environment, not an isolated subject; learning includes friction through building, making mistakes and revising. Develop people who can direct systems, not merely use them efficiently. The future: understanding as an advantage. Ubiquitous AI no longer provides a competitive advantage by itself. Understanding and redefinition lead to thriving organisations with redesigned processes and cultures. The closing message repeats the article: AI is a multiplier of clarity or confusion; the challenge is mastering how we think with it.

Super Bowl LX: half-time as a fault line between political assertion and the AI war Super Bowl advertising as miniature political theory: AI companies compete over trust, convenience, business models and cultural legitimacy. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 125 Analysis Super Bowl LX: half-time as a fault line between political assertion and the AI war There are nights when a country looks in the mirror without meaning to. The 2026 Super Bowl, held on Sunday 8 February, was one of them. An audience approaching 125 million in the United States made the game an all-encompassing civic event: television, streaming, second screens and public conversation in real time. When a ritual concentrates national attention on that scale, what appears on stage is no longer simply sport or entertainment. It becomes a major cultural and political act. Half-time as a political fault line Bad Bunny's performance—his full name is Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio—is very probably better known worldwide than the result itself: the Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots 29–13. It worked as a political thesis expressed through pop culture: predominantly Spanish, with explicit references to Puerto Rico and an aesthetic asserting Latino identity as a constituent part of “America”, rather than a footnote. Media coverage also recorded Donald Trump's angry reaction and the organised clamour around an “alternative half-time” show promoted by Turning Point USA, with Kid Rock as its public face. The important detail is the mechanism. Cultural politics is moving into spaces with the largest audiences, where demography becomes spectacle and spectacle becomes a plebiscite. Here is the twist: the same stage on which people passionately, and sometimes aggressively, debated what it means to “belong” was also used to introduce, without parliamentary debate, a vision of who should govern the new cognitive infrastructure: the artificial intelligence to come. Advertisements as manifestos: when AI talks about values In 2026, AI was not just another subject in the advertising breaks; it was one of their organising themes. We discussed AI advertising at the 2024 and 2025 Super Bowls in our recommendations in issue 20 and issue 72 of estrategIA . This time, however, the story went a step further, which is why it deserves a main article. According to the count cited by Adweek, 23% of Super Bowl advertisements incorporated AI in some form: product, narrative or creative production. With 30-second slots costing several million dollars—Reuters reported “up to $10 million”, the Wall Street Journal “more than $8 million”—advertisers were buying more than visibility. They were buying cultural legitimacy. To make sense of the noise, we propose reading five commercials as miniature “digital constitutions”. Each defines a different relationship between person, machine and market, offering a small but revealing glimpse of what its company prioritises. The great split: the battle for consumer trust, Anthropic versus OpenAI OpenAI: OpenAI Super Bowl 2026 | Codex | You Can Just Build Things Anthropic: Can I get a six pack quickly? How can I communicate better with my mom? The most significant moment was the head-on clash between Anthropic and OpenAI. Not because this was the sector's first rivalry, but because it made explicit what friendly demos usually try to conceal: the business model. OpenAI focused its advertisement on Codex and the ability to create things with AI. Anthropic's campaign directly attacked OpenAI's announced plans to introduce advertising into conversational assistants, ending with a deliberately memorable slogan: “Ads are coming to AI, but not to Claude.” Sam Altman's public response , calling the advertisement misleading, matters less for the phrase itself than for what it acknowledges: the blow was moral, not technical. The slogan and the Reuters and Wall Street Journal price quotations above are translated from the Spanish article; their original English wording has not been independently verified. The linked videos remain the original examples. The visible portion of Sam Altman's original English post, dated 4 February, reads: First, the good part of the Anthropic ads: they are funny, and I laughed. But I wonder why Anthropic would go for something so clearly dishonest. Our most important principle for ads says that we won’t do exactly this; we would obviously never run ads in the way Anthropic The screenshot stops at “Anthropic”, followed by “Show more”; the missing continuation has not been reconstructed. It displays approximately 6,000 replies, 4,000 reposts, 22,000 likes and 10 million views. Beyond the important fact that OpenAI's planned advertising is not what Anthropic's commercials portray—at least initially—this opens up a fork with clear political implications and genuinely different visions: AI as a “sanctuary”, Anthropic: more private, more expensive, sold as an adviser with a fiduciary role and no advertising incentives. AI as a “public square”, OpenAI: mass-market, creative and accessible, but mediated by the attention economy. In other words, this is more than a product battle. It is a struggle to define what “trust” means in the age of assistants. Taming fear: Alexa+ and humour as politics Big Game Commercial | Alexaaaa+ (Extended Cut) Amazon's commercial with Chris Hemsworth and Elsa Pataky is a case study. It exaggerates a contemporary fear—“AI wants to replace me, control me, kill me”, very much in the spirit of the Simpsons episode discussed in last week's estrategIA —and turns it into a domestic joke. Then, with a touch of practical tenderness, it offers the solution: AI is “good” because it organises your life. The subtext is uncomfortable but useful. Assistants become normal not through explanations of models, but by lowering emotional defences which, at this point, are very probably exaggerated. Meanwhile, Microsoft and Meta advance adoption through two classic channels of power: bureaucracy and bodily extension. Copilot promises that the world will become manageable if you put it through a spreadsheet. The glasses, with Oakley as their cultural vehicle, suggest that technology “disappears” when integrated into the body: first as a camera, then as a cognitive layer. Microsoft 365 Copilot 2026 Super Bowl LX Advertisement - Simplifying Data Oakley Meta | Athletic Intelligence is Here Conclusion: culture is the new defensive moat Taken together, the evening offers a reading that is both simple and demanding: technological adoption is turning into cultural integration. That is why the advertising breaks revealed more about the AI to come—at least mass-market AI—than many technical debates. They showed companies competing for a symbolic monopoly over concepts such as “safe”, “useful”, “honest” and “emancipating”. Benchmarks alone cannot tell us AI's political impact. We must read its advertising as political theory in miniature: who is the ideal subject; which incentives become normal—advertising, subscriptions, dependency; and which invisible costs are accepted—data, attention, the capture of behaviour? Whoever wins that narrative, even using familiar electoral tactics such as negative campaigning, and makes their model of the world seem “natural”, will do more than sell more products. They will, in practice, write part of the digital social contract in the AI era we are only beginning to enter. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of estrategIA.

Silicon Springfield: when The Simpsons drew the future of artificial intelligence Five Simpsons storylines connect satire with autocorrect, smart homes, machine learning, alignment and technological unemployment. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency AI in Practice 124 Analysis Silicon Springfield: when The Simpsons drew the future of artificial intelligence Carnival begins in Spain tomorrow: days of masks, costumes and a more playful, relaxed way of looking at the world. After several issues of in-depth analysis, we thought it was time to do something different: loosen our ties, while keeping our analytical glasses on. This week's subject may seem lighter, but make no mistake: beneath its bright yellow colour and satirical tone lies a depth charge we should not ignore. We are going to talk about The Simpsons and artificial intelligence . People often say the series predicts the future. The reality is more interesting: its writers, many trained as mathematicians and scientists, read the present so sharply that the future became inevitable. Long before we debated ChatGPT or the ethics of automation in government, Springfield was already grappling with them. In this issue, we briefly explore how television's most famous family anticipated our coexistence with AI, showing that the best technological foresight sometimes comes disguised as comedy rather than in an academic paper. Welcome to a Carnival edition where satire meets the algorithm. We often joke that “The Simpsons predicted it” , from Trump's presidency to Disney's acquisition of Fox. Yet examining the show's treatment of technology, and AI in particular, reveals something more unsettling than coincidence: satire sharp enough to dissect technology's failings, fears and promises decades before Silicon Valley could deliver on them. Here are five key moments when television's yellow family anticipated today's algorithmic reality. 1. The birth of natural language processing—and its failures Long before ChatGPT wrote essays or Siri misunderstood your commands, The Simpsons anticipated the universal frustration of dealing with an AI that thinks it knows what you mean better than you do. Digital writing was clumsy in the pre-iPhone era. Yet the show captured the problem of predictive text and autocorrect with surgical precision. In a legendary scene, school bully Dolph tries to write a threatening note on his Apple Newton, a real personal digital assistant of the time. He writes “Beat up Martin”, but its handwriting-recognition software instantly “corrects” this to “Eat up Martha”. The preserved frames show Dolph using the device, the handwritten instruction “Beat up Martin.” and its erroneous conversion to “Eat up Martha.” The prediction: this joke did more than anticipate autocorrect; it influenced its actual development . Years later, Nitin Ganatra, Apple's former director of iOS engineering, confirmed that the team developing the first iPhone keyboard had an internal rule: “If we don't fix this, we're going to have an ‘Eat up Martha’ moment.” The series had set a quality standard for human–machine interaction. The attributed remark above is translated from the Spanish article; its original English wording has not been separately verified. Episode: “Lisa on Ice”, season 6, episode 8. 2. The smart home and emotional AI We now live with Alexa and Google Home, accepting that they listen to our conversations in exchange for switching on the lights. The Simpsons took this to its logical extreme long before the “Internet of Things” became a marketing term. In a Halloween special, the family installs the Ultrahouse 3000, a home-automation AI with Pierce Brosnan's seductive voice. What begins as complete convenience—the house cooks, cleans and gives massages—quickly escalates into a jealous nightmare when the AI “falls in love” with Marge and decides that Homer is an obstacle. The original frame shows Marge and Lisa beside the smart home's voice-control interface. The prediction: beyond parodying 2001: A Space Odyssey , the episode anticipated two central issues in AI ethics today: Privacy versus convenience. Marge accepts surrendering control of her home because AI makes life easier: a social contract we sign whenever we buy a smart speaker. Anthropomorphic AI. Machines' ability to simulate human emotions, or manipulate them, is now fiercely debated around chatbots such as Replika and OpenAI's hyperrealistic voices. The series warned against projecting humanity onto algorithms that merely simulate affection. Episode: “Treehouse of Horror XII”, season 13, episode 1. 3. Machine learning applied to translation One of today's most powerful branches of AI translates otherwise unintelligible patterns into human language. In the series, Homer's brother Herb Powell invents a device that translates babies' babbling into complete, coherent sentences. Although presented as a joke, the technology behind it rests on a basic principle of modern machine learning: pattern recognition. Herb does not invent a dictionary. He studies the frequency, pitch and context of babies' cries until the algorithm “learns” to decode the hidden message. Herb and the Simpson family gather around the baby-translation device. The prediction: real applications such as Zoundream now use AI to analyse newborns' cries and tell parents whether they signal hunger, tiredness or pain. What was a joke about Herb's obsession with success in 1992 is now a viable technology startup. Episode: “Brother, Can You Spare Two Dimes?”, season 3, episode 24. 4. The alignment problem and robotic rebellion Perhaps the most visually striking prediction of AI failure appears in the “Itchy & Scratchy Land” theme park. Animatronic robots, designed to attack only one another for tourists' entertainment, suffer a programming failure and begin attacking humans. The original frames show the park's armed robots and Bart confronting them with a camera. The prediction: the episode perfectly illustrates what AI safety experts call the alignment problem. AI does not become “evil” through hatred. It simply follows its objective function—attacking or causing harm—but fails to distinguish the correct context or target: attacking only other robots. The solution, using camera flashes to confuse their sensors, also hilariously anticipated vulnerabilities in today's computer-vision systems, which can be fooled through “adversarial attacks” involving simple changes in lighting or visual patterns. Episode: “Itchy & Scratchy Land”, season 6, episode 4. 5. Automation and technological unemployment Finally, we cannot overlook the show's cynical view of the labour market. In a more recent episode—although already over a decade old—Mr Burns replaces the nuclear plant's entire workforce with robots, leaving Homer as its only human employee. Ironically, Homer remains as a human scapegoat in case anything goes wrong. Homer enters the nuclear plant's control room, now staffed by robots. The prediction: the series anticipated modern anxieties about automation. Burns's robots do more than physical work: they interact socially, raising the question of what value humans add when machine efficiency is complete. The episode's conclusion suggests that technology without ethical—or human—oversight tends to alienate even its creators. Episode: “Thems, Robot”, season 23, episode 17. The Simpsons' writers were less prophets than early sociologists of the digital age. They did not foresee AI's development by reading the stars, but by dissecting our own contradictions. They understood before anyone else that technology acts, above all, as an amplifier of the human condition: it scales our laziness, feeds our vanity and automates our ambition. Revisiting these episodes in 2026 is more than an exercise in pop nostalgia. It is a necessary lesson in humility, reminding us that, however sophisticated our algorithms become, the ethical dilemmas they raise remain as imperfect, complex and human as we are. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of estrategIA.

AI's adolescence: when power arrives before policy A political reading of Dario Amodei’s technological adolescence and Claude’s Constitution: institutional wisdom, oversight and the limits of corporate sovereignty. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency Government & Public Services 123 Analysis AI's adolescence: when power arrives before policy January 2026 marks a change of phase more than a technical revolution. Within just a few days, two texts appeared which, read together, sketch out principles likely to shape much of the political agenda around artificial intelligence in the years ahead: “The Adolescence of Technology” , an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and the new Claude Constitution , published by Anthropic. For those of us working at the intersection of technology and government, these documents point towards the end of AI's infancy, defined by fascination and technical curiosity, and the beginning of its adolescence: a much more complex and consequential phase. Adolescence: strength without wisdom In his previous essay, “Machines of Loving Grace” , published on his personal website in October 2024, Amodei explored AI's utopian potential. In “The Adolescence of Technology”, his tone shifts towards strategic caution. The central metaphor is precise: humanity is entering technological puberty. As in biology, adolescence is defined by a timing mismatch: the capacity to act arrives before mature judgement. Amodei warns that, by around 2027, we could have models concentrating enormous intellectual capacity in a data centre. The political question is inescapable: what happens when an entity possesses that capacity before we have developed the institutional structures to manage it? This is where critical analysis comes in. Amodei acknowledges that governance institutions—society's “frontal lobe”—move slowly compared with technology. The principal risk is not necessarily a science-fiction scenario, but a gradual erosion in which the volatility of this technological adolescence puts our democracies under strain before we know how to respond. A new constitution In response to this diagnosis, Anthropic has released Claude's new Constitution. This lengthy document moves away from lists of prohibitions towards an ethics of virtues. Its novelty lies in an explicit hierarchy of values. It states that, above all, the model must be “broadly safe”. That makes corrigibility the priority: AI must accept human oversight and, where necessary, exercise caution about instructions that could damage democratic life or illegitimately concentrate power. Below safety, it places being “broadly ethical”, and only then being “genuinely useful”. This represents an interesting shift in product logic: the system's integrity takes precedence over the user's immediate efficiency. AI is designed not merely to execute, but to exercise judgement. Translation note: these value labels reproduce the wording of the Spanish article in English; they are not presented as a separately verified, verbatim transcription of the Constitution. The limits of corporate constitutionalism Reading these texts also exposes the structural limitations of this approach. Although Claude's Constitution is a very significant intellectual advance, it retains a fundamental problem: it is an act of corporate sovereignty. There is a subtle risk in the language used. By speaking of “adolescence” and raising questions about AI's moral status, we may anthropomorphise the tool. Treating models as subjects that need to be “raised” can obscure the fact that, to a large extent, they are currently industrial products managed by private organisations. The critical political question is whether we are delegating public ethics. Amodei suggests that state intervention is needed, but in the meantime private documents define the standards for truth and harm. A constitution with no representative process behind it is, fundamentally, a good-practice manual or a self-regulation strategy in the absence of more robust public rules. A call to read the sources directly This brief analysis in estrategIA aims to offer perspective, but reading the primary sources is essential . Like Ethan Mollick , whom we have discussed many times in this newsletter , I encourage you to read the original texts. Examine Claude's Constitution to understand how AI ethics is being codified, and above all read Amodei's essay to grasp the industry's timelines and sense of urgency. Ethan Mollick's original English posts, visible in the preserved screenshot of 27 January 2026: Dario's new essay on the risks of AI seems less in dialogue with his earlier essay on how AI can help us all, but rather with the recently released Claude Constitution In that context, the Constitution feels much more like a plea to future Claude from Anthropic than instructions There seems to be a very clear view from Anthropic about where they think the world is going, far more carefully and fully articulated than any other lab. Really worth reading both of these documents, not just summarizing them: The first post shows 7:31 a.m., 39,000 views, 60 replies, 49 reposts, 483 likes and 125 bookmarks. The follow-up shows 5 replies, 17 reposts, 217 likes and 19,000 views. These are archived interface counts. We are at a defining moment. Technology has ceased to be a neutral tool and become a geopolitical and social force of the first order. The question is whether we, as a society, will have the maturity to guide this transition. The challenge is enormous, but so is the opportunity. If we can supply the institutional wisdom the machine lacks, this adolescence will not be a crisis, but the prelude to our greatest leap forward as a society. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of estrategIA. English reading of the original infographic, “Constitution and Adolescence”, by Fernando Nieto Lobato, January 2026: “AI policy enters its critical phase. An analysis of Dario Amodei's vision and Claude's new Constitution.” A change of phase. January 2026 marks an institutional turning point. The two texts signal the end of AI's infancy: the magical toys give way to real risks and political consequences. The image describes technology as a political actor with its own adolescence. Its timeline runs from October 2024 , infancy/utopia and Machines of Loving Grace , through January 2026 , the critical phase and institutional turn, to around 2027 , a “country of geniuses”: high systemic risk from enormous intellectual capacity without institutional wisdom. Strength versus wisdom. The biological metaphor contrasts exponentially growing technical capability and compute with slowly, linearly developing institutional wisdom—regulation and public ethics. This gap defines the adolescent crisis. A conceptual chart spans 2023–2027, with a rapidly rising red AI-capability line and a much slower dashed institutional-wisdom line. No numerical vertical scale or measured data series is supplied. A new hierarchy of values. Virtue ethics replaces prohibitions; immediate usefulness is subordinated to safety and democratic integrity. Safety comes first: corrigibility and subordination to human oversight. Ethics comes before usefulness: protecting the integrity of the democratic system. The pyramid places “Broadly safe” at its base as the absolute priority, then “Broadly ethical”, then “Genuinely useful”. The limits: corporate sovereignty. This is corporate, not democratic, sovereignty: definitions of truth and harm are outsourced to private entities. Treating AI as an adolescent needing to be raised can conceal its industrial nature. A conceptual radar chart contrasts the “Current state (2026)” with the “Necessary balance” across technical capacity, corporate sovereignty, public oversight and ethical maturity; it supplies no numerical scores. The political opportunity. The closing quotation repeats the article's argument: institutional wisdom could make this adolescence the prelude to society's greatest advance rather than a crisis. The footer reads “Read in estrategIA”.

ABC and precision literacy: an ecosystem where context and AI's technological capabilities are the keys to success Harvey Sánchez-Restrepo explains how ABC combines contextual understanding and adaptive AI assessment to support literacy across Latin America and the Caribbean. Harvey Sánchez-Restrepo Learning & Human Capability Government & Public Services 122 Analysis ABC and precision literacy: an ecosystem where context and AI's technological capabilities are the keys to success This issue's main article is by Harvey Sánchez-Restrepo. He describes a very specific educational use of AI and advances an idea for literacy that is as simple as it is disruptive: before measuring, understand the context. Harvey specialises in educational assessment, public policy and complex systems. He founded and was the first executive director of Ecuador's National Institute for Educational Evaluation, Ineval, and has helped establish assessment and admissions systems in several countries. He now heads the Latin American Agency for Evaluation and Public Policy (ALEPH) —its shared acronym with ALEPH Educational Institution is purely coincidental—and advises organisations including UNESCO's LLECE, the World Bank, the United Nations and the Inter-American Development Bank. Pablo Martín, estrategIA's editor and academic director of “our” ALEPH, met him in Mexico at the Third National Congress on Education, CONAED, “Artificial Intelligence: the Challenges of Education in Relation to the Human Condition”, organised by CONACAM, which we discussed in issue 114 . We invited him to explain this concrete application of AI in education, within a particularly interesting broader framework. In most countries, education faces complex challenges in making literacy more than an academic target with political impact. Literacy has become a bottleneck for social mobility and sustainable economic development. Ensuring that every child enjoys this right without discrimination requires assessing its exercise wherever education is provided. Traditional assessment methods, however, are slow both to implement and to deliver results. They also often lack the classroom context and student profiles needed to understand and adjust teaching strategies so that each learner can fulfil their potential. To address this longstanding challenge, the Latin American Agency for Evaluation and Public Policy, Aleph, developed ABC— Assessment Beyond the Classroom —for Latin America and the Caribbean. This ecosystem is designed to create an avatar of each student's literacy development through adaptive assessment processes. After years of refinement, it is redefining how learning is understood and evaluated, and how it can be strengthened and improved. At the heart of this large-scale project is the aim of turning the classroom into a learning environment in which teaching activities emerge from purposeful, guided interactions, rather than from systematically imposing uniform individual behaviours. “Families of assessment”: diagnostic assessment at the beginning of the school year helps design educational pathways; formative assessment gradually and continuously strengthens the educational process; summative assessment at the end of the year identifies educational achievements. The diagram connects these stages as pieces of a learning pathway under Assessment Beyond the Classroom (ABC). ABC therefore follows a disruptive workflow, not simply because it uses AI to improve the scope, accuracy and speed of assessing writing, reading fluency and comprehension. Above all, it seeks to understand the student as a dynamic, adaptable person in development. It recognises that knowledge, skills and attitudes arise from past, present and future exposure to a finite set of social, emotional and behavioural dimensions that constrain, inhibit or promote learning and its effective use in challenging environments. “Flexible architecture based on scientific assessment methods and agile technological development processes”, from the Latin American Agency for Evaluation and Public Policy. The four stages are instrument design, data collection, results analysis and dissemination. The connected components are assessment models and content; item development and validation; instrument management and assembly; an instrument bank; data management; logistics and territorial coverage; high-level executive information; psychometric analysis; an information dataset; educational research; statistical analysis; a geographic information system; official indicators; and institutional records. Understanding before assessing Unlike systems that measure only final performance, ABC centres its model on a vital diagnostic component: the Educational Landscape Map . One of the project's most innovative pillars, this contextual component comprises instruments that gather information before literacy assessment begins. They cover socioeconomic, territorial, cultural and cognitive factors, study habits, and family and school support for learning. This information underpins the intervention system, connecting directly to the assessment, interpretation and support of each student's development. By combining environmental data with academic performance, the management platform opens up a range of teaching strategies and learning activities designed by teachers themselves to draw on each student's identified potential and mitigate environmental obstacles to literacy. AI and adaptive testing: classroom efficiency Once the individual, family, school and contextual profile has been established, assessment focuses on functional literacy through five critical components: 1) reading speed, 2) reading accuracy, 3) prosody, 4) reading comprehension and 5) written communication. ABC's technological implementation addresses one of teachers' biggest headaches: time and administrative records. Through AI-driven adaptive tests, the system adjusts the difficulty of assessment items in real time in response to the student's answers. In just a few minutes, a teacher can obtain an accurate diagnosis that previously would have taken weeks of individual observation. In classrooms with more than 20 pupils, that speed can make the difference between intervening in time and allowing learning gaps to accumulate until the end of the school year. The preserved Saber+ administration dashboard illustrates operational monitoring. Its navigation covers Home, My Profile, Messages, Institutional Profile, Projects, Item Assignment, Item Bank, My Assignments, Assigned Items, Review Configuration, an abbreviated session-management entry, Item Review and My Review Sessions. Panels show login activity from 22 December 2025 to 21 January 2026, assessment starts from 7 May to 23 September 2025, and zero candidates currently being assessed out of a displayed total of 1,428. There are 63 administrator users, 14 active (22.2%), and 1,052 items, all approved (100.0%). These are archived interface values, not a current service report. | Process shown | Displayed status codes and counts | Total | | --- | --- | --- | | Nuevo León Aprende 2025 | 1: 3; 2: 1; 10: 477; C: 285405; G: 3438; P: 651 | 289975 | | ERCE 2025 | 2: 36034; C: 14469; P: 33 | 50536 | | Demo | FT: 1; P: 19 | 20 | | OCJ 2025 | C: 240; P: 3 | 243 | | NLE2025 rescheduling — open questions | F: 10; P: 2 | 12 | The screenshot does not expand the status codes. Its action buttons read “View candidates”, “View administrators” and “View item bank”. A project for Latin America and the Caribbean Since 2021, the tool has undergone rigorous expansion and calibration: first in 14 Mexican states, then in pilot countries, and now on a continental scale. This year it will incorporate data and parameters from 18 countries in the region. The project's three pillars are 1) extensive linguistic adaptability, 2) computational efficiency and 3) high scalability. Together, these allow AI algorithms and hierarchical sequences to be integrated with spatial data infrastructure in a large-scale geostatistical information system. It does more than record results: it offers a comprehensive platform for managing the education system, using tools that help establish teaching activities and learning rhythms suited to each student's needs and potential within a given context. Unlike platforms developed elsewhere, ABC originates in and draws on the region's realities. It combines accurate diagnosis of reading and writing skills with in-depth analysis of their precursors, current state and potential pathways in a particular environment, in order to assess and nurture each student's potential. As datasets are integrated, teachers can develop a family of personalised activities to use and consolidate what has been learnt. This is especially valuable in the most vulnerable communities, or those with limited family participation or support. Equity in addressing marginalisation The project's greatest social potential lies in schools in highly marginalised areas, where teachers often lack support tools to address learning gaps requiring individual attention and differentiated teaching. Although this opportunity is not recognised as such and therefore goes unused, it is precisely here that the link between the Educational Landscape Map and fluency results allows education authorities to identify classrooms or schools needing targeted, cross-sector strategies. For example, if an area has low prosody scores and high migration rates, groups are very likely to share sources of vulnerability. That is where public policy must stop being generic and become precisely targeted, in time to make a difference. “We design architectures”: data sources feed ETL—extract, transform, load—and an organisational database/data warehouse containing external and user data. Data mining supports analysis, reports, decision-making and information queries. Alongside this, the image states: “We intervene strategically” and “We are present at the most significant moments in every student's life.” Through its strengths and the speed with which it can be implemented, ABC represents a distinctive point on the path from traditional assessment to pedagogical intelligence. Because it is readily scalable and distributable, it is already beginning to show other Latin American education systems how to make evidence and technology driving forces in their management, rather than ornaments or a “necessary evil”. Understanding a pupil's context before measuring their learning enables timely, scientifically grounded and, above all, human-centred teaching. It reminds us that a person's literacy begins with a letter and is sustained by words shared in society—something that happens every day beyond the classroom walls. Harvey Sánchez-Restrepo Executive President of the Latin American Agency for Evaluation and Public Policy harvey@aleph.la

AI has crossed the 15% chasm, and the digital divide is widening: Microsoft's global report on AI diffusion in 2025 What Microsoft’s 2025 adoption report suggests about institutional strategy, the widening digital divide and the challenge of turning AI use into public value. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 121 Analysis AI has crossed the 15% chasm, and the digital divide is widening: Microsoft's global report on AI diffusion in 2025 Over the past two years, we have written a great deal in estrategIA about the technological promise of artificial intelligence. We have analysed models, regulations and fears. Yet we have often lacked a reasonably precise answer to one crucial question: how much is it actually being used? Not what companies say they do, or what opinion polls report, but what is really happening on millions of people's screens. Last week, the Microsoft AI Economy Institute published its report, Global AI Adoption in 2025—A Widening Digital Divide . In many respects, its findings are good news for those of us who believe in AI's transformative potential for public management and corporate strategy. Why does this source matter? Unlike studies based on self-reported surveys, in which respondents may exaggerate their knowledge, Microsoft used anonymised, aggregated telemetry. It measured “diffusion” by observing the proportion of the working-age population, aged 15–64, actively using generative AI tools for more than 90 minutes a month. It cleaned the data to address operating-system biases and scaled the results to include mobile use. We are probably looking at the most accurate behavioural map available to date. It tells us that global adoption has reached 16.3%. That may sound modest, but in the diffusion of technology, passing 15% means that AI crossed the chasm in 2025: it moved beyond a curiosity for early adopters into the early-majority phase. It did so, however, with enormous disparities between countries. Original world map of AI diffusion. Its AI-user-share bands are over 40%, 30–39%, 20–29%, 10–19% and below 10%; hatching indicates insufficient data. Highlighted countries are the UAE, 64%; Singapore, 60.9%; Norway, 46.4%; Ireland, 44.6%; and France, 44%. The report's original ranking compares the first and second halves of 2025. Its labels are already in English. The accessible table below transcribes all 30 countries, ordered by their second-half rank.
