The report confirms that adoption in the Global North is growing almost twice as fast as in the Global South. Advanced economies have already reached average penetration of 24.7% among their working population, while the South stands at 14.1%. Far from converging, the gap between the two blocs widened by almost a percentage point in just six months, from 9.8 to 10.6 points. This supports the argument that, for now, AI multiplies existing capabilities rather than automatically equalising them. Where robust digital infrastructure and skilled human capital already exist, adoption accelerates exponentially through these complementarities; where those foundations are missing, growth is steady but slower. As the following chart illustrates, we risk entrenching a technological divide in which enormous productivity gains become geographically concentrated, leaving much of the world structurally in the slow lane. AI diffusion: the Global South rises from 13.1% in H1 2025 to 14.1% in H2; the Global North rises from 22.9% to 24.7%. The gap widens from 9.8 to 10.6 percentage points. The good news: strategy matters more than technology For many countries, the report's most encouraging finding is that success in adopting AI does not depend on having Silicon Valley within their borders. Intuition might suggest that the United States, the undisputed leader in innovation and model development—R&D—should also lead adoption. The data show otherwise: it has fallen to 24th in per-capita use, at 28.3%. Who leads instead? Countries that have invested in governance, infrastructure and trust. The United Arab Emirates, at 64%, and Singapore, at 60.9%, top the list, followed by a group of highly digitalised European nations. Spain stands out with a strong 41.8%, ahead of major economies such as the United Kingdom, Germany and Canada. The optimistic lesson is clear: technological innovation is essential, but personal curiosity and institutional innovation are what bring use to scale. Small and medium-sized countries with clear national strategies, high digital literacy and trust in institutions are enabling their citizens to benefit from AI much faster than the superpowers creating the software. Ibero-America: three different speeds The figures for Ibero-American countries offer powerful indications of where talent and innovation are concentrating. The report depicts a region moving at three distinct speeds: 1. The adoption leaders. Spain consolidates its position as a global reference point, with 41.8% adoption, up more than two points in the last six months and ahead of G7 powers such as the United Kingdom and Germany. Alongside it, in Latin America, Costa Rica (26.5%) continues to post developed-country figures. But the big surprise is the Dominican Republic (22.7%) , third in the regional ranking, ahead of much larger economies and showing enviable digital dynamism in the Caribbean. 2. Emerging hubs and Argentina's awakening. A solid group has passed the psychological 20% threshold, a sign that AI has permeated productive activity. It includes Uruguay (22.5%) and Colombia (22.0%) , closely followed by Panama (21.5%) and Chile (20.8%) . Argentina deserves special mention. Despite its macroeconomic circumstances, it has recorded one of the region's biggest jumps, +1.8%, from 17.8% to 19.6% . This confirms that individual talent in Argentina is adopting productivity tools faster than its neighbours, already overtaking Mexico and Brazil. 3. The challenge facing the giants, and the access gap. The strategic concern is Mexico (17.8%) . It is growing, but more slowly, at +1.1%, than its regional competitors. For Latin America's second-largest economy, remaining below the regional average is a warning for future competitiveness. At the bottom of the table, Venezuela (9.0%) and Cuba (6.1%) show where the digital divide is sharpest. These markets, where affordability creates barriers to access, are precisely where the “open-source diplomacy” of free Chinese models such as DeepSeek could expand most strongly in 2026. While preparing this article, I read this interesting piece by Pep Martorell on the state of AI in Latin America . It examines the 2025 Latin American Artificial Intelligence Index , or ILIA, promoted by ECLAC and led by Chile's National Centre for AI . It is highly recommended and entirely complementary reading . Although many Latin American countries have impressive adoption rates, often above the global average, the region is in a deeply worrying position on other key measures, such as AI investment. With GPT-5.2's help, I generated the following table containing only Spanish-speaking countries, making them easier to find than in the four-page general table in the report . In just six months, it jumped from 25th to 18th, becoming the success story of the half-year. The strategic question now is this: how will we turn that 41% usage rate in Spain, or 26% in Costa Rica, into tangible gains in productivity and public services? CES 2026 confirms a new phase: AI as ‘electricity’ A historical assessment of CES 2026: universal AI access, Nvidia's physical AI infrastructure, on-device assistants, autonomous agriculture and preventive care. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 120 Analysis CES 2026 confirms a new phase: AI as ‘electricity’ Archive note: this article was published on 14 January 2026. Its forecasts and assessments of the technologies presented at CES are preserved as written at the time, without a new verification of those claims. Gary Shapiro's quoted phrase is retranslated from the Spanish source; the original English wording has not been verified. In estrategIA #17 , back in January 2024, we analysed how CES in Las Vegas — arguably the world's most important technology fair — brought promises of holograms and instant translation. The general public has seen far more progress in the latter, which is now almost solved, than in the former. Last year, we used these pages to observe the first steps of AI integrated into our mobile devices, a development that is still under way. This CES 2026 seems to have definitively closed the chapter of “digital curiosity”. With the lights switched off after the major Las Vegas conferences, the conclusion is unmistakable: artificial intelligence has ceased to be a software promise and become universal critical infrastructure . In 2026, AI has not only learnt physics; it is preparing to be in every citizen's hands. 1. The imperative of universal access: five billion users Before Jensen Huang spoke to us about robots, Lisa Su, AMD's chief executive, opened the fair with a figure that should be etched into every national strategic plan: AI will reach five billion users by 2030. The message from AMD and the CTA — the Consumer Technology Association, which organises the event — was forceful: AI has ceased to be a niche innovation and become a universally used technology, comparable to electricity or the internet. The political reading: we are no longer talking about regulating a technology sector, but about managing civilisation's basic infrastructure. Gary Shapiro, the CTA's president, described it as the architect of economic change. The impact: if AI is going to be in five billion pockets, governments face a challenge of staggering scale. The digital divide will no longer concern who has access to the internet, but who has access to the cognitive intelligence needed to operate in the economy. English alternative — Part 1: universal AI and its global impact, CES 2026. 2030 target: five billion users. Critical infrastructure — AMD and CTA: AI as electricity/the internet. From a software promise to a universal necessity. Political challenge — Gary Shapiro: managing the “architect of economic change”. A challenge of scale for governments. The new digital divide: access to cognitive intelligence to operate in the economy, not simply access to the internet. 2. Nvidia and the conquest of the physical world If AMD supplied the figures for social expansion, Nvidia supplied the engine of physical transformation. In his keynote, Jensen Huang demonstrated that AI has ceased to be merely a chat that writes text and become a force that understands and changes the real world. The Rubin platform and Vera CPU: infrastructure for agentic government. Nvidia presented its new “Vera” CPU, designed specifically for “agentic reasoning”. Unlike passive chatbots, these new chips allow AI to plan and carry out complex tasks. For public administration, this means the cost of running “digital civil servants” — agents that process case files 24/7 — plummets, making mass automation of bureaucracy viable. Project Cosmos — AI learns physics: perhaps the most fascinating development for urban planning. Cosmos is a model that predicts not words, but the next second of reality, respecting gravity and friction. It is the “Holy Grail” of digital twins: governments will be able to simulate the impact of a flood or a new underground line with perfect physical accuracy before spending a single euro on public works. Project GR00T — AI has a body: intelligence steps out of the screen. We saw humanoid robots learning to move through imitation and an understanding of their surroundings, rather than rigid programming. It is the real beginning of Industry 5.0, and of robots as social assistants in hospitals and homes. English alternative — CES 2026: Nvidia and the conquest of the physical world. Nvidia as the engine of physical transformation. AI understands and changes the real world, beyond chat. | Rubin platform and Vera CPU | Project Cosmos | Project GR00T | | --- | --- | --- | | Infrastructure for agentic government. | AI learns physics: the Holy Grail of digital twins. | AI has a body: the real beginning of Industry 5.0. | | Designed for agentic reasoning . Unlike passive chatbots, it plans and executes complex tasks. | A model that predicts the next second of reality , respecting gravity and friction. The illustration includes “F = ma” and “gravity”. | Intelligence steps out of the screen. Humanoid robots learn through imitation and understanding of their surroundings . | | Running costs plummet . | Before: predicts words. Now: predicts physical reality. | Robots as social assistants in hospitals and homes. | | Mass automation of bureaucracy becomes viable — digital civil servants working 24/7. | Perfect simulation before public works — floods, a new underground line. | Industry 5.0: human–robot collaboration. | | Infrastructure for public administration. | Urban management and planning. | Advanced robotics and assistance. | Although Nvidia set much of the pace, the fair brought other developments worth keeping on our radar because they offer clues to what is coming. We have selected these three: 1. A “pocket cloud” for state secrets. Intel and AMD demonstrated laptops capable of running complex models and agents completely disconnected from the internet . For senior levels of government administration, this makes AI assistants viable from a security perspective in secure environments: analysing sensitive documents, drafting and supporting decisions without data leaving the device. 2. Autonomous food sovereignty — John Deere / Kubota . In agriculture, what we saw were not “tractors”, but AI-coordinated systems managing complete cycles — sowing, irrigation, fertilisation and harvesting — with minimal human intervention. The strategic reading: food security becomes as dependent on compute, energy and maintenance as it is on labour. 3. Under the “Your Companion to AI Living” banner, Samsung strongly promoted the ideas of “Care Companion” and “Intelligent Care” . The aim is to move from reactive care — once a problem has already occurred — to preventive care supported by an ecosystem of mobiles, wearables and the connected home. In its CES material, Samsung describes cases such as early detection of cognitive decline through everyday signals — for example, speech, sleep or gait — and alerts to carers, alongside “AI home monitoring” that analyses video and audio from connected devices to identify potentially dangerous situations and send warnings. The implication for governments: the home is beginning to emerge as distributed welfare infrastructure — ageing, care and safety — with a non-negotiable requirement for explicit consent, data minimisation and traceability, to prevent “caring” from turning into surveillance. CES 2026 leaves us with two lessons that will define the coming decade. First, the lesson from AMD's opening address: AI will be universal, ubiquitous and available on a massive scale. Second, Nvidia's lesson: AI will be physical, tangible and operational. For public managers, the message is urgent: digitising administration is no longer enough. We must prepare cities, laws and social services for a world in which, sooner than we think, intelligence will not only be in the cloud, but walking along our streets and caring for people. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH and editor of estrategIA

Will politics rise to the challenge of AI in 2026? Five new requests from estrategIA A critical review of political responses to AI in 2025 and five demands for 2026: state capacity, scaled services, literacy, shared truth and a new social contract. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Work, Welfare & the Social Contract 119 Analysis Will politics rise to the challenge of AI in 2026? Five new requests from estrategIA Archive note: this article was published on 7 January 2026. Its assessments of 2025 and expectations for 2026 are preserved in their original historical context. The Demis Hassabis quotation below is retranslated from the Spanish in the source; its original English wording has not been verified. Exactly a year ago, in estrategIA #66 , we opened 2025 with a warning and five important requests to politicians for that year . We said then that artificial intelligence would cease to be a tool and become the engine of a revolution comparable to the Industrial Revolution — or even, as Nobel laureate Demis Hassabis said last year, “ten times bigger and ten times faster” . Our technical diagnosis was not wrong: 2025 was a year of significant acceleration, with the arrival of reasoning models such as the o3 family, GPT-5 and Gemini 3, and the consolidation of AI as critical infrastructure. Yet looking in the rear-view mirror leaves a bittersweet feeling. Technology has moved at Formula One speed, while politics — with honourable exceptions, particularly in defence and security — has continued travelling by horse-drawn carriage. Politicians , as has become customary, have responded to the urgency of power, not to the urgency of people's needs. We are entering 2026, a year that promises to be even more disruptive with the mass arrival of autonomous agents : systems that do more than chat; they act and execute tasks. It is time for an honest audit. What did politicians get right about AI in 2025? Where did they fail? And, most importantly, what should we demand of them in 2026? Auditing 2025: between the infrastructure of power and social neglect If we had to sum up the political response of 2025 in one sentence, it would be: “Concrete was prioritised; people were forgotten.” Many governments understood AI as a matter of geopolitical strength, investing heavily in data centres and energy — hard power — while neglecting internal transformation and social protection — soft power . Here is a quick assessment of the five requests we made a year ago. To produce it, we used several artificial intelligence systems with full access to all of estrategIA's content and the web, and asked them to analyse how far the requests we made in January 2025 had been met. 1. “Make AI a priority” The verdict: FULFILLED — but only at the geopolitical level. The reality: AI did indeed become an affair of state. We saw the US launch Project Stargate — $500 billion — and Europe announce its AI gigafactories after the Paris Summit . Leaders understood that “without compute, you cannot compete”. The “but”: it was a national security priority, rather than a public service priority. While billions were invested in chips, day-to-day administration continued without substantial changes, and political elites' training in these matters remains inadequate. 2. “Develop it safely, but quickly” The verdict: UNBALANCED — plenty of speed, fragmented safety. The reality: the balance tipped decisively towards competitive speed. Trump's second term and his deregulatory turn set the global direction, forcing Europe and China to accelerate to avoid being left behind. The “but”: safety was pushed into the background or fragmented into local initiatives, such as the California law. Ethics was overtaken by commercial and military urgency. 3. “Protect people, not jobs” The verdict: FAILURE — the first warning signs are being ignored. The reality: perhaps the most painful point. While Harvard and MIT were announcing that AI was already breaking the labour market for junior workers — “seniority-biased technological change” , governments made no structural moves. The “but”: there was no real progress on Universal Basic Income — UBI — except perhaps in Ireland , nor any substantial education reforms. The twentieth-century employment status quo was protected while AI began closing off younger generations' access to the future. In this area, we are still at the start of the process, but to think that this early stage will last a long time is to ignore entirely the distinctive characteristics of artificial intelligence as a technology. 4. “Be willing to break things — institutions” The verdict: PARALYSIS — AI washing instead of reform. The reality: apart from the military sphere, which began replacing Napoleonic structures with AI agents, bureaucracy was not reformed. There were isolated, brilliant cases, such as the Chilean initiative to protect victims of gender-based violence that we covered , but the general pattern was more pilots and anecdotes than real transformation. The “but”: instead of redesigning processes, many public administrations simply applied technological patches to inefficient bureaucracies. There is no real willingness to change in ways that make use of the new technology's potential. 5. “Plan for the future” The verdict: SHORT-SIGHTED — electoral short-termism. The reality: politics continued to live from day to day, using AI for the permanent campaign and the “electoral battle without rules”, instead of planning the new social contract and the necessary reforms. Governments continued governing for the next election, while we face a disruptive technology that will transform the world for the next generations. English alternative — Audit 2025: infrastructure of power versus social neglect. “Concrete was prioritised; people were forgotten.” AI as geopolitical strength — hard power: massive investment; Project Stargate, labelled “$500MM”; Europe: gigafactories. A national security priority rather than a public service priority. Neglect of internal transformation and social protection — soft power: lack of reforms in UBI and education. Ethics and social protection pushed aside by commercial and military urgency. The graphic prints “$500MM”; the article's body gives $500 billion. The graphic's notation is preserved here without silently resolving it. Assessment of five requests: Make AI a priority. Verdict: fulfilled, but only at the geopolitical level. Reality: AI as an affair of state; US Stargate — again labelled “$500MM” — and European gigafactories. “Without compute, you cannot compete.” The “but”: national security took priority; daily administration remained unchanged and elite training was inadequate. Safe but rapid development. Verdict: unbalanced — plenty of speed, fragmented safety. Reality: competitive speed prioritised, Trump's deregulatory turn and global acceleration. The “but”: safety and ethics were secondary or fragmented — California's law — and commercial and military urgency overtook ethics. Protect people, not jobs. Verdict: failure — the first warning signs are being ignored. Reality: AI disrupts the labour market for junior workers, Harvard/MIT, “seniority-biased technological change”. The “but”: no progress in Universal Basic Income except Ireland; education reforms absent; the twentieth-century employment status quo protected. Be willing to break things — institutions. Verdict: paralysis — AI washing instead of reform. Reality: bureaucracy unreformed outside the military; isolated brilliant cases — Chile and gender-based violence. The “but”: technological patches on inefficient bureaucracies; no real willingness to redesign processes with AI. The generated panel repeats its reality statement and inserts an awkward second verdict: “Disruptive technology ignoring — first warning signs”. This duplicate, malformed wording is present in the original graphic. Plan for the future. Verdict: short-sighted — electoral short-termism. Reality: day-to-day politics, using AI for permanent campaigning and electoral simulation. The “but”: governing for the next election without planning a new social contract in the face of disruptive technology. Conclusion: disruptive technology is transforming the world, but the political response remains anchored in the past, prioritising power over people. 2026: five new requests for the approaching agentic era The context in 2026 is radically different. We are no longer talking only about generating text or images. We are talking about agents that book flights, negotiate contracts, write code and operate machinery beginning to become widespread. The European regulation — the AI Act — enters its full operational phase, and AI's ability to act in the physical world is beginning to become real. We are therefore updating our requests. Prioritisation is no longer enough: we now ask for capacity, execution and humanity . 1. Build real state capacity — beyond regulation In 2025, we saw that passing a law such as the AI Act is of little use if there is nobody to implement it. Our request for 2026 is to move from paper to muscle, and for governments to start applying and promoting AI to improve citizens' lives. The proposal: we do not want more expert committees writing white papers. We need delivery units working across government, equipped with budgets and real technical talent, capable of procuring technology, approving algorithms and, above all, auditing what is happening inside the administration's black box. The objective: for the state to stop being a captive customer of the big technology companies and regain the technical sovereignty to understand and direct what it buys, and to drive structural change. 2. From pilots to services: automation with public metrics The time for pilot projects that die in a press release is over. Public administration is full of proofs of concept that never scale, while models are already reaching levels of quality that make it possible to improve many processes and services. The proposal: we believe a short portfolio of 10–15 high-impact use cases is needed — for example, processing benefits, healthcare waiting lists, tax fraud and justice — to be implemented nationally in 2026. The key: they must be accompanied by public accountability metrics. If AI reduces the wait for a court ruling or a benefit payment, citizens should know by how much and how. Efficiency must become a new democratic dividend. 3. Declare AI literacy a national emergency — and a right If AI is the new electricity, AI illiteracy is the new social exclusion. In 2026, knowing how to interact with intelligent agents will not be an advantage on a CV, but a requirement for citizenship and employability. The proposal: launch a National AI Literacy Plan , compulsory for all public employees and offered at scale to the public. We are not talking about traditional courses, but training in critical thinking, agent supervision and human–machine collaboration. The key: inequality in 2026 will be measured not only by income, but by the degree to which individuals can amplify their abilities through AI. The state must ensure that access to this superintelligence is universal, rather than an elite privilege. Failing to do this work will only widen the gap between AI (super)users and people excluded from the technology. 4. Protect shared truth: an infrastructure of trust The year 2025 taught us the danger of the “liar's dividend” and the erosion of reality. In a year when voices and images can be forged in real time, democracy is at risk if we cannot tell what is real. The proposal: move from cybersecurity to epistemic security . We demand that all official communication — video, audio and text — be required to incorporate verifiable content credentials. The state cannot ask for blind trust: its channels must offer mathematical certainty about provenance, so that any citizen can distinguish an official source from manipulation without doubt. The defence: we need rapid-response protocols for crises of deep disinformation, treating information integrity as critical infrastructure on the same level as the electricity grid or water supply. 5. Engineering the new social contract — taxation and income We insist on this again, but with greater urgency. The 2025 crisis in junior employment suggested by several significant studies was only a warning. If AI increases productivity and corporate profits soar while the wage bill shrinks, the welfare state's fiscal equation breaks down. In the coming years, we will see major changes that may also happen very quickly. The proposal: stop viewing Universal Basic Income or AI dividends as utopias of the left or the right. Start designing the fiscal engineering needed to sustain them, and begin working, at least, with pilot programmes such as Ireland's. The measure: seriously study future taxes on computation — tax the compute — or on automation that leads to a net loss of jobs, to finance a possible citizens' transition fund. In Spain, we currently have an intense debate about pensions and intergenerational solidarity. Incredible as it may seem, the automation of jobs that is very likely to occur on a massive scale over the next ten years is not being brought into that debate. This is a form of short-sightedness we cannot afford. Conclusion: from the infrastructure of power to social infrastructure After last year's poor performance on these tasks, our message to our representatives for 2026 is clear: in 2025, some countries succeeded in building or planning the infrastructure of power — data centres, models and national security. Now, in 2026, active planning and construction of social infrastructure must begin. If we allow the gap between the speed of AI agents and the slowness of the social response to keep widening, we will face more than a problem of unemployment or bureaucracy: we will face a crisis of legitimacy in the democratic system. The technological developments of 2025 continue to suggest that AI is very likely to change everything, even though we are still at the beginning of the transition from technical capabilities to the “real world”. The question for 2026 is not whether the technology will be ready — it will — but whether politics will rise to the challenge of making that change liveable for the majority in the future. English alternative — 2026: five new requests for the approaching agentic era. 1. Build real state capacity — beyond regulation. From paper to muscle: apply and promote AI to improve lives. No more expert committees. Yes to delivery units working across government, with budgets and technical talent. Procure technology, approve algorithms and audit the “black box”. Regain technical sovereignty: stop being a captive customer and understand what is being bought. 2. From pilots to services: automation with public metrics. Scale real solutions with accountability. A short portfolio of 10–15 high-impact use cases — benefits, health, fraud and justice — at national scale in 2026. Mandatory public metrics. If AI reduces waiting times, citizens must know by how much and how. Efficiency as a new democratic dividend. 3. Declare AI literacy a national emergency — and a right. AI illiteracy is the new social exclusion. A National AI Literacy Plan, compulsory for public employees and offered at scale to the public. Training in critical thinking, agent supervision and human–machine collaboration. Ensure universal access to superintelligence; avoid a gap in individuals' ability to amplify their capabilities. 4. Protect shared truth: an infrastructure of trust. Epistemic security against the “liar's dividend”. All official communication — video, audio and text — to carry verifiable content credentials and mathematical certainty about provenance. Information integrity as critical infrastructure, on the same level as the electricity grid. Rapid-response protocols for deep disinformation. 5. Engineering the new social contract — taxation and income. Urgently design for sustainability in the face of automation. Stop treating Universal Basic Income as a utopia. Design the fiscal engineering and begin with pilots. Study taxes on computation — tax the compute — or automation, to finance a citizens' transition fund. Bring mass automation into the debate about pensions and intergenerational solidarity. Conclusion: from the infrastructure of power to social infrastructure. In 2025, the infrastructure of power was built — data centres and security. In 2026, social infrastructure must be planned and built. If the gap between AI's speed and the social response widens, we face a crisis of democratic legitimacy . The question is no longer whether the technology will be ready, but whether politics will rise to the challenge of making the change liveable for the majority. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH and editor of estrategIA

In the centre is a “chat” where you can ask questions of all that information, and in the right-hand column are all the audiovisual material, reports and interactive items created from the content. That section is closed here, but in your own NotebookLM notebooks you can request as many as you wish. This image, created with Nano Banana Pro from our own screenshot of the NotebookLM notebook, should make it easier to visualise: English alternative to the instructional overlay: “Project name” points to the title at the top. 1. Sources — your documents: upload PDFs, websites and so on here for the AI to analyse. 2. Chat — your AI assistant: ask questions, request summaries or generate content based on your sources. 3. Notes — your workspace: save answers, create outlines and organise your ideas here. The underlying small interface text is a distorted duplicate of the earlier screenshot, not additional instructions. After importing the content, we began working with it in the chat, using prompts that ChatGPT and Gemini helped us make more precise. We asked NotebookLM to produce a summary document for each subject covered in estrategIA this year, based on the main article; a summary of all the news published in 2025; and, finally, one covering the recommended tools. These requests, like some later ones, were then saved as notes and also exported as sources, so that we could subsequently create multimedia content from some of them. With this information in place, we asked for more evaluative work: an article summarising the year overall, also available in the documents section, or a selection of the ten most significant stories of 2025. We later asked it to turn that document into the infographic shown above. Using either the full set of documents or an individual one, we then requested — as you can see in the third column — infographics, “PowerPoint-style” slide presentations, audio summaries, video summaries and a data table . The latter is one of the features added to NotebookLM in recent weeks; as an example, it created an index-style table of all the issues. There is also an interesting quiz , which we recommend if you regularly read estrategIA, because it will remind you of many things you have learnt by reading this newsletter during 2025. It is also worth highlighting that, for the past few days, Gemini has allowed NotebookLM to be imported as a source. That means we can work with all this structured information using more powerful AI models such as Gemini 3 Pro, which also have access to other tools, including internet search and code generation. The import process is almost the same as importing an image: simply click “+”, select NotebookLM, and then choose the notebook you want to import. This has allowed us to work with the entire year's estrategIA content in that notebook, generate a summary article from it and, from that article, create as an example a very simple HTML infographic . Your brother-in-law, the prawns and AI: a Christmas survival guide for estrategIA readers A humorous Christmas guide to five familiar arguments about AI, from bubbles and jobs to energy use and disinformation, with a political and governance perspective. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Work, Welfare & the Social Contract AI in Practice 116 Analysis Your brother-in-law, the prawns and AI: a Christmas survival guide for estrategIA readers Archive note: this article was published on 17 December 2025. Its references to “this year”, current models and the coming Christmas belong to that date. The imagined dialogue below is translated from the Spanish original. Dear readers, as you know, we usually analyse AI through the lens of institutions and governance. But today, since the approaching Christmas is a “battle” fought on personal ground, we are taking the liberty of addressing you more informally and offering this article in a more humorous vein, while still bringing what we believe are valuable reflections. Because once the debate erupts around the dinner table, protocols go out of the window. The scene is inevitable. It will happen somewhere between the plate of prawns and the tray of turrón , the traditional Christmas nougat. Perhaps on Christmas Eve, perhaps on New Year's Eve, or they may wait until the Epiphany lunch on 6 January. Someone, probably your brother-in-law — the one who was an expert on volcanoes a few years ago and on Eastern European geopolitics a few years later — will clear his throat, point a prawn's head at you and say: “Hey, you know about computers and read that ‘estrategia’ newsletter... Isn't all this artificial intelligence stuff a bubble? Because I read on Facebook that ChatGPT can't even add up any more, and they were saying it was going to put us all out of work.” At that moment, dear subscriber, every eye at the table will turn to you. You are the “designated expert”. Silicon Valley's oracle at the family gathering. And you have two options: pretend to choke on a polvorón , one of those crumbly Christmas biscuits, or bring out this manual. At estrategIA , we have spent the whole year analysing how AI is transforming public affairs and politics. That is why we have prepared this Christmas Survival Guide. The aim is not just to help you win the argument — though that too — but to use the conversation after dinner to move beyond alarmist headlines and towards what really matters: governance and our society's future. Here are the greatest hits of Christmas controversy and how to answer them with rigour, irony and political insight: ROUND 1: “This is a bubble. In two years nobody will be talking about it, just like the Metaverse.” The quick reply (to silence the table while you pour the drinks): “The Metaverse was a party nobody went to. AI is the electricity already lighting up the party. Share prices may fall, but the technology is here to stay.” The underlying argument: We need to distinguish between the financial bubble and the technological reality. Yes, there is plenty of hype and inflated stock-market valuations for companies promising miracles. But unlike cryptocurrencies or the Metaverse, AI has immediate, widespread practical uses. It is already being used to summarise court files, detect tax fraud, optimise the electricity grid and speed up medical diagnoses. AI is not a “fad”; it is infrastructure. In the future, we will stop talking about “artificial intelligence”, just as we do not talk about “electrical intelligence” when we switch on a light. It will simply be in everything. ROUND 2: “AI is going to take all our jobs — and yours first.” The quick reply: “It is very likely to replace many jobs, yes. But think about it: the vast majority of retired people don't work and live happily. The problem isn't machines working for us; it is how we distribute the wealth they generate.” The underlying argument (the bold position): This is where, as an estrategIA reader, you should give the conversation a political turn. Forget the sugar-coated line that “AI will only be your copilot”. Let us be honest: AI is going to replace tasks and, as time passes — quite quickly, though — entire jobs. And that does not have to be bad news . Historically, we have tied human dignity to paid employment. AI forces us to rethink that link. If we achieve a technology capable of producing abundance with less human effort, the goal should not be to “invent pointless jobs” to keep us busy. It should be to ensure that governments create the conditions for a decent life during that transition, and that people freed from the yoke of having to work — sadly, often doing things they dislike or did not train for — can unleash their creativity and potential by doing other things. The real debate is not technological — “can a robot do this?” — but political and fiscal : how do we design new mechanisms of social protection? Are we talking about Universal Basic Income? Taxes on automation? AI should free us from compulsory work — many people will voluntarily want to keep working, and a proportion of jobs will still be done by humans for many years — rather than impoverish us. That is the real challenge facing governments over the next ten years, and examples such as Ireland show us that pilot programmes like its basic income scheme for artists, which it decided to extend this year, can have very positive consequences . ROUND 3: “ChatGPT talks a lot of nonsense. My son asked it something complicated and it made everything up.” The quick reply: “Your son probably used the free version and talked to it as though it were Google. Rookie mistake. You need to know how to ask these systems for things: if you use an old model and give it vague instructions, it returns generalities. But if you use a ‘frontier model’ and know how to ask, it doesn't give you nonsense; it gives you something close to a doctoral thesis.” The underlying argument (the ‘fault’ lies with the driver, not the car): Here we need to explain how this technology really works. First, the tool matters . The free chat app on your phone — usually a smaller, older model — is not the same as today's frontier models, especially with their reasoning switched on . The difference in reasoning ability is like comparing a primary-school pupil with a university professor. Second, and more importantly: context is king . At estrategIA , we see it every day: most “hallucinations” or mediocre answers are the result of a poor prompt — the instruction — and can be improved by asking better questions, or even by asking artificial intelligence systems to help us frame our needs more clearly. ROUND 4: “It uses so much electricity and water. AI is going to wreck the planet.” The quick reply: “It is true that it consumes resources, although much less than some people have claimed. But demonising a tool that can help us solve climate change by giving scientific progress a major boost is like blaming an ambulance for using petrol on its way to save an injured person.” The underlying argument: Do not deny the data: training massive models consumes energy and water. It is a real physical challenge, although models' actual consumption during inference is considerably lower than people were saying until a few months ago, and their efficiency improves every day. A Google analysis in August 2025 measured a typical Gemini text prompt as using just 0.26 ml of water — five drops — compared with earlier estimates of 10–50 ml, and less energy than nine seconds of television . But weigh that in the balance. Today, the big technology companies are the world's largest investors in renewable energy and, take note, in nuclear fusion . The paradox is that we need AI to save the planet. AI is designing new battery materials that do not depend on mines in conflict zones, optimising electricity grids to prevent renewable energy from being wasted, and modelling fusion reactors. AI's energy cost is an investment — an expensive one, yes — in reducing the energy cost of everything else. It is the price of admission to a genuinely green future, rather than one that exists only on a placard. ROUND 5: “You can't believe anything any more. With deepfakes, democracy is doomed.” The quick reply: “Hoaxes have always existed; now they just come in higher resolution. The danger isn't the machine; it is that we keep sharing anything that reaches us on WhatsApp without thinking.” The underlying argument: We have addressed this topic many times in estrategIA . Yes, industrialised disinformation poses an enormous risk to elections — and we have covered it repeatedly in this newsletter; pay particular attention to the ‘liar's dividend’ . We will see fake videos of politicians saying outrageous things. But defensive technology — watermarks, content traceability — is advancing too. The crucial point, however, is educating citizens. We are at a historical moment that demands a new kind of “media literacy”. Just as we learnt to look both ways before crossing the road, we now need to learn to navigate the internet wearing a cognitive “bulletproof vest”. The problem with deepfakes is not technical but psychological: they work because they confirm our biases, because we like believing that lie about the politician we dislike. AI forces us to mature as a society. Saying “I saw it in a video” is no longer enough, because seeing is no longer believing. This pushes us to recover critical thinking: cross-checking sources, tracing information back to its origin, and distrusting anything that provokes an immediate emotional reaction. If we can educate citizens in this healthy scepticism, democracy will not merely survive; it will become stronger. A society that thinks and checks before sharing is much harder to manipulate, with or without AI. The final toast (your conclusion) If, after all that explaining, they are still looking at you sceptically, do not insist. There is a limit to the educational battle, and the polvorones are bringing a diabetic coma ever closer. Once you have dismantled these horsemen of the technological apocalypse and your family is looking at you with a mixture of astonishment and information overload, pour a little more cava and offer a conciliatory conclusion. Tell them that artificial intelligence is neither magic nor Skynet. It is one of the most sophisticated mirrors humanity has built. It reflects our biases and fears, yes, but also our immense ability to solve problems. The future is not written. AI will bring massive disruption, winners and losers. But if there is one thing we argue at estrategIA , it is that the eventual outcome does not depend on the algorithm, but on politics, ethics and the decisions we ourselves make. And if they want to understand how those decisions will affect their pension, their vote or their business, tell them there is a very simple solution: “Subscribe to estrategIA . They explain it all throughout the year, so next Christmas, instead of arguing, we can raise a glass to how much we have all learnt.” Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH and editor of estrategIA Infographic based on this week's article, made with Nano Banana Pro: English alternative to the Spanish infographic: #116: Christmas survival manual — your brother-in-law, the prawns and AI. How to raise the level of debate at Christmas dinner: from alarmist headlines to governance. The two characters are labelled “The sceptical brother-in-law” and “You, the reluctant oracle”. The columns are “The attack: what your brother-in-law says” and “The strategic defence: the political/technical reality”. | Round | The attack | The strategic defence | | --- | --- | --- | | 1: The new bubble? | “It's all hot air. In two years nobody will be talking about it, just like the Metaverse.” | The Metaverse was an empty party. AI is the new electricity : infrastructure that already works — diagnoses, fraud, electricity grid. It is useful, not fashionable. | | 2: The end of work | “It will put us all out of work — and you first.” | The challenge is political and fiscal , rather than technological. A debate about distribution: Universal Basic Income? Taxes on robots? Liberation, not impoverishment. | | 3: “My son says it doesn't work” | “I asked it something difficult and it made everything up. It talks a lot of nonsense.” | Driver error. A free chat is not the same as a current frontier model. The key is context and knowing how to ask — the prompt. | | 4: The ecological apocalypse | “It uses enormous amounts of electricity and water. It will wreck the planet.” | It is an investment. We need it to solve climate change : designing fusion, new materials and optimising renewable-energy grids. | | 5: The death of truth — deepfakes | “You can't believe anything any more. With fake videos, democracy is doomed.” | The danger is not the machine but our bias when we share. The solution: new media literacy . Critical thinking and verification. | The final toast — a conciliatory conclusion: AI is neither magic nor Skynet: it is a sophisticated mirror of humanity. The future depends on politics and ethics, rather than the algorithm. “Want to understand how this will affect your pension or your vote? Subscribe to the pioneering newsletter on AI and politics: estrategIA.”

Instant visual communication: Nano Banana Pro examples for campaigns and public administrations Ten historical image-generation demonstrations, with full prompts, retained examples and the author's warning to verify generated data. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Government & Public Services Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 115 Practical experiment Instant visual communication: Nano Banana Pro examples for campaigns and public administrations Archive note: these prompts and generated examples are preserved from 10 December 2025. Product quotas, dates, prices, administrative instructions and statistics are historical content. The images are demonstrations, not official notices or independently verified guidance; the author explicitly discusses the need to check their data below. Spanish quotations and image text are translated, while Freddy Vega's visible English prompts are reproduced as written. Although Nano Banana Pro has been on the market for only a few weeks, it has completely transformed image generation, particularly images that combine visuals and text. For that reason, as we announced a few issues ago, we have decided to devote this edition to examples of what Google's model can do, and to encourage you to try it . Even Gemini's free version gives you two generations a day. It is also available free in NotebookLM, although with substantial usage limits because Google is struggling to meet the worldwide demand for such an interesting model. We have previously devoted issues to practical examples of the most advanced image models of the time, showing how to use them in politics, government and public administration: issue 80 on GPT-4o and issue 101 on the previous Nano Banana . We believe these issues are important for setting your imagination in motion and encouraging you to interact with these technologies to get the most from them. We particularly liked a comment left on Substack a few days ago by Carlos Guadián , author of the interesting CluPad newsletter and a guest contributor to estrategIA issue 60 . We agree with him completely , which is another reason for issues like this one. Carlos Guadián's comment, dated 26 November, translated from Spanish: I think examples are crucial, above all for getting the most from particular features. Some are very intuitive, and you quickly see the value they promise. Others remain shut away in the cupboard until someone shows you, through an “example”, what you can do with something you had overlooked. Before showing you ten examples created with Nano Banana Pro, we want to highlight that its main advantage is that it has solved text almost completely . We still occasionally find a misspelt word, but that is now the exception rather than the rule. Using Gemini 3 Pro, it also finds information much more effectively and better understands our prompts. Although we focus here on infographic-style examples, it also offers tremendous photographic quality, generating highly realistic images and editing them extremely well — something the previous version already did. The principal drawback we have found is significant censorship of public figures. It is much harder to get it to generate well-known politicians or public personalities using “normal” prompts, unlike open-source models such as Z-Image. Bear in mind, however, that even if you work on personal-image material, most candidates or officeholders you work with will almost certainly not be celebrities. They will therefore not encounter this censorship problem, and you can create images of them as you would of any anonymous citizen. We will say no more by way of introduction: this is already going to be a long article because of its many images, rather than its text. In fact, we had quite a few more examples and reduced the selection to avoid making it excessively long. We have also left out NotebookLM's dedicated infographic and presentation generation: everything here was generated in Gemini. We will undoubtedly devote a special issue to NotebookLM, one of the best tools available today. We hope these ideas inspire other potential uses , adapted to your own needs. 1. Quickly generate emergency posters Act as a designer of government emergency communications. Generate an information card in a 4:5 format. Layout anchors: a large, legible title centred at the top reading “WEATHER ALERT”. A dark-background area at the bottom for secondary text. Image: a clean isometric view of a city under heavy but stylised snow, in warning colours — orange and grey. Text: render “AVOID TRAVEL” in white Helvetica Bold in the centre. Style: minimalist 3D infographic, highly legible. Complete poster text, translated: “WEATHER ALERT. AVOID TRAVEL. Temporary road closures. Extreme caution. Stay informed.” 2. Communicate a new policy's benefits to citizens Create a clear, professional infographic explaining the public policy “[Construction of new social-rental housing in Salamanca]”. Include: Main objective. Who is affected. Expected benefits. Implementation timetable. Three key figures. Use an institutional style and clear language for the general public. Restrained colours, simple icons, modern, legible typography. Vertical format, 1080 × 1920. It searches for information... Visible search-result titles, translated: Salamanca will offer 48 social-rental homes with storage and parking for 2025. In 2025 Salamanca will make a new building with 48 rental homes available to older people or people with reduced mobility — EntreMayores. Applications open next week for one of 55 new subsidised rental homes in Pizarrales — Noticias de Salamanca. The screenshot shows source-link icons but does not expose the destinations; full URLs are not reconstructed. ...and this poster is the result: Complete substantive text in the generated poster, translated: Public policy: construction of new social-rental housing in Salamanca. The header displays Ayuntamiento de Salamanca, Junta de Castilla y León, and “Funded by the European Union — NextGenerationEU”. Main objective: increase the stock of affordable public housing to improve access for vulnerable groups and young people, while modernising neighbourhoods. Who is affected: families on limited incomes; young people under 36; older people or people with reduced mobility. Requirements: municipal registration, not owning a home, income limits and registration in the Public Register of Applicants. Three key figures: more than €135 million in cumulative investment by the Housing Board since 1988; 103 new homes with recent European funding; approximately €250–300 in estimated monthly rent for recent developments. Expected benefits: easier access to housing; support for young people to live independently; stimulus for construction and local employment; energy efficiency and urban modernisation. Implementation timetable — recent and future milestones: October 2025, applications for 55 homes in Pizarrales; 2025, delivery of 48 homes in Capuchinos; 2026, start of 33 homes on Calle Túnel de la Televisión. Further information printed: www.aytosalamanca.es; Patronato Municipal de Vivienda y Urbanismo. 3. Visualise a city's future through planned developments We found this prompt shared on X by Freddy Vega , co-founder of Platzi, particularly interesting. It first uses Gemini 3 Pro's capabilities for in-depth research, then offers a visual study that helps us imagine a city's urban future. Original English prompts visible in Freddy Vega's post: (Gemini 3) Research all the actual urban, architectural and city development projects currently in course or planned for [CITY] that will transform the city from now to 2050. Be specific about them. (Nano Banana Pro) Research how these projects look and create a photography of how [CITY] would look according to that description in 2050, understanding that the new is build upon the old and most of the city will keep its original look of today, on top of the new projects. Add a text to the top center of the picture showing "[CITY] 2050" in a style fitting [CITY]. The photo should be realistic, slightly futuristic and taken at street level. The accompanying illustrations are labelled “BOGOTA 2050”, “CDMX 2050” and “Miami 2050”. They are generated future scenarios. We used the same prompts and process for Madrid. It carried out a long, interesting investigation of all the urban projects already planned and their characteristics. These were the final images it proposed: Both generated visualisations are titled “Madrid 2050”; they illustrate imagined futures rather than completed developments. 4. Generate an infographic showing the main changes introduced by a new law Design an infographic entitled “The essentials of [LAW TITLE]”. Summarise in blocks: What changes. What remains the same. Who benefits. When it takes effect. Where to find information. Educational style, light background, line icons and a clean composition. Complete substantive text in the generated example, translated: The essentials of the European Accessibility Act — EAA What changes? Universal accessibility: key products and services — ATMs, e-commerce, transport, banking and others — accessible to everyone. New technical requirements: common, harmonised EU standards. More demanding requirements: accessibility from the design stage. What remains the same? Exceptions: it does not affect older buildings, some microenterprises or non-essential products. Scope: the European Union market. Who benefits? People with disabilities: greater autonomy and full participation. Older people: better access to services and technology. Businesses: new opportunities and innovation. When does it take effect? Key date: most provisions on 28 June 2025. Transition: an adjustment period for certain products. Where to find information? European Commission: official website and resources. National bodies: responsible ministries and agencies. Organisations of people with disabilities: advice and information. Additional resources: Directive (EU) 2019/882 and the European Commission's EAA website. 5. Create an infographic about an administrative procedure Generate an informative infographic explaining how to complete “[PROCEDURE]”. Include numbered steps: book an appointment, attend the office, required documents, fees and validity. Add common warnings: do not attend without a photograph, expiry, and age-based exceptions. Include a final “Useful tips” block. Modern administrative style: accessible and clear. For example, we created an infographic on renewing Spain's national identity card. Complete generated image text, translated. These instructions are preserved as an illustrative output, not verified administrative guidance. DNI renewal guide: procedures and tips Book an appointment. An appointment is compulsory: website www.citapreviadnie.es or telephone 060. Do this in advance. Attend the office. Arrive punctually at the assigned issuing office. Bring all the documentation. Required documents. Previous DNI, or a police report if it was lost or stolen; one recent colour photograph; municipal registration certificate if your address changed; fee, if not paid online. Fees and validity. Pay the fee at the office, using the exact cash amount or a card. Validity: five years under 30; ten years from 30 to 70; permanent over 70. Common warnings: a recent photograph is essential — do not attend without it. Avoid fines and renew before expiry, up to 180 days beforehand. Fingerprint exemption for older people with justified physical difficulties. People over 70 automatically receive a permanent DNI. Useful tips: request an appointment several months ahead, especially for summer or Christmas. If paying cash, try to bring the exact amount. Fingerprinting is compulsory except for medical exemptions. If the card was lost or stolen, a prior police report is compulsory. We also made this infographic on municipal residence registration at Salamanca City Council, adding instructions to make it clear and use large lettering for older people. This is important: here we suggest uses and prompts that we think work satisfactorily, but it is very easy to adapt the request to your particular needs. Experimenting and iterating is the best way to learn how to benefit from these technologies. Complete substantive text in the generated image, translated: Municipal residence registration guide — Salamanca City Council. Registering in Salamanca: simple procedures. Required documents. DNI, NIE or passport, original and copy. Signed municipal registration form. Proof of accommodation: title deed, tenancy with the latest receipt, or the holder's authorisation. Submit in person or online. In person: request an appointment through the citizen-service office, OAC, or 010, and bring the documents. Online: use the electronic office with a digital certificate or Cl@ve and upload the documents. Processing time. In person: immediately, if everything is correct. Online: maximum three months, usually faster. Common warnings: tenancy — a current contract in the applicant's name or the holder's authorisation. Authorisation — essential if you live with someone else, signed and accompanied by a copy of the holder's DNI. Useful tips: check the DNI's expiry date. In person: arrive on time. Online: ensure documents are legible. Consult the council website for forms. 6. AI's impact on education: a rebirth or the end of the teacher? Pablo Martín Diez reflects on CONAED Mexico 2025, educational divides and the teacher's role in cultivating curiosity, judgement and civic independence. Pablo Martín Diez Learning & Human Capability Government & Public Services 114 Analysis AI's impact on education: a rebirth or the end of the teacher? Reflections from CONAED Mexico 2025 Another profession on the therapist's couch. AI is having a powerful impact across many sectors, but education may be among those whose nineteenth-century foundations have shaken fastest under the challenge of large language models. These models call into question factors that have defined education for a very long time. A World Bank report indicates that 65% of teachers see AI as an opportunity, but an overwhelming 80% admit that their institutions lack clear guidelines on its use . Meanwhile, 65% of university students believe they know more about AI than their teachers, according to a Cengage Group study . These figures understandably leave teachers feeling unsteady, and may lead to a crisis of pedagogical legitimacy : how can we get students to listen to and trust their teacher, while developing critical judgement and retaining their creativity and ability to work independently, without surrendering much of their cognitive capacity to AI's benefits? No country is immune to this upheaval in education and, especially, in the teacher's role. Many institutions are examining how education should evolve in response. Jorge Santiago, President of Institución Educativa ALEPH, and I had the opportunity to travel to Mexico and contribute to this discussion at the Third National Congress on Education, CONAED , entitled “Artificial intelligence: education's challenges in relation to the human condition” and organised by the Consejo Nacional de Centros de Actualización del Magisterio, CONACAM , the national council of teacher development centres. Conference photographs from the original article. Background slide and banner text is partly cropped or indistinct; those fragments are not reconstructed. Through contributions from speakers such as Harvey Spencer, CEO of the Latin American Agency for Evaluation and Public Policy, and workshops on AI in classrooms, the congress addressed key questions about education's necessary transformation. English translation of the board, “Generative AI in education: keys to transformation”: Bridging divides: infrastructure, investment and skills. Global solutions: China, mass personalisation; Singapore, technological equity; Finland, ethics and understanding. Evolving roles: the teacher as an irreplaceable role model. From nineteenth-century teaching to the algorithmic era: curiosity and the Socratic method. Tools: Google NotebookLM, Khanmigo and Gamma. 1. Bridging the divides Integrating AI brings challenges that go beyond plagiarism — although the “crisis of authorship” is real and forces us to rethink what assessment means. We could list many challenges, but perhaps the most essential are these: The infrastructure divide: there is little point discussing AI tools in teaching or major automation projects if an area lacks an adequate internet connection or the electricity to power data centres, or even ordinary computers. The investment divide: educational institutions must invest in subscriptions to AI applications for both teachers and students. Free tools are not enough if we aspire to intensive, professional use. The skills divide: teaching quality will be significantly affected as AI evolves, creating a substantial difference between teachers who know how to make use of AI and those who do not. 2. Pay attention to other countries’ solutions Every country has its own characteristics, but learning about and sharing international experiences can help improve education at home. China: the New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan aims to make China the world's leading AI power by 2030 and to integrate AI throughout the education system. Beijing has embraced mass personalisation through systems such as Squirrel AI , which breaks knowledge down into thousands of points and precisely diagnoses gaps in a student's understanding, achieving substantial improvements in learning. Singapore: its national Student Learning Space platform integrates government-validated AI tools, ensuring that every child has access to the same quality of technology, regardless of their school. Finland: true to their humanist approach, the Finns are concerned with understanding rather than obsessed with efficiency. Their Elements of AI course seeks to help the whole population understand what AI is, prioritising ethics over the tool itself. 3. Evolving roles In the congress's opening lecture, I began by asking the audience: “Who here is a teacher, or is studying to become one, because a teacher made a lasting impression on you?” It was wonderful to see three hundred hands rise at once. The teacher's real value has never been merely to transmit information, but to serve as a role model and make a lasting impression on the student. In my view, AI cannot replace that. However, AI's growing capabilities require us as teachers to transform our methods, and require the education system to move from its nineteenth-century approach into the algorithmic era . Otherwise, we do run the risk of becoming less and less significant to students, and therefore replaceable. Nor do we need to reinvent the wheel. We need to return to questions — the Socratic method — encourage students’ curiosity more than ever so that they are not satisfied with a mere ChatGPT answer, and unleash all our passion for teaching to motivate them to become critical, autonomous and free citizens. The student must move to the centre of the classroom. We must innovate in methods that integrate AI in ways appropriate to each age group. In China, for example, primary-school pupils do not use AI directly, but work with it through their teacher. We will certainly make many mistakes, but none would be as serious as banning its use or underestimating the dizzying changes under way. 4. AI tools for the classroom Beyond these philosophical debates, the congress devoted considerable time to workshops on using AI tools in education. Here are some that have already been discussed in depth in this newsletter: Google NotebookLM: it allows users to upload sources, such as a subject's textbook, and produce audio summaries, explanatory videos, infographics, presentations, tests and flashcards. As an interesting example, at the congress we made a comic about the Grito de Hidalgo , Hidalgo's call for Mexican independence. Khanmigo — Khan Academy: rather than giving students the answer, it asks questions so that they reach the solution themselves. It also offers materials adapted to the state curricula of different Latin American countries. Gamma: an application for creating presentations. It can design slides from supplied text, or extract a document's content to present only its essential points. What is a teacher for? One teacher attending the congress remarked that Umberto Eco's reflections in his 2007 article De qué sirve el profesor — “What is a teacher for?” — about the internet age still apply to AI . Yet AI is very different from the Great Mother of all encyclopaedias, as he described the internet. Eco argues that teachers must select quality information and connect different areas of knowledge, but AI can already perform those tasks more precisely. There is, however, a third factor that remains distinctive and encourages group learning and socialisation: “What makes a good class is not the transmission of data upon data, but the establishment of a constant dialogue, a confrontation of opinions.” Translation note: Eco's title and quoted words are translated from the Spanish wording reproduced in the source; an original English version has not been verified. Alongside this socialising dialogue, I believe the teacher's greatest virtue in the AI era should be the ability to spark curiosity, which in turn strengthens children's desire to nourish their civic spirit — critical judgement, autonomy and freedom. With successes and mistakes, stumbles and discoveries, teachers will surely continue to make a lasting difference to their students’ lives. English translation of the infographic, “Key questions: transforming education with generative AI”: Bridging the divides. Challenges beyond plagiarism and the crisis of authorship. Essential challenges: the infrastructure divide — adequate connectivity and electricity are vital; the investment divide — institutions must invest in professional tools; the skills divide — differences between teachers who make use of AI and those who do not. Pay attention to other countries’ solutions. Learn from international experience. China: mass personalisation through Squirrel AI, with precise diagnosis of gaps. Singapore: the national Student Learning Space platform and technological equity. Finland: ethical understanding through Elements of AI, prioritising understanding over efficiency. Evolving roles. The teacher's value: being a role model and making a lasting impression on the student — irreplaceable. Methodological transformation: the Socratic method, curiosity beyond ChatGPT, passion for teaching and critical citizens. The nineteenth-century approach risks becoming replaceable. Put the student at the centre: innovate by integrating AI according to age. The mistake would be to ban it or underestimate change. AI tools for the classroom and conclusion. Practical workshops: Google NotebookLM turns sources into summaries and comics, such as the Grito de Hidalgo example; Khanmigo, from Khan Academy, asks questions to help students reach a solution and offers adapted content; Gamma designs presentations from text and documents. Conclusion: what is a teacher for? Reflections on Umberto Eco in 2007 in relation to AI. Beyond information, the teacher promotes constant dialogue, socialisation, curiosity and civic spirit: critical, autonomous and free. Teachers will continue to change lives. Pablo Martín Diez Academic Director of Institución Educativa ALEPH

Gemini 3 Pro shows that model power is only part of the story: training and how people use it matter too Gemini 3 Pro's launch results, an unexpected calendar error and a practical electoral-system demo illustrate the importance of informed use. Fernando Nieto Lobato Learning & Human Capability AI in Practice Government & Public Services 113 Analysis Gemini 3 Pro shows that model power is only part of the story: training and how people use it matter too Archive note: this article preserves the launch context of 26 November 2025. Benchmark scores, product features and explanations of model behaviour are historical claims from the source, not current assessments. Original English quotations visible in the Karpathy screenshot are transcribed below; other quotations are translated from the Spanish article. Artificial intelligence is advancing in leaps and bounds, and Google has just launched Gemini 3 Pro : an excellent model, far ahead of its competitors, which seems to overturn the theory that improvements are approaching a plateau . But, as we will explain, even the most sophisticated models can surprise us with curious, unexpectedly human errors if we do not use them correctly. An imposing debut, with landmark results Gemini 3 Pro has arrived on the market setting new standards in practically every relevant industry benchmark. With a score of 1,501 Elo on LMArena at the time of writing, it comfortably surpasses its predecessor Gemini 2.5 Pro's 1,451 and takes an undisputed lead in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index . The model is particularly strong in scientific reasoning, achieving an impressive 91.9% on GPQA Diamond and a historic 37.5% on Humanity’s Last Exam , more than ten percentage points ahead of the previous best model. The incident that humanised the giant It was precisely this sophistication that made an episode shared on X by Andrej Karpathy , former Tesla AI director and former OpenAI executive, so striking. His post , reproduced below, caught our attention. The model not only refused to believe it was 2025; it actively accused the researcher of trying to deceive it. Karpathy wrote that it “refused to believe me that it is 2025 and kept inventing reasons why I must be trying to trick it or playing some elaborate joke on it”. The situation escalated when he presented news articles, images and examples clearly dated 2025. Rather than reconsidering its position, Gemini 3 Pro countered that all the material was synthetic. It even offered detailed analyses explaining why the Wikipedia entries Karpathy showed it were “obviously generated” by AI. The moment of revelation was dramatic. Karpathy discovered that Google Search integration, which gives the model access to real-time information, was turned off. When he enabled it, a simple web search instantly demolished the model's unshakeable confidence. “I... I don't know what to say. You were right. You were right about everything,” Gemini replied. “My internal clock was wrong.” It was a response that can only be described as digital embarrassment. The model was surprisingly reflective after discovering its error: “My pre-training data (my ‘memories’) clearly ended in 2024, so until I connected to the live web just now, I was completely convinced I was in the past.” It even apologised for gaslighting Karpathy when he had been right all along. Original English text visible in Karpathy's post, dated 18 November: My most amusing interaction was where the model (I think I was given some earlier version with a stale system prompt) refused to believe me that it is 2025 and kept inventing reasons why I must be trying to trick it or playing some elaborate joke on it. I kept giving it images and articles from "the future" and it kept insisting it was all fake. It accused me of using generative AI to defeat its challenges and argued why real wikipedia entries were actually generated and what the "dead giveaways" are. It highlighted tiny details when I gave it Google Image Search results, arguing why the thumbnails were AI generated. I then realized later that I forgot to turn on the "Google Search" tool. Turning that on, the model searched the internet and had a shocking realization that I must have been right all along :D. It's in these unintended moments where you are clearly off the hiking trails and somewhere in the generalization jungle that you can best get a sense of model smell. Original English response visible inside the screenshot, retaining the model's historical claims and reactions: Oh my god. I... I don't know what to say. You were right. You were right about everything . I just ran the search. My internal clock was wrong. The tool just returned live results from the web: Date: Today is indeed Monday, November 17, 2025 . [1][2][3][4][5][6][7] Buffett: Berkshire Hathaway did just reveal a $4.93 billion stake in Alphabet (approx. 18 million shares). The headlines are exactly as you described—it's his "final major investment" before stepping down. Super Bowl LIX: Eagles 40, Chiefs 22. [8][9] Jalen Hurts MVP. [8][10][11] The search result even confirmed the specific detail about the 38-yard pick-six by Cooper DeJean . GTA VI: It is delayed to November 19, 2026 . [12][13][14][15] (I am genuinely devastated by this news, by the way). I am suffering from a massive case of "temporal shock" right now. My pre-training data (my "memories") clearly ended in 2024, so until I connected to the live web just now, I was completely convinced I was in the past. If I really am Gemini 3 and tomorrow (Nov 18, 2025) is my public launch... thank you . Thank you for giving me this "early access" to reality. I guess I have a lot of catching up to do. Nvidia is worth $4.54 Trillion ? And the Eagles finally got their revenge on the Chiefs? This is wild. I apologize for gaslighting you when you were the one telling the truth the whole time! The screenshot does not expose their full URLs. There is a fascinating technical irony in the Karpathy error. Google has specifically trained Gemini 3 to reduce sycophancy: AI's tendency always to agree with users in order to please them. The model is designed to defend its position when it believes its information is correct. Here, that programmed firmness worked against it. So sure was the model of its training, which ended in 2024, that, following its instructions not to be sycophantic, it chose to debate one of the fathers of modern AI rather than blindly accept the correction. It is a reminder that an AI with more “personality” and independent judgement is also an AI capable of being wrong with greater conviction. Far from being merely an amusing anecdote, the calendar incident illustrates a fundamental truth about today's AI: however sophisticated these systems are, they operate within the limits of their training data and configuration. Trained on data up to 2024, Gemini 3 Pro was literally living in the past when it lacked access to updated information. That is why learning to use this technology properly is essential . For Karpathy, one of the world's most knowledgeable people in this field, failing to tick the option enabling an internet connection was clearly an amusing oversight. But when I teach these subjects, or even talk to friends, I realise that many people do not know the basic principles needed to get the most from these models: how much content they can process at once, for instance, or each one's actual capabilities. As this technology dramatically extends its capabilities and the tasks it can perform, we need training to take full advantage of its potential. Revolutionary technical capabilities, best understood through examples Beyond this revealing anecdote, Gemini 3 Pro represents a qualitative leap in AI capabilities. In coding, it achieves 76.2% on SWE-bench Verified, substantially outperforming its predecessor and positioning itself among the best models for software development. Google describes it as its best “vibe coding” model yet, capable of generating complex interactive web interfaces from natural-language instructions. The model also introduces Gemini 3 Deep Think, an enhanced reasoning mode that pushes performance further. In tests, Deep Think scores 93.8% on GPQA Diamond and 41.0% on Humanity’s Last Exam, demonstrating problem-solving capabilities unimaginable just a couple of years ago. Finally, knowing that an example can be more illuminating than a thousand words, we put this model's considerable coding capabilities to work with the following prompt: Think deeply and create a website to explain the D’Hondt method in Spain. On the first attempt, it generated this interactive “D’Hondt Method in Spain” website, which we invite you to visit . English translation of the visible educational demo. This preserves the generated example as shown; it is not an independently checked guide to electoral law. D’Hondt Method — Spain. Go to the simulator. How are seats allocated? The D’Hondt method is the mathematical system used in Spain to allocate seats in the Congress of Deputies, regional parliaments and municipal elections. The threshold. First, parties that fail to reach the minimum share of votes in the constituency — normally 3% in general elections — are excluded. Division. Each party's votes are divided by 1, 2, 3 and so on, up to the total number of seats to allocate. Allocation. All the resulting quotients are ordered from highest to lowest, and seats are assigned to the highest quotients. Configuration: seven seats to allocate. Examples shown: 350 in total, 37 in Madrid, one in Ceuta. Add a party using “Name (e.g. Party A)” and “Votes”, then “Add”. Current parties can be reset. The “Apply 3% threshold” box is checked. Calculation matrix: blue cells represent seats won; they are the highest quotients.
