ChatGPT, the flagship of this wave, now has more than 800 million weekly active users . Globally, AI adoption, especially outside North America, is even faster than internet adoption in its early years. Meanwhile, the major technology companies are investing colossal sums. Capital expenditure, or CapEx, by the US “Big Six” — Apple, NVIDIA, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta — has soared 63% over the past year. They now devote 15% of revenue to it, compared with 8% a decade ago. NVIDIA is emerging as one of the main beneficiaries, capturing a growing share, more than 25%, of worldwide spending on data centres: the new cathedrals of the digital age. The great dilemma: the cost of creating AI and the challenge of monetising it Training the most advanced AI models is a colossal undertaking, costing hundreds of millions of dollars per model. Yet once they have been created, the cost of using them, known as “inference”, is plummeting. Thanks to much more efficient chips — such as NVIDIA’s, which consume 105,000 times less energy per generated “word” than a decade ago — and smarter algorithms, inference costs have fallen by an astonishing 99.7% in just two years. This dramatic reduction is excellent news for users and developers, who are seeing AI become more accessible. For the companies investing fortunes in creating these models, however, it raises a crucial question: how do you make a return on a technology that is becoming cheaper to use and faces ever greater competition? Fierce competition and the momentum of open source Fortunately for us as users, the AI race is not the private preserve of a few giants. New models from multiple players are continually emerging, creating a vibrant, highly competitive ecosystem. A crucial factor is the rise of open-source models, whose designs are public and which anyone can use and modify. Although “closed” or proprietary models, such as those powering ChatGPT or Gemini, remain the most popular among consumers, open-source alternatives are gaining ground rapidly, especially among developers and in countries seeking to build their own AI capabilities without depending on others. Platforms such as Hugging Face have become universal libraries facilitating this trend. This chart, for example, shows the enormous download success of Meta’s Llama models, although their most recent versions fall short of today’s best open-source models, especially the Chinese ones, in performance. China’s unstoppable rise in AI BOND’s report does not hesitate to describe the current situation as a new “space race”, with China emerging as a formidable competitor to the United States. The Asian giant is advancing in leaps and bounds, particularly in open-source AI models such as DeepSeek and Qwen, which we have discussed and recommended in earlier issues. It often achieves performance comparable to US models but with lower training costs, increasingly using semiconductors of its own design. Indeed, alongside the United States, China leads the ranking for the creation of large-scale AI systems, leaving the rest of the world behind. Moreover, the country already has an installed base of industrial robots larger than the rest of the world combined, and its citizens are notably more optimistic about AI’s benefits than Americans . This technological competition will undoubtedly have profound geopolitical implications. AI is reimagining work and will conquer the physical world AI’s influence extends beyond the digital sphere. It is increasingly being integrated into the tangible world: autonomous vehicles such as Tesla’s and Waymo’s, defence systems, precision agriculture with weed-removing robots, and even mineral exploration. This penetration is fundamentally changing how we work. Productivity is expected to rise — a Stanford HAI study already showed a 14% increase in customer-support tasks — and, although the future of employment remains debated, job postings requiring AI skills have increased more than fivefold, up 448%, over the past seven years, while other traditional technology jobs have already seen a slight contraction. Companies such as Shopify already consider proficiency with AI a basic employee skill. The next frontiers: autonomous agents, artificial general intelligence and connecting the unconnected Looking ahead, the report sees several promising frontiers. One is the evolution towards “AI agents”: systems that will not merely answer our questions but perform complex tasks autonomously, acting as truly proactive assistants. Further ahead, artificial general intelligence, AGI — machines with cognitive capabilities comparable to humans’ — is increasingly seen less as a distant utopia and more as an attainable horizon. Finally, one of the most transformative prospects is AI’s potential, combined with low-cost satellite connectivity such as SpaceX’s Starlink, to connect the 2.6 billion people currently living without internet access. Their first experience online could be through conversational AI interfaces in their own language: a revolution in itself. BOND’s report is a wake-up call about the speed and magnitude of AI disruption. Although optimistic about its potential, it does not shy away from economic and geopolitical uncertainties. AI is here, its development is exponential and its implications are profound. Businesses, investors and governments face a landscape of immense opportunities and non-trivial risks. Monetisation remains a complex puzzle for many, competition is fierce, and the struggle between the United States and China for AI leadership has only just begun. As the report concludes, “the genie is out of the bottle”, and the world is entering, at an unprecedented speed, a new era defined by machine intelligence. Google Cloud Summit Madrid 2025: generative AI and the future of the public sector, with ALEPH Educational Institution as VIP guest and reporter Gabriela Ortega Jarrín reports from Madrid on public services, sovereign cloud, AI skills, regulation and competition between cloud providers. Gabriela Ortega Jarrín Government & Public Services Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics Learning & Human Capability 088 Report Google Cloud Summit Madrid 2025: generative AI and the future of the public sector, with ALEPH Educational Institution as VIP guest and reporter Editorial introduction: this week’s main article is by Gabriela Ortega Jarrín , who holds a doctorate in Communication and is a political consultant specialising in election campaigns and public institutions’ communications, a brand management specialist, and Director of Strategy at ALEPH Educational Institution. Gabriela gives us her first-hand account of the special event Google held in Madrid to follow up on I/O 2025, which we covered in last week’s newsletter . Historical context: this report was published on 4 June 2025 and retains the announcements, projections and regulatory framing of that time. Quotations below are translated from the preserved Spanish article. English text: “Google Cloud Summit”, “22 May 2025”, “Madrid”. First impressions count. When we arrived at Google Cloud Summit 2025 , thousands of professionals were waiting to enter Hall 12 at IFEMA to explore Google’s latest innovations and their real-world applications. Inside, we found a futuristic, stadium-like stage which, after the opening talks and presentations of the company’s new services and products, became six simultaneous stages. Six talks ran at once, and through headphones you chose the colour of the room and the speaker you wanted to hear, presenting real cases of Google solutions in use. As though we were in a film set in the future, we were all at the same conference, all listening closely to a speaker. None of the attendees were talking to one another; only non-verbal communication conveyed how impressive some applications were, or sought a knowing response from colleagues, as if to ask: what if we did this in our company or organisation? Visible demonstration text, already in English: “Books”; “Find by book title and author”; “Search”; “Clear”; columns “Title”, “Author”, “Summary”, “Edit”, “Delete”, and an add button marked “+”. The four entries shown are: The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn — Mark Twain. “Huck Finn, the protagonist, escapes his abusive and drunken father and runs away with a slave named Jim. The two have many adventures on a raft on the Mississippi River, including traveling with the antagonists, the king and the duke, two con artists who go from town to town stealing from people.” Treasure Island — Robert Louis Stevenson. “While going through the possessions of a deceased guest who owed them money, the mistress of the inn and her son find a treasure map that leads to a pirate fortune as well as great danger.” Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll. “This edition brings together the complete and unabridged text with more than 70 stunning illustrations by Robert Ingpen, each reflecting his unique style and extraordinary imagination in visualising this enchanting story.” Don Quixote — Miguel de Cervantes. “Novel about a man named Alonso Quijano who, after reading countless chivalric romances, becomes convinced he is a knight-errant named Don Quixote and sets out on a series of misadventures with his squire, Sancho Panza.” Generative AI serving the public sector: savings, efficiency and new roles Below, we summarise the main developments presented for the public sector. If one thing is certain, it is that public administration and its relationship with citizens are being redefined. Perhaps we already knew that; now let us see how. Efficiency and quality in the public sector through the automation of repetitive tasks First, the technologies presented promise a substantial improvement in the efficiency and quality of public services. Esade and Implement presented a report on AI’s impact on Spain’s public sector , whose conclusions quantify a saving of 9% of each public employee’s time through the automation of repetitive tasks, translating into around €7 billion in annual added value . In addition, civil servants could shift towards higher-value functions , such as personalised assistance for citizens, strategic policy analysis and so on. Cumbersome bureaucratic processes could be streamlined with natural-language tools that draft reports or summarise case files in seconds. As the study notes, implementing AI strategically would make it possible to “optimise operations, improve decision-making and ultimately deliver better services to citizens more efficiently”. Some institutional caution still prevails, however: almost 60% of respondents feel their organisations are not fully prepared to integrate AI into their operations. In other words, there is optimism about AI’s transformative potential — three in four anticipate a positive impact — but also awareness of the remaining challenges in training, regulation and technological adaptation . Digital sovereignty and data security: the response from Google Cloud and its partners Digital sovereignty in the cloud and data security were prominent themes at the Summit , especially relevant to governments and regulated sectors in Europe. This allows public administrations to benefit from the cloud’s scalability and resilience without surrendering control over sensitive data. It is crucial in critical fields such as emergency services, defence, taxation and healthcare, among other sectors handling information that requires the strongest safeguards. Google Cloud reinforced its commitment to sovereign cloud: cloud services that guarantee local control of data and strict regulatory compliance. Notable offerings include Google Cloud Data Boundary, which can restrict the exact location of data and provides advanced key-management controls; Google Cloud Dedicated, cloud environments operated by local partners and adapted to specific sovereign requirements, already operating in France and coming soon to Germany; and Google Cloud Air-Gapped, a completely isolated cloud designed for highly sensitive sectors. On security and compliance, one concrete example presented at the Summit was the Canary Islands’ 112 emergency service project . The Canary Islands Emergency and Security Coordination Centre, 112 — CECOES , is migrating the management of its critical data to a sovereign public-cloud solution provided by Google Cloud in collaboration with Minsait Cyber, Indra’s cybersecurity subsidiary, and the GuardedBox platform. This makes the Canary Islands’ 112 service one of Spain’s first public administrations to use the public cloud for critical services under an advanced sovereignty framework. The solution guarantees that sensitive data is stored and managed entirely within national territory, with fully auditable encryption and access controls. “For a service like ours, it is essential to have real control over our data, among the most sensitive and critical for citizens […] to know how and where the data is stored and protected,” explained Carlos García, the 112 service’s head of IT. Many public institutions still use older systems and operate infrastructure locally rather than in the cloud, making cloud solutions or advanced AI harder to adopt. Technological modernisation requires sustained investment and updates not only to equipment but also to data architectures suitable for training and hosting AI models. Security, although strengthened in the cloud, remains a constant concern, since trust must be built between administrations and cloud providers. Pilot experiences such as the Canary Islands project demonstrate that a model replicable by other public bodies is possible. The availability of local cloud regions — Madrid has hosted a Google Cloud region since 2022, the first from a hyperscaler in Spain — and trusted national partners such as Minsait and Telefónica Tech makes it easier for more public data to migrate to certified cloud environments. Public administration could thereby gain business continuity, with round-the-clock data centres and disaster recovery, and greater agility in deploying new digital services, without compromising sovereignty over its data. AI to break down language barriers, and writing assistants to improve communication and productivity in organisations Another central theme was the improvement in communication and productivity achieved through AI in Google’s platforms. Google Meet , its videoconferencing tool, deserves particular mention for adding AI features intended to break down language barriers and improve communication. A new real-time speech translation feature for meetings was announced: the speaker’s voice is automatically translated into the listener’s preferred language while retaining its original tone and timbre. This AI simultaneous translation debuted in beta for users of certain Google One plans, AI Pro and Ultra, in languages such as English, Spanish, French, Italian and Portuguese, with plans to extend it soon to business uses. Meet also demonstrated automatic AI-generated meeting summaries. At the end of a video call, the platform can provide a written summary of the main points discussed, agreed actions and next steps, all produced through natural-language processing. For example, simultaneous translation in videoconferences and automatic transcription and summaries can facilitate collaboration between international bodies or different autonomous communities with co-official languages. They could also improve accessibility: imagine local council meetings or government webinars subtitled and translated live to reach a wider audience . Tools such as writing assistants in Gmail and Docs could help spokespeople and public communicators produce clearer messages, or help managers draft quick but carefully worded replies to citizens . Together, these generative AI communication capabilities can strengthen both internal coordination within the state and external communication with citizens, making them more inclusive and efficient. Talent, regulation and multicloud competition: Europe’s new playing field Google Cloud accompanied its technological announcements with institutional initiatives to prepare for responsible AI adoption. One of its most notable commitments concerned training and digital skills: the company announced a target of training one million people in Spain in cloud and AI skills by 2027. For ALEPH Educational Institution, taking part also offers an opportunity to turn training into practice and demonstrate improvements from applying AI in government and politics. We are therefore already working on a collaboration with Google Cloud. We will share further news… Other institutions involved include ASTIC, the body of public-sector ICT professionals, whose members will have access to Google Cloud Skills Boost resources and official certifications. Training programmes in AI are also being extended to teachers through Google for Education and to healthcare personnel in collaboration with professional associations such as ANDE and SEMERGEN. Google.org, Google’s philanthropic arm, also awarded a $1 million grant to Fundación General CSIC to support open-source AI projects for scientific and healthcare purposes, from virtual-reality avatars for cerebral palsy therapies to drug-discovery software for neglected tropical diseases. On regulation , Spain has positioned itself as a pioneering country by launching the first AI regulatory sandbox in line with the EU AI Act . This sandbox, a controlled testing environment, seeks to help start-ups and organisations develop and implement high-risk AI systems while meeting demanding European regulatory requirements. Google Cloud announced its active participation as a collaborator, providing a secure environment in its cloud alongside a toolkit for responsible AI. Specifically, Google will give the sandbox access to advanced capabilities such as Vertex AI, its platform for developing and managing models, and confidential computing services, enabling developers to test algorithms under conditions of maximum security and privacy. The sandbox’s ultimate goal is to balance AI innovation and regulation. Spain is thus serving as a testing ground for two purposes: supporting responsible AI innovation , accelerating projects with potential positive social impact; and refining the practical rules that will guide the application of future European AI legislation . For Google Cloud, participation is also an opportunity to make concrete improvements to its own AI governance tools and develop a distinctive “responsible” cloud offering aligned with Spain’s demands for digital sovereignty. In the same vein, regulation and the ethical use of generative AI raise questions about accountability, transparency and potential bias in automated decisions. Integrating AI into administrative processes, whether to propose draft decisions or prioritise cases, will require clear limits and human oversight. The EU AI Act will impose obligations, especially where “high-risk” systems are used in areas such as justice or employment. Participation in the regulatory sandbox is an advantage for Spain, enabling regulators and developers to learn together and adjust requirements before the law is widely applied. Practical questions remain, however: how can complex algorithms be audited? How can we ensure models used by a public administration meet criteria for non-discrimination, explainability and data protection? Institutions will need to create AI ethics committees, algorithm validation protocols and guidance for civil servants on responsible use. Meanwhile, compliance with rules such as the GDPR must continue to be guaranteed when personal data is used in models. Hence the importance of tools such as Data Boundary and confidential computing, presented by Google, which provide technical controls to support that compliance. English text of the photographed slide: “Gemini: leader in all categories”. The vertical axis is “Higher performance — LMArena Elo Score”, with labelled ticks at 1,300, 1,350, 1,400 and 1,450. The horizontal axis is “Lower cost (log)”, running from 100 through 10 and 1 to 0.1; its measure is “$ price per million tokens, 3:1 input:output”. Blue points connected by a line are labelled Gemini-2.5-Pro-Preview-05-06, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Preview-5-20, Gemini-2.0-Flash-001 and Gemini-2.0-Flash-Lite, in that order from higher performance/higher cost to lower performance/lower cost. Other comparison points are unlabelled. Exact coordinates are not printed, so none are supplied here. The surrounding banner reads “22 May 2025” and “Hello, Madrid”. The announcements at Summit Madrid 2025 paint an ambitious picture of what we may see: public administrations enhanced by generative AI, operating in secure sovereign clouds, with civil servants trained in new digital skills. Yet Google Cloud is one part of an ecosystem that includes other major players, notably global hyperscalers AWS, Amazon Web Services, and Microsoft Azure, all competing for the trust of European businesses and governments. Google Cloud Summit 2025 was therefore more than a product showcase: it was also a strategic positioning of Google in Europe’s digital ecosystem. Competition is intense, and Google Cloud seems determined to distinguish itself by placing AI at the centre of its value proposition. As Isaac Hernández, Director of Google Cloud Iberia, put it, “AI has changed everything all over again”, and Google takes a different approach from its rivals thanks to its own “integrated stack”, spanning specialised chips and advanced AI models . In particular, Google champions its Gemini model, claiming that version 2.5, presented globally, “is above any” alternative model in performance and cost. The company maintains that its latest TPU chip generations enable low-cost AI, with Gemini up to “seven times cheaper” than equivalent competing models. Google also stresses that it is the only cloud provider currently offering large AI models in every modality — text, image, audio and video — within its platform, giving it a very comprehensive catalogue. Its competitors are not standing still, however, and are also adapting their strategies to Europe. AWS, for example, has announced plans for a “European sovereign cloud” separate from its global regions, designed specifically for public-sector and highly regulated customers in Europe. This AWS sovereign cloud will operate independently, with data centres solely in the EU — the first region is due in Germany at the end of 2025 — and incorporate controls to meet European regulators’ requirements for data residency and operational autonomy. Microsoft, meanwhile, presented its Microsoft Cloud for Sovereignty initiative in 2022: a public-cloud offering for governments and public administrations promising greater control, transparency and regulatory compliance. To develop it, Microsoft partnered with European companies, including defence firm Leonardo in Italy and Proximus in Belgium, to ensure local trust, and explicitly acknowledged that the move “intensifies competition” with AWS and Google in public-sector cloud services. European players are also making moves: consortia and local providers are promoting initiatives such as GAIA-X, a framework for cloud interoperability, and sovereign cloud federations such as VirtuRA, a project backed by European funding that brings together companies including OVHcloud, T-Systems, Telefónica and Scaleway to provide federated, open-source cloud infrastructure in several EU countries. All this reflects how digital sovereignty has become an unavoidable requirement for competing in a European market that demands guarantees of legal compliance and local control, especially from public administrations. Global providers are adapting their services accordingly. To the extent that Google aligns with EU priorities — fostering local innovation, technological sovereignty and ethical AI — it can distinguish itself from competitors and possibly gain ground in public contracts and strategic alliances. But Europe values competition and diversification: one company, however innovative, is unlikely to dominate the public digital ecosystem. A multicloud environment is foreseeable, with different global and local providers supplying interoperable services. Google will therefore need to keep integrating into this network, participating in open standards and ensuring customers can “take their data” and models wherever they wish. In summary, Google Cloud Summit Madrid 2025 showcased abundant AI to improve efficiency, strong emphasis on sovereignty to respect legislation and local preferences, and a message of public–private collaboration on training and ethics. For public decision-makers, the message is encouraging: the technology needed to modernise institutions exists and is available. The main challenge is leading the organisational and regulatory change required to incorporate these tools safely and effectively. The next few years will be crucial in showing how many of these pilot projects become large-scale realities. With initiatives like these, Spain could place itself at the forefront of public-sector AI adoption, offering Europe an example of combining innovation with sovereignty and service to citizens. As always in digital transformation, technology is only part of the equation. Institutional leadership, continuous training and good governance will determine the real impact of this “AI wave” on public administration. For now, Google has not only made its move: it has set out the board. It is now public administrations’ turn to accept it, “kick it over”, or negotiate the rules of the game. Google I/O 2025: artificial intelligence at the heart of innovation and the future Google’s May 2025 announcements, from Gemini and Veo to local AI models, and their implications for creating, searching and communicating. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Futures, Safety & Human Agency 087 Analysis Google I/O 2025: artificial intelligence at the heart of innovation and the future Historical context: this article was published on 28 May 2025. Product availability, comparative rankings and forecasts reflect that moment. Google I/O 2025 , held on 20 May, marked a turning point in Google’s trajectory, placing AI not merely among its key technologies but at the centre of its strategy, as the driving force behind all its future innovations, with the aim of making AI very easy for everyone to use. It was also the first moment in many years when Google appeared to be leading AI worldwide, with products outperforming its competitors in almost every field. Google, although it may have spent years “asleep”, is the great pioneer of generative AI, with its foundational 2017 paper on transformers . Text of the slide: “#1 across all LMArena categories”. Our students were able to use it extensively in the experiment creating a political party and election campaign that we described last week . It offers improved reasoning and multimodal understanding. Features such as Deep Think mode for complex problems, the nimble Flash version optimised for fast tasks, and Gemini Live’s conversational interactivity seek to establish Gemini in our daily lives, integrating it into everyday tools such as Gmail, search and Chrome. This is a strategic move to make AI not only powerful but also ubiquitous and useful. New diffusion models for text and video: Gemini Diffusion and Veo 3 In content generation, Google presented two advances that struck us as especially significant: Gemini Diffusion for text, an incredible model for the technical progress it promises for the future; and Veo 3 for video, a genuine revolution that is already here. Gemini Diffusion: this new text diffusion model is extremely fast. In demonstrations, it generated text five times faster than Google’s fastest model to date, while maintaining strong performance on coding tasks. Unlike traditional language models, which generate tokens sequentially — and this is the particularly significant point — Gemini Diffusion refines noise over multiple steps, using a method inspired by image generation. It can thus begin with an approximation and improve it iteratively, making it especially useful for tasks that benefit from this approach. Veo 3: this is the latest generation of Google’s video model, capable of creating highly realistic videos with visual effects and, among its most notable new features, native audio generation. Veo 3 can therefore generate videos containing dialogue, ambient sounds and synchronised music directly, without additional editing steps. This puts Veo 3 a step ahead of competitors such as Sora or Kling. Although initial access to Veo 3 will be limited and require an AI Ultra subscription, its potential for film and video creation is enormous . In the recommendation of the week section, we have collected some of the best creations users are already generating with Veo 3. They are extraordinary: do not miss them. Editorial note: the recommendation section mentioned above is a separate part of the original Spanish newsletter and is outside this main-article translation. To complement Veo 3 and Imagen 4, Google’s improved image-generation model, Google introduced Flow. Flow is an AI filmmaking tool that allows users to design complete narratives, scene by scene, combining Veo, Imagen and Gemini to maintain visual and narrative coherence. It also includes tools to control the camera and transitions, helping give clips a more cinematic look. Redefining search and interaction The search experience, Google’s flagship product and principal source of revenue, is also being reimagined as AI advances as a new way to find information. A new “AI Mode” will enable more complex conversational searches, while “AI Overviews” will provide AI-generated summaries at the top of results. Other notable announcements Alongside these developments, Google I/O 2025 brought a wave of AI-powered innovations: Project Astra: an ambitious initiative seeking to create a universal AI assistant that can understand the context of the world around us, help with complex tasks, find information and even act on the user’s behalf. Imagen 4: the new version of Google’s image-generation model, with improvements in photorealism, cleaner detail and a wider variety of artistic styles, plus the promise of better spelling and typography in generated images. In our initial tests, however, it is not yet at the level of OpenAI’s model. Gemma 3n: an open, fast, efficient multimodal model, designed to run without a network connection on devices such as phones , laptops and tablets, supporting audio, text, images and video. I have already been able to test it on my own phone with Google AI Edge Gallery . For us, this was another of the event’s major advances. It makes clear that, trailing the most powerful giant AI models by only a few months — or around a year in the case of phones — we will be able to have artificial intelligences at almost the same level running locally on our own devices, with the enormous advantages for privacy and control that this brings. Google Beam, the evolution of Project Starline: a new AI-based video communications platform using a state-of-the-art video model to transform 2D video streams into realistic 3D experiences in real time, aiming to create a more authentic sense of presence in video calls. AI advances for developers: given this newsletter’s nature and focus, we have chosen not to cover the enormous advances in programming, tools and technical protocols here. But it is worth highlighting the major competitive advantage Google gains from having its own “computers” to train models and serve them to users: its seventh-generation TPU, Ironwood, enables faster, more efficient models at competitive prices. Ultimately, Google I/O 2025 made clear that the company is fully committed to an AI-powered future in which artificial intelligence is not merely a tool but an essential “partner” in almost every aspect of our lives. The advances presented — especially Veo 3, already transforming the audiovisual industry completely, and Gemini’s evolution towards models leading competitors in benchmarks — will continue to redefine how we create, interact with information and communicate, marking a significant milestone in AI’s continuing, dizzying progress. Connecting the global vision with local impact: Google Cloud Summit Madrid 2025, which we will cover in the next issue English text of the event graphic: “Google Cloud Summit”, “22 May 2025”, “Madrid”. The transformative vision and wave of AI innovations presented at Google I/O 2025 were not confined to global announcements from Mountain View. These advances have a direct echo and practical application in local settings, exemplified by Google Cloud Summit Madrid 2025 , held in Madrid on Thursday 22 May . To offer a first-hand perspective and analysis of what happened there, our next issue will feature a valuable contribution from Gabriela Ortega , Director of Strategy at ALEPH Educational Institution, who attended the event in Madrid. Next week, she will tell us about her experience of getting to know Google’s approach to artificial intelligence first-hand. Repeating the AI election experiment a year later — with our students: what has changed in twelve months A repeat of estrategIA’s election experiment with ALEPH students explores human judgement, reasoning models, deep research and new campaign tools. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Learning & Human Capability Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 086 Practical experiment Repeating the AI election experiment a year later — with our students: what has changed in twelve months Historical context: this article was published on 21 May 2025. Its tools, assessments and forecasts refer to that date. “Yesterday” means 20 May 2025; the classroom exercise deliberately recreates a US election scenario beginning on 1 January 2024. A year ago, in four issues of estrategIA published between April and June 2024 ( 28 , 29 , 30 and 36 — we recommend reading them if you did not do so at the time), we used the best AI tools and models then available to create a political party and a female candidate, and simulated several key campaign tasks for the European Parliament elections held on 9 June. The “experiment” was also presented in September in Málaga at the ACOP conference — the Political Communication Association — where it attracted considerable interest. Now, a year later, we have recreated that experiment to observe and assess the capabilities of the new AI models and how far things have advanced in just one year. The main difference is that this time I was not the only person creating the party, candidate and campaign. I also set it as an academic assignment for several groups of students on ALEPH Educational Institution’s Master’s in Marketing, Communication and Political Consultancy and Diploma in Digital Election Campaign Management , because I consider it an excellent practical way to learn how to integrate AI into real work. English text of the slide: “EXERCISE: Creating a political party, a candidate and key elements of an election campaign using AI.” “Directly inspired by the experiment we carried out at estrategIA in spring 2024, creating a party, a female candidate and key elements of an election campaign with AI.” It lists estrategIA issues 28, 29, 30 and 36, linked above, and a compilation document: “estrategIA compilation: creating Europa Estoica Unida and its candidate with AI”. The party logo reads “Europa Estoica Unida” (“United Stoic Europe”). The preserved slide does not supply the compilation document’s destination. The biggest change, intended to make the task easier for students who mainly come from Latin America — while retaining a real setting that allowed them to go deeper into political and sociological data — was to move the scenario to the United States and propose creating a third political party there , one that could offer, to some extent, an alternative to the two traditional parties . English text of the slide: “EXERCISE: Creating a political party, a candidate and key elements of an election campaign using AI.” “CLASSROOM SCENARIO: ‘OPERATION DISRUPTION 2024 USA’.” “Start date: 1 January 2024.” The context is the United States approaching presidential and legislative elections in November 2024, with intense polarisation between the Democratic Party, presumably with Joe Biden seeking re-election, and the Republican Party, dominated by Donald Trump despite other contenders. Widespread fatigue with polarisation, dissatisfaction with traditional options and a search for alternatives affect significant parts of the electorate: independents, younger voters and moderates in both parties. The illustration labels read “DEMOCRATIC PARTY”, “REPUBLICAN PARTY” and “ALTERNATIVES”. These are the premises of the historical classroom simulation. Without going into every detail of the extensive exercise, which is not especially relevant to this article, after a theoretical introduction to AI and its possibilities the students received some additional contextual pointers and a collection of the frontier generative AI tools publicly available today. Alongside creating the party, candidate and key campaign materials such as speeches, talking points and posters, they were asked to write a brief reflection on using AI for these tasks. And because when one person teaches, two people learn, I learnt a great deal from this excellent group of students, with their interesting and varied professional backgrounds. I want to share that with you, our readers, before offering my own reflections on generative AI’s progress over the past year. Notable reflections from — and with — the students after the exercise 1. AI brings a very substantial improvement to 70% of processes and tasks, but the human 30% remains crucial today and is probably what makes the difference. I must say that I very much agree with this student’s reflection, shared by most of the group. It is before working with AI — knowing what to ask it, how to ask, having the imagination to devise scenarios — and after its answer — our ability to evaluate it, check the information, ask follow-up questions or challenge the AI again — that we find a very substantial difference in the final results of AI-assisted processes in 2025. That said, over a five- or ten-year horizon, this crucial human contribution is very likely to diminish progressively as models become more capable and intelligent, acquire highly advanced memories of our habits and preferences, and transform the process. Even so, at least until artificial intelligences reach that still-distant point of having a will of their own, human initiative will remain essential. 2. AI improves when it is “pushed”. Both in last year’s experiment and in several tests I carried out in 2025, you can see that AI’s initial answers are not bad, and are improving as the models improve, as I will discuss below. Yet they can be somewhat generic or “soulless”. Some student groups said they had observed the same thing. Several groups’ work also showed that when human ingenuity puts these models under pressure, pushes them in different directions and uses several AIs creatively at the same time, more innovative and distinctive answers and solutions emerge. As we discussed in the first point, the human contribution following the AI process makes a difference today, even though AI already does the vast majority of the work. 3. The more someone knows about a subject, the better equipped they are to get good results from working with AI. Several students with advanced knowledge in particular fields demonstrated highly complex, finely tuned workflows in their presentations that would never have occurred to me, for example, despite spending many hours every day working with AIs. These more precise, specific approaches, drawing on all that expert knowledge, produce excellent results beyond what AI might generate from general queries. As an anecdotal example of the opposite, one election poster a group proposed in its presentation had some interesting elements, but used a typeface that would have made my university design lecturer’s eyes bleed: he would never have approved such an atrocity. 4. AI is being used much more — and better — than a year ago, but we are still a long way from making full use of its potential. Many students have already integrated AI thoroughly into their everyday work. I ran a survey before the classes both this year and last to establish their starting point, and between 2024 and 2025 the number of people using AI daily, and also paying for at least one AI tool, grew very significantly. AI is already seen as a fully valid ally in political consultancy, yet many people said they used it almost on autopilot. I think one benefit of this exercise is that it can help people open their minds to using more AI, but above all to using it more creatively: working with several models at once, getting different models — even those from very different cultures, such as Silicon Valley, China and Europe — to generate ideas, debate and correct one another. The technology is improving very rapidly. One student who had used Gemini some time ago, for example, said she had tried it again after I mentioned its enormous improvement in the first class and had noticed a huge difference. We need to retain a beginner’s mindset towards it and never tire of testing and experimenting. 5. Using AI: that moment of discovery From a teacher’s perspective, it has been fascinating to see how some people who had never used AI, or had barely used it, were beginning in just a few days to find it useful and improve their capabilities, without losing a critical, balanced view of it. One of the final questions, which I could not explore fully for lack of time, concerned how to persuade other colleagues to use it, or introduce it to people who barely do. My main recommendation here, which I also gave the students in our first class, is Wharton professor Ethan Mollick’s book, Co-Intelligence , with its four basic rules for using AI, still very valid today: “always invite AI to the table; be the human in the process; treat AI like a person; assume it is the worst AI you will ever use”. It was this last point that I particularly emphasised in the theoretical part of the classes, because I feel that even these postgraduate students, whose average use of AI is notably advanced, are still far from understanding “what is coming” and the new possibilities they will have in the years ahead. Translation note: the four rules attributed to Mollick above are translated from the Spanish wording in this article; they are not presented as verified quotations from the English original. English text of the mind map — “Notable reflections from (and with) students after the exercise”; centre: “AI reflections with students”: 1. AI’s impact: 70% of processes versus a crucial human 30%. 70% improvement in processes/tasks; the human 30% as the differentiating factor, currently. 5. A moment of discovery. New users, within a few days: find it useful, improve their capabilities and retain a critical perspective. 2. AI improves with human ingenuity. Humans “push” models; the result is more innovative solutions. 4. The evolution of AI use. Much greater use than a year ago; potential still remains untapped. 3. Prior knowledge strengthens AI use. Greater knowledge of the subject leads to better results with AI. How AI has progressed over the past year in political consultancy My own reflections, many of them formed before the classes and confirmed afterwards, focus on comparing where we are with where we were a year ago. Before setting the exercise for the students, I completed its entire text component with five different AI models, then ran many tests with other tools for images, music and so on. 1. Reasoning models make an enormous difference. The leap brought by o1 and o1-preview late last year, and now by models such as o3 and Gemini Pro 2.5, gives us a substantial increase in quality compared with this time in 2024, especially on complex tasks. Meanwhile, improvements in “normal” models, through the almost monthly iteration of, for example, 4o, ChatGPT’s default model, also mean that results are better than a year ago even when we use models that do not “think”. For more complex tasks, however, the quality achieved with AIs that use “time to think” is much higher. 2. “Deep research” is a turning point in working with data and analysing the political context. Using OpenAI’s Deep Research with o3, or Google’s with Gemini 2.5 Pro, with good direction, means having an initial report of 40 or 50 pages containing key statistical data — in this case, on the US context in 2024. Even so, it is essential to check the data carefully and remember that these advanced models still hallucinate and may invent things. They remain far from perfect and entirely reliable, but offer enormous power to grasp context and broaden our perspective in the tens of minutes they take to conduct research that would take an average person many hours. And we must always remember: they are “the worst model we will use for the rest of our lives”. 3. A larger context window means much more coherent results. Improvements in context windows — these models’ ability to work with ever more data — make all the difference. We can now work while carrying forward all the information from previous stages. This enables models, especially reasoning models, to give much more coherent answers, drawing on all the knowledge generated rather than having to start almost from scratch with every interaction and question. 4. Many more high-quality models for generating images. There has been a noticeable leap in image generation, perhaps less in the quality of the image itself — although that too has improved, and Midjourney 6, which we used in 2024, was already a very interesting tool — than in the range of possibilities. There are now many more models capable of generating high-quality, even photorealistic images. Above all, there is the ease of use and adherence to prompts — following our instructions — of models such as OpenAI’s in ChatGPT or Imagen 4, which Google introduced yesterday, 20 May. 5. Notable improvements across all fields and tools. There has also been a notable leap in other AI-powered tools, such as audio, infographics and presentations. Above all, this will enable us to do new things professionally in the near future . English text of the mind map — “AI in political consultancy: progress over the past year”; centre: “AI in political consultancy”: 1. Reasoning models. o3 or Gemini Pro 2.5 compared with 2024: higher quality on complex tasks. Normal models such as 4o also improve. Reasoning AIs are superior on complex tasks. 2. Deep research. Deep Research with o3 or Gemini: extensive, good reports. Time savings compared with human work. Crucial: review, because they still hallucinate. Potential: grasping context quickly. 3. Larger context windows. More data makes a difference. Carrying previous information forward produces more coherent answers. 4. Images. OpenAI and Google models: easier to use and follow prompts. Variety and photorealism: Midjourney 6 was already good. 5. Other AI tools. Audio and other formats. New professional possibilities across multiple fields. To illustrate this last point, I generated a very simple video game , fitting the context of the students’ exercise, mainly using o3 and o4-mini. I also made a very similar alternative version with Gemini 2.5 Pro. I invite you to have a quick game — it may not display well on mobile phones, depending on the model — and try to bring the third party to electoral victory by jumping over the Democrats’ and Republicans’ traditional symbols, the donkey and the elephant , and collecting ballot papers. English text of the game screen: “Third Party Runner”; ballot papers: “10/10”; record: “10”; “Citizens’ victory!”; “Citizens’ victory”; “Total ballot papers: 10”; “Record: 10”; “Restart”. The game features a female character jumping over donkey and elephant obstacles. Clearly, it is a very simple, “bad” game, a sort of extremely basic side-scrolling sketch of Mario Bros . Yet I did not touch a single line of code to make this example , and finishing it took no more than a couple of hours. Most of that time was not spent generating the game itself: I wanted a platform where I could make it publicly available for you to see and play. I eventually used Websim for its simplicity, after first trying Firebase and Bolt.new. Creating the first version in ChatGPT took less than three-quarters of an hour. The entire game was created simply by giving the AI models general text instructions. Beyond the modest, simple result, the point is that in future we will be able to create video documentaries about candidates, games and virtual environments as easily as we now create images or songs. One student said that last year they had already generated a song with Suno for an election campaign that was perfectly usable and that they had actually booked airtime for on the radio. Even in very modest campaigns, we will be able to see surprising innovations in creative communication. Final reflections and trends Beyond the incremental yet very significant year-on-year improvements in generated content, and the addition of deep research as a major advance, it is essential to recognise that these developments will by no means stop at this level . We will see further major improvements in reasoning models’ intelligence and capabilities , in deep research powered by those new models — one key to understanding its ceiling will be whether higher-quality data can be accessed — and, above all, in the memories and context windows of these models . According to statements from several researchers, these will grow very significantly in the coming months and years, allowing AIs to develop much more personalised, finely tuned knowledge, another highly significant improvement. In other fields, such as images , where we are already very close to models that recreate reality and make doing so easy, as well as video, interactivity, virtual and augmented reality, we will undoubtedly see decisive improvements in the next few years . Already, the Veo 3 model Google presented yesterday is an extraordinary advance . So next year or the year after, I will surely be able to ask students to generate campaign videos almost as easily as they now make images or songs, and possibly also to create much more elaborate video games or key applications that improve campaigns’ efficiency or reach. To sum up, AI’s dizzying evolution suggests that we will very probably be able to do things we could not previously even have dreamed of . Pioneers who make use of all these new possibilities, drawing fully on their own knowledge and that of the AIs they work with, will have an enormous competitive advantage. I will close this article with the same two sentences I used to end my theoretical class: Artificial intelligence is quite likely to transform the world profoundly and rapidly over the next few years. In that scenario, learning about this technology and integrating it into our professional work seems the best possible option for “enjoying” the change rather than “suffering” it. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, ALEPH Educational Institution

Who should decide in the age of artificial intelligence? Ethics, prudence and human dignity in the face of algorithmic power Pablo Martín Diez reviews Adela Cortina's case for an ethical, democratic approach to AI grounded in human dignity, practical wisdom and public dialogue. Pablo Martín Diez Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Government & Public Services Learning & Human Capability 085 Review & commentary Who should decide in the age of artificial intelligence? Ethics, prudence and human dignity in the face of algorithmic power Translation note: quotations from Adela Cortina below are translated from the Spanish article. English renderings of the book’s title and subtitle are explanatory, not the titles of a verified English-language edition. Almost every week, we encounter grandiose promises and predictions, often expressed boastfully, by technology gurus and magnates. In the face of this hubris — the ancient excess the Greeks associated with the arrogance of those who believed themselves above fate — Adela Cortina, Professor of Ethics and Political Philosophy at the University of Valencia and a member of Spain’s Royal Academy of Moral and Political Sciences, offers a critical, prudent and wise perspective that helps us look beyond the dizzying spiral of technological innovations and impacts. In her book ¿Ética o ideología de la inteligencia artificial? — “Ethics or ideology of artificial intelligence?” — the philosopher proposes an ethical framework for AI’s advance, while warning of the risks currently facing society and democracy. Ours is an age that prizes a misguided boldness rooted in arrogance over prudence, which Aristotle called the greatest intellectual virtue. Cover text: Adela Cortina, author of Aporofobia. Title: ¿Ética o ideología de la inteligencia artificial? — “Ethics or ideology of artificial intelligence?” Subtitle: El eclipse de la razón comunicativa en una sociedad tecnologizada — “The eclipse of communicative reason in a technological society”. Publisher/series: Paidós, Estado y Sociedad — “State and Society”. The ethical principles of the 4.0 revolution Adela Cortina argues that this new technological wave should adhere to the following ethical principles: 1) Beneficence: the benefits must reach everyone, not just a few. To achieve this, the author maintains, the state must intervene. 2) Autonomy and dignity: in the opening pages, Cortina draws attention to a crucial issue: “the immense difference between using intelligent systems when making decisions and delegating to those intelligent systems decisions that are significant for the lives of people and nature”. In this regard, she reminds us that “intelligent systems are not autonomous; they do not have free will”. Therefore, “decisions affecting people’s lives cannot be placed in the hands of intelligent machines without human oversight […] A human being must always make the final decision and be able to account for it, if necessary. Machines lack context and an environment; an environment can be created, but they lack common sense”. What if technology advances and AI acquires common sense? The philosopher argues that general intelligence cannot exist without a body: “machines lack the common-sense knowledge made possible by our embodied experiences”. 3) Explainability and accountability: we have a right to know how our data are used and how the algorithm handles them. “Believing that technologies are neutral is pure ideology.” “As Habermas rightly said, science and technology can become ideology: that distorted and distorting view of reality that allows the powerful to satisfy their illegitimate interests and exercise domination.” 4) Do no harm: full digital citizenship rights to address challenges such as cybersecurity, data protection, privacy, the protection of intimate life and protection from harmful content. 5) Promote a just world: particularly in relation to the impact on the labour market. The author refers to several solutions already examined in detail in this newsletter . Full translation of “Ethical principles of the 4.0 revolution”: Beneficence: ensure that technological benefits reach everyone, with state intervention. Autonomy and dignity: maintain human oversight of AI decisions to protect autonomy. Explainability: require transparency in the use of data and algorithms. Do no harm: protect digital citizens from cyber threats and harmful content. Promote a just world: address the impact on the labour market and promote fairness. Alongside establishing moral principles, the author reviews ethical frameworks that could be applied to intelligent systems . Cortina argues that “a deontological framework for integrating ethical rules into machines’ ‘brains’ is the most appropriate because, although the machine is not conscious of it, it will try to protect beings that are valuable in themselves […] My proposal is a dialogical deontology that uses the method of critical hermeneutics ”. In other words, some things are right as a matter of principle, such as respect for human dignity . The remaining principles and rules should be developed through complex public debate, rather than imposed by a handful of companies or governments. Those principles must also be subject to critical interpretation, to ensure that AI rests on ethics rather than on an ideology imposed through science or technology. Not just ethics and philosophy, but politics too Given this article’s limited space, I will confine myself to two key political issues, although Adela Cortina’s book contains many references to this field that I am sure will interest this newsletter’s readers. Geostrategy: the AI race is also a race for global hegemony. Presenting certain developments as inevitable or inherently “ethical” can serve to justify massive investment, selective deregulation or the adoption of technologies that ultimately concentrate power in a few corporations or states. In any event, she is very clear about the strategy the European Union should pursue: “in accordance with the basic principle of respect for human dignity, promoting AI is a moral, political and economic obligation for the European Union. If Europe does not rise to this challenge, it will be condemned to irrelevance”. The eclipse of communicative reason: this is perhaps the book’s most powerful concept for understanding AI’s impact on democracy. Cortina, a follower of Habermas, argues that the “technological society” is undergoing an “eclipse of communicative reason”. Connectivity intensified by social media and digital platforms does not necessarily translate into better, truthful and deliberative communication. On the contrary, “strategic reason” — manipulation, disinformation and polarisation — often prevails, seeking illegitimate advantage rather than mutual understanding. This eclipse is a “radical challenge to democracy”, because it makes it harder to build an inclusive “we” capable of taking decisions together. Public policy should therefore foster a digital ecosystem that promotes informed dialogue and “plain language”, rather than encouraging fragmentation, dogmatism and moralism — cancel culture. Finally, in response to these challenges, Adela Cortina turns to the crucial role of education . She recognises AI’s potential benefits in education, such as personalisation and access to knowledge, but issues a forceful warning about its risks: a widening digital divide, algorithmic bias and, fundamentally, the erosion of personal autonomy and critical thinking. Cortina proposes that education should help us think for ourselves while connecting well with others, encouraging public conversation and criticism . Until now, a robot’s morality belonged to science fiction. But we live in remarkable times, which have led even one of the most important philosophers in the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking world to reflect on AI’s ethical foundations. Read this book. It is straightforward, written for everyone , not for advanced readers of philosophy. I am sure you will enjoy it as much as I did and appreciate the significance of wisdom built on humility. Pablo Martín Diez Academic Director of Institución Educativa ALEPH and Editor of estrategIA

From innovation to action: artificial intelligence serving public administration in Chile Mauricio Pilleux describes an AI assistance system for Chilean women facing gender-based violence abroad and the incremental approach behind its development. Mauricio Pilleux Government & Public Services AI in Practice 084 Analysis From innovation to action: artificial intelligence serving public administration in Chile Archive note: published on 7 May 2025. This guest account preserves the author’s descriptions of the system, its results and its security arrangements at that time. The ECLAC quotation is translated from the Spanish source; its original English wording has not been verified. Violence against women continues to corrode our societies in 2025. Yet artificial intelligence can help us offer tangible responses in this field too. This week, estrategIA gives the floor to Mauricio Pilleux , CEO of Coderhub , to explain first-hand how his team, together with the Chilean government, has created a system to protect Chilean women who experience gender-based violence abroad. With promising early results, the project shows how AI, used well, can help us improve our society. In a world where digital transformation is advancing in leaps and bounds, Chile has already begun to establish itself as a regional leader in implementing AI-based solutions to improve the efficiency and quality of its public services. AI is already changing how the state interacts with citizens, optimising processes and creating new capabilities to address complex social challenges. Applying AI to the fight against gender-based violence States’ responsibility to protect their female citizens against gender-based violence extends beyond national borders. It is both a moral and a legal imperative within the human rights framework. According to the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), it is essential to “create an institutionalised mechanism at consular level, coordinated with national and local bodies, to assist and protect women who are victims of gender-based violence and migrant family members” . This recommendation, set out in the 2013 Montevideo Consensus on Population and Development, recognises that women moving across international borders face specific vulnerabilities. Gender-based violence is a serious global social problem. According to a UN Women study cited by the OECD, approximately 600 million women live in states that do not adequately criminalise domestic violence. This underlines the importance of countries extending protection to their female citizens regardless of their geographical location. In this context, Chile developed a technological solution to address this global challenge. Within the framework of the National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2021–2030, Chile’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Women and Gender Equity implemented an AI-based assistance system. This initiative marked an advance in how the Chilean state supports women experiencing violence abroad. Translation of the substantive text in the screenshot: Skip >> We provide information and guidance to Chilean women experiencing gender-based violence in another country. To improve your safety and experience in the app, we need to know your location. Enable GPS Continue without enabling GPS An AI assistance system for responding to gender-based violence abroad Translation of the substantive text in the screenshot: Chatbot Virtual Guidance Assistant for Chilean Women Abroad Usually responds within a few minutes. We are online Usually responds within a few minutes. Start conversation Navigation: Home · Chatbot · Networks How it works and its technological innovation What distinguishes this solution is its ability to go beyond simply providing information. The system uses advanced natural-language processing algorithms to: 1. Understand the user’s account: the platform analyses the narrative provided by the woman seeking help, identifying key elements that indicate the nature and severity of the situation. 2. Complete a case record in real time: as the interaction develops, the system asks questions, gathers relevant information and structures it into a case record, similar to one a trained official would complete. Translation of the substantive text in the screenshot. The contact details below are those displayed in the archived image, not verified contact routes for the service. Chatbot Virtual Guidance Assistant for Chilean Women Abroad Usually responds within a few seconds. User: I confirm that I am in a situation of risk. Assistant: We have collected the following information for your request for assistance: Contact information for the affected person Country: Germany City: Berlin Email: mila@mail.com Telephone number: +4971184850 Personal information for the affected person Please review the information and confirm whether it is correct. If you would like to change anything, please say so. Assistant label: Coni Message field: Write your message Developed by ContactsHub Navigation: Home · Chatbot · Networks 3. Assess whether referral is needed: using predefined protocols, the system determines whether the case requires in-person attention or specialist follow-up. 4. Provide location-specific information: the system identifies and provides details of the Chilean consulate nearest the user, as well as information about local support networks. 5. Transfer the information collected: when in-person attention is deemed necessary, the complete case record is automatically transferred to the relevant consulate. This entire process strictly follows the protocols established by Chile’s Ministry of Women and Ministry of Foreign Affairs, ensuring that the automated response maintains the necessary quality standards. Protecting sensitive data is crucial to this process. It implements end-to-end encryption and strict security protocols in accordance with Chilean Law 19.628, while also following the information security policies specified in ISO 27001. Impact and results The results of this implementation were immediate. In its first three months of operation, the system handled dozens of conversations, providing immediate guidance to women who needed information about what to do when experiencing violence abroad. The solution has proved particularly effective in: Removing barriers to access: women who could not have accessed traditional consular services because of distance, opening hours or fear have found an accessible route to help through the platform. Reducing response times: the system’s round-the-clock availability enables immediate attention, crucial in crisis situations. Improving the quality of referrals: by gathering structured information, it enables more accurate and effective referrals where necessary. Optimising consular resources: consular staff can focus on cases requiring specialist attention while the system handles information requests and the initial data-gathering stage. An incremental approach and lessons learnt This system was not developed in isolation, but as part of an incremental strategy. The first step was to implement a chatbot for self-service access by the general public to Chile’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. This reduced the volume of interactions that staff had to handle directly from 700 to 200 a day, representing not only a significant optimisation of resources but also an improvement in users’ experience and the coverage of their needs. Indeed, during 2024, 64% of interactions were handled through the interactive voice response system, or IVR, with only 36% requiring contact with a human agent. This gradual approach allows public institutions to learn, adjust and optimise technological solutions nimbly, ensuring not only operational efficiency but also sensitivity and adaptation to complex human circumstances. Ultimately, the future of AI in public administration can be built on this incremental model: start with simple solutions, demonstrate measurable value, then move towards deeper and more sophisticated AI integration. This approach can ensure that AI not only improves the state’s efficiency but also strengthens citizens’ trust in institutions and improves the quality of life of those who need it. The dawn of artificial muscle: how a new wave of intelligent robots could redraw the employment map On the eve of International Workers' Day, a look at humanoid robotics, its possible effects on jobs and the policies needed to manage the transition. Fernando Nieto Lobato Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Futures, Safety & Human Agency Government & Public Services 083 Analysis The dawn of artificial muscle: how a new wave of intelligent robots could redraw the employment map Archive note: published on 30 April 2025. Forecasts, robot specifications and policy references retain that date’s perspective. The quotation attributed to Marina Bill is translated from the Spanish source; its original English wording has not been verified. From steam to silicon: why we are talking about robots — and AI — today Tomorrow is 1 May, International Workers’ Day, a date born amid the clamour of nineteenth-century factories to demand an eight-hour working day . Almost a century and a half later, the very concept of work is beginning to enter a new phase. We are at another technological crossroads: the emergence of AI and a new generation of intelligent robots. Their true muscle is not just metal, but the advanced artificial intelligence — including generative approaches — that enables them to understand natural-language instructions, move nimbly on two legs and, most disruptively, learn complex tasks in a matter of hours, often training in hyperrealistic AI-generated simulations before interacting with the physical environment. This fusion of AI and robotics is what radically distinguishes the new humanoids and cobots — collaborative robots designed to work alongside humans in a shared environment — from their predecessors. Publishing this analysis today, on the eve of International Workers’ Day, is an urgent invitation to reflect on the nature of the work ahead of us. Following AI’s initial disruption of intellectual or “office” jobs, already under way, we can see another, equally powerful disruption reaching other kinds of employment within a few years as new generations of robots become widespread. A silent tsunami: the scale of the phenomenon Robotisation, as a general concept, is not merely a future promise: it is a reality accelerating at an unprecedented pace. The latest World Robotics (2024) report from the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) puts the number of operational industrial robots at 4.28 million worldwide, up 10% on the previous year . New installations have exceeded half a million a year for three consecutive years. Although Asia remains the epicentre, accounting for 70% of new installations, Europe, at 17%, and the Americas, at 10%, are also breaking their own records. “We have never seen such a rapid pace of adoption,” said IFR president Marina Bill. The robotic tide, driven by AI, is rising — and fast. Snapshots of a future already here: recent examples What distinguishes this new generation of robots is not just their number, but their intelligence and versatility. They are no longer merely mechanical arms inside cages. Let us look at several recent examples illustrating different aspects of this qualitative leap. Although this is by no means a systematic selection, we believe, dear readers, that seeing these prototypes in action can often be worth a thousand words: Archive media note: the Spanish article refers to demonstration videos that are not preserved as playable media or linked assets in the local source. No missing video destinations have been reconstructed. The humanoid arrives in the warehouse: recently, Digit , Agility Robotics’ bipedal robot, began working shoulder to shoulder with human operators in logistics centres belonging to giants such as Amazon. Handling containers weighing up to 16 kg, this scaled pilot marks humanoids’ entry into logistics, fertile ground for automating repetitive tasks. And it reaches the factory too: as can already be seen in this BMW video from just three weeks ago, humanoid robots are being integrated into vehicle assembly lines. The example also shows how striking technological advances in this field can be over just a few months. Robots that replicate themselves: in February, Apptronik announced an agreement with Jabil for its humanoid, Apollo , to take part in the assembly line. What is new? Among the parts it will assemble will be those of other Apollo robots. This milestone points not only to a drastic reduction in costs, but also to the emergence of general-purpose robots capable of adapting to different manufacturing tasks, including making their own “species”. Mastering fine dexterity: the last human stronghold? Delicate manipulation. Sanctuary AI challenged it in March by unveiling the seventh generation of its Phoenix robot, demonstrating how advanced tactile sensors and sophisticated multimodal AI models , capable of rapid learning, allow a task to be mastered in less than 24 hours. The barrier of manual dexterity is beginning to crack. A robot half-marathon in Beijing: at an event held on 19 April 2025, 21 humanoid robots joined 12,000 human runners in the Beijing half-marathon , marking the first time bipedal machines had competed in a 21-kilometre race. Developed by companies such as Noetix Robotics and DroidVP, the robots varied in size and design. Although many encountered difficulties such as falls and overheating, six completed the course. The standout was Tiangong Ultra, from the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre, which finished in 2 hours and 40 minutes thanks to its optimised design and an advanced algorithm imitating the human stride. Although most required constant human assistance, the event symbolises a significant advance in integrating AI and robotics into complex human activities, revealing both the progress achieved and the remaining challenges in humanoid robots’ autonomy and adaptability. The employment equation: destruction, creation and adaptation These examples are not mere anecdotes. They are the spearhead of a profound transformation. The robots already being developed, equipped with computer vision, natural-language processing and autonomous planning, are beginning to possess a “cognitive” capacity driven by the latest AI advances — from computer vision to language processing and reinforcement learning — that greatly expands the range of tasks that can be automated. Debate about their impact on employment is intense and polarised, with often conflicting views: The scale: the IMF warns that 40% of jobs worldwide (and up to 60% in advanced economies) contain tasks susceptible to full or partial automation by AI and advanced robotics in the coming years . The net balance: however, the World Economic Forum projects that, although 92 million jobs will be displaced by 2030, 170 million will be created in new occupational categories , from robot maintenance technicians and AI programmers to digital twin designers and robotics ethics specialists. Forecasting is extraordinarily difficult at a time of such rapid change, but many experts suggest that employment automation will follow a two-stage pattern: first, generative AI and agent systems will multiply productivity in intellectual and office tasks; a few years later, we will see more extensive robotisation of physical work, because the need to manufacture the machines physically creates significant bottlenecks for mass global adoption. When agile, low-cost, general-purpose robots become widespread in factories, warehouses and services, many manual functions will require only minimal supervisory teams. Although new occupations will emerge around the design, maintenance and ethical governance of these technologies, their rate of creation will struggle to offset, in the short and medium term, the net destruction of traditional jobs brought about by this twin productivity boost. The real challenge will be less about slowing technical progress than managing a transition that, without agile policies for redistribution, new skills training and social protection, could lead to structural unemployment and ever-deeper inequalities. Towards 2030–2035: five key trends to watch The current pace of robotics development, combined with AI, suggests acceleration over the next five years. Five trends could set the direction: Mass deployment of humanoids: China’s ambitious plan to establish a complete supply chain for bipedal robots in 2025 and integrate them deeply into its economy by 2027 will push prices down and accelerate global adoption. Cobots for everyone: falling sensor prices and easier programming, even by voice, will mean collaborative robots cease to be the exclusive preserve of large corporations and reach small and medium-sized businesses, becoming as commonplace as 3D printers are today. Deep AI–robotics convergence and generative training: generative AI , driven by Nvidia, OpenAI, Google and others, not only strengthens robots’ “brains” but revolutionises their training . It is used to create vast simulations in which robots learn complex skills, such as fine manipulation or bipedal navigation, before deployment. These foundation models for robotics will also make it possible to transfer skills almost effortlessly between different robot body types, creating far more versatile physical agents. New capital–labour dynamics: when an advanced robot costs less than the average annual salary in a developed country, capital–labour elasticity will increase. This could intensify downward pressure on wages for tasks that machines can easily replicate. Proactive regulation: the entry into force of rules such as the European AI Act will classify many workplace robots as high-risk systems. This will require safety audits, impact assessments and greater algorithmic transparency before they can be marketed. Navigating the transition: towards a robotic social pact To ensure that the promise of a “robotic dividend” over the coming decades — higher productivity and freedom from arduous tasks — does not widen the social divide, action on several fronts is surely crucial , as various international organisations recommend: Radical lifelong learning: strong tax incentives for companies investing in reskilling and upskilling, and agile micro-credential systems that allow workers to acquire new skills quickly. Adaptive safety nets: modernise social protection through sectoral transition funds, perhaps financed by a tax on extreme automation or the resulting profits, to support workers during retraining. Shared algorithmic governance: encourage trade union and worker participation in overseeing algorithms that manage shifts, allocate tasks, assess performance or even contribute to dismissal decisions. Ethics and safety by design: require safe-by-design principles for robots that physically interact with humans, and explainability obligations for those making autonomous decisions with a significant impact. Conclusions Robots that load pallets at Amazon, assemble themselves or run half-marathons are no longer science fiction: they are at the forefront of the present and foreshadow a qualitative shift in the relationship between humans and machines at work. History teaches us that societies prosper by embracing innovation while investing in their human capital and robust safety nets. The key question is not whether they will arrive, but when and, above all, how we will collectively manage their impact. On this eve of Workers’ Day, the best way to honour past struggles is not to fear machines, but to prepare ourselves to think actively about our place alongside them. The aim is for artificial muscle to free us from the tedious and dangerous, boost productivity and generate resources to invest more in what is distinctly human: creativity, care, strategy and, yes, leisure too.
