AI Index 2025: the state of AI in politics and public power Stanford's AI Index 2025 through the lens of regulation, public investment, geopolitical competition, responsible AI and public trust. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 082 Analysis AI Index 2025: the state of AI in politics and public power Archive note: published on 23 April 2025. This analysis preserves the report figures, policy timelines and investment announcements as described in the original article; it is not an update on their subsequent implementation. The year 2024 marked a turning point in the relationship between artificial intelligence, politics and global governance. What until recently had been theoretical debates and nascent national strategies became a wave of concrete action: binding regulations, massive public investment and an unprecedented intensification of international cooperation — and competition. The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025 , published on 7 April by Stanford University’s Institute for Human-Centered AI, documents this ferment and offers a detailed picture of a technological field that is no longer the future, but a present reality demanding urgent political attention. For estrategIA, this report is essential reading : last year’s edition was our “recommendation of the week” in issue 30 of estrategIA . In this issue, we unpack the key findings of the 2025 edition, focusing chiefly on what its more than 450 pages tell us about the intersection of AI and public power . Chapter 6 is devoted to “Policy and Governance”, but many questions relevant to government and politics also appear elsewhere in the report. The regulatory explosion: from debate to concrete action If 2023 was the year generative AI entered global public consciousness, 2024 was the year governments and legislators began responding. The AI Index reveals a dramatic increase in regulatory activity. Worldwide, mentions of “artificial intelligence” in legislative proceedings across 75 countries rose by 21.3% in 2024 alone , reaching nine times their 2016 level. Figure 6.2.14, original English title: “Number of mentions of AI in legislative proceedings in 75 select geographic areas, 2016–24”. Source: AI Index, 2025; chart: 2025 AI Index report. The horizontal axis runs annually from 2016 to 2024; the vertical axis is the number of mentions. The line rises from roughly 200 in 2016 to around 860 in 2018, falls slightly and levels off in 2019–20, rises in 2021, dips in 2022, then climbs sharply in 2023–24. Its explicitly labelled final value is 1,889. Intermediate values are unlabelled in the image; the approximate descriptions here are not an exact data transcription. In the United States, the trend is even more pronounced. At federal level, 59 AI-related regulations were introduced in 2024 , more than double the 25 in 2023, with twice as many government agencies involved. Although the passage of comprehensive federal laws remains slow — only four passed in 2024 out of 221 proposals — the regulatory machinery of executive orders and agency guidance is in full operation. Yet the true legislative epicentre in the US lies in the states: the number of state AI laws soared from 49 in 2023 to 131 in 2024 . California leads the charge, but many other states are actively legislating, particularly on immediate concerns such as deepfakes . By the end of 2024, 24 states already had specific laws regulating or penalising the malicious use of AI-generated synthetic content, up from just five the previous year: a direct response to fears about electoral integrity and personal protection. Internationally, the European Union reached a milestone with the final approval of its ambitious Artificial Intelligence Act , the world’s first horizontal, risk-based regulatory framework. Although it will take full effect progressively through 2026, its approach sets a global precedent by classifying AI systems by risk level and imposing strict obligations on those deemed “high risk”. Massive public investment in AI Alongside regulation, 2024 saw an unprecedented financial commitment by states to strengthening their AI ecosystems. AI has become established as a strategic national asset, and governments are investing billions to avoid falling behind. Canada announced a $2.4 billion package to secure its “AI advantage”. France committed €109 billion to a wider technology plan prioritising AI. India launched its “IndiaAI Mission” with $1.25 billion . Saudi Arabia unveiled “Project Transcendence”, an ambitious $100 billion strategic project to establish itself as a global technology hub, including a strong commitment to Arabic-language AI models in collaboration with Google. China, meanwhile, created a new $47.5 billion state fund focused on advanced semiconductors, which are crucial to AI. These astronomical sums contrast with public investment in previous years and reflect a new doctrine: technological sovereignty in AI is a matter of national security and economic competitiveness. Interestingly, the AI Index highlights differences in how that money is spent. In the United States, analysis of public contracts shows a strong concentration in the Department of Defense —75% of spending in 2023 . In Europe, public AI investment is more evenly distributed among general public services, education and health, with defence still accounting for less than 1%. The geopolitics of AI: intense competition and new cooperation AI is inevitably a new arena of geopolitics. The United States retains its lead at the frontier of innovation , producing 40 of the 58 notable AI models in 2024, and attracts the most private investment , at $109 billion. China, however, leads in the volume of scientific output , accounting for 23.2% of global publications, and patents , at almost 70% of the global total. Crucially, it has dramatically narrowed the technical performance gap between its models and their rivals. By the end of 2024, the best Chinese models had reached near-parity with Western ones on key benchmarks such as MMLU and HumanEval . Competition is fierce, as reflected in measures such as US controls on exports of advanced semiconductors to China. Original English chart: “Performance of top United States vs. Chinese models on LMSYS Chatbot Arena”. Source: LMSYS, 2025; chart: 2025 AI Index report. Monthly dates run from January 2024 to February 2025 on the horizontal axis, with score on the vertical axis. The US line stays above China’s throughout. Both rise overall: the US series has plateaux early in 2024 and in May–July, then an October dip before rising again; the Chinese series jumps in May, is nearly flat through August, and rises strongly late in the period. The printed endpoint scores are 1,385 for the United States and 1,362 for China. Other plotted points do not have exact numerical labels. But 2024 was not only about competition. International cooperation to address shared risks also intensified. The most visible milestone was the creation of the International Network of AI Safety Institutes , formally launched in November 2024, bringing together bodies from the United States, the United Kingdom, the EU, Canada, France, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Australia and Kenya. Its aim is to coordinate research on the safety of advanced models, manage synthetic-content risks and develop common standards. Similar initiatives emerged from the G7, through the Hiroshima AI Process, and the OECD, seeking a shared language and shared expectations for responsible AI. In search of responsible AI Much of the political and regulatory activity in 2024 revolved around the need for responsible AI, or RAI. The principles of transparency, explainability, fairness, safety and accountability recur in almost every national strategy and international framework. This responds both to ethical concerns and to the pragmatic need to build public trust so that AI can be adopted. The AI Index reveals that, although corporate awareness of RAI risks has increased — privacy and cybersecurity are the main concerns — effective implementation of mitigation measures is lagging behind . Only a small proportion of companies systematically carry out rigorous bias audits or impact assessments. This is where public policy has a crucial role to play, encouraging or requiring better practice. New technical benchmarks for evaluating models’ safety and factual accuracy emerged, and developers’ transparency improved, but opaque areas remain. One emerging challenge with political implications is the shrinking of the “data commons” : growing restrictions on scraping public web data could limit the diversity and quality of data available to train future models, potentially affecting competition and fairness. Public perceptions: trust or caution? Public opinion, the central subject of the report’s eighth and final chapter, is a key gauge of AI’s political viability. The document presents a complex picture: Growing but uneven optimism: globally, 55% believe AI will bring more benefits than drawbacks, up from 52% in 2022. Yet regional differences are enormous: 83% in China versus 39% in the United States. Strikingly, optimism has grown most in previously sceptical countries, with Germany up 10% and France up 10%. Usefulness versus risk: people value AI for saving time and for entertainment, but are wary of its impact on health, the economy and job quality. Support for regulation: both the general public and local legislators in the US show strong support for AI regulation. Low institutional trust: mistrust persists towards technology companies and their ability to protect personal data — only 47% trust them globally — and ensure fairness, with belief in AI’s impartiality declining. Those are the main messages the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025 offers on AI, politics and government, but the report also contains a series of highly significant general conclusions . Its own summary is available on its website and in the report’s opening pages. Below, we offer our own condensed version , prepared, like the rest of this article, with o3 and Gemini Pro 2.5, with the infographic generated using Napkin.ai. Full translation of “Key findings of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025”: Acceleration and integration: AI is deeply integrated into the economy, science and daily life. The coming years promise major changes. Technical performance: AI models consistently surpass benchmarks, even the newest and most difficult ones. Improvement is accelerating. Government action: global regulatory activity is rapidly intensifying. Multiple nations are making massive public investments in AI infrastructure and development. Impact on science: AI is revolutionising drug discovery and medicine, opening new scientific horizons and earning recognition such as Nobel Prizes. Public opinion: global sentiment towards AI is positive, though it varies greatly between countries. Concern about ethics, privacy and fairness is growing. Business investment and adoption: private investment in AI is breaking records, and corporate adoption has soared. Responsible AI: AI-related incidents and concern about ethics, bias and safety are increasing. Efficiency and accessibility: AI is becoming cheaper and more efficient, lowering barriers to entry and widening access. Industrial dominance: industry develops powerful AI models. Academia remains highly important in research. Persistent challenges: reasoning, reliability and disinformation remain challenges. Conclusions The AI Index Report 2025 confirms that 2024 was the year the intersection of AI, politics and government reached critical mass. The speed of technical advances is forcing public actors to move with unprecedented agility. Good regulation is no longer optional, but a need perceived around the world. Public investment has become a fundamental geopolitical instrument. And international cooperation, though still emerging, is recognised as indispensable for addressing cross-border challenges such as the safety of advanced models and disinformation. Yet the challenges are immense. How can we regulate effectively without killing innovation in a technology that evolves every few months? How can we ensure that massive public investment delivers broad social benefits rather than narrow competitive advantages? How can we make sure responsible AI goes beyond statements of principle and is embedded in how systems are actually designed and deployed? And how can we manage the gap between AI’s technical capabilities and the understanding — and trust — of the public and many decision-makers? The Stanford report offers no easy answers, but it does provide crucial data to inform the debate. It shows a world that has decisively awoken to the AI age and is beginning to construct the rules of the game, rapidly and sometimes chaotically. The next few years will be decisive in determining whether we can forge adaptive, evidence-based, human-centred global governance that allows us to navigate the most profound transformation since the Industrial Revolution. For estrategIA readers, the report’s message is already clear: AI is no longer merely a technical or economic matter. It is also, and very significantly, a matter of politics and global governance. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

The old and the new: the Catholic Church confronts artificial intelligence A Holy Week reflection on Antiqua et Nova, the Vatican's view of AI, and the place of human dignity, solidarity and philosophical judgement in technological change. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency 081 Review & commentary The old and the new: the Catholic Church confronts artificial intelligence Archive note: published on 16 April 2025. This essay retains its Holy Week context and the author’s contemporary account of the Vatican’s position. The final quotation from Demis Hassabis is retranslated from the author’s Spanish translation; its original English wording has not been verified. Last January, while technology leaders were presenting their latest artificial intelligence creations at global technology fairs, the Vatican quietly published a document that few had expected. Under the Latin title Antiqua et Nova , the Holy See set out its official position on artificial intelligence . Since this newsletter is being sent during Holy Week, several weeks ago we set aside this Holy Wednesday to examine it and reflect on the unexpected marriage between ancient religious wisdom and dizzying technological innovation. This document , signed by the Dicasteries for the Doctrine of the Faith and for Culture and Education, is perhaps the Catholic Church’s most ambitious effort to date to engage with the ethical and social questions raised by AI. Unlike other religious institutions, which have maintained a cautious or distant stance, the Church has decided to intervene actively in the debate. At first sight, it might seem anachronistic for a two-thousand-year-old institution to take a position in debates dominated by companies such as Google or Microsoft. Yet this move has not come out of nowhere. Back in 2020, the Vatican promoted the Rome Call for AI Ethics , establishing principles such as transparency, inclusion and responsibility. Now, five years later, Antiqua et Nova explores these issues in considerably greater depth, adding theological and ethical nuances that go beyond simple technical recommendations. The Vatican’s central concern is defending human dignity in the face of technology’s omnipresence. At a time when AI can imitate human texts, images and voices with alarming accuracy, the Church warns of the risk of what it calls “algorithmic post-truth”: the loss of a shared, objective truth as a point of reference. Far from trivial, this problem strikes at the very heart of an institution that has historically defended the existence of universal, immutable truths. But the Church does not stop at general warnings. It specifically criticises concrete AI applications such as the use of lethal autonomous weapons, a concern Pope Francis has already expressed publicly in international forums. In clear and forceful terms, the Vatican states that no decision about human life should ever be delegated to a machine. The document also addresses AI’s economic and social impact at length, highlighting the ethical dilemma of job displacement caused by automation. The Vatican’s view is clear: if automation displaces jobs, society has a moral obligation to ensure that nobody is excluded. In a nod to contemporary debates, the text mentions, albeit only indirectly, the possibility of introducing measures such as universal basic income, in line with earlier remarks by Pope Francis in September 2024 , when he suggested that guaranteeing a basic income in an age of automation is not mere charity, but social justice. It is significant that Antiqua et Nova returns to traditional ethical concepts such as justice, prudence and solidarity, applying them directly to a modern technological context. The aim is not simply to prevent AI’s most obvious abuses, but to ensure that technological progress truly serves the common good, strengthening the social fabric rather than eroding it. The Church also offers practical guidance to ensure that AI does not replace what is essentially human, particularly in areas such as education, healthcare and environmental stewardship. It recognises the potential benefits, from improving access to education to enabling more accurate medical diagnoses, or even helping to fight climate change through advanced predictive systems. Yet it warns that these advantages must always be used to complement, rather than replace, conscious and ethical human decisions. One particularly striking point is the warning about technological idolatry. The Church cautions against the modern temptation to see AI as a substitute for God, something more dangerous than traditional idols precisely because machines can imitate human intelligence. Ultimately, the Church insists on maintaining the correct hierarchy: artificial intelligence, however powerful, must always remain a tool in the service of human beings, never the other way round. This position is not merely theoretical. The Vatican has decided to lead by example, implementing internal regulations within its own territory that explicitly prohibit any AI application that could harm human dignity or foster inequalities. By establishing a special AI Commission, the Holy See seeks to show the world that technological advances can be integrated within robust, coherent ethical governance. Translation of the original table, “Pillars of the position set out in Antiqua et Nova”. The two columns list principles and concerns; the final two cells in the principles column are empty in the original. | Guiding principles of the Vatican’s position | Key concerns / warnings | | --- | --- | | Human dignity as the supreme value | Dehumanisation: relationships, work, health | | AI as a tool/product, not equal to a human being | Inequality and discrimination | | Service to humanity and the common good | Job displacement / deskilling | | Human responsibility and oversight are essential | Disinformation and erosion of truth | | Need for an ethical framework: “algor-ethics” | Privacy violations and surveillance | | Importance of the “wisdom of the heart” | Loss of human agency / autonomy | | Promotion of integral human development | Risks of anthropomorphism | | Defence of truth and trust | Lethal autonomous weapons | | | Environmental impact | | | Potential for idolatry | Translation of the original diagram, “Principles of the Vatican’s position”: Human dignity: emphasises the inherent worth of every individual. AI as a tool: recognises AI as a tool, not an equal. Service to humanity: prioritises the common good and service to others. Responsibility: stresses the essential role of human oversight in AI. Ethical framework: advocates ethics in AI development. Wisdom of the heart: promotes emotional intelligence and empathy. Integral human development: supports individuals’ holistic growth. Defence of truth: defends truth and trust in information. The reception of Antiqua et Nova has been mixed. Some technology ethics experts see it as a valuable contribution to the global debate, particularly given the Church’s moral authority. Others, however, have questioned the Vatican’s real ability to influence an industry dominated by technology giants and governments with agendas of their own. Regardless of these criticisms, the Church has achieved something important: firmly placing the central ethical question surrounding AI on the table. At its heart, this document asks fundamental questions. What kind of society do we want to build with the help of artificial intelligence? What does “progress” really mean when we are talking about machines capable of replicating and even surpassing human abilities? The Vatican’s answer is that true progress places human beings at the centre, recognising and defending their inherent dignity in the face of any technological innovation. In an age of rapid change, perhaps it is precisely this ancient wisdom that we most need to hear so that, even if we do not agree with everything it proposes, we can ask the right questions. As the document’s title suggests, perhaps the meeting of the old and the new is where we can find the ethical and philosophical answers that the age of artificial intelligence so desperately demands. This connects with recent remarks by last year’s Nobel laureate in Chemistry and Google’s AI leader, Demis Hassabis — translated here from our Spanish rendering : “I think we need great philosophers. Where are they? The next great thinkers… the equivalents of Kant, Wittgenstein, even Aristotle. I think we are going to need them to help society navigate the next step. AGI and ASI are going to change humanity and the human condition.” Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

Ten uses for ChatGPT's new image-generation system: how easy AI image creation could redraw political communication Thirty-one preserved images illustrate ten historical GPT-4o experiments in visual political communication, with complete prompts and accessible English text. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Government & Public Services 080 Practical experiment Ten uses for ChatGPT's new image-generation system: how easy AI image creation could redraw political communication Archive note: this visual exploration was published on 9 April 2025. It preserves the original experiments, prompts, synthetic examples and historical claims about GPT-4o; the retained images have not been regenerated. Translations of their text appear alongside them. Original newsletter note: because this week's newsletter contains dozens of images , it will be very long and probably will not arrive complete in your email. If you find that the content has been cut off, please open the Substack app to read it . This time, we are also not providing an audio version of the main article: because it is so predominantly visual, simply listening to it would make little sense. After last week's dense and important article about the debate on universal basic income amid AI's rapid advance , this week we have decided to bring you almost the opposite: an imaginative exploration of the impressive possibilities offered by GPT-4o's new image-generation model, even to those of us without advanced design knowledge or skills in drawing or complex computer image editing . That said, as in any other field where AI is developing rapidly, experts and people with greater knowledge of the subject are very likely to get the most out of it. These developments are also likely to have much less impact on high-budget presidential or national campaigns, or communications by large governments, which can afford extensive teams of specialist professionals—many of whom will also use and make the most of these new technologies. But for many rank-and-file politicians and small governments, these new tools could directly and substantially multiply the impact of their visual communication strategies. Best of all, every one of you can already use this model in ChatGPT, even free of charge, albeit with a daily usage limit. This article's main purpose is to encourage you to try it and experiment. Before showing you the results of our exploration and the examples we have created over the past few days, we would like to highlight briefly what makes this image generator stand out “above the competition”: its strong fidelity to what it is asked to do , technically known as “prompt adherence”, and the remarkable visual quality of the results , even when it is asked to include text within the image. Coupled with enormous ease of use—you simply use it within ChatGPT with very straightforward instructions, as we will see—this makes it an excellent model. As always, remember that this is the worst AI we will use for the rest of our lives, and that these systems improve very quickly. It can do a great many interesting things beyond filling social media with beautiful “Ghibli-style” images. Retained example post by Andy Orsow, @andyorsow. Its original English caption reads: “Ghibli is over, muppets are now.” The screenshot is dated 26 March 2025 at 15:41 and shows 3.1 million views. The synthetic image depicts three puppet-like figures in a presidential setting; a box bears the generated wording “PRESIDENT PRESIDENTIAL”. One brief point before we begin looking at the interesting or curious examples we have created over the past few days: although the model works with very simple, short prompts—instructions—you can achieve much better results if you know exactly what to ask for and compose more detailed instructions. This is one area in which image and design professionals bring clear added value. Even so, you can always iterate from a simple starting point. In general, all the prompts we used in this exploration are direct, one-line instructions, unless we explicitly state otherwise. One concrete example of how different instructions can sometimes lead to more advanced results is another style that has been highly successful on social media: generating marble sculptures from any photograph, even in a particular colour, which could be that of a political party. To begin with, I would simply give the model Obama's image from Wikipedia and ask something like: “Transform that image into a marble sculpture.” The result of the simple prompt: a synthetic marble treatment of the portrait described above. The result is not bad. But a creator with expertise in these matters, Umesh , would write instructions such as the following and obtain more advanced effects. Instructions in this format were also necessary to obtain good results with other image models such as Midjourney or Stable Diffusion. The 4o model is infinitely more intelligent in its comprehension because of the kind of AI model it is, although we will not get into technical discussions here. A photorealistic image of an ultra-detailed [COLOR] calacatta elegant sculpture bust of the subject in image made of shining marble. The sculpture should display smooth and reflective marble surface, emphasizing its luster and artistic craftsmanship. The design is elegant, highlighting the beauty and depth of marble. The lighting in the image should enhance the sculpture's contours and textures, creating a visually stunning and mesmerizing effect The prompt above was already in English in the original article and is reproduced unchanged. The more detailed prompt's white-marble bust, with a polished, reflective surface. And in the party's colour, replacing white with blue in the [COLOR] parameter: The blue-marble variation of the same synthetic portrait treatment. Best of all, you are not limited to textual instructions. Those who can draw—I probably could not even manage a diagram like the one below—can make a sketch on paper, give ChatGPT a photograph of it, and obtain a result like this: The original English prompt in the screenshot reads: turn this sketch into a hyper realistic youtube thumbnail 1920x1080. the ONLY text that should stay during the creation process is "1000 MPH" and the arrow right next to it. the rest of the text are instructions about details for you to follow The sketch labels a light, hat, blue sky, baseball bat, baseball, flames/fire, jersey and trees, alongside “1000 MPH” and its arrow. The result, labelled “Image created”, shows a batter hitting a flaming baseball, with “1000 MPH” and the arrow retained. The labels function as drawing instructions rather than a factual sports claim. Ten interesting or unusual possible uses of 4o's image-generation model in ChatGPT for politics and government 1. Make campaign posters in different visual styles simply by asking in the prompt I simply ask ChatGPT for a campaign poster, it suggests different styles, and I try them out… The images below are utopian retrofuturist propaganda—the first one it generates, with text it also writes—then a Simpsons-style version, and finally futuristic pre-Columbian art, a style suggested by ChatGPT. Imagination is the limit, and AI itself can suggest styles. Retrofuturist example. Poster text: “Imagine a better tomorrow. Today, we're backing you.” Simpsons-style example, with the same text: “Imagine a better tomorrow. Today, we're backing you.” Futuristic pre-Columbian example. The readable wording says: “Imagine … a better tomorrow. We're backing you.” Some generated lettering after “IMAGINA” is malformed; it has not been reconstructed as a clean original slogan. 2. Turn any image into a poster, advertisement or social media asset, using one of the model's main strengths: handling text, even in Spanish For this example, we use an image of Elena Vidal, the virtual candidate we created with AI last year for the fictional party Europa Estoica Unida, ahead of the European elections . The original synthetic portrait of Elena Vidal used as input. We give the model a very simple instruction along with the image: Transform that image into an advertisement for the fictional party “Europa Estoica Unida”. And here is the result. Nothing spectacular, but it took 30 seconds and required no design software. The generated poster reads “Europa Estoica Unida”—“United Stoic Europe”—and “For a strong and serene Europe”. This is the fictional party described above. 3. Create an action figure, for example of a party leader This is another style that has been highly successful on social media, and it is fairly simple. We can generate the figure with or without packaging. The main point to specify in the prompt is the list of items we want alongside it. Boxed synthetic action figure labelled “BARACK OBAMA”, with a laptop, mug, phone, cap and sunglasses. The mug and cap also carry the name “OBAMA”. Unboxed variation, with a cap, mug, notebook and sunglasses; the name “OBAMA” appears on the first three accessories. It can also create group action figures from images such as this one of a US–EU summit in 2023: The source photograph used for the group example, showing three leaders at the summit described in the article. The generated boxed group version. The packaging reads “Action figures”. 4. Add objects to images The new image model is also fairly good at adding any object to an image. This could be used, for example, to present documents—a budget, a new law… In our example, we have simply set Obama reading Don Quixote . Synthetic reading scene. The book cover reads “Miguel de Cervantes”, “Don Quijote de la Mancha” and “Edition by Francisco Rico”; the small generated publisher lettering is distorted. This is an image-editing demonstration, not a documentary photograph. 5. Create comics that explain concepts There are still occasional errors in the text, which will surely improve in later versions. But you can ask the new model to generate comics without even providing a script, because it draws on GPT-4o's capabilities and knowledge. Undoubtedly one of our favourite functions. Translation of the prompt in the screenshot: “Create a four-panel comic in Spanish explaining what inflation is.” The interface says “Image created”. The four panels read: “What is inflation?” “It is the general rise in prices”, illustrated by bread increasing from $10 to $12. “With inflation, shopping becomes more expensive.” “Money is worth less over time.” Complete translation of the generated comic “How to vote in Spain”: Voting location: the building is labelled “Polling station”. Identification: a voter shows an identity document. Selected ballot paper: the visible paper is labelled “Ballot paper”; another label is cut off. Booth. Vote: a paper labelled “Vote” is shown being marked with an X. Insert the vote: a paper labelled “Ballot paper” is placed in a ballot box. Complete translation of the generated comic “Functions of the Prime Minister”: | Panel heading | Panel text | | --- | --- | | Direct the government's work | Coordinates and supervises the work of ministers. | | Represent the state | Acts on Spain's behalf in international relations. | | Propose candidates | Submits proposals to the King for the appointment of office-holders. | | Draw up a bill | Promotes the creation of laws and presents them for debate. The document shown is labelled “Bill”. | | Resolve conflicts between administrations | Settles disputes that may arise between public administrations. | | Request a vote of confidence | May ask Congress for a vote reaffirming its support. | These are the original generated panels' claims, translated for accessibility; they are not a verified account of constitutional powers. 6. Create cartoons, political panels and caricatures We asked for a political cartoon and it generated these two. The script is entirely ChatGPT's, and this is part of its explanation of what it created: “The cartoon criticises depersonalisation and narcissism in modern politics. It portrays politicians as prefabricated products, without critical thought, obsessed with their own image, incapable of representing anything beyond themselves… when they do not even have an identity of their own.” The explanation above is translated from ChatGPT's Spanish wording quoted in the original article. Complete cartoon text: “The politician who did not exist.” A spectator asks, “And where does he live?” The answer is, “On the campaign servers.” The headless politician's speech bubble reads, literally: “The person you admire most of all is, of course, me.” The Spanish uses “admira”, with its subject left unstated; this wording is retained rather than silently changed to “I admire”. The model is also very capable at generating caricatures, such as this one of Barack Obama based on his Wikipedia image: The generated caricature retains the portrait's crossed-arm pose, exaggerating the smile and facial features. 7. Generate memes, for example through contrasts or popular-culture references The new model can also be excellent for making simple contrast memes, even exaggerated ones, of the kind familiar in party politics. This one, related to last week's article, came to mind readily: Complete meme text: “2030. Without universal basic income. With universal basic income.” The upper panel depicts distress and deprivation; the lower depicts smiling people beside a home. This is the article's illustrative contrast, not an observed result. And, of course, it can generate it in a Ghibli style too: The same meme, restyled: “2030. Without universal basic income. With universal basic income.” It is also a rich resource for creating memes around trending concepts or ones deeply rooted in popular culture. The following example was generated automatically simply by uploading the image of TVE's four-way debate in 2019 and asking it to turn the participants into members of the Hogwarts houses: The synthetic edit gives the four debate participants robes in the colours of the Hogwarts houses; it is not a photograph of an actual costumed debate. Or putting anyone into a film, following this prompt by Javi López : The screenshot shows two input photographs and a synthetic boxing-film result. Its interface labels mean “Create an image” and “Image created”. The prompt itself is already in English and reads: "Edit the cinematic image while keeping the same aspect ratio and without changing the colors. Make sure to do a proper white balance (don’t push it toward that yellow tint again, seriously mfkr, you always do that). Also, edit the face area to replace the woman's face with the one from the other photo (the one with the woman alone) but whatever it takes so it doesn't look pasted or badly done in Photoshop, making sure the body proportions are perfect and he even looks handsome on top of that." 8. Transform any space to see how it would look This is a prompt I have seen online in the context of home renovation and furnishing rooms, and it works very well. But it can be applied to any space—in this example, the press room of Spain's Congress of Deputies. It could have very interesting applications in designing stages for rallies, backdrops for special campaigns… Complete translation of the prompt shown beside “Create an image”: “Change the background of this press room to a different one, for example a brick wall, to see how it would look.” The response is labelled “Image created”. Create awareness campaigns GPT-4o can suggest and generate very powerful images to express ideas visually, such as this example: The original generated awareness poster reads: “This is what happens when we do not recycle.” It depicts a globe surrounded by rubbish beneath a smoky sky. 10. Visualise the future, especially infrastructure For example, by generating a new sports complex on a map: Complete translation of the prompt in the screenshot: “Create a sports complex in the southern part of this satellite image. The aim is to show what a development planned for that area would look like.” The interface labels read “Create image” and “Image created”. The generated result adds a running track, football pitch, courts, a building and parking. Small place labels in the generated map are distorted; this is a concept demonstration rather than a verified site plan. It can create a concept to help people visualise it: Generated concept image. The heading reads “New health centre” and the building is labelled “Health centre”. And it can produce visually powerful “before and after” images for the public, for example showing how a run-down neighbourhood would change following a public intervention. The synthetic comparison is labelled “Before” and “After”, contrasting deteriorated housing with a renewed neighbourhood. It illustrates a possible transformation rather than documenting completed works. These are just a few examples. Imagination, common sense and ethics—crucial here, because not everything that can easily be done should be done—are the only limits to a technology that is already excellent in its ease of use and results . Moreover, because it can be used directly within ChatGPT with 4o, the model itself offers new suggestions and options. We encourage you to try, experiment and create. And if you would like more ideas or need inspiration, here is an interesting list I have put together of visual artists specialising in AI on X.
