Rewriting the social contract in the age of thinking machines: universal basic income in the AI storm An argument for debating universal basic income before large-scale AI disruption, covering its history, purposes, funding, uncertainties and social meaning. Fernando Nieto Lobato Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency 079 Essay Rewriting the social contract in the age of thinking machines: universal basic income in the AI storm Introduction: why this important article matters In recent weeks, we have seen numerous statements by prominent figures and experts drawing direct attention to something that those of us who follow AI closely already know, but that we believe most of the population knows almost nothing about: the disruptive potential of the artificial intelligence revolution we are living through. To give a few examples: Bill Gates said on The Tonight Show that, within ten years, AI would provide everyone with top-level medical advice and personalised education for free, and that the other side of this “free intelligence” would be that AI could take over most jobs . A few days earlier, Dario Amodei, Anthropic's CEO, said that AI could write all programming code within a year . Javi López , one of Spain's leading AI entrepreneurs, reflected on X, as ChatGPT's new image-generation system arrived, that “we are heading towards a world in which we will be able to create anything using nothing more than natural language and gestures” . On the occasion of that same release, AI communicator Jon Hernández , whose interview with José María Lassalle discussing these issues we recommended a few issues ago , made this blunt statement on X: “Joking aside, making Totoro-style pictures is cool and all, but today a whole load of companies have been wrecked and another profession has been put at risk of extinction. Let that sink in, and maybe we'll fucking wake up at last and realise what's coming.” Translation note: quotations in this introduction are translated from the Spanish wording reproduced in the original article. No original English wording or recordings have been independently verified for this edition. These are just four recent examples, but there are many more. In truth, major AI companies and laboratories have been warning us for years about this technology's transformative power. Everything seems to suggest that, in less than a decade, we will be living in a rather different world, one in which work as we know it could be a very different reality for most people. In this context, one of the main tools considered for addressing the socioeconomic earthquake is the introduction of universal basic income , although, as you will see, the idea is centuries old. We think the concept is far less widely understood than it deserves to be, given the revolution ahead . It is crucial to begin discussing this solution and how to implement it—or how to devise alternatives, because changing nothing will not do. We have therefore devoted this article to an initial introduction , with help from all the deep-research tools we recommended in issue 75 : what universal basic income is, why it might be badly needed with the arrival of artificial general intelligence (AGI), and some key ideas about its meaning and implementation. Crucially , beyond recognising the intrinsic dignity of human beings in its own right, this would be a world in which it is not that people do not want to work: there may very well be no work for the majority . Universal basic income: a key option as artificial general intelligence approaches Progress in artificial intelligence is no longer measured in decades but in months. From algorithms that optimise logistics to language models that write code or poetry, AI is reshaping entire industries . Yet the horizon holds an even more profound transformation: the arrival of artificial general intelligence, systems with cognitive capabilities comparable to, or even greater than, those of humans across a broad range of tasks. This prospect, together with the hypothetical superintelligence that would follow shortly afterwards, raises fundamental questions about the very structure of our economies and societies, particularly the future of work . Faced with the increasingly real possibility of automation on a massive scale, an idea once relegated to the margins of political debate—universal basic income, or UBI—emerges as a proposal demanding urgent, pragmatic consideration. What is universal basic income? In essence, universal basic income is a regular, individual, unconditional cash payment made by the state to all its citizens or residents . Its universality and unconditionality distinguish it sharply from traditional benefits, which tend to be selective and temporary, and require something in return, such as actively seeking employment or demonstrating need. UBI, by contrast, is conceived as a citizen's right: a guaranteed economic floor that would simplify the welfare state's complex architecture, reduce bureaucracy and eliminate the stigma associated with receiving assistance . Graphic created with GPT-4o's new image model using simply this prompt: “Could you make a four-panel infographic about universal basic income in the era of the arrival of artificial general intelligence, please?” Full English rendering of the four panels, headed “Universal basic income”: Income for everyone: the state provides unconditional income to the entire population. The original graphic truncates the Spanish adjective “unconditional”; its intended meaning is also explicit in the article's definition above. No conditions: the payment is not subject to requirements such as looking for work. A response to AGI: introducing basic income may become relevant with the arrival of artificial general intelligence. Economic security: the aim is to reduce poverty and provide economic stability. The idea is not new . Its intellectual roots are surprisingly diverse. To mention just a few figures, Thomas Paine was already advocating a “citizen's dividend” in the eighteenth century as compensation for the privatisation of land. In the twentieth century, figures as different as civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. , who saw it as a direct tool for abolishing poverty, and liberal economist Milton Friedman , who championed a “negative income tax” as an efficient alternative to welfare bureaucracy, supported similar concepts. More recently, philosophers such as Philippe Van Parijs have articulated UBI in terms of “real freedom”, arguing that material security is a prerequisite for everyone to be genuinely able to exercise their choices in life. Beyond theory, numerous limited-scale basic-income “experiments” have taken place in recent years , in Finland, Ontario, India, Germany and elsewhere. But we must understand that the context will be very different . One fear among the political proponents of these prototypes was that UBI might discourage work and thereby have negative effects. Here, however, we may very well find ourselves in a scenario in which much of the population will not be “able” to work , at least under conditions similar to today's. That changes the perspective completely and removes that “fear”. Bearing this enormous difference in mind , what those studies broadly showed was that UBI reduces extreme poverty and financial stress without producing a mass withdrawal from employment. Its positive effects are seen above all in security, mental health and the ability to start businesses or acquire skills . Questions remain, however, about how to fund an adequate UBI at scale and whether it might have inflationary effects. The age of artificial intelligence: why is universal basic income returning to the forefront? If UBI has been a recurring theme in the history of thought across many traditions and perspectives over recent centuries, and quite a few pilots have been conducted, why has it gained so much traction recently? The answer , obvious if you have read this article's introduction, lies in AI's exponential acceleration . Unlike previous technological waves, today's AI automates not only routine or manual tasks but also cognitive and creative ones. Moreover, it is a technology that will soon be able to “improve itself”: we will have AI models training better models, which will in turn train the next generation, accelerating development still further . Reports by consultancies such as McKinsey project hundreds of millions of job displacements worldwide by 2030 , while Accenture estimates that models such as ChatGPT could affect up to 40% of working hours . Both studies date from 2023—ancient in AI terms, when the pace accelerates every year. The prospect of AGI intensifies these concerns. If intelligent machines can perform most human tasks more efficiently and cheaply, the traditional model of employment as the main mechanism for distributing income begins to falter. The risk is not only mass unemployment but also a dramatic exacerbation of inequality , as José María Lassalle highlighted in his book and in his conversation with Jon Hernández . As economists such as Daron Acemoglu have pointed out, automation tends to favour capital over labour, concentrating the wealth it generates in the hands of those who own the technology . Without corrective mechanisms, we could face a future of technological abundance coexisting with widespread insecurity. In this scenario, UBI presents itself as a strategic tool for several interconnected reasons: Economic and social stabilisation: it would act as an essential safety net for millions of displaced people, preventing mass poverty and sustaining the aggregate demand necessary to keep the increasingly automated economy functioning . Without consumption, our entire capitalist economy collapses: if people have no money, they cannot consume. Giving them purchasing power, even if limited at first, is therefore key to maintaining the system as we know it . This would happen while prices fell through technological improvements and reduced labour input, and while the amount received as UBI could progressively rise as more wealth was generated globally. How this would work in a post-scarcity economy, in a later phase, is another question for a somewhat more distant future. Redistribution: it would channel a share of AI-generated productivity gains to the entire population , acting as a “technological dividend” that recognises the collective nature of progress. Technology-sector figures such as Elon Musk and Sam Altman, who has even funded his own research on the subject , have publicly supported UBI on this basis. Facilitating the transition: it would ease individuals' economic pressures, allowing them to invest in training, adapt to new roles or explore alternative forms of social contribution—care, art, volunteering—that the market does not always reward adequately . The equally crucial question of meaning in life , in a context where we have tied our identity so closely to work and that work disappears or changes profoundly, would undoubtedly warrant another article . At least UBI would provide a minimum response to economic needs and allow more options for addressing these extremely important existential questions too. Strengthening labour bargaining power: it would give workers greater power to reject precarious conditions, encouraging an overall improvement in the quality of the jobs that remain . People without the economic resources to survive are far more vulnerable to an unscrupulous employer threatening to replace them with AI or a robot unless they work twice the hours or accept a pay cut. UBI could thus make a significant contribution to safeguarding the dignity and working conditions of those who remain in employment. Intergenerational justice: this is particularly relevant to young people. If AI leads firms to limit new hiring rather than dismiss existing staff, which is much more costly—a pattern we are already beginning to see among major technology companies that have sharply reduced their plans to hire programmers—new generations would face substantial barriers to entering the labour market. The proposed reductions in working time discussed in recent years could run into the same wall in an AGI context: hours are reduced and conditions protected and improved for those already employed, but AI fills the working time they leave vacant, rather than new workers, who become still more exposed. UBI would give young people an essential economic foundation and could provide the security some need to launch their own projects, encouraging entrepreneurship, or direct their lives towards socially valuable but unpaid activities. Graphic created automatically from the text with Napkin.ai. Full translation of “The role of universal basic income in an AI-driven economy”. At the centre: “Economic and social stability”. The five surrounding roles are: Economic stabiliser: keeps the economy—and consumption—functioning by preventing poverty. Wealth redistribution: channels AI's enormous productivity gains to the population. Facilitating the transition in work and personal life: enables training, retraining and a shift into unpaid roles. Bargaining power: improves working conditions by empowering the workers who remain. Intergenerational justice: provides a foundation for young people who would struggle to enter the labour market. The crucial question of funding The million-dollar question remains how to fund a meaningful universal basic income capable of addressing the social change that AGI's arrival could bring. Proposals range from traditional tax reforms—progressive increases in personal income tax, VAT and corporation tax—to more innovative ideas adapted to the emerging digital economy: Taxes on capital and wealth: taxing capital income and large fortunes more heavily, as their concentration is expected to increase with AI. A “robot tax”: taxing the use of robots or algorithms that replace human jobs, as Bill Gates suggested many years ago , and Bernie Sanders supported more recently . Technological dividends: requiring major technology companies to contribute a share of their profits or equity to a public fund financing UBI, as proposed by Yanis Varoufakis . Taxes on personal data or digital services: capturing some of the value generated by the data economy, which uses our personal data to create wealth on major platforms. Although the challenge is monumental, AI itself could generate the additional wealth required by dramatically increasing productivity. The key will lie in the political will to design tax systems that effectively capture and redistribute that wealth without destroying innovation and growth. Challenging myths about UBI amid mass AI adoption: beyond left and right, towards freedom and entrepreneurship Interestingly, UBI attracts support from opposing ideological directions . While the left sees it as an instrument of social justice and equality , some liberals and conservatives defend it in the name of individual freedom and efficiency . They argue that giving people money directly empowers them to make their own decisions, reduces the welfare state's paternalistic bureaucracy and eliminates “poverty traps” . The analogy with a school voucher is relevant: individuals are trusted to manage their resources and make decisions, rather than becoming completely dependent on the state. Far from encouraging laziness, UBI could also catalyse entrepreneurship . By providing a basic safety net, it would reduce the financial risk of starting a business, democratising the opportunity to innovate . Evidence from several UBI pilots, such as the one conducted in India , showing an increase in small businesses, supports this hypothesis. In a world where traditional work will be scarce, encouraging individual initiative will be crucial. Some exceptional individuals or small groups, making the most of AI's power, will undoubtedly be able to develop projects of great economic and social value to humanity. Finally, UBI opens the door to deep reflection on the meaning of work. In societies where, unfortunately, a high proportion of people report dissatisfaction with their jobs , guaranteeing subsistence could free many individuals from the “biblical curse” of labour, allowing them to pursue activities more closely aligned with their vocations and values, redefine social contribution beyond paid employment, and recover the notion that individuals have value simply by existing, not solely through their ability to produce wealth . That notion is deeply rooted in many ancient philosophical traditions, including, close to home, the humanism of Christian and classical origin that underpins European and Western values. Conclusion: preparing for the storm before the downpour begins Universal basic income is no magic solution, nor is it free of challenges. Implementing it requires careful design, sustainable funding and cultural adaptation. Legitimate doubts remain about its long-term effects on inflation and broader economic dynamics. Nevertheless, given the scale of the disruption promised by AGI and the absence, for now, of clear alternatives from politics and governments—which we hope will also begin to be discussed and developed—UBI emerges as one of the most relevant and potentially necessary policy tools for navigating the transition. Its complexity means it cannot be deployed optimally from one year to the next, and would involve reshaping or abolishing most existing benefits. Yet we probably do not have much time before we begin to see enormous disruption from AI in employment: first in “intellectual” work, then years later in other fields as AI-controlled robots advance. UBI offers a pragmatic way to address the risks of mass unemployment, extreme inequality and social unrest simultaneously, while strengthening individual freedom and adaptability . Ignoring UBI or dismissing it outright as an impossible utopia would be imprudent . Governments, international institutions and civil society must intensify research, experimentation and informed debate about its different forms and funding mechanisms, and do so soon. It goes without saying that, as a relatively simple mechanism to understand—a universal payment to each individual— UBI could readily win electoral support at a time of considerable labour-market tension . Even so, actually implementing it would require cross-party political alliances and substantial tax reform, as well as rethinking other issues that will also be profoundly shaken by the transformation brought by the AI revolution, such as pensions, unemployment and training. Beginning to develop frameworks for a possible universal basic income , alongside studying other possible alternatives, is not a concession to laziness but strategic preparation for a future in which the relationship between humans, technology and work will very probably change irreversibly. The AGI storm is approaching, and UBI could be the anchor that allows us to weather it and build a fairer, more resilient society in a new age of intelligent machines. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at the ALEPH Educational Institution

AI on official accounts: viral play, threat or distortion? Martín Sosa Dirié examines AI imagery on official political accounts and asks whether viral reach enriches or trivialises public discourse. Martín Sosa Dirié Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 078 Analysis AI on official accounts: viral play, threat or distortion? This week, our main article once again features a contribution from Martín Sosa Dirié , a journalist, communications consultant and graduate of the Master's in Image Advising and Political Consultancy directed by Jorge Santiago. He also wrote the interesting lead article in issue 67 of estrategIA . Much of the debate about artificial intelligence and political communication has centred on its potential risks, especially the spread of disinformation through artificially generated images, videos and voices. But to what extent have these warnings materialised? Has AI established itself as an effective tool for manipulating public discourse, or has its impact taken unexpected directions, creating new forms of risk and distortion? I invite you to join me in reviewing some recent cases in which the official accounts of presidents and political parties have used AI in their communications. 1. AI: the bizarre and its impact On 26 February, Trump once again shook the international agenda with a social media post. This time, it was not an affront, a threat or a sarcastic criticism of an opposing politician, as we have grown accustomed to, but the arrival of the “Trump Gaza” reel. realdonaldtrump A post shared by @realdonaldtrump . The retained still shows an AI-generated golden statue in the reel's imagined resort setting; it is not a photograph of a real development. The video lasts 33 seconds and begins with images of a ruined city in which children are pursued with rifles. The caption “Gaza 2025/What's next” locates the images in that area of the Middle East, before switching to a sequence of scenes of Gaza transformed into a kind of holiday paradise, with clear-water beaches, white sand, gold statues of Trump, five-star resorts and even a Trump Tower. The short features Donald Trump , Elon Musk and Benjamin Netanyahu , with a soundtrack whose lyrics say: “Donald is coming to set you free, bringing life for all to see. No more tunnels, no more fear, Trump Gaza is finally here. Trump Gaza shining bright, a golden future, a whole new light. Feast and dance, the deal is done, Trump Gaza number one.” Translation note: these lyrics are translated from the Spanish quotation reproduced in the original article; they have not been verified against the original audio. The piece exceeded 60 million views on Instagram alone, twelve times the average his regular content had been receiving there. 2. AI as an extension of personal branding and a reinforcement of identity Another interesting case is Javier Milei, probably the serving president who makes the greatest use of AI tools . Since his 2021 election campaign, when he built a strong personal brand associated with the figure of the lion —projecting strength, courage, boldness and leadership—Milei has continually reinforced that association through AI. He uses these tools frequently to depict a wide variety of political events, whether defending a government measure , marking a bilateral meeting with a foreign president, or portraying his government's heroism and bravery through playful references to popular-culture figures: Terminator, Superman, Rocky, Neo from The Matrix , and so on. Translation of the substantive text in this montage of posts from Javier Milei's account: Terminator image: “Belliboni detected. Trade unionist detected. Governor detected. Member of parliament detected. Caste in sight, baby.” “Caste” refers here to the political establishment in Milei's rhetoric; the last line plays on a Terminator catchphrase. The artwork bears the signature “Nik”. Caption beside it: “The caste is trembling. Freedom advances. Long live freedom, damn it.” Visible comments beneath that caption: “How you lulled us with the lies you promised, eh!!! In the end I was the caste, you petty thief”; “When your term ends in 2027, I'm going to post ‘SE TERMINATOR’”—a pun on se terminó , “it's over”; “Hey, hasn't this meme aged badly? In the end the caste was the people and the goblin came to sell EVERYTHING THAT ‘DOES NOT BELONG TO HIM’. In other words, another thief, only a white-gloved one. Still a thief”; and “Now NIK is lending himself to this nonsense.” Caption beside the superhero image: “Impossible not to adore my followers. And now they are bringing in the magic of AI as well. Long live freedom, damn it.” Visible comments beneath it: “They went to vote three times and this seemed the best choice”; “Urgent therapy”; and “I want to defend you, but you're not helping.” These translations document the posts and reactions visible in the original screenshot; the statements are those of their respective posters. He has also used AI to reinforce strategic points in his narrative: the defence of freedom ; “awakening lions” ; and the fight against communism and against the caste , among others. The left post, from @JMilei, reads “Defending the cash box…” and depicts a lion in ceremonial dress with a sword, banknotes, rats and the Argentine flag. The right-hand image shows a lion drinking from a mug labelled “Leftists' tears”. Both are synthetic illustrations used in the original article as examples of political messaging. It is also worth recalling the 2023 presidential campaign , when Milei depicted one of its key moments , his alliance with Patricia Bullrich for the run-off against Sergio Massa, through an AI-generated image . The original post from @JMilei is dated 25 October 2023 at 13:16. It shows the synthetic illustration discussed below. The image, showing a duck representing Bullrich and a lion representing Milei embracing, illustrated the political alliance in a novel way. 3. AI as a tool for political denunciation and promotion Another recent case with considerable impact was launched by Spain's Partido Popular (PP) at the beginning of the month to denounce alleged corruption within the PSOE and Pedro Sánchez's government. Entitled “The Island of Corruption” , the campaign used an AI montage to recreate the opening of the popular television programme “Temptation Island” . In the video, political figures associated with the PSOE, including Pedro Sánchez, his wife Begoña Gómez and others, are introduced as “contestants” on an island where “corruption, lust, ambition and lies” reign. The video exceeded two million views on the PP's X account in its first 24 hours, multiplying by 75—yes, 75!—the views of some of the same account's most-watched videos that week. Something similar happened on Instagram , where it accumulated more than 10,000 likes and 350,000 views in just one day, between eight and ten times the average. The PP later deleted it following an oversight that prompted a complaint from the Dominican Republic's embassy . Macron , too, recently experimented with AI by publishing a video full of deepfakes of himself to promote the AI Action Summit held in Paris in February. emmanuelmacron A post shared by @emmanuelmacron . The retained still is from the deepfake video discussed in the article; it is not presented as an authentic scene. It reached 8.4 million views , eight times the reach of his most-watched reels. 4. Beyond volume As the cases examined show, AI—at least so far—has not been used in political communication with the aim of deliberately deceiving or spreading disinformation. Not, at least, from official accounts, which are what we have explored here. The applications we have seen tend to focus on creating exaggerated, surreal and fantastical scenes that do not seek to pass themselves off as real. Instead, they aim to exploit the humorous, satirical or memetic avenues of digital culture. This content seeks to amplify its impact through virality—and succeeds—by taking situations to the limit or even beyond, creating material that borders on the bizarre, the disruptive and the extravagant. Yet evaluating these pieces solely from a quantitative perspective, such as their volume of views or plays, is not enough. Every piece of political communication serves strategic objectives , both communicational and political . Although AI creations clearly achieve greater reach in terms of views and engagement, the key question is whether this kind of content contributes to political discourse or, instead, degrades and trivialises it . It is therefore essential not to allow qualitative analysis to be eclipsed by the dominance of volume and virality. Indeed, a broader, more systematic study combining quantitative data—views, plays, shares, engagement and so on—with in-depth qualitative analysis would be highly valuable. It would allow a more rigorous assessment of AI-created pieces in political communication, not only in terms of reach, but also in relation to the quality and meaning of the political message they convey. Martín Sosa Dirié Journalist and communications consultant Author of @conversacioncontinua .

The age of thinking machines: navigating Lassalle's “Artificial Civilisation” A review of José María Lassalle's Civilización artificial, its case for technological humanism and its account of AI, power and the future of work. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics Work, Welfare & the Social Contract 077 Review & commentary The age of thinking machines: navigating Lassalle's “Artificial Civilisation” As you know, our recommendation of the week in the last issue of estrategIA was a stimulating video conversation between Jon Hernández and José María Lassalle . Following that recommendation, and thinking particularly of those who enjoyed it as much as we did and wanted to explore the excellent questions it raised more deeply, I have spent the past few days reading Lassalle's latest book, Civilización artificial , or Artificial Civilisation . Here is a short review that might also whet your reading appetite. The original Spanish cover reads “Civilización artificial”, by José María Lassalle, published by Arpa. The title and subtitle translate as “Artificial civilisation: wisdom or replacement—the human dilemma in the face of AI”. These are translations for this review, not a claim that an English edition exists. Unlike many other books we have examined in estrategIA, this is neither a practical manual nor a conventional technological manifesto. It is a deep philosophical and political immersion in the AI tsunami that is already soaking us to the bone. Lassalle , wearing the twin hats of a former Secretary of State for the Information Society and the Digital Agenda—and, before that, Secretary of State for Culture—and a seasoned scholar, offers a privileged perspective. His high-level political career, combined with a solid academic grounding, makes him an exceptional observer of this silent but seismic revolution. Before delving into the core of his argument, I would offer two preliminary observations that I consider important. First, “Artificial Civilisation” is not light reading. Prepare for a dense book, a veritable intellectual banquet featuring more than 30 philosophers and thinkers, from the Greek classics to major contemporary minds. It demands attention and reflection, but amply rewards the patient reader willing to navigate its pages . Paradoxically, however, this depth is also one of its strengths, offering a robust conceptual framework for understanding the magnitude of the change we are living through. Second—and this is perhaps our principal reservation—we wholeheartedly agree with the constructive disagreement Jon Hernández raised in the interview: timing. The book , published in April 2024 and probably written the previous year, may err towards a certain “slowness” in its chronology . At that time, some academic circles still placed strong artificial intelligence on a horizon two decades away, and certain additional biases concerning the potential “danger of AI” were more pronounced. The reality, as events in recent months have shown with dizzying speed, is that acceleration is the norm. Even within “academia”, forecasts for the arrival of artificial general intelligence or even superintelligence have been brought forward dramatically, to the end of this decade or the beginning of the next at the latest. Another question, given the complexity of the terminology, is whether Lassalle means only AI with consciousness similar to ours when he refers to strong AI. That is very difficult to place on a timeline, and might not even occur as such in the coming decades. AI with capabilities superior to ours will not be knocking on the door in twenty years: it is already sitting on the sofa, beginning to redesign the house as it pleases. This temporal urgency, which the book perhaps does not emphasise as forcefully as current events warrant, in no way invalidates its analysis. But it does require us to read with a stopwatch in hand, aware that the future it describes is converging on us at breakneck speed. Full translation of the infographic, “Artificial civilisation”: Civilisational transition: the shift from industrial to artificial civilisation. Ethical dilemma: the struggle between nihilism and humanism in AI. Geopolitical competition: the race between nations for dominance in AI. The transformation of capitalism: the move towards data-driven cognitive capitalism. Technological humanism: integrating human values into AI development. With those considerations addressed, Artificial Civilisation unfolds a fascinating conceptual map for understanding the age of the thinking machine. To avoid overwhelming you with the nuances of its philosophical depth, we can distil the book's central ideas , which set its course from chapter to chapter, into the following key points. 1. The advent of artificial civilisation Lassalle argues that we are witnessing a civilisational transition of historic proportions, comparable to the Neolithic Revolution, the invention of the printing press or the Industrial Revolution. AI is not merely another tool but the catalyst for a new paradigm: an “artificial civilisation” that redefines the coordinates of our existence. This new era marks the twilight of the industrial and liberal civilisation born of the Enlightenment, replaced by an ecosystem in which artificial intelligence becomes the foundational infrastructure of society, the economy and politics. 2. AI's Faustian dilemma: humanism versus technological nihilism At the heart of the book lies a fundamental ethical question: should AI develop without restriction, autonomously maximising its capabilities and power, or should it be subordinated to a higher human purpose? Lassalle places us before a “Faustian dilemma”, a crossroads at which we must choose between nihilistic AI, driven solely by efficiency and technical progress without an ethical horizon, and humanistic AI serving humanity's overall well-being. The drift towards nihilism, he warns, leads us towards an “AI-cracy” in which machines, devoid of wisdom and transcendent purpose, could displace human beings as the axis of existence, creating a profound crisis of existence and meaning. 3. The geopolitics of AI: the struggle for hegemony in the algorithmic age AI development is not a neutral process; it is intrinsically bound to geopolitical competition between the great powers, principally the United States and China. Lassalle describes a “race for hegemony” in which both countries seek to lead AI innovation to gain military, economic and political advantages. Given its publication date, the book naturally does not incorporate the new parameters Trump adds to the equation, but it sets out a general framework that does not seem to have changed very much. This competition, lacking a global ethical framework and fuelled by the logic of power, accelerates AI development while increasing the risks of global fragmentation and potential conflict, particularly in autonomous weapons. On this global chessboard, Europe seeks a difficult balance, trying to position itself through a model that prioritises ethics and regulation. Its ability to influence this dynamic without missing the train to the future remains uncertain, all the more so following Trump's victory. Yet, both in the book and in the interview, Lassalle advocates a “European path” towards AGI that we at estrategIA fully share: one that, without anchoring us in the past and while firmly embracing all the good this technology brings, projects a new humanism rooted in Europe's intellectual tradition into the emerging civilisation. 4. The transformation of capitalism and the future of work AI transforms not only politics and society but also the foundations of capitalism. Lassalle explains how artificial intelligence, together with earlier developments such as the internet and its platform economy, is turning industrial capitalism into “cognitive capitalism”, in which data and algorithms become the new factors of production. This transformation radically changes the nature of work, replacing intellectual and creative tasks previously regarded as the exclusive preserve of human beings. The result is a potential destabilisation of the welfare state and liberal democracy, with the risk of growing social inequality and erosion of the middle classes, traditionally the foundation of social peace. In this context, the author presents basic income as an interesting tool, perhaps inevitable and necessary but insufficient, in a scenario where AI radically redefines the concepts of value and social participation. Implementing it would require rethinking distributive justice in a world where algorithmic capital replaces human labour as the primary source of wealth. 5. The need for technological humanism Faced with the risks of uncontrolled and potentially dehumanising AI, Lassalle advocates a “technological humanism” that places artificial intelligence at the service of human well-being and dignity. This technological humanism means recovering the concept of wisdom, understood as a higher level of understanding that transcends mere specialist knowledge and is connected to purpose, meaning and transcendence. Human wisdom, grounded in experience, reflection and awareness of our own limitations, must guide AI's development and governance, preventing the purely rational, efficient logic of machines from stripping us of our humanity. This new humanism means subordinating AI to transcendent ends, regulating its development through global ethical standards—certainly without paralysing or obstructing it—and rejecting the utopia of machine perfection, embracing imperfection and vulnerability as essential features of the human condition. I think a good way to conclude this review of a work whose value lies far more in how it invites us to think about the existential issues AI brings than in giving clear answers to questions we cannot yet define is to put the following question directly to you. Lassalle asks it towards the end of his introduction, and it neatly encapsulates the central dilemma posed by the arrival of this new artificial civilisation waiting just around the corner: Do we want to prevent the imposition of a technological nihilism that maximises AI's will to power as its own apotheosis? Or do we wish to offer a human alternative that places AI's power at the service of a higher purpose, allowing us to evolve from the Homo digitalis we are into the Homo deus we could become? Translation note: the closing quotation is translated from the Spanish excerpt reproduced in the original article, not from a verified English edition. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at the ALEPH Educational Institution

AI takes the lead: what Mobile World Congress 2025 tells us about the digital future MWC 2025's AI announcements and the implications for mobile networks, public administration, regulation and future services. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 076 Report AI takes the lead: what Mobile World Congress 2025 tells us about the digital future Mobile World Congress (MWC) 2025, held in Barcelona from 3 to 6 March, has closed its doors with a palpable sense that artificial intelligence is no longer a futuristic promise but the mobile industry's ubiquitous leitmotif. From the chips powering the smartphones in our pockets to the strategies of major operators and government policies, AI dominated conversations in the halls of Fira de Barcelona. Yet behind the dazzling demonstrations and grand announcements, a crucial question emerges: are we witnessing a genuine technological transformation in the present, or an elaborate performance designed simply to seduce investors and voters alike? This year's event, which drew more than 109,000 attendees, was characterised by an “overabundance of artificial intelligence”. Mobile-device manufacturers presented their handsets as “AI companions”, integrating advanced features ranging from instant call translation to conversational assistants capable of natural, complex dialogue. The power of new chips, such as Qualcomm's Snapdragon X85 5G, with dedicated AI processors, promises to bring these capabilities directly onto the device, reducing reliance on the cloud and improving user privacy. But AI is not confined to consumer gadgets. Major telecommunications operators also showed how they are using it to optimise their 5G networks and prepare the ground for 6G. Huawei, for example, presented “AI-centred 5.5G” solutions, promising smarter, more autonomous and more energy-efficient networks. Samsung, meanwhile, showcased CognitiV NOS, its network-automation platform, capable of managing the network lifecycle autonomously, anticipating congestion and adjusting resources in real time. Even start-ups such as DeepSig are revolutionising the physical layer of communications, replacing traditional algorithms with neural networks that learn and adapt to wireless-channel conditions , with substantial improvements in spectral efficiency. In cybersecurity , AI emerges as a double-edged sword. While companies such as Telefónica Tech showed how AI can detect and neutralise cyberthreats in record time, experts warn that malicious actors are also using it to make their attacks more sophisticated. The industry is engaged in a digital arms race in which defensive AI must stay one step ahead of new forms of cybercrime. AI's ethical imperative: navigating the fine line between innovation and regulation The technological euphoria that swept through MWC 2025 did not eclipse an increasingly urgent debate: the need for a robust ethical and regulatory framework for artificial intelligence. As AI spreads into every area of life, from health to government, the question is no longer whether we should regulate it, but how to do so effectively without stifling innovation. A pivotal moment in this debate was the contribution of Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak. Far from adopting a Luddite position, he advocated “more honest AI” . A longstanding advocate of technological oversight, Wozniak stressed the importance of algorithmic transparency: “To judge what we consume more effectively, we need to know whether the information comes from technology, how the AI has been trained, or which sources it has used.” His call echoed an underlying concern at the congress: users' right to know when they are interacting with AI and the ethical parameters or biases under which it has been trained. Translation note: Wozniak's quoted remarks are translated from the Spanish wording in the original article; their original English wording has not been independently verified. At MWC 2025, many companies showed a growing awareness of the need to adapt to this new regulatory landscape. Samsung, for example, stressed that all the AI features in its Galaxy S25 devices are designed with privacy in mind. The company presented its “Personal Data Engine”, an architecture that processes personal data locally on the device and deletes it if the user wishes. Spain, seeking to position itself as a significant player in the AI ecosystem, also made important announcements on ethics and regulation. The Secretariat of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence launched an open-source community for the development of ALIA, the family of foundation AI models in Spanish and Spain's co-official languages. Opening ALIA's code aims to foster transparency, auditability and collaboration around AI “made in Spain”, incorporating European values such as privacy and inclusivity by design. Questions remain, however, about the feasibility of effective regulation in a technological field evolving at breakneck speed. Will the EU AI Act be flexible enough to adapt to future innovations? How will compliance be guaranteed globally, given AI's cross-border nature? And perhaps the most fundamental question: how can the need for regulation be balanced with the imperative to foster innovation and economic growth? Far from having easy answers, these questions will shape the political and technological agenda in the years ahead. The intelligent state: governments trying to ride the AI wave MWC 2025 made clear that artificial intelligence is not merely a technological toy for the private sector, but an instrument of power with transformative potential for governments and public administrations. In a global context of accelerating digitalisation and increasingly complex social challenges, states are beginning to see AI as a strategic ally in modernising services, improving administrative efficiency and, ultimately, strengthening their legitimacy in citizens' eyes. Spain once again emerged as an example of this trend. The Minister for Digital Transformation announced an ambitious €200 million package at MWC to integrate AI into the Spanish economy . The investment, part of the Digital Spain 2026 agenda and the National AI Plan, seeks to advance AI projects in businesses across sectors, from manufacturing to tourism and healthcare. A notable element is the €67 million investment in Multiverse Computing, a Spanish pioneer in efficient AI, in a clear attempt to advance AI's energy sustainability and put Spain “at the forefront of Europe” in this field, in Minister López's words. Beyond investment, MWC 2025 also offered concrete examples of how AI could revolutionise public administration . Discussions covered the potential of intelligent virtual assistants to simplify bureaucratic procedures and provide round-the-clock citizen services, following countries such as Estonia, which have already implemented government chatbots. At local level, Barcelona, MWC's host city, reinforced its ambition to become an AI technology hub through a strategic agreement with Huawei. The agreement envisages training centres for advanced digital skills and the development of AI-based smart-city pilots, such as predictive urban traffic-management systems or urban maintenance using computer vision to detect damage to streets. The GSMA Ministerial Programme , held alongside the congress by the organisation representing the mobile industry worldwide, provided a platform for ministers and representatives from more than 40 countries to discuss digital policies and AI's role in governance. They discussed public-administration use cases such as analysing public data to improve urban transport planning or detect tax fraud. There was broad agreement that governments should lead by example in ethical AI adoption, using open, privacy-respecting solutions. In this context, the European Commission presented Digital Europe Programme initiatives in its pavilion, including a demonstration of AI serving social inclusion: a computer-vision system to help people with disabilities navigate events. AI's influence was visible even in institutional promotion. The Spanish government's pavilion at MWC, which attracted 30% more visitors than the previous year, featured an interactive AI hologram that welcomed visitors and recommended companies to visit according to their interests. Beyond the novelty, it illustrates how AI is beginning to permeate every aspect of public life, from citizen services to promoting the national brand. Government adoption of AI is not without challenges, however. A shortage of specialist AI talent in the public sector, resistance to change within traditional administrative structures, and concerns about the security and privacy of citizens' data are obstacles that must be overcome. There is also a continuing risk that AI will be used to reinforce state control and surveillance, rather than empower citizens and improve public services. The key to an “intelligent state” lies in a delicate balance between technological efficiency and democratic values. Future trends glimpsed at the congress The innovations presented at MWC 2025 offer a glimpse of several future trends in AI: Ubiquitous AI in personal devices: flagship smartphones already act as proactive assistants, and these functions can be expected to reach mid-range and entry-level devices in the coming years. We will see more sophisticated AI running offline on our phones, thanks to increasingly powerful chips and compressed models. Users will become accustomed to interacting with their phones by voice for all kinds of tasks, blurring the line between phone and virtual assistant. Autonomous networks on the road to 6G: AI integration into networks will continue to grow. Operators will seek self-managing networks that optimise and repair themselves without human intervention. The idea of neural networks for communications could take hold if experiments such as DeepSig's continue to bear fruit. This could shorten innovation cycles in telecommunications. We will also see AI in services running over the network: for example, 5G network slices dedicated to AI-powered extended-reality services, or adaptive quality of service depending on whether the network detects a critical application—an autonomous car, for example—or a non-critical one. More human-like assistants and bots: the next generation of assistants—Siri, Alexa and Google Assistant—will probably incorporate advances from ChatGPT and Gemini. After what we saw at MWC, we expect more conversational, context-aware and multimodal assistants. “Metabots” could emerge, combining several specialised AIs, as with Deutsche Telekom , T-Mobile's parent company, which presented its innovative “AI Phone”, combining Perplexity, Google AI, ElevenLabs and Picsart . Generative AI in every sector: we saw AI applications in health, education, finance, government and more. The trend is for no sector to remain untouched. Traditional companies are moving from pilots to real deployments, albeit slowly. As regulation matures and successful use cases emerge, future editions of MWC could show large-scale implementations: cities with AI-controlled traffic lights responding to real-time flows, health systems using AI for diagnosis in primary care, and courts applying AI to case management, always with human oversight. Public–private collaboration will be important in scaling these projects swiftly. An emphasis on ethics, privacy and sustainability: AI's future will be shaped by how well its ethical challenges are addressed. Privacy will remain a hot topic: local AI use may increase so that data does not leave the device. We will also see efforts towards “green” AI, optimising models to consume less energy in view of the growing environmental costs of large AI data centres. Full translation of the infographic, “Future AI trends seen at Mobile World Congress 2025”: | Trend | Description | | --- | --- | | AI in devices | Smartphones will become proactive assistants. | | Autonomous networks | AI integration into self-managing networks will grow. | | Human-like assistants | New assistants will be more conversational and context-aware. | | Generative AI | AI will be implemented in every sector. | | Ethics and sustainability | AI's ethical and privacy challenges will be addressed. | MWC 2025 made clear that artificial intelligence has moved from promise to the central axis of mobile technological innovation. From the most basic chip to the most strategic government decisions, AI lay at the heart of every announcement. Improvements in hardware, the maturity of language models and the post-pandemic urgency to digitalise processes have converged to make 2025 the year of AI's explosion in connected mobility. Users can expect smarter devices and more personalised services; operators, more efficient networks; businesses, new opportunities; and governments, tools to serve citizens better. Challenges remain—interoperability, regulation and developing AI talent—but the direction is clear. AI is no longer just a trend: it is a reality cutting across sectors that will probably continue to dominate headlines at future editions of MWC, perhaps with less hype and more concrete results. As Barcelona showed, we are entering a stage of “AI in practice”: moving beyond the laboratory and the demo to integrating it fully into our lives, usefully and responsibly. The cards have been dealt, and future editions of the congress will reveal how much of what was announced becomes real products and policies in the global AI market. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at the ALEPH Educational Institution

February, the month of AI “deep research”: introducing and testing three major tools A March 2025 test of OpenAI, Perplexity and xAI research tools on electoral systems and Spanish polling, with complete historical evaluation tables. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Government & Public Services Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 075 Practical experiment February, the month of AI “deep research”: introducing and testing three major tools Archive note: this comparison was published on 5 March 2025. Model capabilities, prices, access limits and interface screenshots are preserved as described at that time. The evaluations below are historical AI-generated assessments, not current product recommendations. February 2025 marked a milestone in artificial intelligence with the launch of three deep-research tools: OpenAI Deep Research , Perplexity Deep Research and xAI DeepSearch . During the month, the race to transform how we explore and analyse information reached new heights. In this article, we introduce them and offer an initial evaluation of capabilities that we believe could be tremendously useful in politics and government. The pioneer in launching a deep-research tool was Google, with Deep Research on 11 December 2024 . We have not included it in this comparison because, although it deserves considerable credit for being first, it is still powered by Gemini Pro 1.5, a previous-generation AI model, and it would be unfair to compare it here with deep-research tools using far more powerful and advanced reasoning models . Google is very likely to update the model soon, however, just as it has developed an even more complex and powerful model for scientific research, Co-scientist, which we discussed last week . The term “deep research” refers to AI models' ability to carry out advanced searches, analyse multiple sources and synthesise information into understandable reports, often using deep-learning techniques and advanced reasoning. These models, with the differences we will discuss, are especially useful for professional tasks such as financial analysis, scientific research and product development. We believe they could also be useful in academic and professional work in politics and government. Introducing the models First, let us recap the models introduced in February 2025 and their main features. 1. OpenAI Deep Research: the power of the most advanced reasoning Launched on 2 February , this tool, powered by the o3 model—the most powerful AI publicly accessible anywhere in the world today—stands out for its focus on logical reasoning and its ability to generate long, detailed reports. Aimed at professionals, it was initially available only to Pro users, at $200 a month. Fortunately, since 26 February, Plus subscribers, paying $20—or €20—plus tax a month, have been able to carry out ten investigations a month. Screenshot text: “How can I help you?”; “Ask anything”; “Search”; “Deep research”. The tooltip reads: “10 available until 30 March. Get detailed insights on any topic.” Other fully visible controls include “Analyse images” and “More”; some shortcut labels are obscured by the tooltip. 2. Perplexity Deep Research: accessibility and efficiency On 14 February, Perplexity introduced its advanced-research offering , based on the Chinese DeepSeek R1 model, an open-source transformer optimised for reasoning. Its main advantage over competitors is that it can be used free, albeit with usage limits. Screenshot text: “What do you want to know?”; “Ask something…” The model menu offers: Auto: best for everyday searches. Pro Search: three times more sources and detailed answers. Deep research: in-depth reports on complex topics. Reasoning with R1: new DeepSeek model hosted in the United States. Reasoning with o3-mini: OpenAI's latest reasoning model. The fully visible background headline reads “Amazon launches quantum chip”; other background cards are partly hidden by the menu. 3. xAI DeepSearch: next-generation search Just a few days later, xAI launched DeepSearch on 18 February as part of Grok 3. Integrated with real-time data from X and the web, it is available to Premium+ subscribers at $30 a month and, temporarily, to free accounts too . We encourage you to try it while that remains the case. The original English interface reads “How can Grok help?”, with “DeepSearch” selected beside “Think”, and “Grok 3” as the model. Comparison at a glance English translation of the complete historical comparison table: | Model | Launch date | Underlying model | Access | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | OpenAI Deep Research | 2 February 2025 | o3 | Pro subscription, $200/month; from 26 February 2025, Plus includes ten investigations a month | | Perplexity Deep Research | 14 February 2025 | DeepSeek R1 | Free with usage limits; coming soon to mobile apps | | xAI DeepSearch | 18 February 2025 | Grok 3 | Premium+ subscription on X, $30/month; currently also available to free accounts | Preliminary tests of these models To give you more information about these deep-research tools—all interesting, but with enormous differences in their results that make them more or less suitable for different uses— we carried out two preliminary but in-depth tests. First, we asked for a more “theoretical and academic” investigation comparing electoral systems in different countries. Second, we requested a more applied, practical investigation closely tied to current affairs: an analysis of Spain's current electoral polling picture. As I had previously read from prominent experts and scientists such as Ethan Mollick and Derya Unutmaz, considerable subject expertise is needed to judge the research produced by OpenAI's model because of its power and quality. To make this preliminary analysis more impartial , I took advantage of our decision not to evaluate Google's advanced-research model, for the reasons explained at the beginning, and used its most capable reasoning model to help make the question we put to the three models as effective as possible and, especially, to evaluate the content obtained after using all three systems for the same task . Below we share the question , links to each model's response , which you can and should examine for yourselves—we consider that the best way to get a sense of these models—and a summary table of Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking Experimental's evaluation of the answers . We also invite you to consult this 119-page document containing the full questions—the prompts we submitted—the responses collected from the three models, and the complete evaluation by Google's most advanced reasoning model . Remember that the full request—the prompt—is quite long and detailed and is available in the document . The wording above is only its title. The models' responses: click each name to access its original response, which we recommend reading. OpenAI Deep Research : one key detail, which we will return to, is the very different amount of time these tools take. OpenAI's system spent more than eleven minutes producing that extensive answer.
