AI’s future at stake: the challenge between Gary Marcus and Miles Brundage Gary Marcus and Miles Brundage put money behind competing expectations for AI, with ten tasks and a deadline at the end of 2027. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency 068 Analysis AI’s future at stake: the challenge between Gary Marcus and Miles Brundage Archive note: this essay was published on 15 January 2025. The wager, its terms and the author’s interpretation are presented as described at that time; this translation does not assess subsequent progress towards the challenge. We are at the beginning of 2025 and, as often happens at the start of a year, predictions about artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are proliferating. Yet AI has proved one of the hardest areas to predict, because of its multidisciplinary nature — spanning everything from computing to philosophy — and the dizzying pace of innovation. The debate about the arrival of artificial general intelligence (AGI) ranges from the enthusiasm of those who believe it is just around the corner to the scepticism of those who doubt its feasibility in the short or even the long term. Into this landscape comes the intriguing wager between researcher and well-known sceptic Gary Marcus and AI policy expert Miles Brundage . Why all the excitement? Because this is not simply “another prediction”: both have put real money on the table, with a charitable component at stake. It is a true example of “skin in the game”, a concept popularised by Nassim Nicholas Taleb that means risking something valuable — reputation, money or anything else — when you make a claim or take a decision. The mechanics are simple but revealing. If, by the end of 2027, AI meets a series of ambitious criteria that we set out below, Marcus will donate $2,000 to a charity chosen by Brundage. If AI fails the challenge, Brundage will instead pay $20,000 to a cause selected by Marcus. Beyond the amounts involved, this structure of milestones brings seriousness to the debate by focusing on concrete, tangible results. The contenders: pragmatic scepticism versus grounded optimism Gary Marcus , author of influential books such as Rebooting AI , is an influential sceptic. While he acknowledges advances in areas such as language processing, he insists that today’s AI still lacks the contextual understanding and capacity for generalisation required to achieve AGI. His participation in the wager is not merely a criticism but a challenge to the industry to demonstrate real, measurable progress. In the other corner is Miles Brundage , a pragmatic optimist. With first-hand experience gained over several years at OpenAI, Brundage has confidence in rapid technological progress. Although he advocates an ambitious roadmap, he also stresses the crucial need for controls and regulation to mitigate potential risks. His wager reflects his conviction that AGI-related milestones are achievable in the coming years. The terms of the challenge The wager centres on ten specific tasks that, both agree, could serve as clear indicators that AGI has been achieved. Under the agreement, Marcus will lose if AI systems can perform at least eight of these tasks before the end of 2027. The selected tasks include: Complex narrative understanding: watch a film for the first time and summarise it without spoilers, identifying characters, conflicts, motivations and plot twists. Literary analysis: read new novels and answer questions about characters, plots and conflicts, going beyond the literal meaning. Professional writing: produce obituaries or short biographies with the quality and rigour of The New York Times . Adaptation in video games: quickly learn and master the basic mechanics of almost any new video game. Legal writing: write persuasive, error-free legal arguments. Advanced programming: produce working code of more than 10,000 lines from natural-language specifications, without relying solely on existing libraries. Literary and cinematic creation: write Pulitzer-calibre books and Oscar-calibre screenplays with little or no human intervention. Scientific discoveries: propose paradigm-shifting discoveries worthy of a Nobel Prize. Mathematical translation: convert mathematical proofs written in natural language into verifiable symbolic formats. Solving video-game puzzles: solve original puzzles in alternative worlds within video games. A panel of independent judges will decide whether the tasks have been accomplished , taking account of factors such as reasonable costs and the system’s adaptability. This approach seeks to prevent the results from depending on particular technological advances or an excessively specialised design. Beyond the wager: a gauge of AI’s future Although Marcus has been a vocal critic of the narrative that AGI is imminent, his participation in the wager reflects a tacit acknowledgement of the technology’s potential. By accepting that AI could perform several of these tasks — though, in his view, fewer than eight — before the end of 2027, Marcus shows a willingness to revise his pronounced scepticism in the light of concrete evidence. Brundage, for his part, is betting confidently on AI’s accelerating progress, reflecting a position common among those who have worked in leading organisations in the sector and have privileged inside knowledge of how these technologies are developing. Far from being a mere clash of opinions, the wager between Gary Marcus and Miles Brundage offers a measurable, realistic method for assessing advances in artificial intelligence. Introducing “skin in the game” — and donations to charitable causes — adds credibility to a debate that too often amounts to “predictions without consequences”. Regardless of who wins, there is one point on which both sides agree: AI continues to scale at a dizzying pace, and its implications for society will be enormous over the coming years. Even sceptical voices such as Marcus acknowledge that we are entering territory where what once seemed impossible is beginning to knock at the door. Would you dare to place a bet? Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

From simulation to strategy: new AI developments that will transform political communication A guest essay on simulated populations, AI agents and the opportunities and limits of predicting human behaviour for political communication. Martín Sosa Dirié Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 067 Analysis From simulation to strategy: new AI developments that will transform political communication Archive note: this guest essay was published on 8 January 2025. Its account of the studies and its interpretation of their implications are preserved as written. Quotations from research are translated from the Spanish article, rather than presented as verified wording from the original papers. In this issue of estrategIA, we welcome a contribution from Martín Sosa Dirié , a journalist, communications consultant and graduate of the Master’s in Image Advice and Political Consultancy directed by Jorge Santiago. As our guest author, Martín examines how advances in AI simulation are transforming political communication. In November, researchers published a study from the universities of Washington, Northwestern and Stanford, and Google DeepMind, in which they conducted qualitative interviews with 1,052 people and created the same number of AI agents to try to simulate their attitudes and behaviour. The results were surprising and lend support to using AI to conduct social experiments and, ultimately, try to predict human behaviour . 1. The study The researchers explained that, to assemble the study, they recruited “more than 1,000 participants using stratified sampling to create a representative sample of the United States in terms of age, gender, race, region, educational attainment and political ideology”. “We present a generative agent architecture that simulates more than 1,000 real individuals using two-hour qualitative interviews,” they stated. They also noted that “large language models (LLMs), which encapsulate extensive knowledge of human behaviour”, make it possible “to build an architecture that can accurately simulate behaviour across multiple contexts”. What is striking is that the generative agents replicated “participants’ responses to the General Social Survey with 85% accuracy , comparable to the accuracy with which the participants themselves reproduce their responses two weeks later”. They also achieved “similar performance in predicting personality traits and outcomes in experimental replications”. In addition, across a series of five social science experiments, the researchers compared human responses with those of AI agents. In four of these studies, the AI-generated responses closely resembled the human ones. Statistical analyses revealed a correlation coefficient of 0.98 . 2. Some context The study represents another advance in simulation and social experimentation through AI agents, a field in which Project Sid and AI Town had already stood out — and which began almost four decades ago with the legendary Little Computer People on the Commodore 64. LITTLE COMPUTER PEOPLE | Commodore 64 (1985) Project Sid succeeded in creating a complex virtual society within Minecraft, populated by 1,000 autonomous AI agents. These agents developed sophisticated social behaviours : they formed alliances, established trading networks and created a currency system using gems to exchange goods and services. Power dynamics even emerged, including instances of “corrupt priests”, reflecting complex social structures. AI Town grew out of a study published in August 2023 that analysed the interactions of 25 AI agents over two days in Smallville. What made this research interesting was observing how the agents formed — and broke off — relationships, collaborated, learnt through dialogue with one another and resolved conflicts. 3. Predicting human behaviour: the decision-maker’s dream Political communication will not be the only field seeking to make the most of these innovative uses of AI , which bring together programming, mathematics, sociology and political science. In commerce, marketing and advertising , for example, this technology could mark a turning point: a paradigm shift. Being able to simulate the emotional and behavioural responses of real consumers would make it possible to test different messages, formats and approaches in a virtual environment before a major market launch. This would not only reduce the costs associated with trial and error but also increase effectiveness by creating personalised campaigns aligned with consumers’ motivations, maximising impact and loyalty. In political communication , tools of this kind are undoubtedly a fundamental development that will affect election campaigns in the short term, as well as government management . Faced with particular situations, politicians and consultants used to commission opinion research — generally online or by telephone, and sometimes face to face. Now, once we have conducted a substantial study using this approach, we will be able to put an endless range of questions and issues to it over a given period. This could become an indispensable tool for politicians and consultants seeking advance insight into the reception of particular government measures or potential electoral alliances. Yet, like every innovative technological tool, it also has a downside . It could encourage a cautious political leadership, excessively preoccupied with the public mood, shying away from the slightest conflict and lacking the resolve or boldness that political action often demands. 4. A call for professionalism AI agents can provide a way of approaching the thoughts — and, above all, the feelings — of particular social groups. But we must not embrace their results blindly. This is not simply because, like any study, they are not infallible and still have a considerable margin of error. Their findings must never be analysed in isolation . Growing up in a family steeped in sociology, I have always carried with me the idea that the fullest and most accurate interpretations emerge from dialogue between different studies and findings. Likewise, the human role in critically analysing information still cannot be delegated. A scene in the film Irresistible , starring Steve Carell, illustrates this very well. The film is a satire of contemporary political campaigns. An election is approaching in a small Wisconsin district and, a few days before polling day, the polls predict a tie. Then — spoiler alert — a member of the Democratic campaign team, immersed in the war room, notices that a very specific part of the district has a high concentration of single women who live alone. Rather than examine these profiles — based on age, gender and marital status — more closely or compare them with other sources or colleagues’ assessments, he accepts them uncritically and decides to mount a last-minute campaign in that area in favour of contraception. The result? Complete rejection: it turns out to be a neighbourhood of nuns. This example simply highlights the importance of building interdisciplinary teams that work thoroughly. Data analysed without due rigour lead to the wrong strategy and, consequently, poor results. 5. AI and the social sciences AI is already bringing about a paradigm shift in molecular biology , where tools such as AlphaFold — recognised by the Nobel Prize — have predicted protein structures with unprecedented accuracy. Similarly, in physics , machine-learning algorithms are helping to analyse the immense quantities of data generated by particle accelerator experiments, such as those at CERN , making it possible to identify patterns and discover phenomena that might otherwise have gone unnoticed. In computational chemistry — the branch of chemistry that uses mathematical models to simulate interactions between the atoms of substances and thereby solve chemical problems — AI models can predict the properties of new materials, accelerating the search for sustainable solutions to global problems such as energy and climate change. Research such as the work on AI agents also opens up opportunities to intensify collaboration between AI and the social sciences. In short, AI has already demonstrated its capacity to revolutionise the basic sciences. Now it is time for it to strengthen the social sciences , where AI can help analyse and understand complex social situations and generate valuable input for decision-making. Martín Sosa Dirié Journalist and communications consultant @conversacioncontinua — his newsletter on Substack.

Five essential priorities for politicians facing the AI revolution in 2025 and beyond Five policy requests for 2025: make AI a priority, develop it safely and quickly, protect people, redesign institutions and plan for the long term. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Futures, Safety & Human Agency 066 Analysis Five essential priorities for politicians facing the AI revolution in 2025 and beyond Archive note: this essay was published on 1 January 2025. Its forecasts and policy arguments are preserved in their original context. The Tony Blair quotations below are translated from the Spanish article, except for the sentence about government and process, which already appeared in English in the source. The description of Hinton as “this year’s” Nobel laureate is retained from the source despite its January 2025 publication date. Artificial intelligence is not simply a technological tool; in all likelihood, it will drive a revolution — at least comparable in scope to the agricultural or industrial revolutions — that will completely reshape society, the economy and politics over the coming decades. At a time when 2025 could, in light of developments as fascinating as o3 , mark the beginning of the arrival of artificial general intelligence (AGI), political leaders must take bold, courageous decisions to prepare societies for a highly probable, though not certain, near future in which change will unfold at breakneck speed. Original diagram: “Five key requests to politicians on artificial intelligence for 2025”. Its pillars are: make AI a priority; develop it safely and quickly; protect people; adapt institutions; and start planning for the future now. These are five fundamental requests that we at estrategIA put to them, drawing on the knowledge gained from following this subject closely, week by week, to address this historic challenge. 1. Make artificial intelligence a priority It should probably be “the priority”, given its innovative potential and exponential pace of development, but I would already settle for politicians treating it as something important. Very few are aware of the transformations that are very likely coming. One of those who has expressed this best is former British prime minister Tony Blair, who declared several months ago that “ artificial intelligence means there has never been a better time to govern ”, for reasons such as these: There is absolutely no doubt that we are in an era of transformation. Things that were previously impossible will become possible; advances that would have taken decades will happen in a few years or even months; the value we can add, the efficiency improvements we can achieve and the radical improvements in outcomes we can secure could be truly revolutionary. Over the coming years, AI will affect every field of science, the economy and society in ways we cannot yet even begin to imagine. Failing to make it a priority in 2025 would be a catastrophe, and seeing how entangled our representatives are in their “same old” disputes and problems does not inspire much optimism. Countries or regions that properly grasp the scale of change and the priority AI requires will enjoy a distinctive advantage for a long time, because of the field’s own accelerating character: over the next few years, perhaps beginning as early as 2025, AIs themselves will train and improve the next generations of artificial intelligence, accelerating development still further . This is a crucial distinction from every other technology in history and must not be underestimated. This calls for comprehensive policies with international coordination, as well as training for political leaders and senior technical staff in public administration. Prioritising AI is not enough: politicians need at least a basic understanding of its technical, ethical and social foundations . Continuing education for politicians, civil servants and advisers could be crucial to improving decision-making quickly. The public sector also needs to commit firmly to making AI development a priority. Understanding, regulating and legislating are not enough: we need to develop, promote and apply AI in politics and government, and make it easier for businesses in the sector to emerge and grow in our countries and regions. 2. Promote safe AI development — as quickly as safety allows Safety in AI development is crucial, but so is moving quickly to benefit from it. As Oxford professor Nick Bostrom points out in this video clip, which we strongly recommend , every day we delay the responsible implementation of these technologies, we unnecessarily prolong human suffering . Humanity has a moral imperative to help people as soon as possible, and that should lead to responsible acceleration . Speed should come from the conviction that AI can alleviate suffering. In healthcare, for example, applying AI to early diagnosis, drug discovery or the optimisation of health systems will very probably save millions of lives. Delaying these benefits out of fear, without sound justification, can be seen as a moral failure towards citizens. This must be compatible with developing safe AI that takes account of the needs of society as a whole and of every individual, rather than only the interests of the powerful or large corporations, which might be tempted to appropriate both AI and its fruits, producing a deeply unequal society , as this year’s Nobel Prize in Physics laureate Geoffrey Hinton warns . Democratising AI and access to it is therefore also essential. Some proposals even seek to ensure that every citizen has a state-guaranteed allocation of computing capacity, because it could become as basic a need, and as decisive a source of advantage, as access to running water, electricity or the internet is today. 3. Protect people, not jobs We no longer have night watchmen, lamplighters or horse-drawn carriage drivers as we did at the end of the nineteenth century. We have been through repeated industrial restructuring, much of it in Spain, unfortunately, extraordinarily painful and unsuccessful because of the approach taken. History teaches us that protecting obsolete jobs or anachronistic institutions is inefficient and does not work in the medium term. Instead of trying to preserve a twentieth-century employment system, we should focus on protecting people by guaranteeing their dignity and basic living conditions. During the industrial revolution, many restructuring efforts failed because maintaining jobs took precedence over preparing people for new realities. Today, measures such as universal basic income (UBI) offer a more modern and effective way to support the transition — which could be deeply traumatic because of its speed — towards a post-scarcity world in which AI-powered machines do most of the work, while scientific innovation and new technological developments make products and services vastly more affordable . It seems vital for politicians to begin studying measures in 2025 that, because they are novel and technically complex to design and implement, cannot be improvised overnight when, as we anticipate, large-scale job destruction begins within a few years. We would highlight two particularly urgent priorities: Introduce universal basic income when AIs and robots begin performing jobs on a massive scale — something that will happen over the coming years and decades — as an economic safety net and a guarantee of equality that, at the very least, covers the population’s basic needs. It would also release people’s creative capacity from the yoke of paid work, which, unfortunately, is not an activity that most humans find satisfying. It is also fairer than alternatives that might protect those already in work but leave unprotected people who are unemployed or lose their jobs to automation, and who would find it very difficult to obtain paid employment in a context in which AIs become better, more efficient and cheaper every year. Universal basic income focuses on preserving everyone’s dignity on a universal basis and is very likely — whatever final model is adopted, since there are many ways to implement and finance it — to be the best transitional solution during the initial arrival of AGI and the development of artificial superintelligence (ASI). Redesign education to prepare people for a future in which human skills complement AI and possible new jobs emerge in new and different areas. It must also prepare us mentally for life in a society in which much of our identity is no longer defined, as it is today, by paid work — work that AIs and robots will in the vast majority of cases perform better. Economic history shows that trying to maintain anachronistic jobs is inefficient and often doomed to failure. Instead of sustaining the employment structures of the past, politics must safeguard people’s wellbeing, rather than perpetuate inefficient jobs or structures that will disappear sooner or later. It must begin studying and adopting new solutions to a situation completely unlike anything we have experienced. 4. Be willing to “break things”: many surviving nineteenth-century institutions, or older ones, will not work well, and changing or removing them will be essential Closely linked to the previous point, this recommendation could also draw directly on another pertinent observation by former Labour prime minister Tony Blair: “ Government is all about process, and AI is all about automating process .” Many areas of public administration could be largely automated, greatly improving efficiency and generating budget savings that could be used to protect citizens more broadly through proposals such as universal basic income. Such measures will become feasible partly thanks to these efficiency gains and the enormous savings in administrative structures. Today’s bureaucracy and institutional machinery, inherited from the Industrial Revolution, could become obsolete in the face of AGI’s dynamism. Tony Blair stresses that AI can automate government processes, rendering many existing structures slow, expensive and ineffective. This new reality, which will arrive very quickly over the coming years, raises the following requirements: Institutional redesign: we need to rethink governance, from more agile parliaments and ministries to flexible oversight agencies capable of responding to emerging problems. Automation of administrative processes: digital government has been the first step; AI makes it possible to go much further. Automating tedious, repetitive tasks would not only save money but also allow resources to be redirected towards more personalised social services. This will mean reassessing roles, hierarchies and responsibilities in the civil service. The European Union already offers a very clear example of the survival of an institution that is “obsolete” for its purpose: several European countries still require notarial procedures to set up a company. This is provoking a fierce response on social media from entrepreneurs’ associations calling for procedures suited to the year we live in and the technology available, as already exist elsewhere, including in many EU countries such as Estonia. 5. Start planning for the future now: do not pass the problem on to the next government It is impossible to address a transformation as enormous as the one AI will bring to our lives in the period ahead without thinking, for once, about the next ten years, rather than the ten months that may remain in a parliamentary term or the ten weeks of an election campaign. The transformation that artificial intelligence will bring requires bold measures that cannot be improvised or put in place in a fortnight; the entire welfare state in Europe and many other countries will probably need to be redefined. The timescales of this technology and the companies driving it are nothing like those to which governments and public administrations are accustomed. Exploring measures such as universal basic income or similar arrangements is crucial , in anticipation of the likely automation of the vast majority of jobs. UBI could guarantee everyone’s subsistence and grow in purchasing power as scientific and technological advances reduce the cost of products and services. Alternatives to the simpler, more direct option of a cash income include giving citizens a stake in public AI companies or organisations, or guaranteeing access to resources such as computing time or robots that work on their behalf. Properly implemented, these measures could lead to a post-scarcity society with a significantly higher quality of life than today, while mitigating the enormous problem of rising inequality that AI’s advance makes possible as human labour becomes increasingly irrelevant. At the same time, redesigning the tax system is essential to adapt it to this new reality. AI will generate enormous corporate profits that must be taxed proportionately, while taxes on labour income in their current form will become far less important — whether agents or robots should be taxed is a separate question. This new tax framework must not only guarantee fairness but also encourage innovation and universal access to AI’s benefits. The social contract between citizens and the state will need to be updated to ensure that the fruits of AI are shared fairly. Governments’ legitimacy will depend on their ability to protect people, rather than obsolete employment or administrative structures, and to manage change with foresight, always putting collective wellbeing before particular interests. A final reflection The arrival of AGI — assuming it materialises within a very few years, as everything currently seems to suggest, although science and technology offer no dogmas or absolute certainty, and we must work with the available evidence, which clearly points in this direction — demands a radical transformation in how governments act. The five requests set out here revolve around the same idea: AI and AGI are not simply additional tools, but transformative forces that require a profound rethinking of political priorities, structures and ways of working. Prioritising AI, developing it safely but quickly, protecting people ahead of outdated institutions, being willing to redesign the state and public administration, and planning for the long term form an ambitious but necessary framework for action. Politics cannot confine itself to obstructing technological change or watching it passively. It must take its place at the centre of events, anticipating risks, seizing opportunities and, above all, making human dignity and global wellbeing the ultimate guiding principles of public action. Only then, as we reach the end of this decade, will we be able to say that the AI revolution has been steered towards a fairer, more prosperous and more humane future. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH English reading guide to the original infographic, “Five key requests to politicians on artificial intelligence for 2025”. Some lines are clipped at the right edge of the original image; the complete argument is available in the article above. Prioritise artificial intelligence. Politicians must recognise AI’s innovative potential and pace of development. Failing to understand the coming transformations could leave countries at a significant disadvantage. Develop AI safely and at speed. Balance safety with the urgency of delivering benefits. Delay driven by fear can cause unnecessary human suffering; prompt, responsible action should benefit society as a whole. Protect people, not jobs. Focus on human dignity and measures such as universal basic income, while preparing people for a future in which AI performs many work tasks. Redesign institutions and processes. Review and modernise government institutions that could become obsolete with AGI. Automation could increase efficiency and redirect resources towards social wellbeing. Plan now for the medium and long term. Do not leave long-term planning to future governments. Consider innovative measures and tax reforms to prepare society for the changes AI will bring.

Where do I begin? A step-by-step guide to adopting AI in your organisation Pablo Martín Diez outlines five stages of organisational AI adoption, from focused pilots and an internal team to staff training, strategy and communication. Pablo Martín Diez Government & Public Services AI in Practice Learning & Human Capability 064 Practical guide Where do I begin? A step-by-step guide to adopting AI in your organisation Throughout the year, the estrategIA newsletter has examined tools, pioneering cases, emerging trends and critical perspectives on AI’s impact on politics and government. In this issue, however, taking the end of the year as an opportunity to reflect, we want to address a question many of our readers often ask: “This is all very well, but… where do I begin if I want to apply AI in my organisation?” To answer that question, it is useful to turn to the methodology proposed by Andrew Ng — Stanford professor and co-founder of Coursera, recognised worldwide for his contribution to AI — who sets out a practical, staged process for incorporating AI into any organisation. This methodology proposes an iterative cycle that begins with specific experiments and culminates in a strategy for transformation across the organisation. 1. Run successful, engaging pilot projects The starting point should be a clearly defined pilot project, limited in scope and with a specific objective that produces tangible results. For example, a government department could automate document analysis to generate reports, or automate the processing of certain grants, freeing its analysts from repetitive tasks. What matters is that this initial project builds confidence internally. A successful pilot demonstrates that AI is more than theory: it is a practical tool that adds value, encouraging different parts of the organisation to join the transformation. 2. Establish an internal AI team Once the benefits have been demonstrated on a small scale, the next step is to build a specialist internal team. Although it is tempting to rely mainly on external consultants for immediate results, investing in internal talent lays the foundations for sustained innovation. An in-house team understands the organisation’s culture, its political priorities and the social dynamics around it. For a public institution or political party, this has strategic value. Having an internal AI team means technological autonomy and the ability to respond to new needs. This team can work closely with communication specialists, political analysts and policymakers, ensuring that AI-based solutions address local realities and social priorities. 3. Provide AI training for all employees AI should not be the preserve of a small technical group. Basic knowledge of what AI is, how it works, and its possibilities and limitations must spread throughout the organisation. The aim is not to turn everyone into an expert, but into an informed user, able to identify opportunities for improvement and understand recommendations generated by automated systems. In politics, this technological literacy is essential. Senior managers, civil servants, advisers, administrative staff and communication professionals must understand the fundamentals of AI to assess its outputs critically and propose new applications. Training across the workforce creates an internal culture open to innovation and reduces resistance to change. 4. Develop a robust, realistic strategy Once the previous steps — pilots, an internal team and training — have been completed, the organisation has enough experience to design a comprehensive AI strategy, which should take account of these four pillars: Alignment with the mission: every strategy must serve the institution’s overarching objectives and fundamental values. For example, a political party with a social focus might prioritise identifying citizens’ needs or automating citizen participation. Identifying opportunities: which processes can be automated or improved with AI? Where are there large volumes of data that have yet to be used? Scalability and prioritisation: not everything can be done at once. Projects should be prioritised according to their impact, technological feasibility and the resources available. Regulatory and ethical framework: particularly in the public sector, an AI strategy must address personal data protection, transparency in algorithmic decision-making and the assessment of potential biases. 5. Develop internal and external communications AI transforms not only processes, but also perceptions of the organisation, both inside and outside it. Communicating this change strategically is essential. Internal communication: explain to staff how AI can improve working conditions, avoiding fears about automation. It is important to highlight new opportunities for training and growth. External communication: show citizens or clients AI’s tangible benefits: faster procedures, more accurate decisions and better services. A clear, transparent narrative builds trust and legitimises AI adoption. Social legitimacy: through effective communication, organisations gain public support and minimise resistance to change. Diagram translation — “Implementing AI in public organisations”. Downward arrows connect initial AI awareness to five successive layers: Run pilot projects. Build an internal team. Train employees. Develop an AI strategy. Communicate. The arrows continue to the final outcome: organisational transformation. How Institución Educativa ALEPH can contribute Allow us briefly to explain that Institución Educativa ALEPH, with a large team of experts bringing more than two decades of experience in political communication and specific knowledge of the sector, reflected in more than sixty editions of the estrategIA newsletter and several research articles, stands as a relevant potential partner for organisations seeking to strengthen their AI capabilities. Our work focuses specifically on incorporating AI into training processes and improving communication, both internal and external. The central question is whether your organisation is ready to meet the challenges AI presents. Readiness means not only adopting technological tools, but also transforming organisational culture, training teams and rethinking communication strategies. Drawing on its record and experience, Institución Educativa ALEPH offers specialist support in each of these areas to help organisations successfully navigate the changes demanded by today’s environment. Conclusions In the not-too-distant future, the gap between organisations that know how to make use of AI’s advantages and those that fall behind will grow ever wider. Institutions that adopt AI systematically will have greater efficiency, better results and a greater capacity to respond to new challenges. These organisations will set the standard for the quality and reach of the services they offer, particularly in sectors where citizens demand faster, more efficient and more transparent responses. AI is not an option, but an imperative for organisations seeking to remain competitive and relevant in the twenty-first century. This article, which aims to be a practical and comprehensive guide, is a call to action for organisations wishing to embark on the fascinating journey of digital transformation. AI is not a technology of the future, but a present reality that is already transforming how we live, work and govern. The organisations that embrace this reality and adapt to its changes will be the ones that set the course in the years ahead. Pablo Martín Diez Academic Director of Institución Educativa ALEPH Translation note: the opening question is translated from the Spanish source.

“Don’t look up”: artificial intelligence is overtaking us. What about our governments? Fernando Nieto Lobato argues that rapid advances in AI reasoning demand serious preparation by governments, businesses and individuals, including for a possible transformation of work. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Futures, Safety & Human Agency 063 Opinion “Don’t look up”: artificial intelligence is overtaking us. What about our governments? Historical note: this essay was published on 11 December 2024. Its references to recent releases, prices and the coming years retain that date’s perspective. The English wording in the screenshots is transcribed from the preserved images; quoted wording elsewhere is translated from the Spanish unless the visible English original is reproduced. In these first days of December, we have witnessed an enormous explosion in the development of artificial intelligence. Among the most significant announcements are the launch of the o1 model and its o1 Pro version (with more computing time and tied to a $200 monthly subscription), as well as this past Monday’s launch of Sora and a system with advanced vision capabilities integrated into voice applications, whose demo was presented last Sunday on “60 Minutes” . All of this comes from OpenAI , as part of a 12-day series of product announcements reminiscent of those Apple used to run during the Christmas season years ago. But the other companies have also presented some very interesting advances in the past week : Google : It has released the latest preview version of Gemini in its open AI lab , a model that outperforms the latest version of GPT-4 and, according to leaks, might simply be the smallest Gemini 2 model. Grok from X.ai : It is now free . Aurora integrated into Grok : X.ai’s AI launched a new image model capable of an extraordinary degree of realism . Although it was quickly withdrawn over the weekend, it returned on Monday, without a model name, integrated directly into Grok. Meta : It has released an open model with just 70 billion parameters , just as powerful as the previous 405-billion-parameter model it presented only a few months ago, despite being almost six times smaller. Microsoft : It has presented a system that allows AI to see your PC screen, for now integrated into the browser, and assist you by voice in real time. These advances matter not only for their present capabilities but, above all, because they point to a clear path towards artificial general intelligence, or AGI, in the coming years or even months. According to some OpenAI researchers, models such as o1 Pro already outperform the average human across a wide range of tasks. Original English in the screenshot — Vahid Kazemi (@VahidK), 6 December 2024: In my opinion we have already achieved AGI and it’s even more clear with O1. We have not achieved “better than any human at any task” but what we have is “better than most humans at most tasks”. Some say LLMs only know how to follow a recipe. Firstly, no one can really explain what a trillion parameter deep neural net can learn. But even if you believe that, the whole scientific method can be summarized as a recipe: observe, hypothesize, and verify. Good scientists can produce better hypothesis based on their intuition, but that intuition itself was built by many trial and errors. There’s nothing that can’t be learned with examples. But even if we take the stronger definition of AGI, “better than any human at every task”, last week’s technological revelations tell us that we are not too far away. The major AI labs also tell us that they already know the path to get there, because o1, and even more so in its Pro implementation, is already capable of things like these . So much so that we already need the best experts in each field to judge the true capabilities of these reasoning models . They are “too clever” for us to find tasks that can readily challenge them, and their main uses lie in science, mathematics and highly complex tasks requiring very advanced reasoning, as Wharton professor and AI expert Ethan Mollick points out in these tweets: Original English in the screenshot — Ethan Mollick (@emollick), 10 December 2024: I have now had multiple instances where professors have told me that they are pretty sure that o1 found something novel in their field, but that the results are technical, non-obvious and complex enough that they can't be sure without considerable checking Interesting challenge We have already had the opportunity to run quite a few tests with o1, though not with its even more powerful Pro system, which costs $200 a month and is aimed at very specific fields that can make the most of its extra computing time. It is truly impressive, but it is very hard to find “everyday” professional use cases that really exploit the model’s full power. Thanks to Carlos López Arístegui, Vice-Rector for Academic Affairs at ESIC, who very kindly shared his latest business case study so that we could test the model, we have seen that it needs even more complex challenges to make it “think”. One of our goals for 2025 is to try to build a small collection of especially complex political cases, ideally without pre-existing data on the internet that might “rig” the models’ performance: they should not have been trained on the answers or on what “happened” afterwards — for example, if we are discussing electoral analysis and a subsequent election produced a particular result. This would allow us to test whether these new models can really make a difference in politics and government, which is enormously likely, but above all how we can use them well, even to live up to this observation by Peter Welinder, one of OpenAI’s senior executives: “It’s exhilarating—and maybe a bit humiliating—to take direction from a model that’s clearly smarter than you.” Original English in the screenshot — Peter Welinder (@npew), 9 December 2024: It’s exhilarating—and maybe a bit humiliating—to take direction from a model that’s clearly smarter than you. In politics and government, we will have to consider how to obtain valuable data and complex problems that allow us to ask genuinely difficult questions that can really benefit from the greater intelligence of reasoning models. This reflection on politics and government brings us to the key question. AI is advancing in leaps and bounds. We are beginning to have models more intelligent than the average human, which will soon be able to carry out tasks as agents — that is probably where we will see the next great leap in their adoption across society — and meanwhile, what are our representatives doing? Are they not looking up? What about politicians? We already have models more intelligent than humans in a great many activities. We know they are improving at a speed that is hard to believe: every few months we see major leaps in their reasoning, capabilities and integrations. We know these models can already underpin agents that, as early as next year, will go beyond chat-style interaction to carry out complex tasks requiring several steps and different tools. Yet when one looks at the political class close to home, and with very few exceptions across the world, the impression is that almost nothing is being done — at least publicly; there is always the hope that much more preparation is taking place in private, without our being told about it. Some countries have proposed rather generic legislation with room for improvement. In cases such as the European Union, it is full of good intentions but poses enormous problems for the competitive development of AI — for now, for example, Sora is being released in almost every country in the world except the United Kingdom and the European Union… And little else. Meanwhile, the world’s major corporations are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into developing new AI models, with Chinese investment comparable in scale. Yet we see our politicians embroiled in their usual power struggles, concerned with gaining or retaining power, with nineteenth-century questions of identity or territory, or with the perennial corruption scandals. And is nobody looking up ? Does that meteorite, which will soon bring the AI explosion and is already about to strike, mean nothing to them? As I know that many politicians read these lines every week, from my position as a mere lookout watching the advance of AI, I have little option other than to be especially clear in a newsletter like today’s: to climb the ship’s mainmast and shout “Land! Land!”, without much hope that anything will be done. At least I trust that, a few years from now, none of those reading these lines will say that nobody warned them about the “meteorite”. More than that, I hope many will at least begin thinking about how to adapt to the change. Against this backdrop of AI progress, the question is not so much whether it will have a massive transformative effect on our society, our politics and employment, but when. One cannot help asking: what are politicians waiting for before commissioning multiple serious studies and developing real funding mechanisms for life in a world where humans are not the only intelligent species on Earth, and probably not even the most intelligent in a few decades? Are we going to wait until unemployment starts spiralling out of control before we begin studying how to fund and implement a universal basic income that protects citizens’ most basic living standards? We face astonishing technologies that could be democratised and give us all power unlike anything we have ever had, but that also carry an enormous risk of becoming systems that concentrate still more power and wealth in the hands of a few countries and billionaires. This is easier to understand with an example , so here is a very simple one of my own devising, showing a clear route to jobs disappearing. Very soon — I do not think I am taking much of a risk in saying that fewer than five years will pass — three executives at company X, a bank, for example, will decide to leave and set up company Z. Unlike X, a large multinational, this new company Z will not have 30,000 employees. It will have 300, assisted by the latest AIs, and will do the same work as X, or even better, with much lower labour and technology costs and far greater agility because of its smaller organisational size. Its products will therefore be more attractive, with lower fees and higher returns, and it will soon start taking X’s entire market — since consumers generally prefer better, cheaper products. X will respond by implementing more AI and laying off thousands of workers. Perhaps X will save itself in time; perhaps it will not. Along the way, probably tens of thousands of workers will find themselves at home without a job. A few will make use of AI and start new businesses in that sector or others, taking advantage of new opportunities. For most, however, it will be the end of their working lives, because AIs will be better, cheaper, work 24 hours a day, seven days a week, not join unions, not fall ill… Are governments around the world already thinking seriously about this? And here we are considering mainly “white-collar” jobs first, but AI-powered robots are already almost knocking at the door. What will governments do with civil servants in predominantly administrative roles, who will be the first affected? Large companies will dismiss an enormous proportion of their workforce, replacing it with AI. Will the public sector be allowed to retain countless people for whom there is no objective need? How will public administration be restructured? The challenges that politics, governments and the entire public sector will face in the next few years, in direct employment alone, are enormous. Yet the impression is that they continue spending their time and energy on other matters, as though this one did not exist. Believe me, it does. As for universal basic income, or UBI , a very complex subject to which we will probably devote a future article, this is perhaps the approach I find most convincing, developed by Berkeley professor James F. O’Brien . It seeks to balance AI’s growing productivity with social equity, ensuring that the future of automation benefits everyone, not just those who control these technologies. It also fits best with the point at which AIs do most of the work. It cannot be implemented — or at least is not necessary — before widespread unemployment caused by AI begins. On grounds of human dignity, it could be perfectly understandable already, because a person’s value, and this is a personal philosophical position, is independent of their ability to generate money; but that would entail other kinds of costs. We cannot wait much longer, however, because the change is very likely to be rapid, and putting UBI properly into operation means restructuring the entire existing welfare state and benefits system. It is also true that, for this UBI model to work, the companies in your country or region need to be competitive in that post-AGI world and able to pay the levies that would fund UBI under a model such as O’Brien’s. The exception would be a global system, something surely desirable but quite difficult even to conceive of at present. Judging by investment so far, it seems that not much is being done on this front either, apart from in the United States and China. This issue’s news section includes a new European attempt: interesting, but clearly insufficient. Freedom from that “biblical curse” that, for many human beings, is the obligation to work to survive should not be a bad thing if it is managed well — although the transition to a world beyond scarcity could be psychologically traumatic in many ways, given such radical changes in so little time. But AI with advanced reasoning models will probably bring enormous transformations in fields beyond employment, making it essential for governments to start planning ahead now. If lifespans begin to grow longer and longer, as seems quite likely with new technologies and enormous changes in healthcare systems, what happens to the sustainability of pensions? They will probably have to be redefined within a UBI framework or something similar. Simply posing the basic questions about defence would provide material for another enormous and complex article. Then there is education, the infrastructure required… Given the nature of this newsletter, we are focusing here on asking governments and politicians for a swift, decisive response to the approaching meteorite. But it is important that businesses also come to terms — that we come to terms — with the reality of these new AIs as soon as possible, for example by doing what Wharton professor Ethan Mollick proposes, right now: Original English in the screenshot — Ethan Mollick (@emollick), 7 December 2024: A test of how seriously your firm is taking AI: when o-1 (& the new Gemini) came out this week, were there assigned folks who immediately ran the model through internal, validated, firm-specific benchmarks to see how useful it as? Did you update any plans or goals as a result? We must also prepare as individuals to make use of all this new AI potential, integrating it positively and productively into our daily lives and overcoming old habits. I confess that I sometimes still search on Google, as I have for almost the past 25 years of my life, even though I know that ChatGPT’s new search engine and especially Perplexity are clearly superior, unless I simply want a URL. These tools also complement education — another field in which we need radical reflection and change in the period ahead. I particularly like this prompt, which I saw over the weekend and share below, and which I hope to incorporate into my learning conversations with ChatGPT: Original English in the screenshot — Arjun Khemani (@arjunkhemani), 7 December 2024: My favorite ChatGPT prompt is: “I want you to keep talking to me and asking me questions until I understand [any hard topic I want to learn about].” Finally, I simply want to say that “not looking up” is not a good solution. The meteorite that triggers the explosion — in this case, it may be a good explosion in a great many respects — may still be delayed by a few years. It may even pass close by without affecting us structurally, although that now seems highly unlikely. But the answer is NOT to be unprepared, ignore it and act as though it did not exist . This humble journalist and teacher can do no more than put this text forward as a call to action, now, because time is running out and “ the coming wave ” is no longer on the horizon: it is right above us. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH P.S. I saw this short video after finishing the article, but I find it so revealing that I have to share it with you. At the press conference before the 2024 Nobel Prize ceremony, this year’s Nobel laureate in Physics — also referring to the prediction of the Nobel laureate in Chemistry sitting alongside him — says that ASI will arrive in 5–20 years: not AGI, artificial general intelligence, but the next step, superintelligence. And he has been a well-known sceptic in the AI field, despite being one of its fathers. Original English in the screenshot — Tsarathustra (@tsarnick), 9 December 2024: Nobel Laureate Geoffrey Hinton says AI superintelligence is "not hype" and he used to think it was further away but the speed of recent developments have convinced him that it will happen in 5-20 years Visible video subtitle: We will get something like Super Intelligence in about 10 years

Operación Retuit: AI as a shield for Venezuelan journalism César Batiz recounts how Venezuelan and Colombian journalists used AI avatars and media alliances to report under censorship and protect their colleagues. César Batiz Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 062 Analysis Operación Retuit: AI as a shield for Venezuelan journalism This week, estrategIA brings you a very special article on using artificial intelligence to fight censorship in Venezuela , particularly through Operación Retuit , which we discussed in issue 47 . Our contributor is César Batiz ( his Wikipedia entry ), an investigative journalist and director of the Venezuelan digital news outlet El Pitazo . Historical context: this first-person account was published on 4 December 2024. Events, assessments and expectations retain the author's perspective at that time. On 30 November, just two years had passed since the arrival of ChatGPT, the artificial intelligence application built by OpenAI. Yet its emergence set in motion a series of projects being developed in innovation laboratories in countries including the United States, China, the United Kingdom, Canada and Israel. Seven months later, in June 2023, the study “A Survey of Generative AI Applications” counted 350 generative AI applications in use. That growth naturally brought growing pains. Plagiarism, bias and hoaxes emerged, raising the alarm over the risks of using AI. In August 2024, 21 months after ChatGPT's arrival, we Colombian and Venezuelan journalists came together to use artificial intelligence as a shield to defend freedom of expression and protect the staff of 14 media outlets, launching Operación Retuit — Operation Retweet. Operación Retuit is a news report we created in response to the threats arising from the state terrorism imposed by Nicolás Maduro's government after the presidential election of 28 July. Opposition candidate Edmundo González won that election with 67% of the vote, a victory the ruling authorities refused to recognise. Both the initiative and its name turn prevailing narratives on their head in two ways. First, they demonstrate that generative artificial intelligence has a use in journalism when backed by quality and ethics. It is not simply a tool for evil, as a black-and-white view of this innovation's emergence would have it. Second, the initiative puts a new spin on the narrative of terror deployed by Maduro's government and its current interior minister, Diosdado Cabello. For at least two years, intelligence agencies have been carrying out the so-called Operación Tuntún against opposition leaders and citizens. “Tuntún” is the onomatopoeic “knock-knock” of officers arriving at people's homes to arrest those targeted by repression. Hence the name Operación Retuit. Its distinctive feature is that the programme is presented by la Chama and el Pana — colloquial Venezuelan terms for a woman and a man, respectively — two avatars created using generative AI. They present the reporting of Venezuelan journalists, with the support of colleagues at Connectas, the Latin American journalism hub based in Bogotá. Less civic space, more fear Operación Retuit was launched amid shrinking civic space and the persecution of dissent against Maduro's government. Since the start of the year, the National Assembly, dominated by Maduro's supporters, had passed laws threatening NGOs' ability to operate. Political figures and community leaders remained in the sights of Venezuelan intelligence and security agencies, restricting political activity in an election year. Before 28 July, 25 people had been detained for reporting. A further 58 websites were blocked following an order issued by the National Telecommunications Commission (Conatel) to telecommunications operators in Venezuela, including Spain's Telefónica, preventing Venezuelans from accessing digital media and obtaining information. In addition, by June 2024, 14 radio stations had been ordered to close. After 28 July and Maduro's theft of the election, the situation worsened. At midday on 29 July, street protests began in middle-class areas and working-class communities on the hillsides of Caracas. People were protesting against the stolen election. From that point, a plan of state terrorism was set in motion that seemed to follow a prepared script. Maduro announced in advance that 2,000 people would be detained. Police and military personnel went out to meet that target. They arrested people passing protests without taking part, citizens standing outside their homes and, of course, demonstrators whose only weapons were their cries in support of democracy. With the help of a network of informers funded through political patronage, police and military officers searched for those who had toppled statues of Chávez — protesters brought down five in the first 24 hours — or taken photographs and videos of the moment. Around ten journalists were imprisoned. Members of press teams in government bodies run by ruling-party supporters began calling journalists to warn that they could be arrested if they went out to cover the protests. Fear took root in the profession. Few colleagues dared return to the streets. Experienced in working together This escalation of state terrorism came at a time when we in independent digital media had recognised working in alliances as part of our strategy for confronting government censorship. By 2014, there had been other experiences of collaboration in Latin America, but in transnational investigative journalism projects. These followed the recognition that, if criminals join forces to commit crimes, protect one another and launder money, journalists should also work together to scrutinise them. Organisations such as the Instituto Prensa y Sociedad (IPYS) and Fundación Gabo promoted these initiatives. Alliances in Venezuela matured following the creation of independent digital media led by journalists committed to fighting censorship. This helped bring about the Alianza Rebelde Investiga (ARI), comprising El Pitazo, Runrunes and TalCual, which covered eight national electoral processes between 2015 and 2024. It also enabled the emergence, in 2024, of La Hora de Venezuela, an initiative promoted by Connectas, and Venezuela Vota, proposed by El Pitazo. La Hora de Venezuela and Venezuela Vota sought to build alliances that would enable access to and distribution of information both inside and outside Venezuela, involving more than 350 journalists. La Hora de Venezuela brought together 14 media outlets across Latin America to produce 528 pieces. On 27, 28 and 29 July, Venezuela Vota produced a YouTube broadcast with information from more than 90 Venezuelan municipalities and 18 cities around the world. All content was shared with 140 media outlets in Latin America and Europe. Although both alliances were active when the protests and repression began in Venezuela, state terrorism forced a tactical retreat, reflection and a search for alternatives that would allow us to continue our work. That was how Operación Retuit emerged. The face of the media Behind the dialogue between la Chama and el Pana, Operación Retuit's two avatars, lies the work of reporters in Venezuela and the script and voice production of colleagues in Bogotá, who put the finishing touches to the output of this first season. Operación Retuit published 30 episodes in Spanish and English. The first episode alone, released on 14 August, received 400,000 views in 24 hours, and its impact was immediate both in Venezuela and abroad. The initiative's innovative approach attracted coverage from around a hundred media outlets in ten languages worldwide, including The Guardian, the BBC, El País and CNN, as well as international journalism centres such as Nieman Lab, LatAm, IJNet and Journalism Review. Operación Retuit is currently awaiting a second season, which will begin after the inauguration on 10 January. As long as there are stories to tell in confronting Venezuelan authoritarianism, la Chama and el Pana will return. César Batiz Investigative journalist and director of the digital news outlet El Pitazo LinkedIn
