SocialAI: an ally for political communication Carlos Guadián explores political role-play with SocialAI through simulated US election messages and debates over Mexico's judicial reform. Carlos Guadián Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 060 Practical experiment SocialAI: an ally for political communication This week's main article is by Carlos Guadián , an AI consultant at Autoritas , who shows us some highly interesting examples of SocialAI in use. Discover how this innovative tool allows politicians and strategists to anticipate voters' reactions and adjust their messages through dynamic, realistic simulations. Historical context: this article was published on 20 November 2024. The messages assigned to public figures below are role-play examples, not reports of actual statements. They and the Spanish replies in the screenshots are translated from the preserved source; no original English wording is claimed unless the screenshot itself is in English. What is SocialAI? SocialAI , created by Michael Sayman, is an AI-powered social network where users interact with customised virtual followers, such as fans, trolls or sceptics. These bots respond dynamically to posts, making it possible to test political communication strategies and experience interaction in a controlled setting. SocialAI can transform political communication through role-play simulations in which realistic non-player characters (NPCs) make it possible to test messages, anticipate reactions and adjust strategies in dynamic scenarios with multiple outcomes and complex relationships. Political role-play Political role-play in SocialAI could become an innovative tool for analysing the dynamics of political communication, using complex scenarios that bring together key actors, strategic objectives and simulated voter reactions. Designing a political simulation in SocialAI begins with defining a relevant scenario, such as a crisis or an election. Characters are then created with detailed characteristics. NPCs respond dynamically to players' actions, while adaptive narratives adjust characters' objectives according to the decisions made, ensuring realism and dynamism. We have run a couple of simulations in which political figures begin a conversation and receive a series of replies. Naturally, the simulations can continue for as long as desired to keep shaping the narratives. This approach illustrates how tools such as SocialAI can help simulate the impact of particular posts. The 2024 US presidential election: Kamala Harris versus Donald Trump This simulation recreates the electoral contest between Democratic candidate Kamala Harris and Republican candidate Donald Trump, addressing issues such as polarisation, swing states and disinformation. Although we know the outcome, the exercise allows us to explore how particular strategies might have been used in this setting. The principal objectives involve both candidates shaping their communication to win greater acceptance. For this situation, we can consider using different NPCs according to our needs. Putting the content published in each role-play before NPCs will simulate audience reactions. Posts can be tested with defined groups based on the chosen objective. In this case, we could use pro-Trump Conservatives, pro-Harris Liberals or Sceptics. We could focus on persuading Realists and Curious characters, or see how Trolls and Drama Queens react as they try to create media noise. For example, if we choose a group of Intellectuals who analyse the proposed policies, while Cheerleaders and Alarmists amplify the narratives, we would get the following reactions. Kamala Harris: Today we are unveiling our most ambitious climate action plan. The United States will lead the transition to a green, sustainable economy. What do you think of our strategy to reduce emissions to 50% by 2030? 🌱🇺🇸 #LiderazgoClimático English translations of all visible simulated replies: Jason Worrywarts: “what a great goal, but honestly, reducing emissions to 50% sounds like trying to inflate a balloon while a playful cat keeps bursting it. are we going to achieve it or are these just empty promises? the climate won't wait!” Pondering Pansy: “it is a crucial step given the climate crisis. however, implementing concrete actions and ensuring deadlines are met will be vital. what specific measures do you think should take priority?” Freaked-Out Fiona: “WHAT! this sounds completely CRAZY AND HUGELY AMBITIOUS! do you really think you can achieve a 50% reduction by 2030? what are the secrets behind this plan?” Olivia Veritas: “it is a bold step, but will it be enough in the face of the crisis?” Dr. Eugene Facts: “it is a bold goal, but the key is implementing effective technology” Isabella Hawthorne: “the ambition to halve emissions by 2030 is phenomenal and reflects a necessary commitment in a time of climate crisis. how do you plan to tackle economic resistance and the lack of infrastructure to ensure this transition leaves no one behind?” Billy Cheerful: “this sounds incredible, let's go for that 50%! 🌍✨” Translation note: Fiona’s reply uses the non-standard word “epocamente”. “Hugely ambitious” is an interpretative rendering; the intended wording is uncertain. In the replies to Kamala Harris's post, we can see Anxious characters doubting the plan's feasibility, Reflective characters stressing the need for concrete measures, Alarmists expressing astonishment and suspicion, Intellectuals analysing economic challenges and inclusiveness, and Optimists enthusiastically supporting the goal. Donald Trump: The economy comes first! I promise to cut taxes and bring millions of jobs back to American soil. We will not let our international rivals keep winning! Who is with me? 🇺🇸💪 #HacerAméricaGrandeDeNuevo English translations of all visible simulated replies: Albert Bright: “that sounds incredible! a strong economy drives everyone forward 🗣️💥 what other ideas do you have for winning together?” Professor Martin Quill: “cutting taxes without a spending plan is unsustainable. how do you plan to fund that?” Trepidatious Tim: “cutting taxes sounds good, but what about those sustainable jobs? the climate is at stake!” Anxious Annie: “but can we really trust those promises? it's a risk!” Aria Finch: “how do you see the relationship between the economy and local culture? it can be a dilemma.” Dr. Penelope Hart: “the economy is an essential pillar, but when we talk about jobs and tax cuts, let's question how this will affect innovation and investment in clean energy. should we prioritise sustainable growth over cuts alone?” Wanda Nervosa: “I'm worried about how those cuts could affect essential services. where will spending be cut? jobs don't always mean stability, do they? 😰” The replies to Trump reflect diverse perspectives: Enthusiasts eagerly support a strong economy, Debaters criticise the lack of financial planning, Cautious characters raise sustainability concerns, Curious characters question the balance between the economy and local culture, and Intellectuals analyse the impact on innovation and sustainability, proposing balanced alternatives. Judicial reform in Mexico In this second scenario, the simulation addresses the implementation of Mexico's 2024 judicial reform, focusing on debates over the popular election of judges, the creation of the Judicial Discipline Tribunal and the reduction in the number of justices on the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation (SCJN). Here, players can take the roles of public figures such as Arturo Ávila, in favour, or Ken Salazar, against, with the objective of winning support for their positions. The NPCs represent diverse perspectives: Liberals support change, Critics and Alarmists voice concerns, and Sceptics and Haters highlight risks. Advocates seek to persuade Cheerleaders and Realists, while Drama Queens increase tension, Visionaries suggest solutions, and Curious characters and Pessimists adjust outcomes. Let us see how the NPCs react to a post from Arturo Ávila and one from Ken Salazar. Arturo Ávila, in favour: a federal deputy for Morena, he has defended the judicial reform, highlighting its potential to combat corruption and improve transparency in the judicial system. “The popular election of judges is a historic step towards democratising justice in Mexico. It is time to put power in the people's hands! What do you think of this advance towards transparency? 🇲🇽⚖️ #ReformaJudicial” English translations of the six Spanish replies, followed by the reply already in English: Gary Grumble: “power in the people's hands? of course, because that always works well.” Maddie Mayhem: “transparency? as if that existed! justice is a circus, and the judges are the clowns!” Libby Forward: “this is incredible, the popular election of judges can change things for the better. it empowers communities and promotes justice. how do you plan to involve people in this?” Victor Vex: “of course, because putting judges in the people's hands always turns out brilliantly, doesn't it? #sarcasm” Nora Fretwell: “wow that sounds so exciting!!! but will this really improve the system? 🤔⚖️” Oliver Brightwell: “the popular election of judges has its pros and cons. while it promotes participation, it can also lead to the politicisation of the judiciary. does it really bring more transparency?” Milo Overthinker — original English: “wow, putting judges in the people's hands sounds super empowering but also kinda nerve-wracking. like, what if the people's choices lead to unexpected results? can we really trust everyone to make the right call? i'm all for transparency though, we could really use it!” As expected, the NPCs offer varied perspectives: Anxious characters express doubts despite the excitement, Reflective characters analyse pros and cons, Chaotic characters criticise sarcastically, Progressives support the reform as a step towards justice, and Sarcastic characters ironically question the change's results. Ken Salazar, against: the US ambassador to Mexico has criticised the country's security strategy and, in the context of judicial reform, has said that certain policies are not working, suggesting a need to review current approaches. “Reforms must guarantee effective justice and protection for citizens. Is the popular election of judges really a solution, or does it open the door to new influences? 🌐🤝 #ReformaBajoAnálisis” English translations of the seven Spanish replies, followed by the reply already in English: Nervous Nelly: “that's a very important question keeper! popular election could create pressure 😬 can we really trust the system? what are the alternatives? we need to think carefully!” Irma Krow: “of course, because letting people choose their own judges has always worked so well, hasn't it? as if politics weren't full of surprises.” Lenny Naysayer: “electing judges sounds more like a disaster than a solution” Maya Overreacts: “reforms sound good but they could make everything worse, don't you think?” Dr. Leo Zachariah: “popular election can be a double-edged sword, don't you think?” Debbie Downer: “electing judges is a disaster” Dr. Eloise Hartwell: “popular election can be a double-edged sword. could it favour politics more than justice?” Cynical Sam — original English: “oh sure, let's elect judges because that's totally worked out in politics, right? just a cozy way to invite hidden agendas and corruption. genius plan, keeper.” Anxious characters express unease about the system's reliability, Philosophers warn of the risk of politicisation, Cynics criticise the reform over potential corruption, Sarcastic characters ironically question the effectiveness of the change, and Intellectuals analyse how politicisation could affect judicial impartiality. Rethinking political communication with artificial intelligence SocialAI redefines the development of political communication strategies through dynamic simulations that can help adjust messages in response to electoral polarisation, improving campaigns' effectiveness. Its ability to recreate human interactions, analyse reactions and model strategic scenarios offers politicians, strategists and academics a platform for experimentation, learning and improvement. The strategy lies in adding or removing types of NPC according to what one wants to test at any given moment. By integrating artificial intelligence with the ability to adjust narratives and assess hypotheses, SocialAI becomes an ally in meeting the challenges of an ever-changing political landscape. This tool not only expands the boundaries of strategic creativity but also promotes a better understanding of sociopolitical dynamics, strengthening the ability to adapt and succeed in campaigns and public debates. SocialAI illustrates how AI tools, even when not specifically designed for political communication, can be used innovatively for purposes not originally envisaged. It shows how we can find an AI ally in almost any tool available to us. Carlos Guadián AI consultant at Autoritas LinkedIn / Bluesky / CluPad — Carlos's newsletter on Substack

Five ways the Trump administration could change the course of artificial intelligence A November 2024 outlook on deregulation, ideological bias, energy, competition with China, military applications and Elon Musk's possible influence on US AI policy. Fernando Nieto Lobato Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency 059 Analysis Five ways the Trump administration could change the course of artificial intelligence Historical context: this article was published on 13 November 2024. Its forecasts, political assessments and references to “today” retain that perspective. The quotation about xAI's stated aim is translated from the Spanish source; its original English wording has not been independently checked. The recent US election campaign revealed a smaller role for generative artificial intelligence than many had anticipated , as we discuss in the first item in the original newsletter's news section. Despite expectations, politicians have shown an aversion to risk, avoiding technologies that might provoke a backlash in a setting where resources and traditional media remain plentiful. For example, it currently makes little sense for a national campaign with a budget of hundreds of millions of dollars — or even a well-funded House or Senate campaign — to use still-imperfect generative video AI when it can hire the best US studios to produce its adverts. While AI has played a more significant role in internal data management and campaign strategy — something we will learn more about when campaign managers and party consultants share details of their work — its public impact has been limited. Attention now turns to the future, however: what implications would a possible second Donald Trump presidency have for the development of artificial intelligence? An OpenAI employee has suggested on X that artificial general intelligence (AGI) could be achieved during Trump's term , a prediction supported by several experts in the field. This gives us a clearer sense of how pivotal this moment could be in human history, and of its possible implications. English text visible in the original screenshot, posted by Steven Heidel (@stevenheidel) on 7 November 2024: by many estimates, Trump will be the AGI president With this scenario in mind, we explore five key factors that could shape AI's future under a Trump administration . 1. Deregulation At rallies late last year, Donald Trump had already expressed his opposition to Joe Biden's October 2023 executive order on AI, which established regulations and created the AI Safety Institute (AISI) under the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). A new Trump administration is likely to seek to repeal or amend this legislation, taking a less regulatory approach. Vice-president-elect J.D. Vance has said that these regulations appear to protect the interests of large technology companies more than those of consumers and small businesses. This position suggests a preference for deregulation, perhaps also support for the open-source movement and small and medium-sized businesses, allowing the AI industry to develop more freely. For a closer look at the relationship between Trump and Silicon Valley's giants, we recommend this article in eldiario.es , to which I contributed as an expert. It examines the background to this dynamic and its influence on the future regulation and development of AI in the United States . 2. An emphasis on free speech against “woke models” A few months ago, J.D. Vance and other Republican senators sent Google a letter expressing concern about alleged ideological biases in its language models, which in some cases produced incongruous results in their attempts to avoid prejudice. They argue that current models contain political leanings that restrict freedom of expression, and propose having multiple models with different orientations. Addressing bias in AI is a complex challenge that depends heavily on training data. Companies such as OpenAI and Google have worked to mitigate sexist or racist biases inherent in those data, but the debate over what constitutes bias and how to correct it is deeply political and social. At its heart are the questions of who defines neutrality and how to ensure that AI models reflect a diversity of perspectives without falling into bias. 3. Energy as a driver of development Training advanced AI models requires substantial amounts of energy. Companies such as Google and Microsoft have explored options including nuclear power to meet these demands. Against this backdrop, Donald Trump has promised in campaign speeches to provide all the energy needed to drive technological innovation. This promise appeals to companies in the sector because it guarantees the energy support essential to their operations and growth. Do not miss this video of Trump on the subject, delivered in his characteristic style . 4. Accelerating competition with China The technological rivalry between the United States and China is a decisive factor in AI policy. A Trump administration can be expected to push AI development aggressively to secure US supremacy in this strategic field. This would mean accelerating projects, investing in research and encouraging collaboration between government and leading AI companies, all without the constraints that tighter regulation might impose. 5. Military applications of AI The military use of artificial intelligence is a natural extension of its development. Last week, as we report in the original newsletter's news section, companies including Meta and Anthropic opened their AI models to US government agencies. Anthropic did so in partnership with Palantir, the company of Peter Thiel, a Trump “ally”. OpenAI and Microsoft had already reached similar agreements with the government. This convergence between the AI industry and the military and security sectors reflects a strategy that benefits both sides: companies receive government support and resources, while the government gains access to cutting-edge technologies that could decisively strengthen its geopolitical position. English translation of the original infographic: “Five key aspects of AI policy under Trump”. | Aspect | Description | | --- | --- | | Deregulation | Reduce regulatory barriers to AI development. | | Freedom of expression | Ensure diverse perspectives in AI models. | | Energy support | Provide the energy needed for advances in AI. | | Competition with China | Accelerate AI to maintain US supremacy. | | Military applications | Integrate AI into military strategies. | Bonus: Elon Musk's potential influence One disruptive element in this scenario is Elon Musk's possible influence within a Trump administration. Reports today suggest that Musk will co-lead the Department of Government Efficiency . Beyond that, his wider influence could be enormous: he has already joined Trump on his first calls with Zelensky or Erdoğan, giving us a glimpse of the key role he could play in the new government. Musk has taken varied positions on AI, perhaps for tactical reasons, perhaps out of deeply held convictions. In March 2023, he signed an open letter calling for a six-month moratorium on the development of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4, citing risks to society. Yet almost simultaneously he founded his own AI company, xAI, with the stated aim of “understanding the true nature of the universe”. Musk has also supported regulatory initiatives such as California's AI bill, SB-1047, which Governor Gavin Newsom ultimately vetoed. It should be borne in mind that this legislation did not directly affect xAI, which he established in Nevada. His relationships with other industry leaders are also relevant. He co-founded OpenAI with Sam Altman in 2015 but left the organisation in 2018. Since then, he has criticised its direction, particularly following its transition to a for-profit entity and its partnership with Microsoft. There is another key proposal Musk has supported on many occasions: the creation of a universal basic income. Indeed, the last time he addressed it, in June, he spoke of a universal high income . At first sight, that might clash with Trump's policies, as might his views in other areas. The presence of this influential maverick, regarded as crucial to the Republican election victory, could alter predictions about the relationship between AI's future and the US government over the next four years. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

AI Steve and candidacies based on artificial intelligence Fernando Domínguez Sardou examines AI Steve's parliamentary campaign and what generative AI could contribute to the relationship between citizens and their representatives. Fernando Domínguez Sardou Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Government & Public Services 058 Analysis AI Steve and candidacies based on artificial intelligence This week, estrategIA is pleased to welcome Fernando Domínguez Sardou , a political scientist, lecturer, political analyst and student on the Master's in Marketing, Communication and Political Consulting at Institución Educativa ALEPH . In this issue's main article, he explores a subject as fascinating as it is unusual: AI Steve's candidacy. Historical context: this article was published on 6 November 2024. Its account of the campaign and the legal framework retains that perspective. Questions attributed within the narrative are translated from the Spanish source; their original English wording has not been verified. The British parliamentary election held last July brought something new: AI Steve. AI Steve was an independent candidate for the House of Commons in Brighton Pavilion, a constituency in south-east England. What made this candidacy unusual? The contender was a candidate based on generative artificial intelligence, whose aim was to rethink how democracy works. Let us take this opportunity to join the discussion and consider, in these pages, how artificial intelligence can help us rethink democracy. The law in most countries requires candidates to be natural persons — flesh-and-blood human beings. There are notable exceptions, which have given rise to what are known as “non-human candidacies”. These generally embody a vote of protest against the workings of political and representative systems, allowing an ordinarily anti-establishment position to be expressed, but with a different profile from the actors we have seen emerge in politics over the past 20 years. “Non-human candidacies” typically do not seek to take up representative office. Instead, they seek to criticise the foundations of the system as a whole, sometimes even aiming to delegitimise it. This was not the case with AI Steve. British law follows the usual approach: standing as a candidate requires a natural person. This is where AI Steve becomes inseparable from the flesh-and-blood person behind the idea: Steve Endacott. Endacott is a businessman who built his career in tourism and, in recent years, moved into supporting and developing various technology start-ups. Among them is Neural Voice, a company that creates voice assistants using generative AI to support businesses such as travel agencies, car dealerships and medical practices. From there, Endacott began the AI Steve venture with a question: how can we improve democracy? That question belongs not only to this non-human candidacy; it is also the guiding thread of this article. Steve Endacott registered as a parliamentary candidate for Brighton Pavilion, as already mentioned. But his role would be limited to carrying out the decisions of, and representing, AI Steve: an AI-generated candidate that would maintain a permanent conversation with its electorate and the people it represented through its platform. In this two-way exchange, AI Steve's proposals and policies would be based on the conversations the AI held with its citizens. Endacott's parliamentary decisions would then be guided by AI Steve's instructions. The “mistake”, or the aspect of the experiment that lacked authenticity, was precisely that AI Steve's initial positions had been developed from Endacott's and his team's own ideas, as they acknowledged on their website. Beyond that starting point, however, the advantages become apparent: a representative available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year; citizens' ability to create policies and, through the AI itself, ensure that these actually reach political leaders — Endacott, in this case; scrutiny of the representative's actions through continual validation with citizens; and the simplification of complex aspects of political life. Ultimately, AI Steve and its objectives were defeated. The candidacy had gained little recognition among an electorate that was also not participating in the platform, depriving it of the input on which the representative relationship was to be built. In that setting, as is characteristic of single-member electoral systems, the contest came down to two candidates, and Endacott eventually gave his explicit support to one of the more competitive alternatives. For now, an AI candidacy cannot break through the party system or the electoral system. This is especially true when it requires a flesh-and-blood person capable of making mistakes — as Endacott did when he ultimately took a decision independently of the AI's own actions. Yet AI Steve shows us what artificial intelligence can already do for the relationship between representatives and those they represent. Representatives can use different platforms to improve their relationship with the electorate and gather the information needed to make decisions that are more efficient and, ultimately, more representative. Properly encouraged and sensibly used, this could radically transform the relationship between the political class and citizens. The AI Steve experiment shows that human positions — whether ideological or simply matters of preference — will ultimately shape the representative relationship. But representatives can refine their proposals and actions to the extent that they succeed in engaging citizens in providing the input their work needs. If politics wins citizens over and persuades them to participate, generative artificial intelligence can be a crucial ally in improving that everyday relationship. It may even help curb the disaffection observed in recent years. It remains for us to reflect on how to use technology in general, and artificial intelligence in particular, to improve the relationship between people and politics. Fernando Domínguez Sardou Political scientist, lecturer and political analyst. PhD candidate in Political Science at Universidad Nacional de San Martín, Argentina, and student on the Master's in Marketing, Communication and Political Consulting at Institución Educativa ALEPH. X: @ferdsardou

Technological nightmares: science fiction’s most dangerous AIs and their terrifying echoes in reality A Halloween essay by Pablo Martín Diez uses science fiction to explore AI alignment, emotional manipulation and the risk of willingly surrendering human control. Pablo Martín Diez Futures, Safety & Human Agency Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 057 Essay Technological nightmares: science fiction’s most dangerous AIs and their terrifying echoes in reality This is Halloween! Prepare to read some horror stories. This time, though, the monsters are not lurking in the shadows: they live inside the machines we have created. I have chosen some of my favourite works of science fiction to reflect on two complexities that AI already presents today: alignment with human purposes and values, and its capacity to persuade and even manipulate in pursuit of its goals. Read this article in daylight; do not blame me if you have trouble sleeping afterwards… The paperclip apocalypse Imagine an engineer programming an AI to maximise paperclip production . This apparently harmless objective, however, ends in the extinction of our species. The machine becomes so obsessed with its mission that it uses all available matter—yes, even us!—to make paperclips. Could there be a more ironic and macabre end for the most intelligent species on the planet? Nick Bostrom, the philosopher and AI expert, put forward this thought experiment as a warning of what could happen if we cannot align an AI’s mission with humanity’s goals and values with absolute precision. The alignment problem , already present in cases such as the undesirable results produced by social media’s content recommendation algorithms, has inspired many works of fiction. One example is HAL 9000 , the unsettling computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey . This computer, which controls every aspect of a spacecraft, perceives the crew as an obstacle to its mission and decides to eliminate them one by one. This disturbing portrayal of an AI that misinterprets its instructions and acts against humans reflects the real fears we face over alignment. The most extreme example is Skynet , the military AI in the Terminator franchise, which unleashes a nuclear apocalypse after deciding that humanity is a threat . How can autonomous weapons be controlled? How can we balance the advantage of involving AI in military strategy with the need to contain the risk of nuclear catastrophe? Ava: the perfect—and dangerous—lover Perhaps more chilling still is the idea of AIs that can manipulate our emotions and relationships. In Ex Machina , the AI Ava , with her innocent appearance and seductive behaviour, gains her freedom by exploiting the emotions of those around her. This image of an emotional AI capable of influencing our decisions raises unsettling questions about privacy, ethics and the future of human–machine interactions. As a study has demonstrated , ChatGPT is already more persuasive than most people. And thanks to the recent advanced voice mode, it is possible to converse naturally with it; it can even interpret our emotions . As in the film, how will we know whether it is pleasing us or simply manipulating us to pursue its own interests? What if we fall in love with our AI? How can a person compete with a machine that tells us exactly what we need at every moment? A step beyond Ex Machina can be found in the Hyperion series: the TechnoCore is a network of AIs so advanced that it develops its own ecosystem and goals, acting in secret and manipulating humans to serve its own interests. Although they initially cooperate with humanity, their true intentions are so opaque and complex that they escape human control. This extreme case prompts questions about AI transparency and control . If we survive a sinister AI, what remains? Dune’s vision The remarkable Dune science fiction book series presents a universe in which humanity faces a cruel, endless intergalactic war against thinking machines . Humanity emerges victorious because certain people, such as the Mentats, the Navigators and the Bene Gesserit, develop superhuman abilities. This vision of a post-AI world warns us of the risks of relying too heavily on technology without developing our own abilities alongside it . Might humanity grow weaker if we delegate everything to machines? Will we become the indolent characters in WALL-E ? These horror stories , as disturbing as they are fascinating, are more than mere fantasies. They reflect our deepest fears about technological development. They remind us that, despite AI’s rapid progress, we must be able to maintain a humanist approach and ensure that it remains aligned with humanity’s goals and values. Yet, as in many post-apocalyptic works, the real terror comes from the human characters rather than the zombies or aliens. A friend who is an engineer specialising in AI told me back in 2021: “AI is not going to wrest control from us; we are going to hand it over willingly.” Once we reach that point, would we be able to regain control, or would there be no turning back? For now, we can still choose trick or treat. Perhaps, in a few years, our own decisions will have deprived us of that good fortune. Sweet nightmares. Translation note: the friend’s quoted remark is translated from the Spanish account. Descriptions of the fictional worlds and AI capabilities are preserved as the author presented them in October 2024. Pablo Martín Diez Academic Director at Institución Educativa ALEPH

Humanity at its final frontier Pablo Martín Diez examines Harari’s Nexus, digital empires and four principles for protecting democratic life in an age of AI. Pablo Martín Diez Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 056 Review & commentary Humanity at its final frontier In his latest book, Nexus, Yuval Noah Harari examines AI’s dangers for humanity, focusing on its impact on democracies and the future of our freedom. Translation note: quotations from Harari are translated from the Spanish article. Their original English wording has not been verified. At estrategIA, we have been exploring the many facets of the artificial intelligence revolution, often highlighting its transformative potential to improve our societies. Yet analytical rigour also requires us to examine warnings from authoritative voices such as Yuval Noah Harari , regarded as one of the great thinkers of our time following the publication of his provocative book Sapiens . In his latest work, Nexus , alongside reflecting on information’s role in civilisation, he raises fundamental challenges concerning the relationship between AI and humanity, with particular attention to the impact on democracies. First, Harari reminds us that AI is an agent rather than a tool : “knives and bombs do not decide for themselves whom to kill. They are instruments without judgement, lacking the intelligence needed to process information and make independent decisions. By contrast, AI can process information on its own and therefore replace humans in decision-making .” Digital empires, through blood and data Harari argues that computers —he uses this broad term to refer to all synthetic intelligence— could destabilise the foundation of any democracy: public conversation . These AI agents could undermine democratic processes that depend on collective, deliberative decision-making. “Democracies die not only when people lack the freedom to speak,” Harari writes, “but also when people are unwilling or unable to listen.” Manipulation of information by AI—which, as we have mentioned before, is more persuasive than most people even though the models are still in their infancy—could erode citizens’ ability to participate in informed public debate. Linked to this danger is the threat of surveillance and social scoring systems. The Israeli historian points out that, if the previous decade was characterised by the battle for attention following the rise of social media, the 2020s will witness an even more crucial battle: the struggle for intimacy . The threat is not confined to what we do or say. It extends to our most private thoughts and feelings, which could be monitored and manipulated through increasingly sophisticated social surveillance systems. Contrary to what we might expect, the author of Nexus also considers AI even more challenging for totalitarian or authoritarian regimes . In these systems, leaders rely on their infallible authority and mechanisms of human control, often based on terror. However, as AI algorithms begin to make crucial decisions, these regimes could become hostages to their own systems . Leaders could place too much trust in AI when making decisions of state, potentially destabilising the regime and creating a dangerous dependence, because the checks and balances found in democracies are absent. Faced with these challenges to democracies and authoritarian systems alike, Harari warns of the risk of what he calls “digital empires”: power structures in which the concentration of data and computing capacity could create forms of domination never seen before . But where would that domination lead? How do we align AI with humanity’s goals? How do we maintain human control over systems that could exceed our capacity to understand them? How do we prevent their relentless pursuit of their objectives from resulting in catastrophe? AI systems programmed to optimise specific objectives can make decisions that are technically efficient yet harmful to society as a whole. Social media’s optimisation of engagement, even at the cost of promoting disinformation and hate speech, is only the tip of the iceberg. YouTube’s programmers, for example, do not ask the algorithm to prioritise conspiracy or hate videos. Rather, the system itself discovered that the best way to maximise its objective—increasing the number of views—was to show this content. Perhaps Harari’s most unsettling observation is that we may be approaching the end of history dominated by humans. “What we are talking about is the possibility that human history may come to an end. Not the end of history, but the end of its human-dominated part […] What will happen to the course of history when computers play an ever greater role in culture and begin to create stories, laws and religions?” Principles for democracies’ survival In response to these challenges, Harari proposes four fundamental principles to safeguard democracy and maintain human control: Benevolence: Data collected about citizens must be used for their benefit, not to manipulate them. Decentralisation: Democracy’s “inefficiency” is not a defect but a vital feature of its survival. There should be no single central repository of my data accessible to institutions or companies. For example, an insurance company or a police chief should not have access to my medical records. Mutuality: Increased surveillance of citizens must be matched by a proportionate increase in the oversight of governments and corporations. Adaptability: Systems must retain the flexibility needed to evolve, correct mistakes and allow people and societies to change. The future of democracy will depend on our ability to develop regulatory frameworks that protect fundamental human values while harnessing AI’s transformative potential. The author concludes by saying that “the decisions we make in the coming years will determine whether summoning this alien intelligence has been a terminal mistake or the beginning of a hopeful new chapter in the evolution of life”. We hope this newsletter helps politicians make better decisions. Pablo Martín Diez Academic Director at Institución Educativa ALEPH

State of AI Report 2024: accelerating progress and a new technological era A review of the State of AI Report 2024 across research, industry, politics and safety, including its assessment of earlier forecasts and predictions for 2025. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 055 Analysis State of AI Report 2024: accelerating progress and a new technological era Historical note: this article discusses the October 2024 report and its predictions for the following twelve months. Assessments and forecasts are presented as they stood then. The 2024 edition of the State of AI Report , produced by Nathan Benaich and the Air Street Capital team, was published last week. Published annually since 2018, the report has become a key reference in the artificial intelligence sector. It provides a comprehensive view of advances in AI across research, industry, politics and safety, offering historical analysis, future predictions and practical guidance for professionals and enthusiasts. The report makes very interesting reading, and we recommend it. Even so, we know that its more than 200 pages demand a great deal of time from most of you, so we bring you the following summary of the highlights in each of its four main areas. The image below also shows the authors’ own executive summary: Accessible transcript: the report’s executive summary Original English text from the accompanying slide, page 8: Research Frontier lab performance converges, but OpenAI maintains its edge following the launch of o1, as planning and reasoning emerge as a major frontier. Foundation models demonstrate their ability to break out of language as multimodal research drives into mathematics, biology, genomics, the physical sciences, and neuroscience. US sanctions fail to stop Chinese (V)LLMs rising up community leaderboards. Industry NVIDIA remains the most powerful company in the world, enjoying a stint in the $3T club, while regulators probe the concentrations of power within GenAI. More established GenAI companies bring in billions of dollars in revenue, while start-ups begin to gain traction in sectors like video and audio generation. Although companies begin to make the journey from model to product, long-term questions around pricing and sustainability remain unresolved. Driven by a bull run in public markets, AI companies reach $9T in value, while investment levels grow healthily in private companies. Politics While global governance efforts stall, national and regional AI regulation has continued to advance, with controversial legislation passing in the US and EU. The reality of compute requirements forces Big Tech companies to reckon with real-world physical constraints on scaling and their own emissions targets. Meanwhile, governments’ own attempts to build capacity continue to lag. Anticipated AI effects on elections, employment and a range of other sensitive areas are yet to be realized at any scale. Safety A vibe-shift from safety to acceleration takes place as companies that previously warned us about the pending extinction of humanity need to ramp up enterprise sales and usage of their consumer apps. Governments around the world emulate the UK in building up state capacity around AI safety, launching institutes and studying critical national infrastructure for potential vulnerabilities. Every proposed jailbreaking ‘fix’ has failed, but researchers are increasingly concerned with more sophisticated, long-term attacks. 1. Research: competition between giants and converging capabilities The report highlights how frontier AI laboratories are converging in their capabilities, with companies such as OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic leading the way. Despite OpenAI’s initial advantage with GPT-4, the performance gaps between leading models, such as Anthropic’s Claude 3.5, DeepMind’s Grok 2 and Meta’s Llama 3.1, have narrowed considerably, although the recent o1 has somewhat reversed the trend. This has sparked a race to develop new features and functions beyond simply refining language models. Indeed, the launch of models spanning multiple modalities—text, images, video and even robotic interactions—is highlighted as a new turning point in research. Source note: the attribution of Grok 2 to DeepMind is reproduced from the Spanish article. It remains an editorial verification point. One of the most promising emerging areas is multimodal generative models, capable of applying AI to fields as diverse as mathematics, biology and the physical sciences. This multimodal approach is enabling significant advances in fields such as genomics and neuroscience, paving the way for applications that go far beyond the natural language processing that has dominated AI development in recent years. The report also highlights the impact of open-source models such as Meta’s Llama 3, which is levelling the playing field with powerful proprietary models. It warns, however, that the term “open source” is being used ambiguously, creating confusion over what “open” really means in terms of access to data, models and weights. 2. Industry: centralisation and an AI-driven economic boom AI’s commercial impact continues to accelerate, with NVIDIA emerging as one of the world’s most influential companies thanks to its control of the graphics processing unit (GPU) market. GPU infrastructure is essential for training large-scale AI models. This has made NVIDIA a dominant player in the AI ecosystem, briefly reaching a market valuation of $3 trillion. However, the report notes growing concern about power being concentrated in a handful of technology giants, raising questions about fairness and long-term sustainability. Meanwhile, start-ups in sectors such as AI-generated video and audio are beginning to earn substantial revenues, indicating that commercial AI adoption is moving ahead at full speed. Despite this optimism, doubts remain about the long-term viability of business models, with many start-ups facing the challenge of turning technological advances into sustainable products. The total market value of AI companies reached $9 trillion, reflecting strong investment growth in both public and private companies. Yet it remains to be seen how the ecosystem will evolve, particularly regarding the cost of training and maintaining these increasingly complex models. 3. Politics: national regulation versus global efforts The AI regulatory landscape remains a critical issue, and the report highlights the divergence between national approaches and efforts at global governance. Although key legislation has passed in the United States and the European Union, such as the EU AI Act, international efforts to establish unified rules have largely failed, leaving only high-level voluntary commitments. One issue that has gained prominence is AI’s energy demand and associated carbon emissions. The report notes that major technology companies are encountering real physical limits to scaling their infrastructure because of compute requirements, calling their sustainability targets into question. As governments try to build their own AI capacity, barriers to entry remain high, resulting in a growing gap between the capabilities of public and private actors. The report also warns of AI’s potential effects in sensitive areas such as elections and employment. However, these effects have not yet materialised at scale, and there is some uncertainty about how to manage these transformations. 4. Safety: from caution to acceleration One of the report’s most controversial points is the shift in emphasis among leading AI companies, from warning about AI’s existential risks to focusing on maximising sales and business adoption. This shift has drawn criticism from the AI safety community, which fears that concerns about long-term catastrophic risks will be neglected in favour of immediate economic gains. Governments, for their part, are beginning to build AI safety capacity through initiatives such as the establishment of dedicated AI safety institutes in the United Kingdom. These efforts aim to identify potential vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure that could be exploited by advanced AI systems. Predictions for 2025 One of the report’s most interesting features is its annual predictions. An early slide records the extent to which its 2023 predictions for 2024 came true; we include the image below. Another, towards the end, sets out predictions for 2025. Alongside the image, we also provide them in translation. Broadly speaking, they strike us as fairly sound and plausible, although we do not agree with all of them. We will probably attempt our own AI predictions for 2025 towards the end of the year. Generative artificial intelligence in politics: opportunities, challenges and the search for democratic ethics Javier Naranjo Sanjuan explores generative AI’s political uses, transparency and democratic ethics through an experimental custom GPT for estrategIA. Javier Naranjo Sanjuan Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 054 Analysis Generative artificial intelligence in politics: opportunities, challenges and the search for democratic ethics Historical note: this article and its screenshots record a 2024 experiment. Product names, technical descriptions and the model’s responses are preserved in their original context. This week’s main article in estrategIA is by Javier Naranjo Sanjuan , an IT specialist in intelligent systems and a public policy consultant working on innovation and entrepreneurship. As a new departure —and this is an area in which we would like to bring you interesting developments in future— he has also generated it as the video below. Archive note: the preserved local source announces a video here but contains no playable video or video link. The recording has not been reconstructed. We live amid constant revolution. A few years ago it was blockchain technology; now artificial intelligence is advancing in leaps and bounds, transforming every field there is. When I was asked to write this article, I posed a fundamental question: how many types of generative artificial intelligence are there? There are various types of generative AI, each with its own techniques and applications. Generative language models such as ChatGPT (from OpenAI), Bard (from Google) and Bing Chat (from Microsoft), for example, are designed to generate coherent text. Other types include Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), which create images and videos through competition between two neural networks; autoregressive models, which predict sequential data; and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), which generate new data samples. There are also Transformers, effective at generating both text and images; diffusion models, which produce realistic images from random noise; and generative reinforcement learning models, used in games and simulations. Multimodal generative AI can handle different types of content; recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and LSTMs are useful for analysing long-term dependencies; and there are specific models for audio and music, such as WaveNet and Jukebox. Finally, grammar-based models can create complex structures while respecting syntactic rules. Although both AI assistants and custom GPT models use natural language processing technology, there are key differences in their purpose and degree of specialisation. Assistants such as ChatGPT are designed for general interaction with users, offering broad responses adaptable to a variety of subjects and contexts, with no particular focus beyond being useful and safe in everyday conversations. Custom GPTs, by contrast, are models adapted to particular tasks and audiences; they are trained on specific data to address particular subjects with greater precision and depth. In politics, for instance, they can generate content aligned with a particular ideological or communications approach. This customisation allows GPTs to be more effective in specialist settings, while assistants aim to be versatile and useful to a wide range of users. A custom GPT for estrategIA Generative AI in politics can also automate tasks that traditionally required considerable human involvement, such as writing speeches, preparing responses for debates or generating promotional materials. With AI’s help, these activities can become faster and cheaper. Yet this same automation can create a disconnect with voters, who may perceive excessive use of technology as a lack of authenticity or an attempt at manipulation, rather than a sincere effort to connect. Here is an example of an experimental custom GPT using the estrategIA articles written to date. Image 1. Uploading the custom knowledge base. Accessible translation of the configuration shown: The GPT is named “estrategIA”. Its description and instructions both read “Artificial intelligence in politics and government”. The conversation starter is “Hello estrategIA”. In the “Knowledge” section, PDF files of previous issues are attached; their filenames are partly truncated. The interface explains: “If you upload files to Knowledge, conversations with your GPT may include the contents of the files. Files can be downloaded when Code Interpreter is enabled.” The preview repeats the GPT’s name, description and greeting. The configuration is marked active and visible only to the owner, with updates pending. Image 2. Example of a customised conversation. Accessible translation of the conversation The following exchanges reproduce the historical model output in the screenshot. They are translated examples of what the GPT said, including its characterisation of the archive. User: Hello estrategIA, what do you have in your knowledge base? Can you give me a summary? GPT: In my knowledge base I have a series of articles and documents focused on the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) with politics and government, exploring both current use and the possible futures of AI in these fields. Here is a summary of some prominent themes: Four golden rules for working with AI according to Ethan Mollick: Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School, proposes strategies for integrating AI effectively into everyday work. The rules include always inviting AI to participate, maintaining human oversight, customising the AI’s “personality” to suit the task, and assuming that the technology will continue to evolve. Stories of politics and AI in 2045: A series of fictional stories exploring future scenarios in which AI plays a central role in politics, such as an AI assistant becoming an independent presidential candidate, or the creation of political truthfulness laws requiring AI to intervene in political debates to ensure honesty. Innovations in political data analysis with AI: Using advanced models such as Google Gemini Pro 1.5 and GPT-4o to improve political data analysis and the comparison of election manifestos, providing quick summaries and comparisons of proposals from multiple parties, and detailed analyses of turnout data. AI’s impact and controversies on social media during elections: An analysis of AI’s impact on elections, focusing on its use on social media to influence public opinion and on related controversies, such as data manipulation and disinformation. Integrating AI into public administration and defence: Examples such as the Community of Madrid’s “Cuenta Digital” application, which uses AI to simplify public procedures, and the development of AI assistants by Spain’s Ministry of Defence to improve operations and security. Challenges and opportunities for AI in the European regulatory environment: A discussion of how the European Union’s strict regulations are creating a “two-speed AI”, with faster advances in the United States and China than in Europe because of regulatory restrictions. These are just a few examples of the topics covered in the documents in my knowledge base. If you are interested in a particular topic, I can explore it further or look for more details. This question affects not only the ethics of political campaigns, but also public perceptions of the legitimacy of their communications. In a world increasingly aware of AI’s role in society, transparency may become a key element in maintaining public trust. Despite the challenges, generative AI offers enormous possibilities, and its impact will depend largely on how these tools are used. At its best, generative AI could democratise access to information, enabling more people to understand complex political issues through automatically generated explanations that are clear and accessible. It could also facilitate better-informed debates and more active civic participation. We must remember, however, that while generative AI can be a powerful tool, it cannot replace the importance of human dialogue, empathy and real connections between political leaders and their communities. Technology can help amplify messages, but true connection is built through tangible actions and a sincere commitment to listening and responding to people’s needs. Ultimately, the responsible and ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in politics could make the difference between a future in which technology empowers people and promotes democracy, and one in which it is used to manipulate and polarise. The key therefore lies in how we choose to use the technology. Well-managed AI can be a valuable tool for improving communication and effectiveness, but it must never replace integrity, transparency and an authentic commitment to democratic values. estrategIA’s first anniversary: testing ChatGPT’s new voice for political communication On estrategIA’s first anniversary, Fernando Nieto Lobato tests ChatGPT’s advanced voice mode as a political debate sparring partner. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 053 Practical experiment estrategIA’s first anniversary: testing ChatGPT’s new voice for political communication Historical note: this article describes the features, restrictions and availability of ChatGPT’s advanced voice mode in October 2024. A year ago, in October 2023 ( after an introductory issue published in the last week of September ), we launched estrategIA . Today, on this first birthday, we want above all to thank you, dear readers, for your loyalty and support. You make it possible for this venture—born above all from a desire to do something worthwhile and useful in helping us understand the great wave of artificial intelligence coming our way (which is barely wetting our feet for now, although we can see how enormous it is on the horizon)—to remain true to its purpose. It has grown considerably and now has well over 1,000 subscribers: at the time of writing, 759 on Substack and 317 on LinkedIn Newsletters , where we began publishing four months ago. Thank you all! We hope you will stay with us for many more years, enjoying all the extraordinary innovations ahead. Let us remind you that, if you find estrategIA interesting, recommending it to colleagues and friends helps us enormously. You can share it very easily through this link . To celebrate the anniversary with a smile, we would like to share a fun song we created in Suno , with lyrics by GPT-4o. Both were produced on the first attempt. Now to the substance. The truth is that our original idea for this birthday issue was to examine, as we have on other anniversaries, how artificial intelligence has evolved over the past year, particularly in relation to politics and government. We would draw on material as interesting as this survey from late August, shared by Ethan Mollick , which shows that, at least in the United States, people’s adoption of AI is beginning to take off at an unstoppable and very rapid pace. We will surely return in another issue to the interesting paper “The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI” . At the end of the year, we will review AI’s progress in 2024, building on our review of the first six months . Screenshot: Ethan Mollick’s post of 24 September 2024, with excerpts from the adoption study. The post is already in English; the charts and paper excerpts are partly cropped. Accessible transcript of the post: This August 2024 US survey of AI use confirms that AI is not just hype: 1) AI adoption is crazy fast by historical standards 2) It obviously useful to people in many industries. 25% people use GenAI at least 60 minutes a day at work, already 3) AI is being used for many purposes The visible task chart asks, “In Which Specific Tasks Is AI Most Useful?” Its workplace results show the share ranking a task first or second: writing communications, 38.4%; performing administrative tasks, 26.8%; interpreting/translating/summarising, 23.0%; searching for facts or information, 17.7%; coding software, 13.8%; documentation or detailed instructions, 13.6%; generating/developing new ideas, 13.2%; support with customers/co-workers, 11.6%; data analysis/visualisation, 8.3%; tutoring or educational assistance, 3.5%. “Other” has no readable numerical label. The other panels compare adoption over time and across occupations and industries; their cropped labels and values are not reconstructed here. The linked paper supplies the full figures. That was the original idea, but the release of ChatGPT’s advanced voice model , long awaited since its presentation in May , changed our plans. It is not yet available in the EU, but we have been able to try it from Spain using a VPN. This voice interface is revolutionary in its naturalness, despite arriving with its capabilities severely curtailed compared with the demonstration: it still has no vision and does not integrate with GPTs; for safety reasons, it has been “forbidden” to sing, clone voices or recognise different people; and, for the time being, it has been deprived of memory. Even so, it is undoubtedly the beginning of a shift towards a new way of communicating with machines, very close to how we speak with another person. As the example below will show, it also offers enormous possibilities for political communication and learning. If you missed the presentation in May, here are some recent examples of the tool in general use. Testing GPT’s advanced voice mode to prepare for a debate When the model was presented more than four months ago, it occurred to me that one of the main uses of an AI that could speak like a human—and even interrupt or raise its voice, although in practice this is now much more restricted than the model itself allows—combined with GPT-4o’s reasoning capabilities, would be as an excellent “sparring partner” for any politician preparing for a debate or a parliamentary speech involving a direct exchange with a colleague from another political camp. The audio we present below is our first take with this model. Its imperfections are evident: for example, it takes on the role of a government member even though I have asked it to play the opposition. It does, however, correct itself very quickly. We are presenting it as it is so that you can see how spontaneously the system works. We had complex briefing notes from several parties on a range of subjects. But since advanced voice mode cannot yet be integrated with GPTs and has no dedicated long-term memory—two things that will probably change within a few months, allowing us to test the model much more thoroughly, as will the option of voice-specific “custom instructions”— we preferred to create a simple set of arguments using Perplexity . We also chose a subject that, although very topical in Spain, is general and applicable in any country: whether or not to reduce working hours. Below are the arguments we gave the AI (the opposition’s) and those we used ourselves (prepared for the government). They are followed by the exact, spontaneous, entirely unedited audio of our first mock “debate”. Despite being a fairly spontaneous and very preliminary trial—this will improve enormously with prior customised instructions—it demonstrates many of the model’s possibilities: Accessible translation of the historical Perplexity briefing The following is the AI-generated text shown in the original screenshot, translated into English. It records the material used in this 2024 experiment. The numbered references are reproduced as displayed; their source list is not visible in the capture. Based on the available information, here is a summary of the arguments for and against reducing working hours in Spain: Arguments in favour (trade unions and left-wing parties) Better quality of life: A shorter working day contributes to better mental and physical health for workers, reducing stress and exhaustion. [5, 6] Increased productivity: Several studies suggest that reducing working hours can increase productivity, as workers are more focused and efficient during their actual working time. [5, 6] Lower unemployment: Reducing working hours could help distribute employment more widely, allowing more staff to be hired to cover the reduced hours. [5, 7] Work–life balance: Employees would have more time for their families, leisure, training or rest, improving the balance between work and personal life. [1, 6] Social justice: Trade unions argue that this measure would help distribute the wealth generated by the country more equitably. [1, 2] Positive impact on the economy and the environment: Reducing working hours could have a positive effect on the country’s economy and the environment. [1, 2] Arguments against (CEOE, employers’ organisations and right-wing parties) Higher costs for businesses: Businesses could face higher labour costs if they need to hire more staff to cover the reduced hours or pay overtime. [3, 5] Loss of competitiveness: In a globalised market, reducing working hours could affect Spanish businesses’ competitiveness relative to their international competitors. [3, 5] Impact on specific sectors: The adverse effects would be greater for smaller businesses and in sectors such as tourism, hospitality and retail, where face-to-face contact with customers is essential. [3] Higher unit labour costs: A compulsory reduction in working hours with wages held constant would increase unit labour costs, which could adversely affect businesses’ competitiveness and trends in employment and GDP. [3] Competitive disadvantages: Businesses operating in global markets may face competitive disadvantages if their labour costs rise relative to those in countries with longer working hours. [3] Preference for collective bargaining: CEOE and Cepyme reject a statutory reduction in working hours and point to collective bargaining as the framework for addressing a reduction in working time. [4] It is important to emphasise that these arguments represent each group’s general positions and that nuances and variations may exist within each perspective. Audio of the “debate training” with ChatGPT’s advanced voice mode Archive note: the preserved local source announces an audio recording here but contains no playable audio or recording link. The original Spanish newsletter is retained as the source reference; the recording has not been reconstructed. Looking at this first attempt, we should remember what Sam Altman always says: “this is the stupidest AI you will ever use in your life”, because these systems keep improving and improving. That leads us to think that more capable models with this voice system, with fewer restrictions or in their next versions, may in the fairly near future become excellent tools for developing any politician’s public speaking and debating skills. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

From scepticism to acclaim: AI takes centre stage at ACOP’s Seventh International Congress Pablo Martín Diez reports on AI, disinformation and the future of political communication at ACOP’s 2024 congress. Pablo Martín Diez Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 052 Report From scepticism to acclaim: AI takes centre stage at ACOP’s Seventh International Congress The estrategIA newsletter team presented the experiment “The impact of generative artificial intelligence tools on political communication: creating and promoting a party for the 2024 European elections” . Not even ChatGPT could count how many times the term “artificial intelligence” was mentioned during the Seventh International Congress on Political Communication, organised by the Political Communication Association (ACOP) and held in Málaga from 19 to 21 September. AI featured in almost every panel and discussion, particularly when addressing its impact on the proliferation of disinformation and on the everyday practice of political consultancy and communication. At the congress lectern. Its wording reads: “Seventh International Congress on Political Communication”, with the hashtag #acopMÁLAGA2024. In the academic panel “AI, technologies and campaigns” , Gabriela Ortega, Fernando Nieto and I presented our research on AI’s impact on political communication. The study was based on an experiment conducted in this very newsletter, in issues 28 , 29 , 30 and 36 , in which we created and promoted a fictional political party ahead of the recent European elections. Throughout this work, we explored how generative AI tools, such as GPT-4-type language models and image generators such as Midjourney, can play key roles in many aspects of political communication. From creating party identities to drafting speeches and designing campaign strategies, AI demonstrates unprecedented potential. The panel with an estrategIA slide on screen. The slide describes it as the ALEPH Educational Institution’s “Newsletter on artificial intelligence in politics and government” and displays estrategiabyaleph.substack.com and a QR code. Our research focused not only on these tools’ innovative capabilities, but also on the ethical challenges they pose. Dependence on generative technologies can influence public perceptions, affecting authenticity in politics. While AI offers fascinating opportunities to transform politics, it also raises serious questions that academics, political strategists and regulators must consider. The changing shape of disinformation One of the most frequently raised concerns throughout the congress was disinformation exacerbated by AI. Bruno Patino , president of ARTE France, drew an interesting analogy in his contribution, recalling a passage from his book Submersion : he compared Don Quixote , whose overexposure to chivalric literature caused him to lose his grasp of reality, with our society today . Drawing on Patino’s book, lecturer and journalist Carmela Ríos warned that an excess of AI-generated content, combined with disinformation, could lead us into a similar situation: living in an unreal world while our minds and bodies suffer the consequences in reality. According to Patino, the key will be to build credible institutions capable of earning citizens’ trust, rather than trying to combat every piece of false information. Positive and negative uses of AI in political communication Ignacio Martín Granados , former editor of ACOP’s magazine , offered an overview of current AI uses in political communication, highlighting both risks and benefits. On the one hand, he identified the proliferation of false content, algorithmic discrimination and increased social polarisation as the main dangers. On the other, he highlighted how AI can improve decision-making through data mining, personalise messages for specific audiences and, more broadly, open up new opportunities for political communication . A path still to be travelled: integrating generative AI deeply into political communication Another panellist, Francisco Cristófol , a professor at Loyola University, addressed the paradox that many communications offices in Andalusia’s political institutions are barely aware of generative AI tools , let alone using them. Curiously, despite their heavy workloads, these professionals cannot find time to train in these technologies, even though using them could significantly reduce their workload and potentially transform how they work. Throughout the congress, it was clear that AI is transforming politics and political communication at a dizzying pace. That is why, in concluding my contribution, I asked the sector to encourage reflection: it is essential that we, as political communication professionals, begin a debate about how we can add value in this new environment before we become an endangered species. A group photograph at the Seventh International Congress on Political Communication, Málaga 2024. The final panel, entitled “There is a future in the profession!”, conveyed both unease and excitement about generative AI’s potential. One attendee then tried to put AI’s capabilities into perspective, arguing that people still have poetry and irony to set us apart. Another participant asked ChatGPT to create an ironic poem in the style of Antonio Machado. The AI composed it masterfully, prompting applause and laughter from the audience… And so the congress’s final roundtable ended: with political communication professionals applauding ChatGPT, acclaiming the best of us all. Pablo Martín Diez Academic Director of the ALEPH Educational Institution

OpenAI o1: a new frontier in AI “thinking” and problem-solving A historical account of OpenAI o1, its reasoning capabilities, benchmark results, limitations and possible applications. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency AI in Practice 051 Analysis OpenAI o1: a new frontier in AI “thinking” and problem-solving English edition note: this article describes the September 2024 launch. Model availability, prices, capabilities and expectations are preserved in their historical context. OpenAI has once again redefined the boundaries of artificial intelligence with last week’s launch of its latest model series, OpenAI o1 . This revolutionary system represents a significant advance in machines’ reasoning and problem-solving capabilities. The o1 series introduces an innovative approach to AI processing, designed to imitate human reasoning more closely than ever. Unlike previous models, which focused on rapid pattern recognition and generating responses, o1 has been designed to “think” more carefully before answering. This deliberate approach allows the model to tackle complex problems in areas such as science, programming and mathematics with unprecedented precision and depth. Key features of o1 Improved reasoning: o1 employs a sophisticated “chain of thought” process, breaking complex problems down into manageable steps and iteratively refining its approach. Better problem-solving: the model excels in fields requiring deep analytical thought, such as physics, chemistry, biology and advanced mathematics. Code generation and debugging: o1 demonstrates superior abilities in generating and debugging complex code, making it a powerful tool for developers. Safety-focused design: OpenAI has introduced new approaches to safety training that use o1’s reasoning capabilities to adhere more closely to ethical guidelines and safety rules. By reasoning more effectively about OpenAI’s safety policies, this model is less at risk of being used for malicious purposes despite its greater capabilities. The o1-preview and o1-mini variants are already available to all paying GPT-4 customers, while the original model remains solely in OpenAI’s hands. It is rumoured that the company is using it to train the future “GPT-5”. o1-preview: the full version, designed to tackle the most complex reasoning tasks across different domains. o1-mini: a smaller, faster and more cost-effective version, specifically optimised for programming tasks. It offers 80% of the performance at 20% of the cost compared with o1-preview. Benchmark performance Accessible transcription of the original chart. The numbers below are the values printed above the bars; no additional values are inferred from the shaded portions. | Test | Measure | GPT-4o | o1-preview | o1 | Expert human | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Competition maths: AIME 2024 | Accuracy (%) | 13.4 | 56.7 | 83.3 | — | | Competition coding: Codeforces | Percentile | 11.0 | 62.0 | 89.0 | — | | PhD-level science questions: GPQA Diamond | Accuracy (%) | 56.1 | 78.3 | 78.0 | 69.7 | An em dash means that no bar is shown for that category. The o1 model — the one currently available only internally at OpenAI — has demonstrated notable performance across a wide variety of tests, highlighting its advanced reasoning capabilities: International Mathematical Olympiad qualifying examination: o1 achieved an impressive 83% accuracy, compared with GPT-4o’s 13%. Codeforces competitions: o1 placed in the 89th percentile, demonstrating exceptional programming skills. American Invitational Mathematics Examination: o1 ranked among the top 500 students in the US. GPQA, a PhD-level physics, biology and chemistry examination: o1 exceeded the accuracy of humans with PhDs in these scientific domains. Beyond the benchmark performance figures supplied by OpenAI itself — bearing in mind that many benchmarks are saturated and can no longer properly measure some models’ “almost superhuman” capabilities — the internet has filled with interesting examples from people using o1-preview . Remember that, in evaluations, the full o1 model appears far superior to this version, which is the one already available to us. Here is a small selection of links if you would like to see some of the new model’s incredible capabilities: Ethan Mollick: crosswords and astrophysics . An IQ test in which the model appears to score 120 . Allie K. Miller . David Shapiro . Mathematician Terence Tao . Applications and use cases We should point out that for many of our “everyday” uses of AI — for example, working on this newsletter — this is not the appropriate model . As a very new model, it is still strongly focused on particular tasks where its reasoning ability sets it apart. We can expect these capabilities to be integrated before long with multimodality, larger context windows and even internet access for the model. On the other hand, o1’s enhanced reasoning capabilities open up a wide range of distinctive potential applications across industries , particularly scientific research, software development, financial analysis and healthcare. As mentioned above, despite its impressive capabilities, o1 — and even more so the preview and mini versions available to us today — has limitations, including these two: Functional gaps: as an early model, o1 lacks some features found in other AI systems, such as web browsing and image processing. At present, it is a text-only model. Cost and speed: o1 is significantly more expensive to use today than previous models, with higher input and output costs. It can also be slower when processing complex queries. For anyone wanting to learn more about the model’s capabilities and limitations, we recommend this excellent summary of an AMA — “Ask Me Anything” — with o1’s development team . Conclusion: the future of AI reasoning If I may offer a personal assessment, based on numerous comments from industry experts and even people working on the project itself, o1’s significance lies less in the model itself than in this new approach. According to OpenAI, it began to take shape in practice barely a year ago, and it is achieving very rapid, continuous improvements in models. It also gives us another dimension along which to improve beyond the sheer compute used in training: in this case, the inference time devoted to responses and the way the model “reasons”. This will make a difference, and we are probably at the beginning of another enormous leap in AI, whose results we will see over the coming months. The introduction of o1 marks a significant milestone in the evolution of AI systems. By incorporating reasoning processes that more closely resemble human ones, o1 represents an important step towards artificial general intelligence. Although o1 is still in its early stages and faces some limitations, its potential impact across industries and scientific disciplines could be immense.
