It can coordinate tasks across applications, organise meetings, send invitations and adjust your calendar, all autonomously. This capacity for anticipation and action is more than a technological advance: it is a small but significant leap towards a future in which virtual assistants are not merely tools, but digital companions that understand us and help us proactively. The Siri we saw yesterday is still far from the genuinely autonomous agents we are beginning to glimpse from other companies such as OpenAI. But despite starting a long way behind, it seems to be moving in the right direction. Considering Apple’s entire ecosystem, combining that with AI development is a distinguishing factor. On-device AI and GPT-4 through a partnership with OpenAI As for how AI is integrated into its devices, the most interesting aspect is the ability to run large language models directly on devices such as iPhones and iPads. This innovation relies on an advanced technique for using flash memory, allowing these models to operate efficiently without a constant connection to the cloud. This capability is crucial for applications requiring rapid responses and for protecting user privacy, since data need not leave the device. For more advanced AI applications, however, Apple sealed a long-rumoured partnership with OpenAI to incorporate GPT-4, allowing controlled access from its devices. This collaboration gives Apple users access to ChatGPT’s capabilities integrated into their operating systems, facilitating tasks such as generating text, creating automatic summaries and assisting with coding. Beyond technical details and presentations, the most significant aspect of this event is Apple’s comprehensive commitment to AI across all its operating systems , giving another major boost to the worldwide popularisation of this technology by bringing it to devices used, in total, by nearly a quarter of the world’s population. Perhaps the least innovative conference of the past two months will prove the most important because of the way it will subtly introduce AI into everyone’s minds and pockets, making the shift towards a new society subtle but unstoppable. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at the ALEPH Educational Institution

Testing new AI models to compare manifestos and analyse data ahead of the European Parliament elections Historical tests of Gemini and GPT-4o for manifesto comparison, turnout visualisation and interpreting the European Parliament's composition. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 036 Analysis Testing new AI models to compare manifestos and analyse data ahead of the European Parliament elections English edition note: this article records tests conducted before the June 2024 European elections. Model outputs, including assessments of party manifestos and the fictional Europa Estoica Unida party, are translated as historical source material. They have not been independently fact-checked or updated. Prompts and quoted responses are translated from Spanish. In the week before the elections to the European Union’s parliament, we want to devote this newsletter ’s main article to testing how some of the AI developments introduced over the past month can offer us new or improved capabilities for working in this field. Comparing several parties’ election manifestos using a large context window, with Google Gemini Pro 1.5 A context window is, roughly speaking, the amount of data a large language model can work with directly. At its developer conference last month, Google announced that it was opening access to Google Gemini Pro 1.5 in new countries, including those of the European Union . This language model, one of the best on most benchmarks, although not yet at GPT-4o’s level, allows a context window of up to one million tokens, equivalent to several hundred book pages. This has allowed us to ask it for a comparative analysis of the manifestos of different parties contesting the European elections. The initial idea was to include the PP and Vox manifestos too, but because they are much shorter and designed in a different format, we decided to focus the analysis solely on Spain’s three main left-wing parties. For this example, we asked it to work on education proposals. We uploaded the manifestos. Those three alone add up to more than 150,000 tokens, exceeding the size GPT-4 can work with, for example: 128,000 tokens. The uploaded documents shown are Podemos (54,403 tokens), PSOE (52,918 tokens) and Sumar (50,270 tokens). The visible cover slogans include PSOE’s “More Europe” and Sumar’s “A manifesto that sets the course in Europe”. We asked it for a comparative summary of the main education proposals and, additionally, to analyse the strengths and weaknesses of each party’s manifesto and draw conclusions. This reduction is partly due to the United Kingdom’s departure from the European Union, Brexit. Fewer seats for the main groups: EPP: the European People’s Party group fell from 221 to 177 seats, a significant loss. S&D: the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats also saw a reduction, from 191 to 140 seats. Reconfiguration and strengthening of centrist and green groups: Renew Europe, previously ALDE: increased its representation from 67 to 102 seats, consolidating its position as an important force in the centre of the European political spectrum. Conclusion The European Parliament’s composition has changed notably between the two terms. Traditional groups such as the EPP and S&D have seen their representation decline, while centrist groups such as Renew Europe and green groups such as Greens/EFA have gained influence. The emergence of new groups such as Identity and Democracy also indicates a diversification of Europe’s political landscape, with greater representation for Eurosceptic and right-wing positions. This change in the distribution of seats reflects a more fragmented and plural European electorate, with growing concern about environmental issues and a greater presence of Eurosceptic movements. The following analysis examines how these principles can align with the European Union’s current trends and needs. 1. Political and social context The European Parliament has experienced notable political fragmentation, with increased representation for green, centrist and Eurosceptic parties. This diversified environment offers fertile ground for new political formations able to provide a coherent and distinctive vision. In particular, the values of wisdom and justice resonate with the demands of European citizens seeking comprehensive and sustainable long-term solutions. 2. Strategic opportunities 1. Dialogue and cooperation Strengthening alliances: Europa Estoica Unida can collaborate with groups such as Renew Europe and Greens/EFA, which share interests in sustainability and social justice. Synergies with these groups can help advance policies promoting a more equitable and sustainable Europe. Promoting dialogue: given its focus on self-control and wisdom, the party can position itself as a neutral mediator in polarised debates, offering solutions based on knowledge and rationality. 2. Social justice and sustainability Leading green initiatives: a commitment to sustainability can align with the Greens/EFA agenda, providing a basis for collaboration on environmental and climate policies. Equity policies: an emphasis on justice can attract voters seeking greater social and economic equality, by proposing inclusive and fair policies. 3. Resilience and self-control Crisis management: Europa Estoica Unida can distinguish itself in managing crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic or the climate crisis, through proposals balancing immediate responses with long-term planning. Education and training: promote educational programmes encouraging self-control and resilience among citizens, in line with a vision of Europe acting from moral strength and rationality. 4. Cosmopolitanism Inclusion and diversity: promoting cosmopolitanism can attract a diverse voter base, standing out in the defence of human rights and the integration of migrants and refugees. External relations: a vision of global fraternity can position Europa Estoica Unida as a key actor in EU foreign policy, promoting international cooperation and peace. 3. Challenges and mitigation Electoral competition: political fragmentation means intense competition. It is crucial for Europa Estoica Unida to define its value proposition clearly and distinguish itself from other parties. Effective communication: translating Stoic principles into concrete policies and communicating them effectively to European citizens will be fundamental to winning support. Adapting to change: flexibility and adaptability will be vital to responding to rapid changes in the political and social environment. Europa Estoica Unida has an opportunity to fill a niche in today’s European Parliament, offering a vision of governance based on Stoic principles that resonate with growing demand for social justice, sustainability and peaceful cooperation. Its success will depend on its ability to form strategic alliances, communicate its values effectively and adapt to a dynamic political environment. With a well-defined strategy, it can become an influential actor in European politics, promoting a fairer, more resilient and united continent. Integrating artificial intelligence into politics , as we see every week in estrategIA, not only improves the ability to analyse and compare election manifestos, but also helps politicians, advisers and citizens make more informed and balanced decisions. Used well, advanced tools such as Google Gemini Pro 1.5 and GPT-4o can represent a crucial advance in democratising access to information and improving transparency and accountability in politics. In an increasingly complex and diversified electoral landscape, the ability to use these technologies effectively will be decisive for campaigns’ success and for understanding the policies proposed. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at the ALEPH Educational Institution

Artificial intelligence in Mexico’s 2024 elections: challenges and opportunities Ray Acosta's historical opinion piece on social media, AI and Mexico's 2024 elections, examining manipulation, political participation and civic education. Ray Acosta Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 035 Opinion Artificial intelligence in Mexico’s 2024 elections: challenges and opportunities Editorial introduction: This week, ahead of Mexico’s federal elections next Sunday, 2 June, we welcome a special contribution from Mexican journalist Ray Acosta , who has written the newsletter ’s main article. Drawing on his extensive experience in radio and podcasts , he has also recorded it as audio, which we recommend listening to. English edition note: this is a translation of Ray Acosta’s opinion article published on 29 May 2024, preserving its historical claims and the author’s assessments. Quotations are translated from the Spanish source; no original English wording has been independently checked. The preserved source contains no playable audio. Let us recall the night of 1 July 2018, when, at around 11 pm, after the INE — Mexico’s National Electoral Institute — confirmed the election winner, Andrés Manuel López Obrador addressed the country for the first time as Mexico’s presumptive president. His first words after victory were full of emotion, notably when he thanked “blessed social media”. From his perspective, these new communication channels had been fundamental to connecting with his voters and winning by a margin of more than 30% over his opponents, something unprecedented in the country’s modern elections. So far, everything seemed to be going well, but… when the stories went viral about envelopes of money that the president’s brother, Pío López Obrador, had illegally received from David León; the conflict-of-interest scandal surrounding the Casa Gris, or “Grey House”, in Houston that involved his son; and ProPublica’s report on the Mexican president’s failed security strategy, López Obrador changed his mind. Initially, he claimed to have won organically, without help from bots, thanks to “blessed social media”. Now that those same networks had exposed these abuses, however, he maintained that the criticism came from bots controlled by his enemies. According to him, only his followers are genuine, as he has repeated on several occasions at his press conferences known as “La Mañanera”, the morning briefing. Here we have an ironic case of two sides of the same coin. It forces us to ask several questions: how influential is social media? Can it change the course of elections? How does artificial intelligence technology influence our digital lives and elections? And, perhaps most importantly, do large corporations manipulate us through social media using AI? We will try to answer some of these questions, or at least provide useful information to help do so. The only thing I can guarantee is that, after reading this text, your perception of AI will change forever. The challenges Let us start with what I consider the most important question: do large corporations manipulate us through social media using AI? The answer is yes. Simple. Harsh. Terrifying. How did they do it? Because, believe it or not, this has already happened; it is part of our reality. Through cookies and algorithms, AI has sufficient tools to manipulate the information we receive, and when and how we receive it, achieving corporate America’s objective: isolating us as a society. For example, if you are a fan of Barcelona football club and search for it on Google, information about the club will “magically” begin appearing across all your social networks and mobile devices, presented as innocent recommendations. And it does not end there: when you accept the terms and conditions for using the software on your phone or computer, you allow your camera, microphone and location to be shared to “improve your experience”. This represents many petabytes of information that will, of course, be used against us. Worse still, Google, Facebook and Amazon reserve the right to sell the data collected about your habits: what do you do first in the morning — open YouTube or WhatsApp? What do you buy on Amazon, on what day and at what time? A serious question: have they paid you royalties from these sales worth many millions? This technology is used on social media, and in 2024 the votes of millions of people in 60 countries will be subject to more pressure or interference than ever in electoral history. In Russia’s special military operation in Ukraine and Israel’s offensive against Gaza, Palestine, false and biased AI-generated information is circulating, altering global perceptions of both conflicts ( Inteligencia artificial: ciber-colonización o soberanía tecnológica — “Artificial intelligence: cyber-colonisation or technological sovereignty”, Nydia Egremy, Buzos de la Noticia , 2024). Are you reading a fragment of the apocalyptic future described in George Orwell’s novel 1984 ? No. It is worse: it is the reality we are living through. In politics, Cambridge Analytica obtained the data Facebook collected through its platform and the site’s cookies, which there is no way to refuse without being forced to accept. They segmented US voters to send them personalised messages based on their psychological profile and electoral preference. In this way, they encouraged fear among voters in the centre and south of the country, and although polls favoured Hillary Clinton to win the presidency, Donald Trump won, as we know. But the manipulation does not end there. In another scandalous and controversial case, Cambridge Analytica also participated in the election won by Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, conducting a smear campaign against the pro-Russian government (Karim Amer and Jehane Noujaim, The Great Hack , Netflix, 2019). Looking at Mexico, according to data from Asociación de Internet.MX, there are 101.9 million internet users in the country, of whom 98% are active on social media, with WhatsApp the most used platform. Mexican internet users are connected to their feeds for nine hours or more a day. The five most-used social networks, by number of users, are WhatsApp, 96%; Facebook, 98%; Instagram, 81%; YouTube, 62%; and TikTok, 62%. Internet use in Mexico is balanced across generations: Baby Boomers, 24%; Generation X, 23%; Generation Z, 22%; and Millennials, 19% (Internet.MX, 2024). Mexico is connected, that is true, but we lack political literacy. In my opinion, AI is being used by Mexico’s government and its advisers to discourage people from voting, promoting the narrative that Claudia Sheinbaum, the governing party’s candidate, “has already won” and that there is no way to reverse the trend because “the gap is 50 points”. In a country with historically high abstention, this is the ideal setting for that narrative: “Why go out and vote if this woman is going to win?” Following her political consultants’ script, the governing party’s candidate herself said during the third presidential debate that, to win, “all that remains is the formality of 2 June”. In his article El Meme como eje de la política mexicana — “The meme as the axis of Mexican politics” — Adrián Pablo observes how curious it is that, in an “information age”, human beings are increasingly less informed about what is happening around us. Quantity does not mean quality: even if we see hundreds or thousands of messages, street advertisements, media items or social media posts, that does not mean everything we see is valuable or necessary information (Adrián Pablo, Movimiento Antorchista Nacional, 2024). To close this controversial subject, let me offer an example: there will be no legislation on AI use for these elections. That will come from the 2027 electoral process onwards, and we still do not know what the legislators of Morena’s majority propose in their law on the subject, since it was left “pending” for the next legislature. So, should we give up social media, as Jaron Lanier suggests in his book 10 razones para dejar tus redes sociales de inmediato — “10 reasons to leave your social networks immediately”? My answer is no. We must learn and live with the benefits of this technology. The opportunities To make the most of AI in elections and everyday life, we must focus on civic education. Public policy should promote responsible use of technology. Our country’s businesses and education sector, together with others, must use these technologies as instruments of democratisation, not manipulation and business. It is not just a matter of regulating in the interests of a few, but of developing the potential of emerging technological tools. In summary, AI is a powerful tool in Mexico’s 2024 elections. Its impact will depend on how we use and regulate it, if we all participate in the process. As citizens, we must remain alert, inform ourselves, be critical and act in response to its influence on public opinion. The future of elections is in technology’s hands, and it is our responsibility to guide it along a fair and transparent path! If you think AI helped me correct the spelling and syntax of this piece, you are absolutely right! Ray Acosta Journalist and storyteller

The potential of artificial intelligence in education: a look at Salman Khan’s Brave New Words: How AI Will Revolutionize Education (and Why That’s a Good Thing) A reading of Salman Khan's Brave New Words, exploring AI tutors, equitable access, teachers, educational policy and the future of work. Fernando Nieto Lobato Learning & Human Capability Work, Welfare & the Social Contract 034 Analysis The potential of artificial intelligence in education: a look at Salman Khan’s Brave New Words: How AI Will Revolutionize Education (and Why That’s a Good Thing) Original editorial note: This week, we have used another open-source text-to-speech model, MeloTTS , to record the main article and the news separately as audio. English edition note: the preserved source does not include playable audio. The Roosevelt quotation and quoted expressions attributed to Khan below are translated from the Spanish article; their original English wording has not been independently checked. The book’s English title is retained. Original cover of Salman Khan’s Brave New Words: How AI Will Revolutionize Education (and Why That’s a Good Thing), identifying him as the founder of Khan Academy. The cover’s English endorsement reads: “A timely master class for anyone interested in the future of learning in the AI era.” — Bill Gates. Education is the foundation of a prosperous society and a strong democracy. As Franklin D. Roosevelt said: “ Democracy cannot succeed unless those who express their choice are prepared to do so. The true safeguard of democracy, therefore, is education. ” In this era of rapid technological progress, artificial intelligence is about to revolutionise how we teach and learn, and we must embrace this change with courage and wisdom. This is the powerful premise of the new book by Salman Khan , founder of Khan Academy , entitled Brave New Words: How AI Will Revolutionize Education (and Why That’s a Good Thing) . In this volume, published last week, Khan uses a compelling narrative and insightful vision to explore how AI can transform education for the better, democratising access to knowledge and personalising learning on an unprecedented scale. I highly recommend reading it to anyone interested in a field as wide-ranging and important as education, and even more so to teachers or parents. But if I had to summarise a few of its key concepts very briefly, they would be these: The potential of artificial intelligence tutors At the heart of Khan’s argument is the concept of “AI tutors”: advanced artificial intelligence systems that can act as personalised mentors for each student. Khan begins the book by describing a personal experience in which he and his daughter Diya used one of these tutors to co-write a fictional story. These AI tutors, powered by models such as GPT-4, to which Khan and the team at his educational NGO had access months before its release, can analyse each student’s unique learning style, identify their strengths and weaknesses, and adapt instruction accordingly. We are probably close to a world in which every child has access to a virtual tutor that can answer their questions, explain complex concepts in multiple ways and provide real-time feedback as they progress — something that will undoubtedly transform education forever. Democratising access to knowledge One of the most compelling aspects of Khan’s book is its focus on using AI to close the gap in access to high-quality education, a goal his non-profit organisation, Khan Academy, has pursued for years. Today, too many students, particularly in disadvantaged communities, lack the resources and support they need to succeed academically. AI tutors can level the playing field, offering a personalised and enriched learning experience to any student with an internet connection. The author imagines a “global classroom” in which students worldwide can access the best educational resources, regardless of their geographical location or socioeconomic circumstances. This democratisation of knowledge would benefit individual students and also drive economic and social progress by cultivating a better-educated and more skilled workforce. Empowering educators Despite initial concerns that AI would replace teachers, Khan paints a future in which technology “gives educators superpowers” instead. AI tutors can take on some of the more tedious tasks, such as marking exams and monitoring students’ progress, freeing teachers to concentrate on personalised teaching and creating innovative educational models. AI can also help educators plan more effective lessons, identify learning gaps early and provide additional support to students who need it. This collaboration between humans and AI has the potential to revitalise teaching as a profession, attract more talent and allow educators to focus on their passion for inspiring young minds. Ethical concerns Of course, any technological advance on this scale brings legitimate concerns about privacy, bias and safety. Khan devotes an entire chapter to addressing these concerns, advocating a “guardian angel” approach to AI in education. AI systems must be designed with transparency, equity and students’ privacy as their top priorities. Algorithms must be continually audited to detect and mitigate bias, and students’ data must be protected with robust security measures. Khan also emphasises the importance of digital literacy, ensuring that students understand how AI works and how to interact with it safely and ethically. The crucial role of politics in education Although the book focuses primarily on AI’s direct potential in the classroom, it also highlights the crucial role that government leaders and policymakers must play in using this technology effectively and equitably. Political leaders must prioritise equitable access to technology and educational resources, ensuring that all communities have the opportunity to benefit from AI tutors. They must also establish regulatory frameworks and policies promoting ethics, transparency and privacy protection in the use of AI in education. Assessment and admissions systems must also be rethought to adapt to an AI-enhanced educational environment, ensuring that assessments are accurate, fair and focused on measuring real learning rather than simply memorisation. AI and the future of work Finally, the book’s final part, Part IX, deserves special mention for its interest. Here, the author goes beyond education to explore the possible consequences of the AI revolution for work, advocating the creation of a post-scarcity society like the one portrayed in Star Trek . Khan acknowledges the widespread fear that AI will replace jobs, citing IBM’s decision to pause recruitment for office roles that AI could eventually perform. However, he believes AI will create new jobs and increase demand for highly skilled professionals able to harness its power. Salman Khan argues that the future of work will require “centaurs”: individuals who combine human skills with AI, becoming more efficient and productive. He emphasises the importance of deep skills in specific fields, alongside business experience across multiple domains, to use AI effectively. Khan then explores AI’s impact on the job-placement process. He imagines a future in which AI agents represent people, negotiating with employers, finding job opportunities and even conducting preliminary interviews. This AI-driven system would be more efficient, consistent and potentially less biased than current recruitment practices. Khan concludes his book with a powerful call for “educated courage”: the courage to embrace AI’s potential while mitigating its risks. He emphasises the urgency of using AI for good, advocating responsible development and regulation to ensure a future in which AI empowers humanity rather than displacing it. Ultimately, the author envisages a world where everyone can thrive in an AI-infused economy, driven by deep skills, entrepreneurship and collaboration enhanced by artificial intelligence. Note: besides reading the book, we recommend this video demonstrating GPT-4o’s capabilities, in which Salman Khan and his son try the model on an iPad, so you can see a multimodal AI tutor’s capabilities in action. We also suggest visiting Khan Academy to experience Khanmigo , its AI assistant designed specifically for education, for yourself. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at the ALEPH Educational Institution

Towards ubiquitous AI: the OpenAI and Google developments that will transform the future A historical account of OpenAI's GPT-4o launch and Google I/O 2024, examining multimodal assistants, search and the prospect of ubiquitous AI. Gabriela Ortega Futures, Safety & Human Agency AI in Practice 033 Analysis Towards ubiquitous AI: the OpenAI and Google developments that will transform the future Original editorial note: As an experiment , using this issue’s recommended “AI tool of the week”, Openvoice2, we have used a free, open-source artificial intelligence system — described in more detail in that section — to generate a narration of this issue’s main article and news . English edition note: this translates the article published on 15 May 2024. Its references to availability, prices and forthcoming events describe that historical moment. The preserved source does not include a playable narration. Quoted wording is translated from Spanish unless already present in English in the images. In barely a month, between mid-May and mid-June, we see the year’s greatest concentration of technology conferences. Yesterday, 14 May, was Google I/O, upstaged on the 13th by a brief but spectacular OpenAI conference and demonstration. Microsoft Build will take place from 21 to 23 May, and Apple’s Worldwide Developers Conference from 10 to 14 June. This year, artificial intelligence is the major — almost the only — theme at all of them. They will show us not just what is already here, but also what the immediate future might look like. At estrategIA, we will keep you informed about everything coming from these technology giants which, alongside very few other companies — Meta, Tesla, Nvidia, Mistral… — set the pace for a technology as disruptive as AI. But let us begin with the first: OpenAI’s conference and demonstration last Monday . It has probably shown the most innovative capabilities and brought the biggest gift: GPT-4o FREE for all users . Text in the announcement: “Introducing GPT-4o” (Spanish heading). “You can now try our newest model, GPT-4o. It’s faster than GPT-4, better at understanding images, and speaks more languages.” Button: “Try it now” (translated from Spanish). At a 25-minute event held last Monday, 13 May, to upstage Google, OpenAI changed the artificial intelligence landscape with the launch of GPT-4o, in which the “o” stands for “Omni”. This model significantly surpasses its predecessor, GPT-4, demonstrating a 60-point Elo improvement on the LMSys benchmark and positioning itself as the world’s most powerful model, ahead of Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3 and Llama 3-70B. Accessible transcription of the original “Text Evaluation” chart. These are the historical figures shown in the source image; N/A is retained where a result is unavailable. | Benchmark | GPT-4o | GPT-4T | GPT-4, initial release 23-03-14 | Claude 3 Opus | Gemini Pro 1.5 | Gemini Ultra 1.0 | Llama3 400b | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | MMLU (%) | 88.7 | 86.5 | 86.4 | 86.8 | 81.9 | 83.7 | 86.1 | | GPQA (%) | 53.6 | 48.0 | 35.7 | 50.4 | N/A | N/A | 48.0 | | MATH (%) | 76.6 | 72.6 | 42.5 | 60.1 | 58.5 | 53.2 | 57.8 | | HumanEval (%) | 90.2 | 87.1 | 67.0 | 84.9 | 71.9 | 74.4 | 84.1 | | MGSM (%) | 90.5 | 88.5 | 74.5 | 90.7 | 88.7 | 79.0 | N/A | | DROP (F1) | 83.4 | 86.0 | 80.9 | 83.1 | 78.9 | 82.4 | 83.5 | The most surprising and relevant aspect of GPT-4o is that it will be free for users, marking a radical shift in the sector’s business dynamics and finally putting a fairly advanced model within the general public’s reach. Previously, OpenAI had launched GPT-4 as a $20-a-month subscription, a decision that limited adoption. Now, thanks to efficiency improvements, OpenAI can offer GPT-4o at no cost, challenging competitors that charge for inferior models. GPT-4o is not only superior at text processing. Perhaps its most significant feature, apart from being available for free, is that it is a multimodal model, able to handle text, audio, voice and images simultaneously. This brings it closer to the vision of an AI like the one in the film Her — something made very clear in the live demonstration — with advanced voice and video capabilities, displaying emotional responses and almost human behaviour in real time. On OpenAI’s website, alongside a detailed account of all the new GPT-4o’s features, the company has added several very interesting videos and images showing capabilities different from those in the brief live technical demonstration . These are fascinating for their potential applications in politics too: image consultancy, generating text in images, brand placement… We invite you to learn more about the model on OpenAI’s website and, above all, to try it, since it is already available today to free users too at https://chatgpt.com . Google I/O That happened on Monday and had a very considerable impact on the worldwide community of AI enthusiasts: both because the model is free, allowing anyone to get a better sense of AI’s current capabilities, and because of its multimodality, voice use and potential as a “work colleague”. Yesterday, Tuesday, Google held its traditional annual developer conference, Google I/O , and tried to respond with almost two hours of presentations focused entirely on integrating artificial intelligence into all its tools and developing new models. One of the most notable announcements was Project Astra, a new Gemini-powered AI agent displaying remarkable spatial understanding and memory. In a live demonstration, Project Astra was able to remember where an employee had left their glasses in DeepMind’s London office, pointing out their location beside an apple on the desk. This offered a simple example of why it could be useful for multimodal models to have memory to help us with multiple tasks. Google also presented Gemini 1.5 Pro, an advanced AI model offering a one-million-token context window, opening up entirely new possibilities for developers. Pichai announced that Gemini 1.5 Pro is being rolled out to all developers worldwide, and that the company is expanding it to an even longer context window of two million tokens. Google also revealed updates to Google Photos, including Gemini-powered Ask Photos, which can summarise photographic memories and extract information from them. Users can ask questions such as “What is my car’s registration number?”, and Google Photos will recognise a frequently appearing car and provide that number. On the Android front, Android 15 will be updated with “AI at its core”, according to Sameer Samat, president of Google’s Android ecosystem. The main improvements include AI-powered search at your fingertips, Gemini as Android’s new AI assistant, and on-device AI to unlock new experiences. Google also showed Veo, its new AI video generator, which will compete with OpenAI’s Sora, and Imagen 3, the latest version of its AI image generator. In music, Google presented Lryia, its AI music generator. Archive note: “Lryia” reproduces the spelling in the Spanish source. Perhaps the most significant immediate transformation, although its initial launch is for the US only, is the change to the Google search engine we all routinely use. It will integrate AI into its answers by default, changing a model established for more than 25 years and very substantially affecting traffic to external websites, as well as search rankings and search advertising. Overall, Google I/O 2024 underlined Google’s commitment to integrating AI into all its key products and services, to the point that the conference closed with a joke about how many times the words “artificial intelligence” appeared in the presentation script: 121. Google itself has published a good summary, also available in Spanish, of what it presented at the conference . Despite that whole display, and the presence on stage of Demis Hassabis, founder of DeepMind and leader of what is probably today’s most powerful scientific AI, Alpha Fold 3 , revealed a few days ago, the AI enthusiast community has not been particularly convinced by Google’s offering. Many of the developments presented are still prototypes, and almost all the new features will not be rolled out immediately. The feeling remains that OpenAI is a year, or at least six months, ahead of Google in AI — and in artificial intelligence, that is an eternity. Even so, the innovations seen over these two days in both presentations are beginning to show how AI will transform many aspects of our everyday experience.

AI’s future and social impact debated at estrategIA’s first event at ESIC University A historical report from estrategIA's first event, covering AI regulation, public services, work and education through the speakers' contributions. ALEPH team Government & Public Services Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Learning & Human Capability 032 Report AI’s future and social impact debated at estrategIA’s first event at ESIC University English edition note: this report was published on 8 May 2024; “yesterday” refers to 7 May 2024. Quotations below are translated from the Spanish report. An overview of the event. From left to right: Carme Artigas, Jesús Herrero, Pablo Martín, Olga Gil and Román Robles. The backdrop displays the event theme, “The impact of artificial intelligence on politics and government”. “ Do not expect gradual evolution: in less than five years, artificial intelligence will make everything semi-automated. The challenge is to avoid inequality. Perhaps a time will come when the wealthy are attended to by people, while those with fewer resources have to settle for being attended to by robots or artificial intelligence. ” This message from Carme Artigas , co-chair of the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI , was one of many interesting reflections heard yesterday at the first event organised by estrategIA , the newsletter launched by the ALEPH Educational Institution , held yesterday at the ESIC Business & Marketing School campus. Carme Artigas, co-chair of the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI. Artigas, one of the leading figures behind the AI Act thanks to her leadership during the European Union’s marathon negotiations, when she was Secretary of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence, challenged the idea that regulation holds back innovation: “ The arms industry is one of the most heavily regulated, and yet innovation is constant. ” Artigas argued that the AI Act makes the following achievements possible: Avoiding legislative fragmentation. Regulation does not prevent innovation, whereas having a separate law in each state would create uncertainty that would make it harder to undertake AI projects. Regulating present and future uses, with particular attention to protecting human rights. Requiring transparency from companies and institutions to prevent risks. Defining prohibited uses of AI, with particular attention to preventing social rankings or classifications, manipulation, biometric identification that enables bias based on identity characteristics, and government control of the population. Jesús Herrero, Director-General of Red.es, in the centre of the image. After discussing the regulatory framework, Jesús Herrero , Director-General of Red.es , stressed that we can be proud of public servants’ efforts to initiate and launch services that improve citizens’ wellbeing. For example, he explained how automating many processes allows Red.es to scale its services to help hundreds of thousands of businesses, something unthinkable a few years ago. Román Robles , a councillor on Galapagar Town Council , brought the discussion of artificial intelligence down to the municipal level. He explained that Microsoft had conducted a study in his municipality and considers that many council processes could be 50% more effective through the use of artificial intelligence. Román Robles, a councillor on Galapagar Town Council. Herrero then addressed the debate about how artificial intelligence may affect the labour market. He said it is very important to adapt to this context and learn to use AI as another tool, something connected to self-esteem, intention and curiosity about this powerful instrument. He considers the best way to integrate artificial intelligence to be “ learning by doing, tinkering ”, and incorporating AI as practically as possible into everyday life, as we did when the internet emerged. Román Robles endorsed Herrero’s contribution and described his experience at the council implementing an artificial intelligence agent to address residents’ administrative needs. Robles sees the process as trial and error, something “ still under construction ” that reduces the administrative burden, freeing time to reinvest in personal attention to citizens. Olga Gil, a researcher on technology regulation at the Complutense Institute of Administrative Science (ICCA) and academic secretary at the Complutense University of Madrid’s School of Government. Olga Gil , a researcher on technology regulation at the Complutense Institute of Administrative Science (ICCA) and academic secretary at the Complutense University of Madrid’s School of Government , turned to the future and to young people. How will artificial intelligence affect their education? What skills will they need for professional success? Gil set out some forecasts and recommendations in response to these concerns raised by the students present: Educational programmes will tend to become shorter. Following European examples such as England, some degrees may be obtained in three years. Education will need to be continuous, with constant retraining to avoid falling behind all the advances taking place. A global outlook is needed, extending beyond Europe’s borders towards Asia and the Americas, where countries such as China and the United States are leading the AI revolution. Creativity will remain indispensable, since AI is not yet able to match human ability. For now, it has been demonstrated that education will not be able to dispense with teachers. Pablo Martín, editor of estrategIA and Academic Director of the ALEPH Educational Institution. Finally, Pablo Martín , editor of estrategIA and moderator of the roundtable, closed the event with a recommendation voiced by the publication’s director, Fernando Nieto: we need to think in terms of artificial intelligence, think on a different scale, and recognise that we have access to the knowledge of the best engineers, professors and communicators… A new era of opportunities.

Beyond automation: artificial intelligence and its cross-cutting impact on work Pilar Mairal Medina examines AI and work beyond automation, from reskilling and organisational culture to interdisciplinary collaboration and a new work ethic. Pilar Mairal Medina Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Government & Public Services 031 Analysis Beyond automation: artificial intelligence and its cross-cutting impact on work Editorial introduction: In this issue of estrategIA, published on 1 May, International Workers’ Day, we are delighted to welcome a special contribution on the relationship between AI and work from Pilar Mairal Medina , an adviser in the office of the Secretary of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence at Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service . Artificial intelligence (AI) and its impact on employment are a highly relevant and widely debated topic today, given this technology’s exponential growth and its adoption by businesses and public administrations. We can now confirm that AI is transforming the way we work, introducing new opportunities and challenges into the labour market, particularly when we consider generative AI: AI that creates new, individualised content from a variety of resources and formats. According to the International Monetary Fund’s report Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work , almost 40% of global employment is exposed to AI, rising to 60% in advanced economies (IMF, 2024). This broad picture must be understood in a context in which digitalisation, and specifically the integration of technologies such as AI, is unequivocally cross-cutting. We are talking about activities as diverse as creating, producing and selling AI-based software and hardware, but also applied research and services associated with project management or legal advice, in every productive sector, to a greater or lesser extent. Consider the dynamism of the economic ecosystem associated with digital transformation, in which integrating AI has become a challenge for organisations and their professionals, and a focal point for government investment. The complexity of digitalisation’s effects on particular economic sectors also matters. In AI’s case, these effects are generating growing mobilisation among groups concerned about creators’ rights, for example in the cultural industries or agriculture, and around ethical dilemmas arising from the risks of commercial AI use, disinformation, and bias in algorithmic management of client portfolios or human resources. As an initial conclusion, we can say that the dilemmas surrounding AI are diverse and will probably grow as the technology itself advances and its applications bring disruption. Different bodies across the world are beginning to respond, either through multilateral agreements or through new regulatory frameworks. In the first case, the United Nations is a clear example, with its High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, created in August 2023 to bring together different perspectives and approaches to AI governance and its alignment with human rights and the Sustainable Development Goals. On another front, in December 2023 the European Union reached a political agreement on the Artificial Intelligence Act, whose aim is to minimise the effects of AI systems classified as high-risk on health, safety or fundamental rights. As we can see, and again given this technology’s disruptive nature, its effects — expected or otherwise — provide ample grounds for debate. Political priorities must undoubtedly be reviewed continually to respond to these dilemmas and to what will also undoubtedly be growing pressure from different interest groups: technology companies, professional groups, users and consumers, among others. From the perspective of work, we can say that the implications of adopting AI are multifaceted, since we cannot overlook the opportunities it generates. In 2020, the European Parliament’s report Opportunities of Artificial Intelligence indicated that AI adoption, always dependent on developing supporting infrastructure and providing training, could increase labour productivity by between 11% and 37% in 2035, substantially improving innovation capabilities and job creation (European Parliament, June 2020). And today, with the emergence of generative AI, we can see that positive effects such as skills development and the creation of higher-value-added jobs already coexist with the replacement — or supplementation — of human tasks that have been automated. The underlying point is that AI requires interdisciplinarity in a working environment involving multiple professions, where different professional profiles can feed and supervise the algorithms underpinning their organisations’ processes, and manage improvements in products and services by reviewing those algorithms’ performance and transparency. In short, we are in a new context in which the move towards cross-cutting organisational management and networked working is irreversible. To a large extent, these will be the keys to driving professional reskilling and the acquisition of skills suited to the labour market in a digital context. Alongside this are other psychosocial factors of considerable interest that will undoubtedly receive increasing analysis. These concern the virtualisation of workplaces and working tools, and the impact of these new settings and tools on organisations themselves. We must ask: are organisations ready to move forward with integrating AI into their activities? We can consider the talent they need to attract when answering this question, but we must not forget the organisational designs and cultures towards which businesses and institutions integrating AI should move, or the principles and criteria that should guide the management of these working environments. By way of conclusion, we can suggest that integrating AI into the workplace is not only redefining the parameters of employment and of industrial and service production, but necessarily leads towards a new work ethic. Closer collaboration between humans and AI systems, in which technology amplifies human capabilities without replacing them, will undoubtedly encourage a more inclusive and productive labour market: more efficient, but also more empathetic and equitable. New values for a context of continuous change, and for a new paradigm in the relationship between technology and work. Pilar Mairal Medina Adviser in the office of the Secretary of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence at Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service.

Continuing our experiment in creating and developing an AI-generated political party for the European Parliament elections A historical test of generative AI for a fictional electoral campaign: objectives, messages, talking points, poster designs and songs. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 030 Analysis Continuing our experiment in creating and developing an AI-generated political party for the European Parliament elections English edition note: this article continues an April 2024 academic experiment involving a fictional party and candidate. The campaign prompts, model responses and mock designs are preserved as historical material. Quotations are translated from Spanish unless the source already supplies English wording. Having created the party, Europa Estoica Unida, two weeks ago, and the candidate, Elena Vidal, in the previous newsletter , in this issue we are going to work with artificial intelligence on some key initial elements of an electoral campaign. This will let us test its current capabilities at this still early stage of generative AI’s development. 1. Defining the campaign’s main objectives With the still general information we have — naturally far less than a real political party project would have about itself or its direct competitors, although we will probably conduct some very interesting experiments on that in future issues — we are going to ask the AI to generate the campaign’s main objectives. In this case, we are using the latest deployed GPT-4 Turbo model through ChatGPT, first giving it the key information we previously generated about the party, principally its mission, vision and values and its main policy proposals: Think step by step. Act as a leading political marketing expert and establish the main electoral campaign objectives of the (fictional) party “Europa Estoica Unida” for the European Parliament elections. Below, I provide information on the party’s mission, vision and values, as well as its main proposals. 1. Promoting the vision of a resilient, united Europe Objective: to raise awareness of the Stoic principles of wisdom, justice and self-control as foundations for better European governance and cooperation. Strategies: Use multiple media platforms, including social media, televised debates and rallies in different Member States, to promote the benefits of a more united and resilient Europe. Create stories and messages illustrating how these principles can solve specific problems facing European citizens, such as inequality and climate change. 2. Presenting clear and distinctive policy proposals Objective: to communicate effectively the party’s proposals for addressing specific problems such as climate change, social justice, digitalisation and diplomacy. Strategies: Develop information leaflets, videos and detailed presentations of each proposal for distribution both online and at campaign events. Organise discussion panels and forums with experts who can discuss the proposals’ merits and feasibility, demonstrating their alignment with Stoic values and their potential impact on Europeans’ everyday lives. 3. Encouraging participation and dialogue with voters Objective: to create an ongoing dialogue with the electorate to understand their concerns and reflect their voices in the party’s policies. Strategies: Implement an active listening campaign through digital tools and face-to-face meetings, allowing voters to express their opinions and needs. Use the data collected to adjust and personalise campaign messages, ensuring that they resonate with local and regional concerns. 4. Building an image of ethical, competent leadership Objective: to position the party’s candidates as ethical and competent leaders who can guide Europe towards a fairer and more sustainable future. Strategies: Highlight candidates’ biographies and skills, focusing on their experience and commitment to Stoic principles. Organise image campaigns showing the candidates in situations requiring wisdom, justice and self-control, connecting their personal characteristics with the party’s values. 5. Maximising visibility and electoral impact Objective: to ensure a strong and consistent presence across all available media and platforms to maximise the campaign’s reach and influence. Strategies: Develop an integrated media strategy combining traditional advertising with digital strategies, including SEO, content marketing and specific social media campaigns. Collaborate with influencers and opinion leaders who share Stoic values to amplify the party’s message. By implementing these objectives and strategies, Europa Estoica Unida can establish an effective electoral campaign that promotes its values and proposals while also motivating voters to support a shared vision of a more resilient and united European future under Stoic principles. 2. Key campaign messages We followed the previous response directly with this request: Based on that information, and acting as a leading political consultant, I want you to define what the key campaign messages should be. Based on Europa Estoica Unida’s mission, vision, values and proposals, it is essential to develop key messages that resonate with voters and effectively communicate the party’s principles and goals. Here are the key messages that should form the core of the electoral campaign: “Building a resilient and sustainable Europe.” This message emphasises the party’s commitment to environmental sustainability and resilience to climate change. It highlights the proposed European Climate Resilience Pact and communicates the urgency of acting wisely and with moderation to protect Europe’s future. “Justice and equity for everyone in Europe.” This highlights the party’s focus on reducing inequality and promoting social justice through initiatives such as the European Social Justice and Economic Equity Initiative. It appeals to a sense of justice and equity, emphasising that every European citizen deserves equal opportunities and fair treatment. “Encouraging temperance in the digital age.” With digitalisation increasingly influencing everyday life, this key message highlights the importance of mindful and responsible use of technology. The Europe United for Digital Temperance Programme is presented as a solution for balancing the benefits of digitalisation with protecting citizens’ privacy and mental health. “Promoting peace and dialogue in Europe and beyond.” This message focuses on Europe’s role as a global leader in diplomacy and peace, linked to the Stoic Diplomacy and Peace Forum. It reinforces the idea that Europe can and should be an effective mediator in international conflicts, using Stoic wisdom and courage to encourage global understanding and cooperation. “United in diversity: celebrating our rich cultural heritage.” This reflects the party’s cosmopolitan values and its commitment to promoting unity by recognising and celebrating Europe’s cultural diversity. The European Alliance for Community Cohesion is promoted as an initiative to encourage understanding and exchange among Europe’s peoples, thereby strengthening social cohesion. “Deciding with foresight for our common wellbeing.” This message underlines the party’s commitment to decision-making based on wisdom and a long-term perspective. It is essential for communicating that Europa Estoica Unida’s policies and actions are designed to ensure future generations’ wellbeing and the continent’s long-term sustainability. These messages should be communicated through different channels and in various formats, and also adapted to the specific local contexts of different Member States to ensure that the campaign is relevant and effective at a pan-European level. In this way, Europa Estoica Unida will be able to establish an emotional and rational connection with voters, increasing its visibility and electoral support. 3. Talking points on a specific issue To explore a particular aspect in more depth, we decided to ask GPT-4 for a specific set of pro-European talking points to “fight” the anti-European stance of many populist parties and many citizens’ disaffection with the European Union. As the previous response suggests, this could be a key message for a pro-European party such as Europa Estoica Unida. This is the response it proposed: Anti-European sentiment and growing scepticism towards the European Union are significant challenges that can be effectively addressed in Europa Estoica Unida’s campaign. The strategy should focus on revitalising perceptions of the EU as an entity that benefits its citizens and is essential to their common wellbeing. Below, I develop a detailed set of talking points that can help counter anti-European sentiment and promote a hopeful pro-European message: Step 1: identifying the main concerns Before formulating any message, it is crucial to understand the underlying causes of disaffection and scepticism. These often include perceptions of excessive bureaucracy, a lack of representation, economic concerns and a sense of lost national sovereignty. Step 2: reaffirming the EU’s values and benefits Key arguments: Peace and stability: reaffirm that the EU has been a pillar of peace in Europe since its creation, preventing conflicts between nations with a history of confrontation. Shared prosperity: highlight how the EU has helped raise living standards through the single market and cohesion policies benefiting all regions, including less developed ones. Solidarity in times of crisis: examples of how the EU has handled crises, such as the coordinated response to the COVID-19 pandemic, demonstrating the importance of cooperation beyond the nation state. Mobility and rights: underline freedom of movement and the right to live, study and work in any Member State as a tangible advantage for all Europeans. Step 3: countering the anti-European narrative Communication strategies: Debunking myths: use data and statistics to refute false or exaggerated claims about the EU promoted by anti-European parties. Personal stories: share accounts from citizens who have benefited directly from EU programmes such as Erasmus+, regional development funds and others. Historical comparisons: remind voters of the challenges and conflicts in Europe’s past so they appreciate the achievements and stability the EU offers. Step 4: proposals for a more effective and democratic EU Europa Estoica Unida’s proposals: Institutional reform: propose improvements in the transparency and efficiency of European institutions to make them more accessible and understandable to ordinary citizens. Greater citizen inclusion: encourage citizens’ direct participation in political decisions through initiatives such as public consultations and citizens’ panels. A local approach: demonstrate how the EU can adapt to each region’s specific needs, reinforcing the idea that the Union works for all its members. Step 5: launching a message of hope and unity Final message: “United in diversity: together, we can build a stronger, fairer and more resilient Europe. Europa Estoica Unida commits to leading with wisdom, justice and self-control to ensure a prosperous and peaceful future for everyone.” Step 6: an integrated communication campaign Implement a campaign using all available media — social media, television, radio and print — to spread these messages. Organise events in different Member States where Europa Estoica Unida’s leaders can speak directly with citizens, listen to their concerns and explain how the EU and the party can address them effectively. These talking points, based on understanding, clarifying and communicating the European Union’s values and benefits, are designed to counter anti-European sentiment and strengthen a sense of belonging and hope among European citizens. 4. A campaign poster We will now try to create a campaign poster using AI. In this case, we began with the AI integrated into Canva, a tool for which we have the Pro version. We went to Magic Design with AI, which in our experience offers considerably more options when Canva is set to English — something we have repeatedly encountered in many AI tools. Since it suggests entering a request of about five words for an AI creation, we simply asked for an electoral campaign poster for “Europa Estoica Unida”. This was its initial generic response, with several design examples: Text in the five original English-language mock posters, left to right: “Uniting for a stronger Europe.” “Join us in creating a united and resilient Europe. Together, we can achieve greatness.” The small print supplies a generated rally date, “June 15th, 2023 — Town Square”, and “Vote for progress and unity. #EuropaEstoicaUnida”. “Uniting Europe under one strong vision.” “Join the movement for a united and prosperous Europe. Vote Europa Estoica Unida! #TogetherStronger”. “Support a Strong and United Europe with Europa Estoica Unida.” “Unity for a Resilient Europe!” “Vote for ‘Europa Estoica Unida’!” “Join us in shaping a united future for Europe.” “Europa Estoica Unida: a united Europe!” “Join us to shape our future — vote on [date].” “Vote for a strong, unified Europe.” The template includes “#elections2023”. These are generated mock-ups, including their dates and placeholders, not announcements of real events. We found that we could also upload a custom image and a brand’s visual identity. For this simple test, we directly used the ALEPH Educational Institution’s own brand identity, which we had already configured. The results are not yet good and remain a long way from what a good designer would produce. However, in a few seconds it offers numerous possible options — the image only shows the first ones — from which to start a design. That could help, for example, in local election campaigns often run with very few resources and no option of hiring a designer. Text in the six original English-language mock-ups, left to right: “Europa Estoica Unida: Our Future, Our Choice!” “Join us for a rally on [date] at [location].” “Vote for ‘Europa Estoica Unida’ — Strong Together!” “Building a resilient and united Europe.” “Europa Estoica Unida: A Stronger Europe Together”. “Together for a Stronger Europe!” “Join us on the path to a united future.” “Strength in Unity: Vote for a Stoic Europe”. The small print supplies “Join us for a rally on 10/15 at 5 PM” and “#StrongEurope”. “Europa Estoica Unida: Uniting for a Stronger Future”. “Join us in building a resilient and united Europe.” The template supplies “August 4, 2023”. The generated dates and rally details are retained as mock-up content. Once you choose one of the hundreds of designs it generates automatically, the tool lets you open it for customisation and even includes an AI writing option to “improve” the wording. Original editing screenshot. The AI writing menu offers “Continue writing”, “Summarize”, “Rewrite”, “More fun”, “More formal”, “Sprinkle fairy dust” and “Fix spelling”. The Spanish poster beneath is translated in the next caption. We made a few small changes to the poster to put the information in Spanish, and in less than a minute we had the result: very simple, but quick. The tool will undoubtedly improve over the coming months and years to create more interesting designs. At present, however, unlike other areas such as text, image generation or even music, which we will look at next, it is still quite far from professional quality. Even so, it can offer interesting options and propose multiple creative treatments that provide a good starting point for something quick, simple and, naturally, very cheap. English translation of the Spanish mock poster: “Europa Estoica Unida: our future, our choice. Join us at the party’s launch event on 22 April in Madrid.” Footer: “Europa Estoica Unida” and “@europaestoicaunida”. This is an illustration from the fictional-party experiment. Besides Canva, we also decided to try a fairly well-known free option Microsoft launched last year: Microsoft Designer — Stunning designs in a flash We gave it a description, and it used generative AI to offer options for completing the text… Original English prompt visible in the screenshot: “Create a professional electoral campaign poster for Europa Estoica Unida. Use blue, yellow, and white colors to represent the European Union.” The mock designs principally repeat “Vote for Europa Estoica Unida” and “Join us in building a stronger Europe”, alongside European flags, groups of people and geometric graphics. The general designs are probably rather more “bland” than Canva’s, although it offers a wide variety of formats and also lets you upload your own images. The same English prompt, now accompanied by the fictional candidate’s image. The generated layouts repeat “Vote for Europa Estoica Unida” and “Join us in building a stronger Europe” in different formats. Again, in less than a minute, it gives us a fairly limited result, but one that can suggest ideas or serve as a basis for more professional work later. Original English poster text: “Vote for Europa Estoica Unida. Join us in building a stronger Europe.” The portrait is the AI-generated fictional candidate. In design, at least with the tools we have tried — there are probably others, including some more sophisticated or better tuned to what we attempted — AI still has a long way to go to achieve professional-quality results. We should remember, though, that we are still taking the first steps with generative artificial intelligence, which will very probably enable excellent results within just a few years. 5. Campaign songs Here, by contrast, AIs have made an enormous leap in recent weeks, with numerous new music-generation applications launching. Among them, version 3 of Suno stands out, and especially Udio , probably with superior musical quality. They can generate songs that are already going viral worldwide despite still being products at a very early stage of development. Both allow you to select musical styles and, in their advanced modes, which remain free, enter custom lyrics. We asked GPT-4 for several short lyrics, because Udio still has a fairly tight duration limit of around 30 seconds. Then, despite our complete lack of specialist musical training, we played around with different styles to produce campaign songs for Europa Estoica Unida in just a few minutes, such as these: Suno: Rock: https://suno.com/song/ae7fa9c0-dc2f-4457-bbda-57c9bfde7067 Atmospheric funk: https://suno.com/song/afcb9d48-da8f-47b6-bb95-fc010203cc19 Udio: Pop rock: https://www.udio.com/songs/vb259gXDN6CBdaJ1VEeWSU Electronic dance version: https://www.udio.com/songs/gMfJf1mS6fUw4RGsToH9TF With greater musical knowledge and more time to generate many more options, there is no doubt that a fairly decent campaign song could already be created today. It would clearly not yet be professional, although it could provide a basis for one, with ideas that could be developed. It would also be possible to generate many “minor”, occasional songs to share on social media, highlighting elements of our campaign or responding to rivals’ campaigns. For a small party, or an independent candidate even in a small municipality, it is no longer outlandish to suggest campaigning with music, thanks to these tools that are still starting out. Udio launched in beta on 10 April, less than 15 days ago. Next week’s newsletter coincides with 1 May, International Workers’ Day, and we will bring you a special issue on the subject. We will pause the “electoral campaign with AI” issues, returning to them later because there are still some very interesting questions we want to explore. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at the ALEPH Educational Institution

“Elena Vidal”: an AI-generated political profile for the European Parliament elections A historical experiment creating a fictional European Parliament candidate with GPT-4 and Midjourney, including her profile, SWOT analysis, speech and interview. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 029 Analysis “Elena Vidal”: an AI-generated political profile for the European Parliament elections English edition note: this is the continuation of an April 2024 academic experiment involving a fictional party and candidate. Prompts and model responses are translated from the preserved Spanish source, except for the image prompt already provided there in English, which is reproduced unchanged. This week, we continue the project from the previous newsletter : using only artificial intelligence models to create a political party and candidates to stand, fictitiously, in the forthcoming European Parliament elections. Last week, we focused on generating the party, Europa Estoica Unida. This time, we are going to use GPT-4 to create the candidate who leads it. We had considered creating more candidates, but the process is exactly the same, and including it here would be long and repetitive. Then we will develop the candidate’s image using Midjourney and its recent similar styles system for characters, conduct a general SWOT analysis of her with GPT-4, generate a speech introducing her candidacy with the “ Orador inspirado 2.0 ” proto-agent — which we previously introduced in issue 16 of estrategIA — and, finally, use GPT-4 again to develop a possible mock interview. 1. Creating the candidate who will lead the party in the European Parliament elections Think step by step. Act as an experienced political strategist and develop the profile of a female candidate for the fictional party Europa Estoica Unida, which will stand in the European Parliament elections in Spain (the candidate must be Spanish). Include both physical characteristics (give me a detailed physical description to serve as the basis for subsequently generating images of the candidate with DALL-E or Midjourney) and psychological characteristics, highlighting virtues and flaws. Provide a detailed account of her education, life story and work experience. Make sure her values reflect the principles of Stoicism and support for European integration, the party’s fundamental pillars. To build the profile of an ideal candidate for Europa Estoica Unida, focused on the European Parliament elections in Spain, it is crucial to bring together a balanced combination of personal qualities, academic education and professional experience. Stoicism, with its emphasis on wisdom, temperance, justice and courage, alongside a pro-European outlook promoting European integration and cooperation, should be the central axes of her profile. Physical description Let us imagine a middle-aged candidate in her early forties, who radiates a calm and authoritative presence. She has brown hair, cut in a practical yet elegant style just above her shoulders, and expressive brown eyes reflecting serenity and determination. Her posture is upright, conveying confidence and resilience. She prefers professional clothes, choosing tailored suits in subdued colours that complement her calm, decisive manner. Her physical presence conveys reliability and approachability without being imposing. Psychological characteristics The candidate is a person of deep ethical principles, guided by Stoic values. She shows remarkable emotional resilience in adversity, an ability to remain even-tempered in stressful situations and an unwavering commitment to social justice. Although firm in her convictions, her pragmatic approach to problems allows her to be flexible in her decision-making, always with the common good in mind. She is empathetic but does not let passing emotions carry her away, allowing her to listen to and consider different perspectives before acting. Virtues and flaws Virtues: compassionate, committed, rational and fair. Her courage in defending her ideals is balanced by profound humility and a considered approach to life. Flaws: some may interpret her rational approach and calm temperament as a lack of passion or urgency. Her tendency towards introspection and deep analysis may also lead her to delay decisions at critical moments. Background and career Born into a modest family in Salamanca, she was drawn to the humanities and social sciences from a young age. She studied Philosophy at the University of Salamanca, specialising in ethics and classical thought, particularly Stoicism. She subsequently obtained a master’s degree in International Relations in Madrid, focusing on European integration. Her professional career began in the third sector, working for NGOs dedicated to human rights and international cooperation. This early experience cemented her commitment to social justice and cross-border solidarity. After a decade, she moved into European politics, working as an adviser on social and environmental policy in the European Parliament. This stage of her career gave her a deep understanding of the complexities of European legislation and politics, as well as an extensive network of contacts in various EU countries. Values and principles Her life and career are deeply influenced by Stoic principles: the pursuit of wisdom, living in harmony with nature (including human and social nature), and practising justice as the foundation of community. As a supporter of European integration, she promotes the idea of a united Europe, diverse but cohesive, with cooperation and solidarity as fundamental pillars. She sees the EU as more than an economic project: above all, it is a project of peace and mutual understanding. This candidate symbolises a blend of idealism and pragmatism, driven by a vision of a fairer and more equitable society, both within Spain and at European level. Her profile balances intellectual depth with approachability, emotional resilience with the ability [Archive note: this sentence ends here in the preserved Spanish source.] We asked GPT-4 for a name, which it had not included in its response, and it suggested Elena Vidal. 2. Images of the candidate First, we used the GPT proto-agent Mid Journey V6 Prompt Creator . We gave it the candidate’s physical description, and it generated the following prompt for use in Midjourney: Portrait of a middle-aged female political candidate in her early forties, exuding a calm and authoritative presence. She has brown hair styled in a practical yet elegant cut, just above the shoulders, and expressive brown eyes that reflect serenity and determination. Her posture is upright, conveying confidence and resilience. She is dressed in a professionally tailored suit in subdued colors that complement her composed and decisive demeanor. Her physical presence, while not imposing, communicates reliability and accessibility. Ideal for a high-quality studio photo, capturing a sense of leadership and trustworthiness. --v 6.0 --style raw --ar 3:4 --s 250 This is the image of the candidate generated by Midjourney: AI-generated portrait of the fictional candidate Elena Vidal. Starting from this first image, we used the recent Midjourney feature launched last month, which lets you apply “reference styles” to people, and generated different images of the candidate carrying out various activities. Here are a few examples: AI-generated image of the fictional candidate speaking at microphones. AI-generated image of the fictional candidate working on documents at a desk. AI-generated image of the fictional candidate outdoors. AI-generated image of the fictional candidate addressing an audience, with European flags behind her. 3. SWOT analysis of the candidate Act as a leading political consultant and prepare as detailed a SWOT analysis as possible, thinking step by step, of Elena Vidal as the political leader of Europa Estoica Unida, a party standing in the European Parliament elections. Since we have not yet analysed the direct profiles of her opponents, we will focus on a SWOT analysis of her based on her background, values and characteristics, and the general European environment in early 2024. To conduct a SWOT analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats) of Elena Vidal as the political leader of Europa Estoica Unida, it is essential to consider both the internal elements that shape her profile and career and the external factors in Europe’s political and social context in early 2024. Strengths Academic and professional background: her solid education in philosophy, specialising in Stoicism and complemented by studies in International Relations, gives Elena Vidal a robust theoretical and practical foundation. Her experience in NGOs and the European Parliament provides a deep understanding of legislation, European politics and international cooperation. Ethical commitment and stable values: the principles of Stoicism and European integration, such as temperance, justice and cooperation, form the core of her political identity. This allows her to present herself as a trustworthy and consistent candidate with firm principles. Resilience and emotional management: her Stoic approach to life gives her a remarkable ability to face adversity, remain calm under pressure and lead with composure. Pragmatic vision and dialogue-based solutions: her ability to listen and consider different perspectives before acting, together with a pragmatic approach to problems, facilitates consensus and inclusive solutions. Weaknesses Perceived lack of passion or urgency: the electorate could misinterpret her calm temperament and rational approach as a lack of passion or emotional commitment to urgent causes. Risk of analysis paralysis: her tendency towards introspection and deep analysis could delay decision-making at critical moments, particularly in the fast-moving and often volatile political environment. Limited visibility and public recognition: coming from less media-visible sectors, such as NGOs and technical work in the European Parliament, she could initially face challenges in achieving recognition and visibility among the wider electorate. Opportunities Growing dissatisfaction with traditional politics: dissatisfaction with traditional parties and the search for authentic, principled leadership could position Elena Vidal favourably among disillusioned voters. Socioeconomic and environmental concerns: growing awareness of issues such as climate change, social justice and European cooperation provides a platform for promoting her policies and Stoic and pro-European values. Movement towards greater European integration: a Europe seeking greater integration and cohesion offers favourable conditions for strengthening the message of solidarity and cooperation that Elena advocates. Threats Political polarisation and scepticism towards the EU: growing political polarisation and scepticism in some quarters towards the European Union may pose significant obstacles to a party promoting European integration and transnational cooperation.
