Economic or social crises: possible economic, migration or health crises could shift the electorate’s priorities, disadvantaging her campaign’s core issues. Disinformation and smear campaigns: in a digital environment prone to disinformation, Elena Vidal could face smear campaigns that distort her positions and values, damaging her public image. This SWOT analysis underlines the importance of a strategy that maximises Elena Vidal’s strengths and opportunities while mitigating her weaknesses and preparing her to face threats. Her campaign should focus on effectively communicating her values and vision, increasing her visibility and connection with the electorate, and responding swiftly to the challenges of Europe’s political and social context. 4. Introductory speech For the speech, we used our own GPT-4 proto-agent, Orador inspirado 2.0 . We simply gave it all the information above about the candidate and answered its questions. Its full response follows: To write a speech reflecting the importance of the European Union and the role of the European Parliament, centred on Elena Vidal, leader of Europa Estoica Unida, it is essential to capture her ethos, logos and pathos, rooted in her solid academic background, ethical commitment and professional experience. Draft speech Ladies and gentlemen, Today, I stand before you not only as Elena Vidal, but as a living testament to the values our Europe represents. At this crucial moment for our continent, it is imperative to reflect on the unquestionable relevance of our European Union and the decisive role of the European Parliament in our lives. From the depths of history to the present day, Europe has been a melting pot of cultures, ideas and aspirations. Yet it was the vision of a united Europe, beyond borders and differences, that gave us the most lasting peace in our modern history. The European Union is not simply an economic pact; above all, it is a project of fraternity, peace and mutual understanding. At the heart of this Union is the European Parliament, the voice of our citizens. Through it, our hopes, dreams and concerns are echoed in the policies that guide us towards a more prosperous, inclusive and sustainable future. As elected representatives, our duty is not only to listen, but to act with courage and determination on behalf of those who have entrusted us with their vote. Stoicism, the philosophy that guides my life and political vision, teaches us the importance of community, justice and temperance. In this sense, the European Parliament is the setting in which these teachings come to life, where every decision is taken with the common good in mind, beyond particular or national interests. We must, however, acknowledge the challenges we face. Growing polarisation, scepticism towards European integration, and socioeconomic and environmental crises require a renewed commitment from us. It is at moments like this that our Stoic resilience, our commitment to justice and our ability to face adversity must shine most brightly. Through my experience in international cooperation and in the European Parliament, I have seen first-hand what we can achieve when we work together. The solutions to our most complex problems lie in greater integration and cooperation, rather than isolation. Europe must be more than the sum of its parts: it must be a community of shared destiny, strong and united in solidarity. That is why, at Europa Estoica Unida, we commit to strengthening this vision of Europe. A Europe in which social justice, sustainability and solidarity are the pillars on which we build our common future. A Europe in which the European Parliament is a beacon of hope, guiding our continent towards a horizon of peace and prosperity. I invite each of you to be part of this project. Together, we can ensure that the European Union and the European Parliament remain the beating heart of our Europe: a Europe united in its diversity, strong in its unity. Thank you. This speech seeks to reflect Elena Vidal’s personality, values and vision, incorporating elements of her philosophical education and her ethical and professional commitment. It is designed to connect emotionally with the audience, highlighting the importance of European unity and cooperation while aligning with her Stoic principles. Would you like to make any adjustments or add a specific point? 5. A simple interview example Using the information I am about to give you, I would like you to act both as an outstanding journalist and as an intelligent, experienced political leader, and simulate a short introductory interview of five questions from the journalist to Elena Vidal, candidate of the (fictional) party Europa Estoica Unida in the forthcoming European Parliament elections in Spain. I provided the information from the preceding sections, and this is GPT-4’s full response: Introductory interview with Elena Vidal, candidate of Europa Estoica Unida in the European Parliament elections in Spain Journalist: Good afternoon, Elena. As Europa Estoica Unida’s candidate, what do you consider the main challenge facing the European Union today, and how do you propose to address it through the European Parliament? Elena Vidal: Good afternoon. Without doubt, the main challenge we face is growing polarisation and scepticism towards European integration. In the European Parliament, I propose encouraging policies that promote education and mutual understanding among Member States. It is vital to strengthen cohesion through dialogue and solidarity, principles at the heart of Stoicism and my political vision. Journalist: You have mentioned the importance of Stoicism in your life. How does this philosophy influence your political approach, particularly to issues as complex as migration or economic crisis? Elena Vidal: Stoicism teaches the importance of rationality and justice, values I apply to every aspect of my decision-making. On issues such as migration or economic crises, it is crucial to act fairly, seeking solutions that benefit, in the long term, both European Union citizens and those seeking refuge or a better life among us. I promote an open-door policy, but a regulated one, that respects human dignity and encourages effective integration. Journalist: In a political landscape where many feel their voices go unheard, how will you ensure that citizens’ concerns are represented in the European Parliament? Elena Vidal: My commitment is always to be accessible and receptive to citizens’ concerns. I plan to introduce direct participation initiatives in which citizens can express themselves freely and contribute to the legislative process. This not only improves transparency and trust; it also enriches our democracy, allowing us to act with a deeper understanding of the population’s real needs. Journalist: You have worked extensively in NGOs and the European Parliament. How has this experience prepared you to lead and potentially influence European politics? Elena Vidal: My experience in NGOs and the European Parliament has given me an invaluable perspective on how policies can be formulated and implemented effectively. I have learnt the importance of teamwork and transnational alliances, as well as the need to address problems with pragmatic solutions that consider both Europe’s diversity and its unity. Journalist: Finally, what would your message be to voters who are still undecided about how to vote in the forthcoming elections? Elena Vidal: I ask undecided voters to consider the importance of choosing representatives who not only make promises, but demonstrate an unwavering commitment to justice, solidarity and cooperation. My vision is of a united Europe in which every action we take in the European Parliament is guided by the common good, overcoming differences and facing the challenges of the future together. I invite you to join this project, where every voice counts and every action aims to improve our lives and those of future generations. This interview reflects Elena Vidal’s values and vision, providing a platform for discussing her ideas and commitments clearly and effectively. Having created the party and its lead candidate — and all the related material we have developed, in both text and images — next week we will focus on using AI for key aspects of an electoral campaign for Europa Estoica Unida and its candidate Elena Vidal. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at the ALEPH Educational Institution

estrategIA’s “electoral” experiment: generative artificial intelligence as the creator and promoter of a new political party A historical experiment using generative AI to create the identity, policies, logo and website of a fictional pro-European, Stoic political party. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 028 Analysis estrategIA’s “electoral” experiment: generative artificial intelligence as the creator and promoter of a new political party English edition note: this article records an academic experiment from April 2024 involving a fictional party. The prompts and model responses below are translated from the preserved Spanish source; no original English wording has been independently checked. A few weeks ago, Pablo Martín , academic director of the ALEPH Educational Institution and editor of this newsletter , mentioned to me the possibility of creating a political party with AI and entering it in the European elections due to take place this June . We thought the idea was interesting. Setting aside the complex legal process of making it “real”, we proposed doing it simply as an academic experiment to describe in this newsletter . That would let us see, given the current state of artificial intelligence — still very early in its development, but evolving very quickly — what we could do directly using AI, and how good the results would be. With this in mind, we began the actual process of creating a party and candidates, working on all of this from scratch with the AIs currently available. To avoid creating a party entirely out of thin air, we decided to give it a couple of guiding principles: it should be pro-European, which is quite interesting and even logical for European elections, and, to give it a distinctive feature, its principles should be based on Stoicism . This is a philosophy I personally know in some depth , so I can judge whether what the AI generates is reasonable and appropriate. From this starting point, at estrategIA we began the process of generating a party and candidates for the European elections, and developing various key elements of their campaign. In this first issue, we are going to generate the party, its name, mission, vision and values, some of its main general policy proposals, a logo and, finally, even a simple party website, all generated directly with artificial intelligence. We began by working through the initial questions with GPT-4: 1. The party’s name Act as a renowned political consultant specialising in branding and electoral strategy, with a deep knowledge of European political culture and Stoic philosophy. Generate five exceptional and compelling name options for a new pro-European political party, founded on Stoic principles, that intends to stand in Spain in the 2024 European Parliament elections. Make sure each proposed name is innovative, faithfully reflects the party’s values and principles, and has strong potential to resonate with and attract Spanish voters, highlighting the importance of European unity and Stoic wisdom. (That is exactly the prompt used in GPT-4.) When creating names for a new political party seeking to integrate a pro-European outlook with Stoic philosophy, it is essential to approach the task using a method that ensures the proposed names align with the party’s fundamental principles and values. Stoic philosophy, centred on virtue, self-control and understanding what is within our power to change, offers a rich seam of concepts and terminology that can be creatively adapted to resonate in the European political context. This approach must both reflect the party’s unique identity and distinguish it within the Spanish and European political spectrum, appealing to the values of unity, rationality and moral strength. Creative and strategic process Conceptual analysis: integrating Stoic principles with pro-European values suggests a search for harmony between ancient wisdom and modern ideals of cooperation and unity. Fortitude, rationality, justice and community are the pillars on which the names will be based. Cultural and linguistic relevance: ensure the names are culturally resonant and linguistically accessible to the Spanish electorate, making the party easier to identify and remember. Strategic differentiation: the names should be clearly distinguishable from those already present in Spanish politics, avoiding confusion and highlighting the party’s distinctive proposals. Emotional and rational appeal: consider a balance between emotional appeal, which can create an immediate connection with voters, and rational appeal, which reinforces the seriousness and depth of the party’s political and philosophical commitments. Proposed names Europa Estoica Unida (EEU; United Stoic Europe): directly reflects the integration of Stoic philosophy with the European project, suggesting a union founded on moral strength and wisdom. Razón y Virtud para Europa (RVE; Reason and Virtue for Europe): highlights the Stoic principles of rationality and virtue as foundations for building a stronger, fairer Europe. Pórtico Europeo (PE; European Portico): inspired by the Portico in Athens where the Stoics met, it symbolises a meeting place for dialogue and reflection in support of a united Europe. Causa Común Europea (CCE; European Common Cause): emphasises the vision of a European community united by shared values, reflecting both the Stoic ideal of working for the common good and the goal of European integration. Séneca Europeo (SE; European Seneca): taking the name of one of the most illustrious Stoics, this name embodies wisdom and moral strength applied to European unity and cooperation. Each of these names has been designed to capture the essence of a party seeking to combine the philosophical richness of Stoicism with the project of European integration. They are intended to resonate with the Spanish electorate, offering a clear, distinctive proposition that highlights rationality, justice and transnational cooperation. We chose the first: Europa Estoica Unida (EEU). 2. The party’s mission, vision and values Think step by step. Act as a distinguished political consultant with extensive experience in formulating communication and branding strategies for political parties, specialising in bringing together profound philosophies and contemporary political ideals. Develop the mission, vision and values of the party “Europa Estoica Unida” (EEU), effectively encapsulating the essence of integrating Stoic philosophy with the ideal of a united Europe. Your approach should reflect how moral strength and Stoic wisdom can provide the foundation for a more cohesive and resilient European union. Make sure each element (mission, vision, values) is clearly defined, inspiring, and resonates with both adherents of Stoic philosophy and supporters of the European project, promoting a message of unity, moral strength and practical wisdom in the current political context. Mission “To promote a united and resilient Europe, founded on the Stoic principles of wisdom, justice and self-control, to create a fairer, more equitable and sustainable society. Europa Estoica Unida is dedicated to encouraging dialogue, cooperation and peace among all European nations, ensuring that every decision is taken with foresight, integrity and the common good at its centre.” Vision “To build a European future in which every individual and nation acts from a position of moral strength, rationality and compassion, overcoming differences and challenges through practical wisdom and mutual understanding. Europa Estoica Unida aspires to be a catalyst for a Europe that not only prospers economically, but also stands out for its commitment to social justice, sustainability and respect for human dignity in all its forms.” Values Wisdom: we promote decision-making based on knowledge, deep understanding and a long-term perspective, considering the wellbeing of all European citizens. Justice: we commit to working tirelessly for equality, equity and social justice in all our policies and practices, ensuring that every voice is heard and valued. Self-control: we encourage political debate and action guided by reason and self-control, avoiding impulsive decisions or those influenced by passing emotions. Fortitude: we strive to approach challenges with courage and resilience, inspiring others to do the same in the search for sustainable and peaceful solutions. Cosmopolitanism: we embrace diversity and promote European unity, recognising our shared responsibility towards the continent and beyond, in a spirit of global fraternity. Every element of Europa Estoica Unida’s mission, vision and values is designed to reflect how Stoic wisdom and principles can inform and strengthen European governance and cooperation, promoting a fairer, more resilient and united continent. 3. The party’s core public policy proposals Act as an experienced political consultant specialising in designing and developing public policy, with a particular focus on integrating philosophical principles with pragmatic political strategies. Formulate three to five core public policy proposals that “Europa Estoica Unida” (EEU) would promote to strengthen the European Union from its platform in Spain. Each proposal should reflect the distinctive fusion of Stoic philosophy — centred on wisdom, temperance, justice and courage — with the goal of building a more united, resilient and morally strong Europe. Make sure these policies address key aspects such as European integration, sustainability, social and economic cohesion, and diplomacy, demonstrating how Stoic values can guide effective and ethical political decisions for the common good of the European Union. In formulating public policy proposals for Europa Estoica Unida (EEU), it is vital to consider how the Stoic principles of wisdom, temperance, justice and courage can inform and guide a pragmatic and ethical political approach to the European Union’s contemporary challenges. Applying these philosophical principles should focus on promoting greater European integration, sustainability, social and economic cohesion, and effective diplomacy, ensuring that all policies reflect a commitment to the common good and resilience in the face of future challenges. Proposal 1: a European Climate Resilience Pact based on wisdom and temperance Objective: to promote environmental sustainability and adaptation to climate change throughout Europe, drawing on wisdom to recognise our interdependence with the environment and on temperance to moderate our consumption and production. Description: this pact seeks to unite Member States around advanced sustainability policies, encouraging the green economy, renewable energy and energy efficiency. It would promote investment in clean technology and innovation, as well as environmental education, inspired by the Stoic principle of living in harmony with nature. Proposal 2: a European Social Justice and Economic Equity Initiative Objective: to strengthen social and economic cohesion in the EU, ensuring that all citizens have access to fair and equitable opportunities, in line with Stoic principles of justice and equity. Description: this initiative would focus on policies that reduce economic and social inequality, such as European tax harmonisation to ensure that companies contribute fairly, and the introduction of a European minimum wage. It would also promote education and training programmes accessible to everyone, ensuring that social mobility becomes a reality throughout the Union. Proposal 3: a Europe United for Digital Temperance Programme Objective: to address the challenges and risks associated with technology and digitalisation, encouraging more mindful and moderate use of technology in keeping with the Stoic principle of temperance. Description: this programme would seek to balance the benefits of digitalisation with the need to protect citizens’ mental and physical health, privacy and personal data. It would include stricter regulations on data use, campaigns to raise awareness of digital wellbeing, and support for technologies that promote collective wellbeing. Proposal 4: a Stoic Diplomacy and Peace Forum Objective: to strengthen Europe’s role as a global mediator and advocate for peace, drawing on Stoic courage to face conflict and wisdom to resolve it peacefully and constructively. Description: this forum would be dedicated to promoting active diplomacy and dialogue among nations, working towards conflict resolution and a more peaceful and cooperative international community. The EU would lead peace missions, treaty negotiations and development assistance programmes, reflecting its commitment to a foreign policy that values justice and global wellbeing. Proposal 5: a European Alliance for Community Cohesion Objective: to promote unity and solidarity among Member States and their citizens, inspired by Stoic cosmopolitanism, which recognises everyone’s interconnectedness and interdependence. Description: this alliance would focus on programmes that encourage cultural understanding and exchange among EU countries, including educational initiatives promoting multilingualism, student and labour mobility, and joint cultural projects celebrating Europe’s diversity and cultural richness. After this conceptual work with GPT-4, we tried asking different AIs to generate a logo for the party. 4. The party’s logo We started with GPT-4 itself and its DALL-E image generator. The result was interesting, although it did not get the text right: Original DALL-E output: a classical temple surrounded by stars. Its lettering contains errors, including “EUROA ESTOCAA”, instead of the intended party name, Europa Estoica Unida (United Stoic Europe). “UNIDA” appears inside the emblem. We also tried a custom GPT proto-agent called “logo creator”, but the results did not convince us at all. As we also have a paid subscription to Midjourney, very probably the best image generator currently available, we tried that too. With a prompt as simple as “a high-quality logo for a political party called ‘Europa Estoica Unida’”, it generated four initial results, one of which we liked quite a lot: Original Midjourney output: blue brushstrokes, yellow stars and the words “Europa Estoica Unida” (United Stoic Europe). We also tested a couple of AI logo-generation websites and, in our experience, their results are rather generic. These, for example, are from: https://www.logoai.com/make Original LogoAI results: nine typographic and geometric designs using the words “Europa Estoica Unida” (United Stoic Europe), arranged in different orders and sizes. Finally, because of its ability to generate text well, we also tried Ideogram , which is also free. Although it can generate logos with the correct text, we found its designs considerably less imaginative and creative than Midjourney’s: Original Ideogram results: four red or dark-blue emblems using variants of the party name. The second reads “EUROPA ESTÓICA UNIDAA”, retaining the generated spelling error; another omits “Unida”. The visible, truncated prompt reads: “Act as a great designer specialising in political branding. Create a logo of great…” 5. A general website for the party Finally, we decided to try one of the many largely automatic AI website generators we had heard good things about, and it did quite an interesting job: https://landingsite.ai/#getting-started For this proof of concept, all we had to do was enter the party’s name and a six-line description based on the mission we had generated. In less than a minute, it produced the following result. We changed a couple of section headings into Spanish; the rest is just as it was generated: English translation of the substantive text in the first website screenshot (generated material for the fictional party): Navigation: Europa Estoica Unida; Programme; Meet our candidates; Contact. A continent united by wisdom and justice. Encouraging wisdom and justice to build a strong and resilient European community. Learn more. Our values. Every service we offer is imbued with Stoic philosophy, promoting harmony and cooperation among Europe’s nations. Stoic wisdom: we promote informed decisions and wise perspectives as foundations for a prosperous European future. Social justice: we advocate justice and equity, ensuring that every voice is heard and valued in European debate. Constructive dialogue: we facilitate meaningful conversations that build bridges and encourage unity among Europe’s citizens. International cooperation: we encourage cross-border collaboration to face common challenges and achieve shared goals. Common wellbeing: we work to ensure that European progress translates into a better quality of life for everyone. Lasting peace: we strive to maintain and strengthen peace on the continent, honouring cultural diversity and shared history. Join the mission — Be part of the change. Explore how you can help strengthen Stoic values and European unity. Take part now. Six months of AI with estrategIA: discoveries, dilemmas and future directions A six-month retrospective on disinformation, models, European regulation and the AI trends identified for 2024. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency AI in Practice 027 Analysis Six months of AI with estrategIA: discoveries, dilemmas and future directions This week marks six months since the first issue of estrategIA appeared on 4 October 2023, although we had previously created an issue 0 . With this anniversary in mind, we used the Easter break to look back over these months and prepare a brief overview of some of the most important subjects we have covered. Many of you have joined us in recent months and probably have not read those articles. We also want to sketch how some issues have evolved during a period that, although fairly short in human terms, is significant at the speed at which AI technology is beginning to develop. A post we saw in one of Reddit's main AI communities reminded us of precisely this just a few days ago: Original English screenshot: a post in r/singularity by strife38 is headed “Things can change really quickly”. It shares Jon Erlichman's comparison, dated 31 March 2024, of two New York street photographs: “Easter in NYC in 1900: 1 car” and “Easter in NYC in 1913: 1 horse”. The captions are the post's claims, retained here as part of the historical illustration. The problem of disinformation In the first issue of estrategIA , we addressed disinformation, a problem that remains extremely serious and topical — as several news items in this very issue show — particularly in a year so full of elections. I recall that we also examined it from the perspective of Mustafa Suleyman, a co-founder of DeepMind, Google's AI laboratory, which led the field for many years. In our second issue, we took an in-depth look at his highly recommended book The Coming Wave , which had just been published in Spanish. Here, the main change has concerned the author rather than the book's contents, which remain fully relevant: barely a fortnight ago, we learned that Suleyman had left his own AI start-up, Inflection, to join Microsoft as head of a new AI division . OpenAI, GPT-4 and its capabilities In issue 3 , we produced our first major practical article, exploring how GPT-4 V(ision) could analyse posters from Spain's latest general election. This was a particularly interesting application, as was the creation of agents — OpenAI's GPTs — discussed in issue 7 . There has been little new in this area, and we are still waiting for OpenAI's next major model, GPT-4.5 or GPT-5, rumoured for a summer release. Despite the wait, Sam Altman said in a recent interview that it would represent a significant qualitative leap. Meanwhile, OpenAI has been fairly inactive in releasing models publicly, though not privately. Unfortunately, this is probably strongly influenced by this year's US elections and its concerns about the misuse of extremely powerful AI tools such as Sora, which we discussed in issue 21 . In recent weeks, the company has been presenting Sora privately to Hollywood studios and filmmakers. The same applies to the highly sophisticated voice-cloning system unveiled last week , which is not yet publicly accessible: Voice Engine . The other major development at OpenAI — the company which, despite everything, continues to lead the AI revolution it popularised with ChatGPT — is that it appears to have overcome its own “Game of Thrones”, which we described in issue 8 . In recent weeks, it announced a new board of directors . What has changed, and matters greatly within the AI industry, is that GPT-4 is no longer the best language model. It has been surpassed by Claude 3's Opus version, a model we have already tested in depth in estrategIA, specifically in issue 24 . Before that, we had also analysed Google's latest model, Gemini. Its Advanced version did not convince us , for several reasons, but version Pro 1.5 is becoming particularly interesting thanks to its large context window, which lets it work with substantial amounts of external information, such as whole books. How the trends for 2024 are developing Finally, to continue this brief review of some of the main subjects we have addressed during estrategIA's first six months, let us take a quick look at how the AI trends we identified for 2024 in issue 14 are progressing, even though only three months of the year have elapsed. 1. AI will be integrated into our everyday tools, and we will increasingly use it almost without noticing This trend is still developing and has yet to take off. AI applications are certainly becoming more common on our phones, but greater integration and ease of use are still needed. Perhaps we will see major advances in this direction over the coming months — if, for example, the reports of an AI app store that Apple might soon launch are true . The same applies to autonomous agents, of which the interesting Devin is perhaps the best example so far. 2. Open-source models will narrow the gap with large proprietary commercial models still further, although the latter will remain more powerful. An open model might even match the capabilities of today's GPT-4 Here, progress continues to be very rapid. Last week X released Grok 1.0, and the models from the French start-up Mistral in particular are already very close to GPT-4's level. Meta's release of Llama 3 is also expected in July. It will very probably be the most powerful open-source model yet, and might well surpass GPT-4. 3. New mobile phones will have AI, in some cases even running locally We have already seen what the new Samsung Galaxy S24 phones, introduced in January, and Google Pixels can do. This CNET article is worth reading if you want to explore further . The ball is now in Apple's court. Judging by the “announcement” of its Worldwide Developers Conference in June, it intends to go all out on AI with an “(A)bsolutely (I)ncredible” event. It has also just presented a very promising new AI model . Original English screenshot, 26 March 2024. Greg Joswiak: “Mark your calendars for #WWDC24, June 10–14. It’s going to be Absolutely Incredible!” A reply from 9to5Mac reads: “(A)bsolutely (I)ncredible you say”. 4. 2024 will be the year of the great revolution in AI-generated video and audio The unveiling of Sora, which we have already discussed , left everyone astonished because it demonstrated advances in video generation that had been thought to lie years ahead. Extraordinary audio tools are also being created, such as Suno.ai version 3, which we will certainly discuss in a forthcoming issue. 5. Robots Anyone following AI news over recent months can see that this is an unstoppable trend, attracting billions in investment from many of the world's largest companies. Nvidia's developers' conference ended with a focus on robots, and the current landscape is fascinating. Singapore: shaping the future in the light of artificial intelligence Fernando Ujaldón examines Singapore’s national AI strategy, public-service projects, workforce preparation and lessons for other countries. Fernando Ujaldón Government & Public Services Learning & Human Capability Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 026 Analysis Singapore: shaping the future in the light of artificial intelligence In this edition of estrategIA, we welcome a special contribution from consultant Fernando Ujaldón , who introduces the interesting case of Singapore’s transformation. On the global artificial intelligence stage, Singapore is emerging as a clear reference point for innovation and strategic vision. With a population only just above five million, this small state between Malaysia and Indonesia has drawn up an ambitious roadmap balancing citizen protection with encouragement for innovation. At the heart of this strategy is meticulous preparation of its citizens for the AI era, setting a precedent for the rest of the world. The country has achieved a striking economic and technological transition, raising its GDP per capita above even that of powers such as the United States. Driven by a strategy of continuous innovation, this growth has attracted technology giants and positioned Singapore as a magnet for the industry. Now, in a new chapter of its evolution, the country is preparing to embrace the AI era fully. At the intersection of AI and governance, Singapore embodies a model of strategic foresight and adaptability. With a sharp focus on improving services for citizens and optimising administrative processes, its government has adopted AI as a catalyst for efficiency and innovation. Through AI-driven analysis, Singapore has streamlined policymaking, enabling evidence-based decisions and proactive intervention strategies. This paradigm shift towards data-driven governance, as numerous international observers emphasise, is a tangible example of using AI for social good. Image: Singapore Government Agency Website. A robust strategy based on leadership and regulation In 2019, Singapore presented its first National AI Strategy, setting out plans to deepen AI use across different sectors of the economy. Since then, the country has seen significant advances in AI, with approximately 150 research and development teams established, alongside 900 start-ups exploring new applications and opportunities in the field. The National AI Strategy’s success depends heavily on collaboration between citizens, businesses, researchers and government. The year 2023 marked another important milestone with the launch of National AI Strategy 2.0, or NAIS 2.0 . It focuses on three key shifts from the initial strategy: moving from seeing AI as an opportunity to recognising it as a necessity; adopting a global perspective from the outset; and moving from individual projects to integrated systems. To achieve these objectives, Singapore has identified ten key enablers, shown in the image, covering areas such as technological infrastructure, training and international collaboration. These will support AI implementation across practical applications ranging from healthcare to smart urban management. Image: Singapore Government Agency Website. Accessible transcription of the ten enablers: | Group | Enablers | | --- | --- | | Activity Drivers | Industry; Government; Research | | People & Communities | Talent; Capabilities; Placemaking | | Infrastructure & Environment | Compute; Data; Trusted Environment; Leader in Thought and Action | Initiatives such as “ Trailblazers ” have been a cornerstone of this vision, encouraging public–private collaboration to develop AI solutions. Launched in July 2023, the project’s main aim is to catalyse innovation by helping local companies identify and solve problems using AI. In partnership with Google Cloud and other key organisations, Singapore has brought more than a hundred AI projects to life, tackling a broad range of challenges in sectors such as health, transport and education. Social impact: empowering communities through AI Beyond government and the centres of power, AI adoption in Singapore extends into the fabric of society, catalysing transformative change in many areas. From health to transport and from education to urban planning, AI is reshaping everyday life in Singapore. Drawing inspiration from AI 2041 , which imagines a world shaped by AI-driven innovation, the country is determined to lay the foundations for a future in which technology enables equitable growth and inclusive development. Among its many notable projects, the following illustrate how Singapore is using AI for its citizens’ well-being: SELENA+: an advance in AI-assisted medical diagnosis This software system uses deep learning techniques to detect eye conditions with unprecedented accuracy. With SELENA+, doctors can identify eye diseases quickly and accurately, enabling earlier diagnosis and more effective treatment for patients. More information about SELENA+ Project Pensieve: tackling dementia with advanced technology This platform uses AI algorithms to detect early signs of dementia by analysing cognitive and behavioural patterns. By identifying key indicators, Pensieve enables early interventions that can delay the disease’s progression and improve quality of life for patients and their families. More information about Pensieve OneService: transforming municipal service management This initiative is part of Singapore’s commitment to improving urban life through AI. An intelligent chatbot guides citizens in dealing with municipal services, from rubbish collection to infrastructure repairs. AI simplifies and optimises processes, ensuring a faster, more efficient response to the community’s needs. More information about OneService Investing in human capital to prepare citizens Another striking feature of Singapore’s strategy is its emphasis on training and preparing its workforce for the AI era. Recognising the need for adaptation and reskilling or self-directed learning, Singapore has launched innovative programmes, including an initiative subsidising study for people over 40. This proactive approach not only ensures the continued relevance of Singaporean professionals but also strengthens the country’s global competitiveness. SkillsFuture offers a broad range of courses and training programmes in different fields, from technical skills to soft skills such as leadership and communication. These courses are designed to meet the needs of people of all ages and experience levels, including those seeking new skills or a change of career. A notable feature of SkillsFuture is the financial support it offers Singaporean citizens. Through subsidies and scholarships, the government covers a significant share of tuition costs for eligible courses, making training more accessible to everyone, regardless of their financial circumstances. More information about SkillsFuture This interesting video on Twitter , which went viral, including in several Reddit communities , shows MP Tan Wu Meng explaining the programme during Singapore’s budget debate, placing it in the context of the AI revolution. It showed the world that a country was already taking concrete action to adapt to the revolution artificial intelligence is bringing. Practices and lessons from a global perspective Within the wider story of AI in Singapore, certain practices and strategic insights emerge as reference points and guides for professionals and policymakers worldwide. By embracing a culture of experimentation and iterative learning, Singapore has encouraged an ecosystem conducive to innovation and risk-taking. Through strategic partnerships between government, academia and industry, the country has unlocked synergies that fuel AI-driven advances and sustainable growth. Singapore’s leadership in AI adoption and regulation has not gone unnoticed internationally. While other countries are also stepping up their efforts, Singapore demonstrates a balanced approach and a long-term vision. As it moves towards an AI-driven economy, it is positioning itself as a model for nations seeking to embrace the technology’s transformative potential. The road ahead Singapore’s commitment to AI extends beyond the present. The recent publication of National AI Strategy 2.0 demonstrates its determination to remain at the forefront of the technological revolution. This new phase emphasises building a smart nation in which AI drives efficiency and innovation throughout society. By creating AI Centres of Excellence, strengthening government competence and increasing computing power, Singapore is laying the foundations for an AI-driven future. It is also clear that exciting challenges and opportunities are emerging as Singapore progresses towards fully integrating AI into society. Safeguarding ethical values and ensuring equitable access to technology are becoming increasingly pressing. Yet with its pragmatic approach and intended commitment to excellence, Singapore continues to show its resolve to face these challenges with determination and foresight. Its roadmap invites the world to reflect on AI’s role in modern society, remembering that its transformative potential should be viewed with both optimism and caution. Fernando Ujaldón Consultant. Technology Director at OmnicomPR Group Spain.

The AI Act through AI’s eyes: using the most advanced text models—or trying to—to analyse the EU law in full A March 2024 experiment analysing the full AI Act with language models, preserving seven questions and answers, context-window tests and observed costs. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services AI in Practice 025 Practical experiment The AI Act through AI’s eyes: using the most advanced text models—or trying to—to analyse the EU law in full Archive note: this article records an experiment published on 20 March 2024, following the European Parliament’s vote. The questions and model answers are translated from the Spanish source and preserved as historical AI output, not as verified legal analysis or current guidance. The two screenshot answers about Article 30 differ; both are reproduced faithfully below. Last Wednesday, the European Parliament approved the AI Act, the general law that will regulate artificial intelligence in the European Union and become the world’s first major comprehensive transnational law on the subject. As we already examined the text agreed at the end of last year in depth in issue 11 of the newsletter , this time we decided to use the AI Act’s approval as an opportunity for a small experiment with one of AI’s potentially most useful capabilities in politics: analysing and working with legislation . In this way, we can bring you directly the analysis that some of today’s most advanced AI systems make of the new law. Methodology We began with GPT-4, Gemini Ultra—using it in English and translating afterwards, for the reasons explained in issue 20 of estrategIA —and Claude 3, the three most advanced “textual” AI systems currently available. The first task, which all completed successfully, was to act as journalists and generate interesting questions about the AI Act. From the full set, we eventually selected five generated by GPT-4, perhaps because it is the tool we use most often and whose prompts we have the best feel for, and because we tried it first—many questions were quite similar—plus one from Gemini Ultra and another from Claude 3. So far, so good. The problem came when we began working with the law and realised it ran to more than 450 pages . Unfortunately, this let us establish directly that neither GPT-4 nor Gemini Ultra had a large enough context window to work with such a long text. In our tests, GPT-4 could not remember and retrieve complete articles beyond the first 17. The situation with Gemini Ultra was similar: although it searched the internet and could provide some information about a given article, it was not retrieving it directly from the source and therefore analysing it first-hand, which was what we wanted on this occasion. Fortunately, every version of Claude 3 has a context window of up to 200,000 tokens , with more than 99% accuracy when retrieving content. This allows it to work with much larger texts, so we could use it to answer our previously selected questions and produce the analysis below . There was one further setback. Working with so much information—more than 450 pages—has a very high computational cost , and we soon exhausted our available credits for Claude 3 Opus, the most powerful version, in just two queries. One was a context-window check in which we asked it to retrieve a particular article of the law. Fortunately, after the first answer, we were able to generate the rest free using Claude 3 Haiku. It performs very well and may currently be the most recommendable free model. We used it through the Poe website , which we continue to recommend. Analysis of the law The original article reproduces the questions generated by the three large language models and Claude 3’s answers without alteration. Their full translations follow. The first answer is by Opus; the remaining answers are by Haiku, as explained above. 1. Innovation and its impact on AI development Question: From your data-analysis perspective, what are the most innovative aspects of the AI Act, and how do you think they will change the development and deployment of AI systems in the European Union? Claude 3 Opus: After analysing the full text of the AI Act approved by the European Parliament in detail, I consider the following among its most innovative aspects and those likely to have the greatest impact on AI development and deployment in the EU: The risk-based approach, classifying AI systems into categories according to their level of risk: unacceptable, high, limited and minimal. This will allow proportionate regulation, focusing on the highest-risk systems. The explicit prohibition of certain AI practices deemed unacceptable, such as social scoring, subliminal manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities or real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces, subject to exceptions. This sets clear limits on harmful AI applications. Strict requirements for high-risk systems concerning risk management, data quality, documentation, transparency, human oversight, accuracy and cybersecurity. These will significantly raise quality and safety standards. Regulatory sandboxes allowing innovative AI systems to be developed, tested and validated in controlled, supervised environments. These will facilitate innovation and the development of trustworthy AI. Support for SMEs and start-ups, including priority access to sandboxes, awareness-raising activities and dedicated communication channels. This will encourage a more diverse, inclusive AI ecosystem. Specific regulation of general-purpose AI models, with transparency and systemic-risk management requirements. Given their considerable impact, these systems needed to be addressed specifically. An EU-level public database of high-risk AI systems, to promote transparency and oversight. Taken together, I believe the AI Act will create a robust, balanced regulatory framework that increases trust in AI, minimising risks and harm without stifling innovation. It will raise standards of quality, safety, transparency and accountability throughout the EU while providing flexibility according to risk level. It will require a rethink of how AI is designed, developed and used, incorporating safeguards from the outset. More testing, documentation, traceability and human involvement will be needed. AI will have to be more robust, equitable and explainable. It will provide legal certainty and a level playing field for businesses. Harmonising EU rules will make it easier to operate throughout the single market. Ultimately, I believe it will encourage more trustworthy, human-centred AI in the EU, becoming an international reference point. However, compliance will also require investment and new capabilities from businesses and public authorities. 2. Ethical and social concerns Question: Considering the ethical debates and social concerns surrounding artificial intelligence, how does the AI Act address these issues, and what are its potential strengths and weaknesses in ensuring ethical, responsible AI technology? Claude 3 Haiku: The EU AI Act addresses ethical and social issues in several key ways: Strengths: Prohibition of unacceptable AI practices: The law explicitly prohibits certain AI practices considered abusive or manipulative, such as social scoring or remote identification of emotions in the workplace. This establishes clear boundaries for unacceptable AI uses. Requirements for high-risk AI systems: Requirements such as fundamental-rights risk assessments, human oversight and transparency seek to mitigate these systems’ ethical and social risks. Emphasis on human-centred AI: The law insists that AI must serve human well-being and EU values, helping to guide ethical AI development. Stakeholder participation: The law provides for experts, civil society organisations and other actors to participate in developing voluntary AI codes of conduct. Weaknesses: Limited scope: The law focuses mainly on high-risk AI systems, leaving out other AI uses that also raise ethical concerns. Voluntary compliance: Ethical requirements for lower-risk systems are largely left to voluntary compliance through codes of conduct. Implementation challenges: AI’s technical complexity and rapid evolution may make it difficult to apply ethical principles consistently. Lack of strong penalties: Although substantial, fines for non-compliance might not be sufficiently deterrent for large technology companies. 3. Regulation, innovation and competitiveness Question: Analysing the balance between regulation and innovation that the AI Act seeks, how would you assess its potential impact on European companies’ competitiveness in the global AI landscape? Claude 3 Haiku: The European Union’s AI Act attempts to balance AI regulation with the encouragement of innovation, with potentially mixed effects on European companies’ global competitiveness: Positive aspects for competitiveness: A harmonised EU regulatory framework: This provides greater certainty and reduces fragmentation, facilitating the development and marketing of AI systems in the single market. Innovation support: Regulatory sandboxes and targeted assistance for SMEs can help European companies develop and test innovative AI solutions. Emphasis on trust and ethical AI: By setting minimum safety and responsibility requirements, the law can improve European AI’s reputation and consumer acceptance. Negative aspects for competitiveness: Additional compliance requirements: Providers of high-risk AI systems must meet a series of obligations, potentially increasing costs and complexity, especially for SMEs. Restrictions on critical applications: Limits on AI use for remote biometric identification, criminal-risk assessment and similar applications may constrain the development of competitive solutions in certain sectors. Uncertainty over interpretation and practical application: The flexibility left to Member States and rapid technological change may produce implementation disparities and complexity for operators. Possible delays in AI adoption: The transition period and time needed to develop standards could slow the introduction of AI solutions to the European market. 4. Challenges and limitations Question: Based on your analysis of large quantities of data and previous discussions of AI regulation, what do you consider the greatest challenges and limitations facing the AI Act in its aim of creating an effective regulatory framework for AI? Claude 3 Haiku: Some of the greatest challenges and limitations facing the EU AI Act in its aim of creating an effective regulatory framework for artificial intelligence are: 1. The rapid pace of AI innovation: Rapid technological change may quickly make some provisions obsolete. Keeping regulation up to date and relevant will be challenging. 2. AI systems’ technical complexity: The opacity and sophistication of AI algorithms make compliance assessment and monitoring difficult. Appropriate methods and tools for assessing conformity will need to be developed. 3. Scope limited to “high-risk” systems: Many “low-risk” AI applications also raise ethical and social-impact concerns. Limiting the scope may leave problematic uses of the technology uncovered. 4. Difficulties in harmonised implementation: Differences in interpretation and application by Member States may cause fragmentation. Consistent implementation across Europe will be essential. 5. Effective oversight and enforcement: Ensuring adequate oversight and penalties throughout the single market will be a challenge. Fines, although high, may not sufficiently deter large companies. 6. Balancing regulation and innovation: Finding the middle ground between protecting rights and safety and avoiding undue barriers to innovation. Preventing European regulation from losing competitiveness against more flexible frameworks. 5. Adaptation to future innovation Question: Given the rapid pace of development in artificial intelligence, how do you think the AI Act will adapt to future technological innovations, and what provisions or mechanisms in the law enable this adaptability? Claude 3 Haiku: The EU AI Act provides several mechanisms to adapt to future technological innovations in artificial intelligence: 1. Periodic review and updating: Article 112 establishes that the European Commission must evaluate and review the law every four years, taking technical advances into account. This will allow it to identify needs to amend or extend the regulation’s scope. 2. Delegated acts procedure: The law empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts to update certain aspects, such as the conditions for considering an AI system “low risk”, the list of high-risk AI systems, technical requirements and so on. This provides flexibility to adapt the rules without revising the entire law. 3. Development of harmonised standards: The law calls on the Commission to request the development of harmonised standards reflecting the state of the art in AI. These standards can be updated more quickly than the law itself. 4. Common specifications: The Commission may adopt implementing acts establishing “common specifications” when harmonised standards prove insufficient. This allows new technical requirements to be addressed more quickly. 5. Expert and stakeholder participation: The law provides for expert groups and advisory forums to contribute technical knowledge. This facilitates early identification of emerging trends and challenges. 6. Phased entry into force: Some provisions will enter into force before others, allowing more time for implementation. This helps gradual adaptation to changes. Together, these mechanisms give the AI Act some flexibility and capacity to adapt, although the rapid pace of AI innovation will remain a significant practical challenge. Constant review and updating will be fundamental. 6. Risk categories Question: Do you consider classifying AI systems into risk categories—unacceptable, high, limited and minimal—an appropriate approach? Why or why not? Claude 3 Haiku: The AI Act’s approach of classifying AI systems into risk categories—unacceptable, high, low and minimal—is generally appropriate and effective for several reasons: 1. Proportionality and adaptability: It allows requirements and obligations proportionate to each AI system’s risk level. This avoids unnecessary burdens on lower-risk technologies while maintaining flexibility. 2. A risk-based approach: Focusing regulation on systems posing the greatest risks to health, safety and fundamental rights is pragmatic. It allows oversight and control efforts to be prioritised in areas with the greatest potential impact. 3. Transparency and predictability: Explicit classification of unacceptable, high-risk and other systems creates greater clarity and legal certainty. Operators can better understand which requirements will apply to them. 4. Capacity to adapt: The law allows periodic updates to lists of high-risk systems and unacceptable practices. This makes it easier to incorporate new technological developments and emerging risks. Nevertheless, there are also possible limitations: 1. Blurred boundaries between categories: It can sometimes be difficult to determine precisely which category an AI system belongs in. This could create uncertainty and litigation. 2. Exclusion of “lower-risk” systems: Relevant ethical and social concerns also arise in “lower-risk” applications outside the scope. Broader coverage would be desirable, at least through transparency obligations. 3. Rapid technological change: The pace of innovation may outstrip the capacity to update risk classifications. Agile review and adaptation mechanisms will be essential. 7. Global impact Question: Looking ahead, what global impact do you think the AI Act will have once fully in force? Do you expect it to significantly influence how other countries and regions regulate AI, or to become a de facto international standard? Claude 3 Haiku: Once the European Union’s AI Act is fully in force, it is very likely to have a significant global impact on AI regulation. Some of the principal effects that can be expected are: 1. Leadership and a model to follow: The AI Act will establish a comprehensive, pioneering regulatory framework worldwide. Other countries and regions will probably take note and tend to align their own rules with the European model. 2. Spillover effects in the global market: Given the size and economic weight of the European single market, companies will have to comply with AI Act requirements to operate in the EU. This will create pressure to adopt these standards even outside the EU. 3. Effects on interoperability and competitiveness: Harmonised European rules will facilitate the development and marketing of AI systems in the single market. This may give European companies a competitive advantage over competitors in fragmented markets. 4. Influence on international standard-setting: The EU will seek to promote global adoption of the technical and governance standards developed under the AI Act. This could make them de facto international reference points. 5. Pressure towards greater global regulatory convergence: A robust EU regulatory framework will pressure other jurisdictions to develop similar rules. This could encourage greater international harmonisation around common AI principles and requirements. However, there are also risks and limitations: Divergent implementation at national level within the EU. Potential conflicts with other technological powers’ regulatory approaches. Difficulties in regulating AI effectively and uniformly on a global scale. In summary, the EU AI Act has considerable potential to become an influential global model for AI regulation, although its actual impact will depend on consistent implementation and its ability to adapt to a constantly evolving technological environment. Additional observations As a point of interest, here is evidence that both Claude 3 Opus and Haiku could correctly retrieve and translate Article 30 of the law into Spanish. We worked with the English text because it was not yet translated into our language, which is understandable given its length. Article 30 appears on page 248. Until now, models with very large context windows have usually had particular difficulty with material in the middle, while remembering the beginning and end especially well. As we saw in one answer, the model also retrieved correct information from Article 112, on page 411 of the document. First example: urban mobility Historical prompt Act as a political marketing expert specialising in urban election campaigns, applying the PASTOR framework (Problem, Amplify, Story, Testimonials, Offer, Response) to develop a specific strategy for a candidate for mayor of a large city. Present a clear offer of innovative policies and measures that the candidate will implement to improve urban mobility, and end with a call to action aimed at urban voters, encouraging them to support the candidate to achieve tangible, positive change in their city. Endless traffic jams, inefficient and overcrowded public transport, and a lack of adequate infrastructure for cyclists and pedestrians are negatively affecting citizens’ quality of life. Second example: AI and blockchain in public policy Historical prompt Act as a forward-thinking political consultant specialising in integrating emerging technologies into public policy design. Develop detailed strategies to incorporate artificial intelligence and blockchain effectively and ethically into public policy. What best practices and approaches are recommended to ensure that these technologies are used in ways that maximise benefits for society while respecting ethical and legal principles? Include considerations of data privacy, transparency, accessibility and inclusion in your advice, as well as examples of successful use cases and recommendations for collaboration between the public sector, technology experts and key stakeholders. Claude 3 Opus — historical response As a forward-thinking political consultant specialising in integrating emerging technologies into public policy design, I recommend the following approaches and best practices for incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain effectively and ethically: Establish a robust ethical and legal framework. Before implementing any technology, it is crucial to develop clear ethical and legal guidelines that ensure responsible, transparent use of AI and blockchain. This includes principles such as non-discrimination, data privacy, security and accountability. Government bodies, ethics and legal experts, and key stakeholders should collaborate to create this framework. Encourage transparency and explainability. AI systems used in public policy must be transparent and explainable. Citizens have a right to understand how decisions affecting them are made. I recommend mechanisms that allow the reasoning behind AI-based decisions to be audited and explained, fostering public trust. Ensure data privacy and security. The collection and use of personal data must comply with strict privacy and security standards. Techniques such as anonymisation, encryption and controlled access should be applied. Blockchain can be used to create immutable, secure records, particularly in sensitive areas such as health or digital identity. Promote accessibility and inclusion. Implemented technologies must be accessible to all citizens, regardless of socioeconomic status, technical skills or disabilities. Intuitive interfaces, multiple access channels and training programmes can help overcome digital divides. AI can even be used to personalise services according to individual needs. Cross-sector collaboration. Governments, the technology industry, academia and civil society should work together on the design, implementation and monitoring of these technologies. I recommend establishing multidisciplinary working groups and citizen feedback mechanisms to co-create people-centred solutions. Pilots and continuous evaluation. Before large-scale implementation, I suggest pilot testing in controlled settings to assess impacts and risks. Once implemented, initiatives should undergo regular evaluations to measure effectiveness, detect biases and make necessary adjustments. Some promising use cases include: Blockchain for secure, transparent voting systems, such as the pilot conducted in Sierra Leone in 2018. AI to optimise resource allocation and personalise public services, such as the AI-based triage system used in hospitals in Denmark. Blockchain-based digital identity for secure, interoperable access to government services, such as the e-Estonia programme. AI to combat corruption and fraud in public procurement, such as predictive models used in South Korea. In summary, the ethical and effective integration of AI and blockchain into public policy requires a multidisciplinary, people-centred approach grounded in sound principles. With appropriate safeguards and ongoing collaboration, these technologies have the potential to transform governance, improve services and empower citizens. As consultants, our role is to provide expert guidance to harness these benefits while carefully managing the associated risks and challenges. GPT-4 — historical response As a political consultant specialising in incorporating emerging technologies into public policy design, my approach focuses on ethical, effective and equitable implementation. Below are strategies and recommendations for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain into public policy: 1. Ensure transparency in AI algorithms, allowing independent audits and reviews to prevent bias and unfair decisions. 2. Establish accountability mechanisms for AI developers and users, ensuring avenues for redress in the event of errors or abuse. 3. Improve accessibility and inclusion: Ensure user interfaces are accessible to people with disabilities, removing barriers to digital public services. Implement policies that promote digital inclusion, providing training and resources so that all citizens can benefit from new technologies. Use AI to personalise public services and improve their efficiency, adapting them to individual needs. 4. Promote collaboration: Establish partnerships between the public sector, technology companies, academic institutions and civil society organisations to share knowledge and best practices. Create AI working groups or ethics committees that include technology experts, philosophers, legal scholars and other stakeholders to assess technology’s social impact. Examples of successful use cases: AI in public health: AI-assisted diagnostic systems that improve the accuracy and speed of disease identification, enabling a faster response to health emergencies. Blockchain for civil registries: Systems for recording births, marriages and deaths that ensure data integrity and immutability. AI in the administration of justice: AI tools that help review cases and legislation to assist judges and lawyers, improving the judicial system’s efficiency. Blockchain in the management of public funds: Platforms that track government spending in real time, increasing transparency and reducing corruption. Recommendations for collaboration: Organise hackathons and innovation competitions that encourage the technology community to develop solutions to public problems. Create public policy laboratories that act as incubators for AI and blockchain projects, facilitating experimentation and phased implementation. Promote international collaboration, sharing experiences and establishing common standards to address AI and blockchain’s ethical and technical challenges globally. In conclusion, AI and blockchain should be integrated into public policy through a human-centred approach, ensuring that these technologies serve the public interest, respect privacy and fundamental rights, and promote a fairer, more inclusive society. A proof of concept: using generative image AI (Midjourney) to enhance a candidate’s image A March 2024 educational proof of concept using Midjourney images of Emmanuel Macron to examine political narratives, synthetic imagery and deepfake risks. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust AI in Practice 023 Practical experiment A proof of concept: using generative image AI (Midjourney) to enhance a candidate’s image Archive note: this March 2024 article documents an educational proof of concept. All thirteen illustrations below were generated with Midjourney 6 and depict invented scenes or stylised representations. None is a photograph of a real event. Artificial intelligence will radically change political communication over the coming years, offering powerful tools and new possibilities that will transform how politicians connect with their constituents. Among these innovations, the ability to generate high-quality images with AI from nothing more than a text prompt stands out as a significant revolution—one that is practically here already. Generative image AI has reached very high levels of quality and is close to achieving full photorealism. Based on advanced algorithms and large datasets, these systems can create striking visuals that capture, communicate and reinforce political messages effectively and persuasively. The major novelty is that they do so at very low cost, putting these capabilities within anyone’s reach. In a world where images carry considerable weight in shaping opinions and attitudes, the ability to generate convincing pictures tailored to a political campaign’s specific needs can provide a significant advantage in political communication and marketing. With these premises in mind, over the past few days we have been running several proofs of concept with Midjourney , probably the most powerful image-generation AI currently available to the general public. Our aim is not primarily to show what can be done today, but to give a sense of what any councillor in a small town will be able to do in a couple of years, very easily, from their own mobile phone and using their own likeness . That still requires particular effort and technical knowledge today, but will soon be child’s play. For these tests with Midjourney version 6, we chose French President Emmanuel Macron as our “character” . We wanted to move away from the usual US presidents, avoid anyone from Spanish-speaking countries so that the images could not easily be reused outside this educational context, and work with someone Midjourney could represent well natively. That last requirement will disappear in a few months, or would have required advanced techniques today. Before we begin, we want to emphasise that none of the following images is real: all were created with Midjourney 6 . We also used it in “simple” mode. On this occasion, we worked only with text prompts—we may try advanced techniques later—and used no inpainting, special upscaling or local retouching. Again, the idea is less to show what can already be done—despite Midjourney’s quality, small errors remain visible in many images—than what will certainly be easy to do on our own smartphones within a few months or very few years. A prime minister could very probably afford to have all these “real” images without generating them with AI, thanks to photographers following them around and large agencies with photo-retouching and design specialists to edit their pictures. The revolution, however, lies in democratising these capabilities: technology makes them technically straightforward for anyone to use, although a clear idea of what the images should achieve, and which ones to use, will still be needed. 1. “Real” images to strengthen a politician’s image One of the first uses that comes to mind for generative image AI is creating pictures that reinforce a candidate’s positive qualities: leadership, familiarity with other international contexts, or closeness to ordinary people through playing a popular sport, for example. These three scenes are synthetic illustrations from the original proof of concept. 2. Images that support a candidate’s narrative A next step could be to create images that are not perceived as real but whose visual power could help sell particular narratives about a candidate . These might use a more “realistic” style, comic-book designs, or even turn the candidate into an action figure. All four images are invented representations created for the original demonstration. 3. The dangerous world of deepfakes: constructing a candidate’s past One of the major dangers of generative image AI as it approaches full photographic quality is how easily it can create false pictures, such as the meeting with Biden. A mayor or member of a regional parliament would very probably be unable to fake this kind of meeting credibly. They might, however, construct a more interesting past for themselves, supported by visual “evidence”, as in the example of Macron on the day the Berlin Wall fell—obviously setting aside, in this case, the fact that he was not even a teenager at the time. These fabricated scenes illustrate the risk discussed in the article; neither documents an actual event. 4. Deepfakes as an (illegal) way to attack opponents Deepfakes of things a politician might have done in the past, or people they might have had dealings with, clearly cut both ways if others use their likeness without permission. In principle, AI tools’ terms of use reject this—we are using Macron solely for fully educational purposes here—but the capability exists. To avoid creating anything that could cause harm if taken out of context, such as placing Macron alongside a terrorist or drug trafficker, we offer a humorous example of this possibility: An invented scene from the educational demonstration. 5. Critical or caricatured images Political opponents may use a candidate’s image not to create deepfakes intended to pass as real—which will very probably be prohibited at several levels, although we fear it will happen a great deal—but to generate critical or caricatured images . They might depict an opponent as a despotic king, a sad Funko Pop figure, or a conventional caricature emphasising, for example, the candidate’s anger or madness. These are synthetic caricatures, not photographs. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

Challenges and uses of AI in public affairs Gustavo Fedi examines the distinction between generative and predictive AI, the challenges of measurement and six emerging applications in public affairs. Gustavo Fedi Government & Public Services AI in Practice 022 Analysis Challenges and uses of AI in public affairs In this edition of estrategIA, we welcome a special contribution from Gustavo Fedi , who offers his expert perspective on using AI in public affairs. Artificial intelligence challenges professional structures and practices every day, and with increasing depth. From generating text and still images, it is now possible to create long videos, and the first film made entirely with artificial intelligence is even about to be released, giving rise to what some call AI-wood: a Terminator parody . But how does this affect public affairs and the representation of interests? It is useful to distinguish GAI—generative artificial intelligence—from PAI, predictive artificial intelligence . The former, whose best-known examples might be ChatGPT and Midjourney, enables tasks to be automated and has caused an explosion in the production of written content and images. PAI, meanwhile, may hold greater appeal for professionals working to influence decision-making. Whereas GAI creates “new and original” content by learning from patterns and data structures, PAI enables forecasts and predictions about future events using current and historical data . In other words, PAI uses machine learning to extrapolate the future, rather than to create content as GAI does. Although both use statistical analysis based on large volumes of data, algorithms and their interaction, one does so to “predict” which words, images and content belong together; the other to identify patterns and associate them with behaviours or phenomena that may occur in the future. It is precisely this last point that is most interesting and challenging for professionals working in influence management, or public affairs. Opportunities and challenges in public affairs Public affairs is a professional field that draws on multiple disciplines to become more effective: law, political science, communication, marketing, digital strategies, public opinion research and more. All can contribute to informing decision-makers in order to represent a particular interest aligned with the common good. In practice, it has three main objectives : establishing political relationships with influencers, decision-makers and regulators; managing issues within their regulatory and social contexts; and anticipating conflicts to prevent them through tactical or strategic action. Until now, within the mix of methodology and insight employed by public affairs professionals—lobbyists—the ability to anticipate what might happen or how an individual or collective actor might respond, based on knowledge, experience and historical analysis, has been a distinctive asset in the market, beyond their network of contacts. That is precisely why PAI could play a fundamental role for public affairs professionals, much more so than GAI, which helps them generate content or interact with audiences. Alongside general regulatory challenges and fears that AI use could increase inequality, public affairs professionals face two related challenges: for PAI to work, it requires large volumes of data, integration and suitable software development , which is extremely costly; and how to construct robust, concrete KPIs —key performance indicators—and other measures when managing intangible assets. This last point, along with rules governing the role and operation of those who seek to influence decision-making, is widely debated by professionals around the world. SEAP, the Society of European Affairs Professionals, for example, recently presented reports by Transparency International , which gathered information from 27 member countries on the state of transparency and access to public information in Europe. As for developing indicators, there is extensive debate and a strong desire to incorporate AI tools to build smarter, stronger KPIs that can communicate within companies the return on investment that public affairs generates from its budget. In other words, to measure the concrete impact of its work on the business. On measurement in public affairs, readers can consult the latest edition of the study by the Corporate Excellence foundation . Uses and applications Finally, some of the ways public affairs is using and implementing artificial intelligence at this early stage include: Regulatory work: analysing legislation and case law to propose amendments or improvements to decision-makers. Political analysis: anticipating or predicting the behaviour of decision-makers and public authorities, as well as organisations and social groups, through PAI. Data-driven political decision-making: access to and processing of large volumes of information, including predictions, could enable decisions to take account of more factors, blind spots and implications of regulatory changes or measures than is currently possible. Optimised stakeholder relationships: through greater access to data and the possibility of more interactions that are automated yet personalised. Research and analysis: including the development of profiles of public officials, institutions, issues and other variables involved in understanding the context in which one operates. Issue monitoring and crisis management: automation and unprecedented capacity to process and analyse large volumes of information allow better monitoring and detection of news and social media posts associated with an emerging issue.
