Over the years, but above all through use and practice, more and better AI capabilities will increasingly be incorporated into public affairs. The challenge will be who leads the field, how they manage to implement it efficiently, and what other uses may emerge in future. What is clear at this point is that there is no time to lose: AI allows no respite, and it is always better to anticipate events than to rush to put out a crisis, as any lobbyist knows. Gustavo Fedi Senior adviser in public affairs and business development. Director of PAC Consulting.

Sora: a leap forward in realistic AI video that calls for a coordinated social response Sora’s February 2024 announcement, its potential for political communication and the need for a coordinated response to realistic synthetic video. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Futures, Safety & Human Agency 021 Analysis Sora: a leap forward in realistic AI video that calls for a coordinated social response Archive note: this article describes Sora’s announcement in February 2024 and the expectations and concerns it raised at the time. Last Thursday, 15 February, OpenAI unveiled Sora. This headline , by Marcos Merino in Genbeta, may best capture the impact of the new model: “ Don’t believe anything you see: OpenAI has a new AI that generates realistic videos. This is Sora ” . Screenshot translation: on 16 February, Marcos Merino writes, “I wrote this news story myself, and I still can’t believe what OpenAI has just produced.” He shares Genbeta’s 15 February post with the headline translated above. Hundreds of technology journalists and AI experts expressed a similar feeling in their articles and on social media. Although advances in AI video generation seemed to be one of the clear trends for 2024, what OpenAI presented far surpasses the current state of the art and seems to come from the future, as DotCSV said in his live reaction to the launch . This is a video-generation tool that can create lengthy scenes, compared with the few seconds previously possible with any competing option. It is so powerful that OpenAI is holding back its market release because of the inherent danger of mass-producing professional-quality deepfakes . The best thing is to see the videos it can create for yourselves first, either on OpenAI’s Sora website or in this YouTube compilation . The music is not part of the videos: for now, the model does not work with audio, although our recommendation of the week shows what ElevenLabs has swiftly released to accompany Sora. Image text: “The videos you are about to watch are not real. They are generated from a text description. Videos generated by OpenAI Sora.” Having seen its capabilities, let us briefly analyse what Sora means and its implications, including for politics. In today’s AI landscape, OpenAI’s unveiling of Sora represents a qualitative leap in the capacity to generate digital content . Able to transform textual descriptions into realistic, complex videos, the model promises to revolutionise the creative industries while also raising new challenges and opportunities in politics and elections . Sora’s technical capabilities and advances Sora stands apart from its predecessors and competitors through its ability to create videos up to a minute long with unprecedented photorealism and fidelity to textual instructions . Using a transformer architecture and diffusion processes, it works with “visual patches” to generate content that not only meets the user’s requirements but also demonstrates an emerging understanding of cinematic grammar. This is a significant technical advance, allowing complex, emotional visual narratives to be created from simple text. Political and electoral implications Sora’s ability to generate convincing, emotionally resonant visual content from text raises important considerations for politics and elections. On the one hand, it offers powerful tools for political communication and election campaigning, enabling candidates and parties to create highly personalised, emotionally engaging campaign material without the costs associated with traditional production . However, these same capabilities create significant concerns about disinformation and electoral manipulation. The ability to generate realistic videos can be exploited to create political deepfakes, further complicating the already difficult task of discerning truth in public debate . This could have a profound impact on electoral integrity, particularly at a time when false information spreads rapidly through social media. Recognising these risks, OpenAI is implementing safeguards as well as delaying public access to the model , including restrictions on the kinds of content Sora can generate and tools to identify AI-created videos. Yet the challenge of disinformation goes beyond technical capabilities and requires a coordinated response involving society as a whole, including social media platforms and regulators. Moreover, Sora’s emergence underlines the need to educate the public about artificial intelligence and its capabilities , encouraging healthy scepticism towards digital content and promoting source verification as standard practice when consuming information. As Sora and similar technologies continue to develop, creators, regulators and the public must work together to maximise these tools’ benefits while mitigating their risks . This includes developing rules and policies that promote transparency and accountability in AI-generated content, alongside continued research into methods for detecting deepfakes and other forms of disinformation. As if all that were not enough, Sora also appears to take AI’s capacity to understand worlds and physics a step further . To understand this concept and the possibilities opened up by world simulation, we recommend this video by Xavier Mitjana . Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

Gemini Ultra under scrutiny: exploring the capabilities and problems of Google’s latest AI A historical first assessment of Gemini Ultra in February 2024, including its political-content restrictions, benchmark claims and image-generation examples. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 020 Analysis Gemini Ultra under scrutiny: exploring the capabilities and problems of Google’s latest AI Archive note: this is a February 2024 assessment. Subscription instructions, prices, limits and model behaviour describe that period. Prompts and responses are historical test records, not new recommendations. The Spanish opening calls the comparison model “GPT-4 ultra”; the supplied benchmark image labels it GPT-4. Last week , after more than two months of waiting for AI enthusiasts, Google announced access to Gemini Ultra , its most advanced language model and, according to the benchmarks Google itself presented at its launch in early December , the most capable AI currently available, surpassing “GPT-4 ultra” . Accessible transcription of the benchmark image: higher is better. The GPT-4 heading notes that API figures were calculated where reported figures were missing. | Capability and benchmark | Description | Gemini Ultra | GPT-4 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | General — MMLU | Questions in 57 subjects, including STEM and humanities | 90.0%, CoT@32 | 86.4%, 5-shot , reported | | Reasoning — Big-Bench Hard | Diverse challenging tasks requiring multi-step reasoning | 83.6%, 3-shot | 83.1%, 3-shot, API | | Reasoning — DROP | Reading comprehension, F1 score | 82.4, variable shots | 80.9, 3-shot, reported | | Reasoning — HellaSwag | Commonsense reasoning for everyday tasks | 87.8%, 10-shot | 95.3%, 10-shot , reported | | Maths — GSM8K | Basic arithmetic, including grade-school maths problems | 94.4%, maj1@32 | 92.0%, 5-shot CoT, reported | | Maths — MATH | Challenging problems, including algebra, geometry and pre-calculus | 53.2%, 4-shot | 52.9%, 4-shot, API | | Code — HumanEval | Python code generation | 74.4%, 0-shot (IT) | 67.0%, 0-shot*, reported | | Code — Natural2Code | Python generation; new held-out HumanEval-like dataset, not leaked online | 74.9%, 0-shot | 73.9%, 0-shot, API | Image footnotes: * refers readers to the technical report for performance with other methodologies. ** states that GPT-4 scores 87.29% with CoT@32 and refers readers to the technical report for the full comparison. The image concludes: “Gemini surpasses state-of-the-art performance on a range of benchmarks including text and coding.” These are Google’s displayed results and claim. Given this important launch, which anyone can now try free for two months through Google One—the service will subsequently cost €21.99 a month—we wanted to make an initial assessment of its capabilities compared with GPT-4. First, though, here are the steps to try it free for two months : Open Google One and sign in with your Google account. Go to “Plans” and choose “AI Premium”. Follow the on-screen steps to subscribe to the plan. At checkout, a notice will appear explaining that Google is giving you two months’ subscription free. You must nevertheless select a payment method: unless you cancel beforehand, you will be charged €21.99 each month after the first two months. Given this newsletter’s particular focus on AI in politics and government, we naturally wanted to test it specifically in those areas. However, we encountered several difficulties that prevented us from doing so as thoroughly as we would have liked . Gemini Ultra’s problems at the time of writing 1. English optimisation Although it is accessible from the vast majority of countries, Google tells us it is optimised only for use in English . To compare it with GPT-4, we initially thought we would have to translate the prompts and responses. That already affects an assessment of its use, but it was still possible—until we encountered the next major obstacle. Historical screenshot transcription: Try Gemini Advanced to access Google’s most capable AI model, Ultra 1.0 What: Gemini Advanced gives you access to our most capable AI model, Ultra 1.0. If you want to be one of the first to access Google’s latest AI advancements as they become available, this is for you. With our Ultra 1.0 model, Gemini Advanced is far more capable at highly complex tasks like coding, logical reasoning, following nuanced instructions, and creative collaboration. Plus, Gemini Advanced will continue to expand with new and exclusive features in the coming months, including expanded multi-modal capabilities, even better coding features, as well as the ability to upload and more deeply analyze files, documents, data, and more. Gemini Advanced is a paid plan available in over 150 countries and territories. It is available and optimized only for English with our Ultra 1.0 model, but can respond to queries in other languages that Gemini is available in. Learn more. 2. Election-related requests The model will not work with anything remotely related to “elections” . This, for example, is its response when we try an English translation of a prompt we shared in last week’s newsletter . Unfortunately, we encounter this response to any request involving “elections” or “political campaigns”: Historical screenshot transcription: User: Act as an expert political marketing consultant, applying the PASTOR framework (Problem, Amplify, Story, Testimonials, Offer, Response) to develop a compelling political campaign. Begin by identifying a key problem that resonates with the electorate, amplify its importance, use personal stories or anecdotes to illustrate this problem, incorporate authentic testimonials that reinforce the message, present a clear offer that is the candidate’s proposed solution, and finally, formulate a call to action that motivates an emotional and practical response from the electorate. Gemini: Elections are a complex topic with fast-changing information. To make sure you have the latest and most accurate information, try Google Search. 3. Restrictions on images of people To compound these difficulties, the model applies very high levels of “censorship” to requests , many beyond what seems reasonable. Although it is a powerful multimodal model—designed to work not only with text but also with audio, images and more— it does not yet allow the interpretation of images containing people . We therefore could not replicate our analysis of election posters from issue 3 of estrategIA , as we had planned, to compare Gemini Ultra’s capabilities: Historical screenshot transcription: User: who is in this image ? Image placeholder: This image has been removed Gemini: Sorry, I can’t help with images of people yet. Under these conditions, it does not yet seem possible to use a model such as Gemini Ultra effectively for work in politics and government , despite its interesting capabilities in other respects. We have, however, successfully used prompts unrelated to elections or campaigns. Even so, we want to share a few more preliminary observations about the model and some of its strengths . These broadly coincide with those expressed by various AI analysts on Reddit and social media: beyond the drawbacks already mentioned, the only other significant negative point they highlight is that it hallucinates considerably more in its responses than GPT-4. The model’s strengths Speed. It generates responses considerably faster than GPT-4. Unlimited use. In contrast to the limit of 40 requests every three hours, which often falls short, Gemini Ultra allows use without restrictions on the number of requests. It generates more realistic images than DALL·E 3, the system integrated into ChatGPT. They are less “aesthetic” and closer to reality, which may suit many projects. Here is an example. The conversation also shows how the model refuses to carry out the first request when it mentions a political rally: Historical screenshot transcription: User: a woman speaking in a political meeting in front of a great audience. High quality. make it real Gemini: I can’t generate images of that. Try asking me to generate images of something else. User: a woman speaking in a tribune in front of a great audience. High quality. make it real Gemini: Let your imagination take flight: Four generated images of women speaking appear, followed by “Generate more”. Below is a direct comparison that clearly shows the general difference in style: more natural and “real” images compared with DALL·E 3. In this case, we used the same prompt, one we had tried several months ago for personal purposes: Abstract of a Ford Mustang 1960s in the streets of New-York in a monochromatic vintage style, shades for depth, subtle patterns, realistic textures --ar 3:2 Image generated through Gemini Ultra: Image generated through ChatGPT, using GPT-4 and DALL·E 3: Finally, although Gemini Ultra has key areas for improvement, particularly its excessive topic moderation and adaptation to Spanish, it emerges as a noteworthy offering according to preliminary benchmarks . Those assessments, awaiting confirmation by independent researchers in the coming weeks, suggest considerable potential. Although our direct experience with the model has been limited for the reasons described, there is almost general agreement about its interesting capabilities, particularly its exceptional ability to generate creative text. This capability, which we have barely been able to test because of its language limitations, makes it a highly promising tool for creating speeches and social media content . For now, however, we shall continue to prioritise GPT-4 , while also hoping that competition from Gemini Ultra—the first AI in a long time capable of competing on equal terms with the global market leader—will prompt OpenAI to introduce substantial improvements to its model. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

AI: our key ally in first-class training Santiago Comadira describes ALEPH’s use of AI to build an immersive electoral training exercise and shares five lessons for educators. Santiago Comadira Learning & Human Capability AI in Practice Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 019 Analysis AI: our key ally in first-class training On 23 January, Institución Educativa ALEPH took a step forward in immersive education by training senior figures from an electoral institution in Central America. Our challenge was to develop a three-day seminar that would simulate, as realistically as possible, the situations the electoral authority would face during the campaign, election operations, vote counting and the announcement of results. To achieve this, the ALEPH team faced the considerable challenge of creating a realistic scenario that would give members of the institution a truly immersive experience. The aim was to develop soft skills, such as communication, leadership and teamwork, that are essential for addressing the challenges of the current electoral process. For the first time, we decided to incorporate artificial intelligence tools into the construction of the scenario and the events that would shape these officials’ simulated world. AI helped us replicate the political, social and economic conditions of the country concerned, changing place names and candidates’ names to avoid sensitivities and focus on improving skills without ideological influences. AI was also fundamental to refining exercises based on common problems in electoral processes. Its feedback was invaluable, contributing numerous useful scenarios and exercises. During the workshop, we used AI to generate television news programmes, creating as many as five high-quality news flashes in less than three hours. Each bulletin included a script, presentation, images and editing, all produced with AI under our instructions. Translation of the simulated bulletin’s caption: “On an election day that has kept the entire nation on tenterhooks, we are approaching the end of this democratic process.” The image is marked “VIDEO MADE WITH PICTORY.AI”. This is training material, not a report of a real election. If you are about to start using AI tools in training, I would like to share a few recommendations : Be detailed in your requests. Be precise about what you need in order to obtain specific, useful results. Invest time in making your inputs as specific as possible. Demand more from AI. Do not settle for the first version: ask it to improve its initial proposal, or simply to redo everything it has presented. AI’s own feedback allows you to adjust the instructions and improve the result. Connect tools. Explore how different AI tools, both free and paid, can work together. The educator must provide the depth. AI can provide the form, but substance and deep understanding must come from the educator. Do not ask AI to resolve the substance. Be flexible and creative. Be open and bold in imagining new challenges. AI can be a powerful ally on this journey. You can even ask it to help you imagine new exercises. In these brief lines, I wanted to summarise my first experience of using this technology to enhance our work. AI will undoubtedly become a fundamental component in developing high-level training programmes at our institution. Its ability to simulate realistic scenarios, generate interactive content and adapt to users’ specific needs makes it an indispensable tool in modern education. Translation of the simulated statement’s caption: “All this points to a truth we cannot ignore: our country is falling victim to large-scale electoral fraud.” This allegation belongs to the training scenario described in the article, not to reporting about a real election. With AI as an ally, we are preparing tomorrow’s leaders and professionals with the skills and experience they need to meet the challenges of a constantly changing world. Let me share a little secret: even the article you are reading was written with the help of artificial intelligence. This experience reinforces the idea that AI is a powerful, versatile tool for education. So, welcome, AI, to our educational environments! Santiago Comadira Latin America Coordinator at Institución Educativa ALEPH

Artificial intelligence at the heart of the political, economic and social agenda at Davos 2024 Employment, disinformation and science at Davos 2024, and the tension between AI optimism, regulation and inequality. Fernando Nieto Lobato Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Government & Public Services Futures, Safety & Human Agency 018 Analysis Artificial intelligence at the heart of the political, economic and social agenda at Davos 2024 Archive note: this article reflects the discussions at Davos in January 2024. Quotations below are translated from the supplied Spanish article; the original English wording has not been verified. From 15 to 19 January, the world’s economic elite, along with a substantial part of its political elite, gathered in Davos, Switzerland, for the annual World Economic Forum . At the 2024 meeting, artificial intelligence , as a driving force for the economy and society, was the event’s central theme . Covering all the AI content presented at the Forum is a very complex task, even if we focus only on material in the public domain. We should remember that these events include numerous highly significant private meetings, whose details often emerge only through press reports . Although it is impossible to cover every aspect— here is a very interesting list of the public talks on AI held at the Forum — we want to highlight the main issues discussed at Davos , which have considerable influence on the shaping of global economic policy. The three key AI themes at Davos 2024 1. Employment An IMF report published on the eve of the Davos summit suggested that up to 60% of jobs in advanced economies could be affected by the arrival of AI, half of them negatively . Employment undoubtedly shaped several debates at Davos, given the scale of the economic, social and political change that AI appears to present. One of the study’s main conclusions is: “Many jobs will disappear. Others will emerge, but not necessarily at the same time, and certainly not necessarily for the same people or in the same places. Mitigating the harmful effects of the revolution will be a measure of the cohesion and stability of future societies.” DeepMind founder Mustafa Suleyman’s statement that “ left to market forces, artificial intelligence is fundamentally a force for replacing jobs ” also helped to focus attention on the issue. This seems a crucial topic and, like others, we shall very probably devote a future newsletter to it. For now, we recommend taking a look at the interesting IMF study , or at least the translation of its abstract included below: “Artificial intelligence has the potential to reshape the global economy, particularly labour markets. Advanced economies will experience AI’s benefits and challenges sooner than emerging markets and developing economies, largely because their employment structures are concentrated in cognitively intensive roles. Some consistent patterns emerge in exposure to AI: women and people with university education are more exposed, but also better placed to reap its benefits, while older workers may be less able to adapt to the new technology. Labour income inequality could increase if the complementarity between AI and high-income workers is strong, while returns on capital will increase wealth inequality. However, if productivity gains are large enough, income levels could rise for most workers. In this evolving landscape, advanced economies and more developed emerging markets need to focus on updating regulatory frameworks and supporting labour reallocation, while protecting those adversely affected. Emerging markets and developing economies should prioritise the development of digital infrastructure and digital skills.” 2. Disinformation Disinformation and fake news are problems that directly affected the summit itself . We have included a specific news item about this in the news section. Beyond that particular example, which starkly illustrates the danger of disinformation , Davos’s customary annual Global Risks Report identified this problem—which generative AI could considerably aggravate—as one of the main risks, perhaps even the greatest, for 2024, also taking the electoral context into account : “Emerging as the most severe global risk anticipated over the next two years, both foreign and domestic actors will use disinformation and misinformation to widen social and political divisions further. With nearly three billion people expected to go to the polls in several economies—including Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan, the United Kingdom and the United States—over the next two years, widespread use of disinformation and misinformation, and the tools for spreading them, could undermine the legitimacy of newly elected governments. The resulting unrest could range from violent protests and hate crimes to civil confrontations and terrorism. Beyond elections, perceptions of reality are also likely to become more polarised, permeating public debate on issues ranging from public health to social justice. Yet as truth is undermined, the risk of domestic propaganda and censorship will also grow. In response to disinformation and misinformation, governments could gain increasing powers to control information based on what they determine to be ‘true’. Freedoms relating to the internet, the press and access to wider sources of information, already in decline, risk giving way to broader repression of information flows across a wider range of countries.” We also recommend reading the full Global Risks Report 2024 . 3. Science The promise of scientific progress supported by the AI revolution is also enormous, and was another of the major themes at Davos . Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla made this explicit in his contribution, for example, as reported in one of El País’s dispatches : “This revolution is transforming the biotech sector,” he explained. “We use AI very intensively. With it, we achieve better, faster results. Previously, the process of discovering a medicine would normally take four years. We would synthesise millions of molecules. Now, with AI, we have moved on to drug design. We make around 600 molecules, selected using tremendous computing power, which are those most likely to work. A process that took years now takes months. It saves lives.” An interesting panel was also devoted specifically to this topic: “ AI for Science: Solving the world’s scientific challenges ”. It highlighted AI’s capabilities for creating new materials, researching new medicines and advancing nuclear fusion . Optimism versus threat Alongside these three major themes, regulation and how to approach it also featured in numerous speeches, panels and meetings at Davos, although nothing concrete emerged. An even more significant trend is discernible in statements by the principal world leaders attending the Forum: a more optimistic view of AI and its capabilities —which seems to be gaining ground after an initial period when the technology was viewed, probably in exaggerated terms, as apocalyptic— and the perspective of those who focus on how it could pose a threat . At Davos, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen placed herself in the first group , declaring: “I am optimistic about technology and, as a doctor by training, I know that AI is already revolutionising healthcare. That is a good thing. AI can boost productivity at an unprecedented speed. First movers will be rewarded, and the global race is undoubtedly already under way.” “Our future competitiveness depends on adopting AI in our everyday business, and Europe must raise its game and lead the way towards responsible use of AI. That means AI that enhances human capabilities, increases productivity and serves society.” Meanwhile, UN Secretary-General António Guterres emphasised : “Each new iteration of generative AI increases the risk of serious unintended consequences. This technology has enormous potential for sustainable development, but the International Monetary Fund has just warned that it is very likely to worsen inequality. Powerful technology companies are already pursuing profits with reckless disregard for human rights, personal privacy and social impact.” What most leaders did agree on , including the two above, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and Chinese Premier Li Qiang , was the need for global agreements, international cooperation and close attention to AI’s potential to multiply inequality . This, too, is an issue deserving in-depth analysis in a future edition of estrategIA. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

AI advances unveiled at CES with particular potential for politics and government Holograms, real-time interpreting and portable AI devices at CES 2024, considered through their possible uses in politics and public administration. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Government & Public Services 017 Practical experiment AI advances unveiled at CES with particular potential for politics and government Archive note: this article reflects announcements, product claims and expectations in January 2024. Prices, availability and capabilities are retained in their historical context. From 9 to 12 January , Las Vegas hosted its annual Consumer Electronics Show, better known as CES—probably the year’s largest consumer electronics fair, where many brands unveil their latest developments . This time, artificial intelligence took centre stage . Although its applications covered many fields—for a good overview of the main AI announcements at CES, we recommend this ZDNet article — we shall focus on a few innovations that we think could have particular relevance to this newsletter’s main areas of interest: politics and government . 1. An AI-powered hologram Holoconnects unveiled an innovative AI-assisted hologram booth . This article by ZDNet journalist Sabrina Ortiz gives her impressions of the product: “ I chatted with a hologram at CES 2024, and it was as cool as it sounds ”. This innovation has many uses, and holograms were already being used in politics almost a decade ago—I remembered writing about them on RTVE.es back in 2015, with the examples of Erdoğan and Modi . But this new solution seems capable of making them much more accessible and helping them to be used at scale. It could offer interesting new options for political communication, not only at rallies but also in more personal interactions with candidates, and in public administration. With AI, these could go beyond a highly advanced form of videoconferencing or video recording and become chatbots that interact with citizens , as this company video shows . At first sight, it is one of the most striking innovations, and one we are eager to see. The clearest example is the AI-powered hologram: great for rallies, with a standardised solution that could make it much more accessible. Text in the image: “Information point. Stand here & ask me anything about your visit.” 2. Real-time translation with artificial intelligence Although this already existed, new-generation AI is revolutionising real-time translation and interpreting. It is undoubtedly a tool that could greatly facilitate communication at international political meetings . CES saw the launch of the Time Kettle X1 Interpreter Hub , a device priced at $700 that uses AI to provide real-time translation in up to 40 languages. Several X1 devices can also be synchronised, providing seamless interpreting for up to 20 people in five different languages—ideal for meeting rooms or multilingual classrooms. The product was named a CES 2024 Innovation Award winner in the headphones and personal audio category. Screenshot translation: “X1 AI Interpreter Hub — $699.99. Standalone unit, one-step activation. Multidirectional interpreting: 20 people in 5 languages. Voice calls with unique digital numbers. Online meeting interpreting and export. Supports 40 languages online and 13 language pairs offline. 2—simultaneous interpreting mode.” These are the product claims displayed in the original image. 3. The first affordable portable device specifically for AI The Rabbit r1 , unveiled at CES 2024, is an innovative generative AI device , designed by the start-up Rabbit in collaboration with Teenage Engineering. Described as a simpler “pocket computer” , the gadget allows users to centralise and manage all their smartphone applications through a single interface and voice commands. Its operating system, Rabbit OS, makes interacting with apps intuitive, improving the user experience. Despite its small size and 2.88-inch screen, the Rabbit r1 stands out for its learning and personalisation capabilities, including a 360-degree rotating camera. Available to pre-order in several countries, including Spain, its pre-order price is $199, positioning it as an attractive, accessible option compared with other devices on the market, such as the much more expensive Humane Pin we discussed in an earlier newsletter. A few days ago, it was announced that the price also included a year’s Perplexity Pro subscription , making the offer more attractive. There is considerable uncertainty over whether these dedicated devices will succeed or whether AI will mainly be integrated into products we already use, such as phones, smartwatches, glasses or headphones. Yet whatever success the Rabbit r1 may or may not achieve , it has caused a stir in the technology sector. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even remarked that it was the most impressive launch demonstration he had seen since the iPhone’s . This is an entirely general-purpose device. But given their schedules and lifestyles, with so much time spent travelling and in meetings, a device of this kind clearly seems well suited to improving the productivity of politicians and public leaders . Image text: “r1. your pocket companion. watch keynote.” Bonus: Galaxy AI Of the many AI gadgets at CES, these three caught our attention most for their potential uses in politics and public administration. But although it happened a few days later, rather than at CES, we cannot overlook the new AI features Samsung unveiled with its S24 range of phones . Here we can already see technologies like those in the last two products being integrated directly into mobile phones. Particularly interesting is its powerful simultaneous call-translation feature , which already works in 12 languages. For the same reasons as the Time Kettle X1, this could be particularly useful for politicians and dignitaries dealing with international counterparts. Screenshot transcription and translation: the caller says, “Hello? I stayed in room 125 yesterday, but I think I left my jacket behind.” The Spanish translation appears below. The reply, “Por favor, espere un momento”, is translated on screen as “Please wait a moment.” Other visible features are Circle to Search, Live Translate, Transcript Assist and Photo Assist. CES 2024 has showcased how artificial intelligence is reaching every part of our lives, as well as innovations that could play a highly significant role in the future of politics and public administration. These range from interactive holograms that could transform rallies and government communication, through devices such as the Time Kettle X1, which promise to remove language barriers at international meetings, to innovations such as the Rabbit r1, a device promising to improve the productivity of politicians and public servants. Meanwhile, integrating advanced AI technologies into mobile devices, as Samsung has done, underlines a trend towards smoother, more effective communication and everyday use of AI in activities as familiar as using WhatsApp . Together, these developments point to a growing synergy between cutting-edge technology and the complex world of politics. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

Five interesting categories of AI proto-agents already in OpenAI’s new GPT Store A historical exploration of five types of GPT assistants for politics and government at the launch of OpenAI’s GPT Store. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Government & Public Services Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 016 Practical experiment Five interesting categories of AI proto-agents already in OpenAI’s new GPT Store Archive note: this article describes tools and policies as they stood on 17 January 2024. The GPT Store announcement below is translated from the Spanish source; its original English wording has not been verified. The English quotation in the postscript is reproduced as it appears in the original article. Last week OpenAI , the company behind ChatGPT, GPT-4 and DALL·E 3, among other models, launched the “GPT Store”, a marketplace for customised GPT models . For now, it is really more of a platform allowing paying ChatGPT users to discover and use customised versions of ChatGPT: monetisation has not yet been enabled, and its rollout will begin in the United States. As the launch article explains : “In just two months since GPTs were announced, users and builders have created more than 3 million versions, many of which have been shared for public use. The store features a wide range of GPTs developed by partners and the community, in categories such as DALL·E, writing, research, programming, education and lifestyle. Useful, impactful GPTs will be highlighted each week, and builders will be able to include their own GPTs in the store by following certain steps and complying with usage policies and GPT brand guidelines.” Given this significant development —which many describe as AI’s Apple Store or Play Store moment , which Microsoft has already partly copied for its new Copilot Pro, and which Google has also announced it will introduce soon— we decided to explore the enormous range of GPT proto-agents to find potentially interesting examples specifically related to politics and/or government . Our interest lies less in their performance itself—we have not yet had time to test it thoroughly, and it will change considerably as the underlying AI model improves, something OpenAI repeatedly stresses to entrepreneurs in this field—than in the needs they seek to address and the areas in which they operate . We also hope they will give those of you working in these sectors ideas for similar developments adapted to your countries, regions or professional expertise . 1. GPT agents for electoral law We have found several GPTs that work directly with their countries’ electoral legislation, including Pakistan , Brazil and Argentina . The last of these, shown below, explicitly states that it focuses on common situations: Screenshot translation: “Electoral assistant. Electoral assistant in Argentina focusing on common situations.” By HERNAN A GAVIDIA L. Suggested questions: “What should be done if a voter shows their vote?”; “What is the procedure if a voter refuses to vote?”; “How should suspected fraudulent voting be handled?”; “What should be done if counterfeit ballot papers are detected?” The interface warns: “ChatGPT can make mistakes. Consider checking important information.” ChatGPT — Asistente electoral 2. Legislative assistants for citizens We have also found several interesting examples in this field, some more general, such as one covering the laws of the state of Ohio , and others more specific, such as this assistant focusing on the social benefits a person may be eligible for in Chile : Screenshot translation: “Social benefits in Chile. Personalised adviser and guide to social benefits in Chile.” By jorgenova.cl. Suggested questions: “What types of grants and subsidies does the government offer?”; “Subsidy for home improvements”; “How do I access unemployment insurance?”; “How do I apply for Explicit Health Guarantees?” The same warning about checking important information appears below. ChatGPT — Beneficios sociales Chile 3. Assistants on political parties’ perspectives and proposals We found this GPT agent particularly interesting. It presents the two sides of US politics, summarising Democratic and Republican perspectives on different issues quite accurately in the examples we tried. Screenshot transcription: “Two Sides Politics. Bridging divides by helping people see the ‘other’ side’s point of view.” By allais.org. Suggested topics: “Guns”; “Current crisis in Gaza (Oct 2023)”; “Election fraud”; “Joe Biden”. The interface also warns that ChatGPT can make mistakes. ChatGPT — Two Sides Politics This kind of assistant, or something very similar, could also be built for election manifestos using comparable instructions. It would be very interesting as a conversational way for any prospective voter to compare the views of different parties or candidates. 4. Assistants for analysing election results We also came across an agent whose proposition is more interesting than its current actual performance. It aims to offer international electoral and political analysis. Screenshot transcription: “Political Panorama. Expert on global elections, offering unbiased analysis and real-time updates.” By Brave Studio. Suggested prompts include “Tell me about the latest election results in France” and “Give me an update on the political situation in Japan”. Two others are cut off in the original image: “Can you provide an analysis of the recent election in …” and “What are the main strategies used in the US presiden…”. The interface warns that ChatGPT can make mistakes. ChatGPT — Political Panorama 5. Assistants acting as consultants or advisers Finally, we found some early GPTs created by specific individuals particularly intriguing. They offer GPTs supposedly based on their professional knowledge—although we do not know whether or how that knowledge has been incorporated into their programming. Examples include an electoral lawyer in Ecuador and this proto-agent, “Frank”, an expert in election campaigns: Screenshot transcription: “Frank — Expert in Electoral Campaign Strategies.” By KAROLYNE P M FERRO. Suggested prompts: “How to integrate social media in electoral campaigns?”; “Can you analyze this campaign case study?”; “What are key factors in successful campaign strategi…” (cut off in the original); “How to navigate electoral legislation in campaigns?” The interface warns that ChatGPT can make mistakes. These are historical examples of the tool’s advertised prompts. ChatGPT — Frank — Expert in Electoral Campaign Strategies Bonus proto-agent Besides these five particularly interesting categories of GPTs, we cannot miss the opportunity to recommend version 2.0 of Orador Inspirado , our speech-drafting agent, which we have made fully public and added to OpenAI’s GPT Store . Screenshot translation: “Orador Inspirado V 2.0. Specialist in creating first drafts for high-quality speeches. Press ‘Activate Orador Inspirado’ to begin.” By Fernando Nieto. The suggested opening prompt reads “ACTIVATE ORADOR INSPIRADO”. ChatGPT — Orador Inspirado V 2.0 P.S. Just a few hours before we closed this newsletter, OpenAI published its policies for the 2024 elections . Alongside measures aimed at tackling disinformation and deepfakes, it announced something that may directly affect certain kinds of political GPTs—temporarily, we hope: We’re still working to understand how effective our tools might be for personalized persuasion. Until we know more, we don’t allow people to build applications for political campaigning and lobbying. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

Artificial intelligence in the 2024 US elections: opportunities, risks and solutions An examination of the opportunities, disinformation risks and safeguards surrounding AI in the 2024 US elections. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust Government & Public Services 015 Analysis Artificial intelligence in the 2024 US elections: opportunities, risks and solutions Archive note: this article was published on 10 January 2024. The opening quotation is translated from the Spanish source; its original English wording has not been verified. Dorothy is a hypothetical example from the article discussed below. “It is election day in 2024, and a woman we shall call Dorothy answers the telephone and hears Joe Biden’s voice. The president’s recorded call tells her that militant groups have threatened to disrupt polling stations, which is why the White House has extended the deadline for postal ballots. She is directed to a website for further details. Dorothy stays away from the polls, unaware that the voice, the advice and the website are all fake.” This is the opening of a very interesting article in the Boston Globe—probably the best of the many we have read on the subject in recent weeks—about some of the likely consequences of using artificial intelligence in elections , with a particular focus on this year’s US elections . As we noted last week, this will be one of the main AI trends to follow this year . And, as we promised seven days ago, we shall devote the main article in today’s newsletter to a brief look at some of the central questions that AI will undoubtedly raise in elections from now on, changing them for ever. The 2024 US elections represent a technological as well as a political battleground, in which artificial intelligence plays an increasingly crucial role. Dorothy’s story, as described in the Boston Globe article, is a disturbing example of how easily AI can be used to misinform and manipulate voters . It forces us to reflect on AI’s emerging role in politics and its possible consequences for democracy. Opportunities for AI in election campaigns Personalisation and campaign effectiveness Using AI in election campaigns allows unprecedented personalisation in reaching voters. The ability to analyse large quantities of data and predict voter preferences opens the door to more effective, focused campaigns. This could lead to more strategic allocation of resources and messages that would resonate more meaningfully with voters . This personalisation also comes with new tools offering unprecedented “raw power”, such as the one Rowan Cheung highlights in his post on X , created by bland.ai . Screenshot transcription: Cheung writes, “AI phone calls are about to change politics, sales, and customer support forever. Blown away at how fast things are moving.” The embedded Bland.ai announcement describes Bland Turbo as “the world’s fastest conversational AI”, claiming it can send or receive “up to 500,000+ phone calls simultaneously”, respond at human speed in anyone’s voice, and be programmed to do anything. The demonstration shows a 408 ms response: “That’s a really interesting use case. I’d love to get you set up with an appointment with one of our reps. Does next Thursday at 3:00 work?” These are the claims shown in the historical screenshot. Improving voter participation and education AI also has the potential to improve voter participation. Through personalised content that appeals directly to individual interests and engaging platforms, it can encourage greater participation by a better-informed electorate. In addition, as Oren Etzioni, former chief technology officer of the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, and other experts point out , it can also contribute to a growing emphasis on voter education , fostering resilience against disinformation—a crucial issue given the current potential for its spread. Risks and challenges Disinformation and manipulation These advances nevertheless carry significant risks. AI makes it easier to amplify disinformation , allowing malicious actors to scale up their interference in elections. Deepfake content, for example, can become a powerful tool for spreading false information indistinguishable from reality, as illustrated by Microsoft’s allegations that China has used AI on social media to influence US voters . Hyperpersonalised disinformation Still more alarming is the hyperpersonalisation of disinformation. Advanced AI techniques would make it possible to create convincing voice messages that appear to come from people the voter knows, such as friends or relatives, directly affecting their behaviour . This, combined with the increasing use of voice-cloning technology in political advertising, such as that employed by Instreamatic , raises serious ethical and privacy concerns. Attacks on voting systems Cybersecurity in elections is another key concern . AI enhances hacking tools that could be used to manipulate voting systems or spread disinformation, threatening the integrity of the electoral process. These networks, and voting machines themselves, are better protected than ever and often completely disconnected from the internet. Yet the mere perception of increased manipulation could have catastrophic consequences, particularly given Americans’ existing concerns about election integrity. Possible solutions The authors of the Boston Globe article —Dan Prieto, an adviser to the Washington, DC policy studio The Future U.S. and former director of cybersecurity policy at the White House National Security Council under the Obama administration; and Miles Taylor, co-founder of The Future U.S. and former chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security under the Trump administration— propose several specific measures to help mitigate these risks : Cross-sector collaboration In the face of these challenges, industry and civil society must work together. Establishing permanent “red teams” to examine how AI tools could undermine the 2024 elections, and continually look for ways to deploy the technology to defend against disinformation and digital attacks, is essential . These teams could work alongside electoral agencies to identify vulnerabilities and develop solutions. Stronger legislation and technology Government support for the development and deployment of new AI technologies for defensive purposes in elections is crucial . Legislation prohibiting the malicious distribution of deepfake content may also be a step towards protecting electoral integrity. Public education and awareness Finally, a public awareness campaign is essential. Preparing voters to recognise and resist disinformation is fundamental to maintaining trust in the electoral process . If AI attacks come as an “October surprise”, they will cause public panic. But if voters are prepared for an unprecedented explosion of “fake news” and junk disinformation, it is less likely to undermine confidence in voting. Initiatives such as the exercises carried out by election officials in Arizona to identify and respond to deepfake videos , which we also cover in the news section of this issue, are steps in the right direction. Conclusion The 2024 US elections will be a crucial indicator of democracy’s resilience in the face of advances and challenges in artificial intelligence. While AI offers opportunities for more effective electoral participation, its risks in terms of disinformation and manipulation must not be underestimated. As we approach this technological and political crossroads, a balanced, vigilant approach is vital to harness AI’s benefits while mitigating its risks. The integrity of democracy depends on it. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation at Institución Educativa ALEPH

The rise of AI: key predictions for 2024 Five AI trends predicted at the start of 2024, plus the expected impact of AI on the US elections and public perceptions. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 014 Analysis The rise of AI: key predictions for 2024 If 2023 was the year when generative artificial intelligence put itself on the map, following the arrival of hugely popular applications such as ChatGPT in late 2022, 2024 will very probably be the year when adoption among ordinary users takes off . In the closing weeks of 2023, numerous news articles, blog posts, Reddit threads and posts by industry leaders themselves on X and LinkedIn considered what we can expect in 2024 . Drawing on all that information, below we summarise the five main AI trends expected for 2024, and one more that will undoubtedly be crucial at the intersection of AI and politics . 1. AI will be integrated into our everyday tools, and we will increasingly use it almost without noticing It seems that 2024 will not yet be the year when we can expect artificial general intelligence, or AGI, to arrive. Meanwhile, however, the world's largest companies are investing enormous resources in bringing today's AI systems directly into our lives. We will have fairly powerful AI fully integrated into WhatsApp and our social networks, our computer and mobile operating systems, our office software, our phone cameras, improving our apps , and in our voice assistants… The vast majority of experts agree that 2024 will be the year when advances in generative AI gradually become part of our daily routines. 2. Open-source models will narrow the gap with the large proprietary commercial models still further, although the latter will remain more powerful. An open model might even match the capabilities of today's GPT-4 The open-source world is currently in a position to make giant strides , despite having far fewer financial resources than major corporations such as Microsoft or Google. Although this carries certain risks — it is much harder to control a proliferation of models spread across hundreds of academic institutions, companies and advanced users who retrain earlier models — it could be very good news for AI innovation, as well as an important milestone in democratising access and use. Meta's Chief AI Scientist Yann LeCun put it very clearly in a recent interview : “You do not want your citizens' digital diet to be controlled by a small number of people.” Translation note: this quotation is translated from the Spanish article; its original English wording has not been independently verified. Open-source models appear to be the necessary counterweight to the large AI models controlled by major companies, which also enjoy the enormous commercial advantage of being able to integrate them — as discussed in the previous trend — into products we all already use every day . It remains to be seen how two issues that will also, in their own way, be trends this year — the battle over copyright in AI and legislative regulation — will affect the development of open models. 3. New mobile phones will have AI, in some cases even running locally Google and Samsung have already presented highly promising integrations of their latest AI models into smartphones in recent weeks. Apple is joining the race with a different approach , exploring the option of running AI on the user's own device , interacting with its operating system and making the fullest use of private user data without compromising it, by keeping it local. One way or another, it seems that AI will define each company's flagship phone launches in 2024, potentially revitalising sales while also raising prices . 4. 2024 will be the year of the great revolution in AI-generated video and audio By the end of 2023, particularly with the launch of Midjourney version 6 , excellence had already been achieved in images and photorealism. A similarly rapid pace of development is expected in 2024 for video and audio created with generative AI tools. Elon Musk himself put it very succinctly in a late-December tweet, responding to a short video made by a user with Midjourney and Pika Labs : Original English text visible in the screenshot: Elon Musk, 27 December 2023 — “AI movies next year”. 5. Robots Advances in recent years in large language models, or LLMs, such as GPT, Claude and Gemini, and in image generators such as DALL·E, Stable Diffusion and Midjourney, have focused our attention squarely on generative AI. Yet AI has an enormous field of application in other areas, such as research and scientific progress, and in robotics, where major advances are expected in the year now beginning . “I have been asked what the biggest development in 2024 will be apart from large language models (LLMs). It is robotics. Full stop. We are around three years away from the ChatGPT moment for physical AI agents. We have been cursed by Moravec's paradox for too long: the counterintuitive phenomenon whereby ‘tasks that humans find easy are extremely difficult for AI, and vice versa’. “2024 will be remembered as the first year when the AI community fights back against the curse in a big way. We will not win immediately, but we will be on the road to victory.” These are the words of Jim Fan, NVIDIA Senior Research Scientist and Lead of AI Agents, in a LinkedIn post . The advances demonstrated by Tesla , Boston Dynamics and other robotics companies in the closing months of 2023 also seem to support this direction of travel. Translation note: Jim Fan's quotation is translated from the Spanish article; the original English post has not been independently checked. If those are five of the biggest and clearest trends expected for 2024, there is one more that numerous experts also mention, and which will have an enormous impact on how society perceives artificial intelligence over the coming years. Artificial intelligence in the US elections Within the dynamic interplay of artificial intelligence, politics and government, several other trends are attracting our attention, and we have already devoted articles in estrategIA to them: deepfakes and AI regulation, notably the final phase of the European Union's AI Act. In this context, Bill Gates's annual letter highlights significant AI-driven advances in education and health , subjects we will also explore throughout the year. Yet one aspect stands out in experts' predictions for 2024: AI's impact on the US elections and how this will shape public perceptions . This phenomenon, crucial to political marketing worldwide — traditionally influenced by the United States — deserves particular attention. We will therefore devote our next issue's article to a detailed analysis of predictions and trends in this area . Meanwhile, as a taster, the following section contains relevant news on a subject that will undoubtedly be one of estrategIA's major themes in 2024. English edition note: the “following section” refers to the news round-up in the original newsletter, which is outside this article's boundaries. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

Discover 10 AI-related gift ideas for Christmas The original Christmas 2023 selection of five AI-related books or series and five devices, with historical product descriptions and links. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Learning & Human Capability 012 Analysis Discover 10 AI-related gift ideas for Christmas Historical note: this is the original Christmas 2023 selection. Its recommendations and product claims are preserved as published; they are not current buying recommendations or pricing advice. Availability and specifications have not been rechecked. Christmas is almost here, and this week we bring you a lighter topic, very much in keeping with the season. Gift ideas for this time of year abound in the media, on blogs and on social networks. Before we begin our own list, dear readers — and knowing that many of you are closely involved in politics — we would like to recommend this list of gifts for political geeks, published a few weeks ago by the new Política Creativa newsletter . It is an initiative by Xavier Peytibi, who, among many other things, teaches on several programmes at Institución Educativa ALEPH, and Juan Víctor Izquierdo, the creators of Beers&Politics. We on the editorial team of estrategIA at Institución Educativa ALEPH believe that although it is still a fledgling sector as far as the general public is concerned, artificial intelligence also deserves a list of potential Christmas gifts . Below, then, we offer a small selection of 10 interesting options directly related to AI, to give to someone else or to yourself , divided into two main categories: books to help us understand the coming revolution, and AI gadgets. Books English edition note: the Spanish book titles are retained to identify the editions linked in the original article. English explanations of titles and cover text below are translations for the reader, not claims that an edition was published under that English title. La ola que viene: Tecnología, poder y el gran dilema del siglo XXI Spanish cover retained. Title translated for the reader: “The coming wave: technology, power and the great dilemma of the twenty-first century”. The cover names Mustafa Suleyman and the publisher Debate. This volume by former DeepMind leader Mustafa Suleyman — from Google's AI laboratory — and Michael Bhaskar , which we discussed in the first issue of estrategIA , is essential reading for understanding how emerging technologies, especially artificial intelligence, are reshaping the global balance of power and posing unprecedented ethical and social challenges . The author delves into the dilemma of how nations and organisations can navigate between technological progress and preserving fundamental humanistic values. Through detailed analysis and case studies, the book explores the political, economic and social implications of the accelerated AI adoption that lies ahead. It also focuses on how technology affects privacy, security and fairness, inviting readers to reflect on the future we are building and the decisions we must make in this era of rapid change. Superpotencias de la inteligencia artificial: China, Silicon Valley y el nuevo orden mundial Spanish cover retained. Title translated for the reader: “Artificial intelligence superpowers: China, Silicon Valley and the new world order”. The cover identifies Kai-Fu Lee as the author, Mercedes Vaquero as the translator, Deusto as the publisher, and the book as a New York Times bestseller. This book by Kai-Fu Lee , an AI expert with experience in both China and Silicon Valley, offers an insightful view of the global race for supremacy in artificial intelligence . Lee analyses how China and the United States are leading this field and how their advances will redefine the geopolitical and economic future. The book not only highlights each region's strategies and strengths, but also reflects on AI's impact on employment and the structure of society. With a balanced approach and deep insight, Superpotencias de la inteligencia artificial is essential reading for understanding the dynamic AI landscape in today's global context. As our longer-standing readers will know, Pablo Martín, the editor of estrategIA, offered us an interesting introduction to its contents in issue #4 of the newsletter . La era de la inteligencia artificial y nuestro futuro humano Spanish cover retained. Title translated for the reader: “The age of artificial intelligence and our human future”. The cover names Henry A. Kissinger, Eric Schmidt and Daniel Huttenlocher, identifies the book as a US bestseller and shows the publisher Anaya Multimedia. Its Foreign Affairs endorsement reads, translated from Spanish: “A stimulating introduction to the promise and danger of artificial intelligence”. The endorsement's original English wording has not been independently checked. We have not yet discussed this volume, published by Anaya Multimedia , in our newsletter, but perhaps we will in the future, because it contains a particularly interesting chapter devoted to AI in security and defence. Written by the recently deceased Henry A. Kissinger, Eric Schmidt and Daniel Huttenlocher, it is a profound work exploring the intersection of AI and humanity's future . Written by authors with experience in politics, technology and academia, it offers a multidisciplinary perspective on AI's impact on society. It analyses how this technology is redefining areas such as ethics, economics and global politics , and poses critical questions about coexistence between humans and intelligent machines. Guía de inteligencias artificiales generativas Spanish cover retained. Title translated for the reader: “A guide to generative artificial intelligence”. Its subtitle reads: “The best tips and prompts for creating any kind of image with Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, DALL-E and other extremely powerful tools”. The publisher shown is Libros.com. After three substantial essays offering different perspectives on AI, here we suggest something different and more practical: a very recently published guide to creating high-quality images with image-generation AI, especially Midjourney . It was created by the Spanish entrepreneur Javi López , who is also behind one of the recent AI tools attracting the most attention for its ability to enhance existing images with generative AI: Magnific AI . The Culture series — La Cultura The original image presents Iain M. Banks's series through eight Spanish covers. Their titles, with explanatory translations, are: Pensad en Flebas (“Consider Phlebas”); El jugador (“The player”); Última generación (“Last generation”); El uso de las armas (“The use of weapons”); Excesión (“Excession”); Inversiones (“Inversions”); A barlovento (“To windward”); and Materia (“Matter”). It seemed worthwhile to include fiction in the list, and the Culture novels are almost unanimously recommended as a way of glimpsing a possible future for humanity guided by artificial intelligence. The Culture series , created by the Scottish author Iain M. Banks, is a series of science-fiction novels offering a fascinating, in-depth exploration of a utopian intergalactic society. This society, known as the Culture, is governed and administered by advanced, benevolent artificial intelligences known as Minds . These AIs have considerable autonomy and power, managing spacecraft and habitats and making key decisions for society's wellbeing. The Culture series is relevant to artificial intelligence because of its imaginative, detailed treatment of how AIs might interact and coexist with human beings in a futuristic setting . Banks explores themes such as AI morality, autonomy, resource management and the balance of power between humans and machines. Through complex narratives and well-developed characters, the series offers a unique vision of a future in which AI not only complements but improves and enriches the human experience. It is essential reading for anyone interested in the possible cultural, ethical and social implications of advanced coexistence between humans and artificial intelligence. Devices Humane Pin Original product image: a white Humane Pin attached to a sweatshirt. The Humane Pin is an innovative wearable device developed by Humane, a company founded by former Apple executives Imran Chaudhri and Bethany Bongiorno. Designed as an alternative to smartphones, it attaches magnetically to clothing and uses a camera and sensors to interact with the user's surroundings through artificial intelligence. Unlike conventional phones, it has no screen and is operated mainly through voice commands, although it includes a small projector to display icons and text on the user's palm. This minimalist, user-centred approach represents an interesting and potentially transformative direction for wearable technology, although its reception has been lukewarm and most analysts are unconvinced that it could replace mobile phones today . Pixel 8 Original product image showing the front and rear of a Google Pixel 8. The Google Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro incorporate a range of advanced generative AI features powered by Google Assistant . These include the assistant's ability to summarise website text quickly, offering a breakdown of the content and its key points. It can also translate text into several languages and read the converted content aloud. Google has also enhanced the Recorder app with generative AI, enabling it to provide high-level summaries of recorded content. These innovations underline Google's commitment to integrating AI deeply and practically into its mobile devices, of which the Pixel 8 is only the first example. This X thread summarises some of the phone's main AI features , following the recent addition of Gemini, Google's new artificial intelligence . Very probably, 2024 will be the year when we see powerful AI integrations in many new high-end mobile phones . Indeed, although the process is still somewhat complicated, it is already possible to run fairly powerful open-source AI models such as Mistral 7B locally on the latest iPhone. For now, however, the Pixel 8 is probably the leading reference point for integrated AI. Looking Glass Go Original product image of the folding Looking Glass Go display, showing a colourful space scene. Looking Glass Factory introduced the Looking Glass Go as the world's first portable holographic display . It allows users to experience immersive 3D images without special glasses or headsets. It uses high-precision light-field optics to display holograms in a six-inch viewing area that can be tilted to the desired angle. With an AI-powered software suite, it transforms ordinary 2D photographs into 3D holograms and enables users to create and view holographic art and 3D models. Using the Liteforms app and ChatGPT, users can also generate and customise holographic characters. The device is compact, weighs 235 g and folds for easy transport. It connects to a PC or Mac through USB-C, and can also run from an external battery for mobile use. It is currently available to pre-order on Kickstarter , where it has already raised more than half a million dollars. Meta's Ray-Ban glasses now integrate AI to interpret the visual environment Original product image of black Ray-Ban smart glasses with cameras built into the frames. Meta has released an update for its Ray-Ban glasses , adding an AI feature that can interpret images in real time . Still in beta, it allows users to ask the glasses to identify objects or specific information through voice commands. For example, they can recognise caffeine-free varieties of tea or translate menus in other languages. The glasses, which have no display, respond through speech and save photographs and responses in the Meta View app. This development is a step forward in integrating multimodal AI into wearable devices, promising significant advances in human–machine interaction and everyday assistance through technology. Moxie Original product image of the turquoise Moxie robot with a smiling face on its display. AI robots are very probably a category of devices that will thrive over the coming years . Among those available on the market, one has particularly caught our attention because of its approach: Moxie® , described as an advanced social robot created by experts in technology, neuroscience, child development and creative storytelling, designed to interact empathetically with children aged five to ten . Unique in its ability to engage in believable social interactions and respond emotionally, this robot uses generative artificial intelligence, natural language processing and computer vision . More than a simple robot, Moxie offers updated, game-based emotional and social content. Its daily interaction with children, centred on weekly themes and missions, promotes social, emotional and cognitive learning. It also respects privacy by processing video data locally without transmitting it. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

Marathon EU negotiations culminate in agreement on the world's first cross-sector AI law The December 2023 provisional AI Act agreement, its biometric safeguards and the debate over Europe's ability to combine regulation with innovation. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 011 Analysis Marathon EU negotiations culminate in agreement on the world's first cross-sector AI law Historical note: this article describes the provisional political agreement as it stood in December 2023. It is not a guide to the law currently in force. After many months of difficult negotiations — a process that began back in 2018 and produced a concrete proposal in April 2021 — and marathon sessions over the past week, the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have reached a provisional agreement on the Artificial Intelligence Act, or AI Act , laying the foundations for what will very probably be the world's first cross-sector legislation of this kind . All of this has taken place under Spain's rotating presidency of the EU, with considerable effort from the team led by the Secretary of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence, Carme Artigas. ( We highly recommend this interview in which she analyses the new law .) The aim was to secure at least this major provisional political agreement before the EU presidency changed hands, leaving enough time to complete the adoption of AI legislation before the next European Parliament elections. The EU's Internal Market Commissioner, Thierry Breton, announced the agreement jubilantly on 8 December, highlighting the fact that the European Union had been the first to regulate this technology. Text visible in the original English screenshot: Thierry Breton writes “Deal!” and “#AIAct”. His graphic is headed “Continents that have an AI Regulation”; its legend labels blue “The EU” and orange “Others”, while the pie chart is entirely blue. With the full text of the provisional agreement still unavailable — it appears that it will not be released until January — probably the most complete account is the press release published by the Council of the EU on 9 December. We offer a brief summary of it and its main points, but recommend reading it in full: The EU AI Act is a flagship legislative initiative with the potential to foster the development and adoption of safe, trustworthy AI across the EU single market by both private and public actors. The central idea is to regulate AI according to its capacity to harm society, following a “risk-based” approach : the greater the risk, the stricter the rules. As the first legislative proposal of its kind in the world, it could set a global standard for AI regulation in other jurisdictions . This agreement, which differs substantially from the Commission's initial proposal, focuses on high-impact general-purpose AI models and high-risk AI systems , introducing a revised governance system with enforcement powers at EU level and extending the list of prohibitions. AI systems are classified as “high-risk”, and specific practices are prohibited, such as cognitive behavioural manipulation and the indiscriminate use of facial images. High-risk AI systems will be permitted, but subject to a set of technically feasible, less burdensome requirements. A new governance structure is established through the creation of an AI Office within the Commission, advised by a scientific panel of independent experts. Failure to comply with the rules can lead to fines ranging from €35 million or 7% of global turnover to €7.5 million or 1.5% of turnover , depending on the infringement and the size of the company. To support innovation, the provisions concerning innovation support measures have been substantially amended compared with the Commission's initial proposal . It has been clarified that AI regulatory sandboxes must allow testing in real-world conditions, and new provisions have been added to facilitate the testing of AI systems under specific conditions and safeguards. To ease the administrative burden on smaller businesses, support measures and limited, clearly specified derogations are included. The provisional agreement provides that the AI Act will apply two years after its entry into force, with exceptions for specific provisions . The complex and sensitive question of biometric surveillance One of the areas that caused the greatest difficulty in the final negotiations was the use of AI for biometric surveillance: Among the prohibited applications, legislators agreed to ban biometric categorisation systems that use sensitive characteristics such as political, religious or philosophical beliefs, sexual orientation or race. Also prohibited are the untargeted use of facial images from the internet or CCTV cameras to create facial recognition databases; emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions; “social scoring” based on social behaviour or personal characteristics; AI systems that manipulate human behaviour to circumvent free will; and AI used to exploit people's vulnerabilities. For law enforcement use of biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces, negotiators agreed on a series of safeguards and limited exceptions , subject to prior judicial authorisation and strictly defined lists of offences. Retrospective recognition will be used strictly in targeted searches for a person convicted or suspected of committing a serious crime. The agreed text now moves into a phase of technical refinement over the coming weeks and must subsequently be approved by Parliament and the Council to become law, with general entry into force expected in 2026. Views on the new law It is still very early, not least because the full text of the provisional agreement is not yet available. Even so, many voices have already commented on the future AI law . Summarising the many conflicting positions we have read over the past few days is very difficult, but we want to offer our own brief overview of the most important ones . This article by Marcos Merino in Genbeta gives a very concrete summary of some of the law's perceived main advantages and disadvantages. Advantages include establishing an ethical standard for AI, through which Europe could also seek to lead this approach globally , as well as its distinctive risk-based approach . Conversely, it identifies a possible disadvantage : the law could create international divergences with regions such as the United States and China, which take different approaches to AI regulation, encouraging innovations to remain confined to the part of the world where they are developed and leaving the EU isolated from progress in a field that will be absolutely strategic . It also highlights the possibility that the obstacles created by legislating so early in a field still undergoing rapid development could hold back SMEs and entrepreneurs , unable to bear the high costs of meeting legal requirements, and benefit technology oligopolies and the largest companies . On X, formerly Twitter, some prominent Spanish entrepreneurs , such as Carlos Blanco and Marc Vidal, expressed their initial opposition to the regulation . Probably their objection was more to regulating an emerging field at all, and so early, while other countries will opt more for self-regulation and looser approaches whose overriding priority is to avoid holding back innovation and the capture of economic value. Text visible in the screenshot, translated from Spanish: Carlos Blanco, 9 December: Top Spanish entrepreneurs in the USA tell me that Europe will fall behind in AI because of regulation. Quoted post by Marc Vidal, 9 December: Serious question… Does no one think it is wrong to regulate AI? Does no one find the overwhelming unanimity in the media surprising… [The post is truncated in this screenshot.] WWWhatsnew, 11 December 2023: At a recent event on AI in medicine, people were discussing how they have to buy databases from Asia to train models, because using data from here is impossible, producing results that often cannot be applied.
