The well-known Spanish entrepreneur Benjamí Villoslada, co-founder of Meneame, added a brief but significant reflection, using the comparison with a knife that many experts have raised throughout the legislative process: whether the technology itself needs to be regulated, rather than only its applications or outcomes . That is how most technologies are treated, but not all — consider clinical trials in medicine and pharmaceuticals, or safety tests for cars. This is a very complex question, and one likely to receive different legislative approaches in different countries, in a field such as AI whose potential capabilities make it highly unusual, with a capacity for both “good” and “evil” on a scale that some experts even compare with atomic energy. Text visible in the screenshot, translated from Spanish: Marc Vidal, 9 December: Serious question… Does no one think it is wrong to regulate AI? Does no one find the overwhelming unanimity in the media in favour of what was approved yesterday surprising? Benjamí Villoslada, 9 December 2023: I think it is wrong. All the harm AI might cause is already regulated. We never introduced regulations for knives; “you shall not kill or harm anyone” is enough. One of the world's most authoritative voices on AI, Meta's Chief AI Scientist Yann LeCun, also commented on the legislation on X . Like others, he seemed particularly pleased with the changes made during the final round of negotiations in favour of open-source models , very probably one of Europe's main routes to competitiveness in AI against the large technology companies, the vast majority of which are American. Overall , judging by coverage in various media — such as this article in Expansión , which gives a voice to numerous experts — and on X and Reddit, the new version of the law, which moderated some of the initial maximalist positions, has been considerably better received by European entrepreneurs in the sector and by researchers than previous drafts . Transcription of the original English text visible in Yann LeCun's post: The EU AI Act negotiations ended. One contentious issue was the regulation of foundation models, particularly open source ones. Kudos to the French, German, and Italian governments for not giving up on open source models. Juicy part: "The legislation ultimately included restrictions for foundation models but gave broad exemptions to “open-source models,” which are developed using code that’s freely available for developers to alter for their own products and tools. The move could benefit open-source AI companies in Europe that lobbied against the law, including France’s Mistral and Germany’s Aleph Alpha, as well as Meta, which released the open-source model LLaMA." The screenshot also shows a truncated Washington Post link; the complete address is not visible. Perhaps the strongest criticism of the agreement came , to many people's surprise, from human rights groups, who were deeply disappointed by the introduction of exceptions concerning facial and biometric recognition . They believe these exceptions could allow many practices dangerous to citizens and civil rights to slip through, and are particularly concerned that other countries will adopt these technologies on the grounds that they are not categorically prohibited even in the EU. Amnesty International's press release headline is revealing: EU: The bloc's decision not to ban public mass surveillance in the AI Act sets a devastating global precedent Translation note: this headline is translated from the Spanish article; its precise original English wording has not been independently checked. Beyond the terms of the law itself, the most common criticism on social media has concerned the EU's relevance in the AI sector and whether, beyond regulation, it will be able to lead through its vision given its near-irrelevance in business , where efforts at development do not appear to match those devoted to legislation. Of the world's 100 largest technology companies, 60% are American, and many of them — often the largest — lead AI development, whereas Europe accounts for less than 10% of the world's 100 largest technology companies. Many people on X therefore responded ironically to the Internal Market Commissioner's tweet announcing the agreement, offering comparisons highlighting the EU's insignificance in the technology business. It has hurried to become the first to have legislation, yet is far from having a strong AI ecosystem ( despite important advances such as those announced this past week by the French start-up Mistral, which put it at the forefront of open-source AI worldwide ): Text and visual meaning of Matteo Zullo's original English graphic: the heading reads “Continents that have AI development”. The legend assigns orange to “Continents that have AI development” and blue to “The EU”. Two separate circles contrast the two groups, as a satirical response to Breton's graphic. This difference in perception is also visible in the contrast between Europe, where the news has received prominent media coverage — though perhaps not even to the extent one might expect — and elsewhere, particularly in technical AI circles. In one of Reddit's main AI communities, someone opened a thread entitled “ The AI act passed, I don't see much talk here .” Perhaps the best summary for understanding this “criticism”, which goes far beyond the legislative work itself — whose importance, at least for the EU, is generally the subject of broad agreement — is the headline The Economist used to report the news: “Europe, a laggard in AI, seizes the lead in its regulation.” Original English headline checked against the screenshot above. Its subheading reads: “The world’s first AI regulation is a bit of a mixed bag”. P.S. After the text of this newsletter had been finalised, we saw that the Financial Times had reported what are probably the most critical comments on the agreement from within European politics , echoing the issues discussed in the preceding paragraphs. French President Emmanuel Macron has argued that the European law could significantly hold back the sector in the EU, and in particular create a major disadvantage in a field where the United States and China are already well ahead . The French president went so far as to say: “We can decide to regulate much faster and much more forcefully than our main competitors. But we will be regulating things that we will no longer produce or invent. This is never a good idea.” Translation note: Macron's quotation is translated from the Spanish article; its original wording has not been independently verified. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

A year of artificial intelligence: the ChatGPT revolution and its global consequences ChatGPT's first anniversary, viewed from December 2023 through adoption charts, competing models and early evidence about AI in consulting and education. Fernando Nieto Lobato Work, Welfare & the Social Contract Futures, Safety & Human Agency 010 Analysis A year of artificial intelligence: the ChatGPT revolution and its global consequences Historical context: this article was published on 6 December 2023, shortly after ChatGPT's first anniversary. Its assessments, figures and forecasts are preserved in that context. Last week, ChatGPT celebrated its first birthday. In that year, artificial intelligence has moved rapidly and decisively from laboratories into the hands of billions of people around the world, probably driving the fastest global technological revolution in human history. Jim Fan , one of the leading AI researchers at Nvidia , the company whose graphics cards are powering AI's expansion, summed it up eloquently in the following tweet. He was responding to an earlier post by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recalling the night before ChatGPT's launch a year ago: The past year in AI is like leaping from Stone Age to Space Age. 🚀 The quotation above uses the English wording visible in the original screenshot. Sam Altman's embedded post reads: a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning’s launch. what a year it’s been... At estrategIA, we want to use this first anniversary of ChatGPT , the tool that decisively brought AI to a mass audience, to look briefly at how the field has evolved over this period . We will draw particularly on the “ Coatue Artificial Intelligence Full Report ”, a comprehensive analysis of AI's current state and future prospects, with numerous interesting charts. It was presented a couple of weeks ago by Coatue Management, a prominent global investment management firm known for its focus on technology. As we mentioned, this is probably the fastest technological revolution in human history. These charts give an indication of its speed of adoption: Chart text: “We're at Day 1 of AI… and riding on top of past waves.” The vertical axis measures US technology adoption as a percentage; the horizontal axis runs from 1990 to 2025. Blue represents the Internet, purple smartphones and green AI. The dotted extension of the AI curve is a projection, not observed adoption. Sources shown: World Bank and Statista, September 2023; Coatue analysis and opinion, November 2023. Chart text: “Adoption has been twice as fast with each platform shift.” Years to reach 50% user penetration in the US: PCs, 20; Internet, 12; mobile, 6; generative AI, 3, shown with a question mark. The generative AI figure is a projection. Source shown: Morgan Stanley Research, September 2023, reproduced by Coatue. We can also see very clearly ChatGPT's decisive importance in popularising AI. As a telling detail that reinforces its relevance, only yesterday we learned that “ChatGPT” is Wikipedia's most searched-for term in 2023 . Although growth has slowed considerably, its impact was enormous: global AI use went from around 50 million users — many of us were already using GPT-3 or the first publicly accessible image-generation AIs — to 450 million in barely six months , largely thanks to its launch. The following chart shows this clearly, along with some slowing after the initial surge. Chart text: “Has initial AI enthusiasm slowed down?” It plots approximate global AI application user counts by month from January 2022 to late 2023 and notes that growth has slowed since May. One annotation attributes over 60% of the user base to ChatGPT. Another offers possible explanations for slower usage: the student summer break and fading initial excitement as people learn which tasks AI handles well or poorly. These are the chart's hypotheses. Source shown: Coatue analysis and opinion, November 2023, covering a non-exhaustive set of applications. The next chart, on monthly active users, was produced by the fund manager Global X . It illustrates the year's evolution and events very well, both for ChatGPT and for the main moves by competitors seeking to keep up with the sector's leader. Chart annotations, transcribed in readable form. These are the historical chart's claims, not newly verified figures. The vertical axis is monthly active users in millions; the chart labels the estimated total “200M+”. October and November 2023 are marked as forecasts. | Date shown | Annotation | |---|---| | December 2022 | ChatGPT exceeds 1 million users in five days, breaking Instagram's previous record of 2.5 months. | | January 2023 | ChatGPT passes MBA and bar examinations. Microsoft invests US$10 billion in OpenAI. | | February 2023 | Google takes a 10% stake in Anthropic; ChatGPT Plus is released; Meta unveils LLaMA; Microsoft integrates GPT into Bing Search. | | March 2023 | GPT-4 is released. Google launches Bard and Salesforce unveils EinsteinGPT. | | April 2023 | Amazon unveils Bedrock. | | May 2023 | Meta unveils “AI Sandbox”, enabling personalised AI-based advertising. The ChatGPT app launches on iOS. | | June 2023 | McKinsey estimates generative AI's economic potential at US$4.4 trillion per year. Nvidia joins the trillion-dollar valuation club. | | July 2023 | OpenAI unveils Code Interpreter; Anthropic releases Claude 2; Bard becomes multilingual; Meta unveils LLaMA 2. | | August 2023 | Meta introduces Code LLaMA, a state-of-the-art language model for coding. | | September 2023 | Amazon invests US$4 billion in Anthropic and incorporates its technology into various products. | | October 2023 | OpenAI exceeds an annualised revenue rate of US$1.3 billion; Microsoft GitHub Copilot exceeds US$100 million in annual recurring revenue. | | November 2023 | OpenAI introduces GPT-4 Turbo and custom GPTs. Elon Musk's new AI venture, xAI, introduces its chatbot Grok. | Sources listed in the chart: Global X ETFs, drawing on TechCrunch (7 November 2023), Similarweb (September 2023) and McKinsey & Company (25 August 2023). The year 2023 has seen important developments in generative AI, a constantly evolving sector. Although OpenAI, with ChatGPT, retains a dominant market position, its leadership was temporarily affected by its CEO's recent departure and subsequent return, officially confirmed a few days ago . We analysed those events in detail in this newsletter two weeks ago. OpenAI is not the only major player, however. Technology giants including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and Meta also play fundamental roles. Google introduced Bard in March 2023, positioning itself as OpenAI's main rival. Originally designed as a research assistant, Bard has grown stronger following ChatGPT's integration with the Internet, adding Google's own resources, including an innovative YouTube extension in September 2023. Anthropic, meanwhile, launched Claude 2, also in March 2023, distinguishing itself through its focus on user safety and less harmful responses. Until recent weeks, Claude 2 had consistently ranked second in most model benchmarks. Other notable competitors include Microsoft's Bing Chat, based on GPT-4, and Meta's Llama 2, an open-source large language model (LLM) with between 7 billion and 70 billion parameters. Llama 2 has inspired the development of numerous open-source models, driving an innovative field in which improvements appear weekly. Some of these models have surpassed GPT-3.5 and are moving ever closer to the market leader, GPT-4. Recently, Elon Musk announced Grok, a new generative AI seeking to compete in this market. These innovations — even before considering advances in creating images, videos and music — demonstrate growing diversification and specialisation in generative AI, marking a period of unprecedented expansion. Meanwhile, OpenAI also made major advances during 2023, particularly with the launch of GPT-4, a model far superior to its predecessor, especially in reasoning, and still the model to beat. It integrated DALL·E 3 for image generation and enabled the creation of AI proto-agents: the GPTs we discussed last week. Powerful changes at work, including in consulting The figures above make clear the speed of the transformation AI is bringing. Beyond the new models, major technical advances and staggering investment figures, analyses and data are beginning to emerge on AI's integration into work and its capacity to transform fields such as those covered by this newsletter . For example, the Coatue report includes this interesting chart from a study by Harvard Business School and the consultancy BCG . It makes clear the leap in consulting capabilities that AI brings even in its current, still very primitive state: improving the number of tasks completed, the speed of completion and, probably most importantly, the quality of the final result. “For each one of a set of 18 realistic consulting tasks within the frontier of AI capabilities, consultants using AI were significantly more productive (they completed 12.2% more tasks on average, and completed tasks 25.1% more quickly), and produced significantly higher quality results (more than 40% higher quality compared to a control group).” This quotation already appears in English in the Spanish article and is retained as supplied. Chart values: the control group is set to 1 for every measure. With GPT-4, task completion rate is 1.12×, completion speed 1.25× and completion quality 1.40×. The vertical axis contains a break. The chart identifies Harvard Business School and BCG. Another powerful finding, closely connected to the educational purpose of Institución Educativa ALEPH and this newsletter itself, emerged from a recent Salesforce study , whose title the article renders in Spanish as Las Promesas y Dificultades de la AI Generativa en el trabajo — “The promises and difficulties of generative AI at work”. It surveyed more than 14,000 workers in 14 countries, including Spain, and concluded that more than a quarter of workers — specifically, 28% — already use artificial intelligence at work. In many cases, more than half, they have done so using tools not approved by their company and, above all, without specific training. Given AI's enormous productivity benefits in many areas of knowledge work, employees will clearly turn to it quickly. It also seems highly advisable that they do so in an organised way and, above all, with the training needed to make the most of it and avoid many of the risks associated with such a new technology. Those of us involved in education should also bear in mind that future generations will use AI entirely naturally at work . A study published on the Nature website last month, concerning university students in Germany , found that more than two-thirds were already using artificial intelligence in their studies . ChatGPT's launch has dramatically accelerated the AI sector, giving it a pace beyond that of other enormous technological revolutions. Yet it is particularly important to remember that, although the present is already profoundly transformative, this technology is still in the early stages of deployment — even if its scientific origins go back more than 50 years — and has enormous room for improvement , at speeds that humans will struggle to process. We will probably devote another issue to AI's immediate future, again drawing on interesting charts from the Coatue report. But I would like to close with this one, which shows precisely the vast capacity for improvement and learning in the AI systems we are only just beginning to interact with. Chart text: “We are optimistic: AI is getting better, faster.” It presents benchmark trajectories from 1998 towards 2024 against a horizontal “Human parity” line. The labelled tasks are handwriting recognition, speech recognition, image recognition, reading comprehension, language understanding, common sense completion, high school and college subjects, and code generation. The latter three remain below the parity line in the displayed endpoints. The chart's stated message is that the time taken to reach human-level benchmark accuracy is shortening. Source shown: directional data from Contextual.ai, Time and PapersWithCode, November 2023. No additional numerical scores have been inferred from the curves. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

Create your own virtual proto-agent: a guide to developing GPTs for any task A historical November 2023 walkthrough of the GPT Builder, with complete screenshot dialogues for Tweet Master and examples of other customised assistants. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice 009 Practical experiment Create your own virtual proto-agent: a guide to developing GPTs for any task Historical context: this guide preserves ChatGPT's interface, account requirements and examples as described on 29 November 2023. It is an archive of that workflow, not current product guidance. Screenshot dialogues below are historical text translated from Spanish. After two information-packed newsletters — the one on AI agents in Bill Gates's vision and the “Game of Thrones” at OpenAI following Sam Altman's dismissal and subsequent return — this week we want to bring you some straightforward, practical information so that you can create your own GPTs and customise them to perform tasks relevant to your work . Having created several GPT proto-agents internally for various tasks at Institución Educativa ALEPH and for this newsletter, I believe that these early assistants can substantially improve personal productivity and work quality when they are well defined and tailored to each activity's needs. They do not work equally well in every case, and it can often be difficult to find the precise instructions needed to achieve what you want. Even so, they represent another step beyond the prompt engineering we explore each week in our prompts for GPT-4 section. After some general instructions, we will work through a very simple example of creating a GPT through ChatGPT, step by step . A paid account is required, as GPTs use GPT-4. We will also point towards a more advanced method that can produce systems with a greater degree of automation. First, in case you are not yet familiar with what a “GPT” means in this context — although we referred to them directly in the newsletter on agents, since they are still very limited proto-agents — here is a definition: OpenAI's GPTs are customised versions of ChatGPT that users can adapt for specific tasks or topics by combining instructions, knowledge and capabilities. Instructions for creating a GPT These instructions follow the tool's guided mode, which is the simplest approach. Access your OpenAI account : sign in to your OpenAI Plus or Enterprise account at chat.openai.com. If you do not yet have an account, or use the free version, you will need to subscribe to a paid plan. Click “Explore” : once you are signed in, click the “Explore” button in the menu on the left. Create a GPT : in the GPT menu, select “Create a GPT”. Describe the chatbot you want to create : use the GPT Builder to describe the kind of chatbot you want to build. Confirm your choice and choose a name : the builder will present a summary and suggest a name for your chatbot. You can change the description or name. Choose a profile image : while the builder prepares your GPT, select an appropriate profile image. You can use an automatically generated option or upload your own. Adjust your chatbot : the builder will ask questions to customise it, such as how detailed its answers should be or what communication style you want it to use. Test your GPT : try out your new chatbot to make sure it works as you want. Publish the chatbot : if you are satisfied with the results, save it and decide whether to keep it private, share it with a selected group — as we will do here — or make it public. There are also more advanced settings that we can define, including directly in another tab, “Configure”. For example, we can choose whether to give the GPT the ability to browse the Internet, use the code interpreter or access documents we upload containing our information . If you would like more detail on this direct method, it is explained towards the end of this guide written by OpenAI's own team . A very simple example We will create a GPT to write tweets — or posts on X, to use the new terminology — from any content supplied to it, such as a political speech or an election manifesto. Following the instructions above, we will create a GPT and configure it through conversation: the simplest approach, although neither the fastest nor the most powerful . We will give it the following instructions: Historical screenshot. The builder's welcome message is already in English: Hi! I'll help you build a new GPT. You can say something like, “make a creative who helps generate visuals for new products” or “make a software engineer who helps format my code.” What would you like to make? Visible user prompt, translated from Spanish: Good morning. First, I would like you to address me in Spanish while we create this GPT. I want to create an assistant that turns any long piece of content I provide into concise, engaging tweets. To do this, I want you to take a brief breath and, working step by step, write five tweets from each piece of content I provide, acting as an expert community manager. We supply the initial instructions and it begins updating its “programming”. It then replies and suggests a name for this proto-agent . “Tweet Master” is clearly not the best name in the world, but it will do for this very simple example, which we are not going to configure exhaustively, so I tell it to go ahead. It then creates a profile image for the agent , using DALL·E 3 internally: Historical screenshot dialogue, translated from Spanish: GPT Builder: Perfect, I will continue in Spanish. I have configured the GPT to act as an expert community manager, transforming long pieces of content into five concise, engaging tweets. For the name, what do you think of Tweet Master ? Or do you have another suggestion? User: Perfect. GPT Builder: Here is the profile image for Tweet Master . What do you think? Is there anything you would like to change or improve? User: That works for me. Preview text, translated: “Assistant for transforming content into five engaging tweets.” The conversation starters read “Turn this article into tweets”, “Turn this report into interesting tweets…” (truncated in the screenshot), “Create tweets from this text” and “Make five tweets from this content”. Finally, in this very simple configuration method, it asks several questions to personalise the GPT further : Historical screenshot dialogue, translated from Spanish: GPT Builder: Great! Now, to refine Tweet Master's behaviour, I need to understand a few more details: What kind of content do you expect to turn into tweets? For example, news articles, blogs or technical reports. Is there a particular style or tone you would prefer for the tweets: formal, informal or humorous? Would you prefer Tweet Master to focus on particular aspects of the content, such as key points, interesting quotations or statistics? These questions will help me ensure that Tweet Master responds exactly as you need. User: In this case, I would like it to specialise in generating tweets from “political” content: speeches, election manifestos, talking points, etc. I want a warm but formal and respectful tone that can also connect with people. I want you to use your knowledge to choose the aspects of the content you consider most relevant, so as to represent the material I provide accurately and position it well in public opinion. GPT Builder: Perfect, I have updated Tweet Master to specialise in political content, using a warm but formal and respectful tone. It will focus on highlighting the most relevant and strategic aspects of the content to connect effectively with the audience. Now that Tweet Master is configured, would you like to try it in the playground on the right? You can send it political content and see how it turns it into engaging tweets. If you need any adjustments or refinements, I am here to help. What do you think? The preview repeats the description and conversation starters from the preceding screenshot. With these simple steps, our GPT proto-agent is configured. All that remains is to test whether it works as we want. For a professional project, we would very probably use the “Configure” tab to make several more specific choices, but this is enough for a general example. We click Save and make it available to anyone with the link. In this case — although, I repeat, this is not a particularly refined agent, as we simply wanted something easy to configure — I have run an initial test using Pedro Sánchez's full investiture speech . These are the results it gave me from such a long piece of content: Archive note: the source introduces test results at this point, but the preserved article contains no text or screenshot of those results. You can now try it , if you are a paying GPT-4 user, at Tweet Master . I hope this simple example shows that creating a proto-assistant through ChatGPT is really easy. They can also be created through OpenAI's website, but that route requires using the API, with its associated costs. Alongside this very simple proto-agent, over the past few days we have configured a somewhat more advanced assistant that we also want to make openly available — although it is still in beta — for all readers of this newsletter to try . A speech generator that asks for parameters to create personalised speeches Historical screenshot text, translated: “Orador Inspirado” (“Inspired Speaker”). “Specialist in creating first drafts of political speeches. Press ‘Activate Orador Inspirado’ to begin.” By Fernando Nieto. Button: “Activate Orador Inspirado”. You can try it at Orador Inspirado . This one has more developed programming , following the method shown in this video , similar to other templates for generating agents circulating on Reddit. It allows us to create proto-agents that require activation and ask for a set of parameters by default. It can also provide some quite interesting instructions for developing your own projects, although we have made substantial changes to the initial draft to personalise and refine it. GPTs with documents and further examples We have not specifically explored them in this article, but GPTs that use documents included in their configuration are also particularly interesting. Here is one created by the journalist Kiko Llaneras about his book Piensa claro — “Think clearly” : Historical screenshot text, translated from Spanish. Kiko Llaneras, 12 November: I have created a mini ChatGPT that is an expert on my book Piensa claro ! And I am amazed. 😮 How? It has read the book, and now you can ask it for passages, examples or explanations of any of its ideas. It works. Look: GPT description, translated: “I am an expert on the book ‘Piensa claro’ and its ‘Eight rules for deciphering the world through data’. What would you like to know?” The visible conversation starters ask why to read the book, how to apply one of its rules, what the eight rules are, and for an explanation of an interesting concept; three of the button labels are truncated in the screenshot. Try Piensa Claro GPT Finally, if you would like to explore further, many GPTs are being made fully public , although relatively few are really valuable at present. To find those likely to be better, we recommend this GPT directory: Discover the Best GPTs , from The Rundown. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

The end of OpenAI? Sam Altman's dismissal unleashes a storm in the AI world A contemporaneous account of OpenAI's November 2023 leadership crisis and the tensions between research, commercial deployment, safety and corporate power. Fernando Nieto Lobato Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics Government & Public Services 008 Analysis The end of OpenAI? Sam Altman's dismissal unleashes a storm in the AI world Historical context: this article records the rapidly changing situation as the newsletter closed on 22 November 2023. Its updates, uncertainties and possible outcomes are retained as they appeared then. Until well into Friday, when what many people — ourselves included — consider the business story of the year broke, this newsletter's main topic was going to be something else: specifically, the fourth European AI Alliance Assembly, held in Madrid last week . We cover it in two news items, and recordings of its two days of sessions are still available here and here . But late on Friday evening in Spain, the entirely unexpected dismissal of Sam Altman was announced. Altman was CEO of OpenAI, the company with the world's most advanced AI models — at least among those publicly available. So began an AI “ Game of Thrones ” that is still unfolding as we write, although Sam Altman's return to OpenAI appears to be confirmed. Its outcome, and the events themselves, will undoubtedly have a decisive influence on the development of artificial intelligence over the coming years. Before attempting a brief summary of the intense sequence of events surrounding the dismissal and the subsequent twists in OpenAI's crisis, it is important to understand a few basic details about the company behind, among other things, the GPT models, ChatGPT — which will mark its first year on the market in a few days — and DALL·E 3. What is OpenAI? Background to the events GPT-4 itself provides a very interesting brief summary: OpenAI is an artificial intelligence research organisation founded in 2015. Its main focus is developing advanced and ethical AI technologies, with the aim of ensuring that AI's benefits are widely shared across society. OpenAI is known for significant advances in deep learning and natural language processing. It seeks a balance between open collaboration and safety, advocating careful and ethical regulation of AI. The organisation has evolved from a non-profit model to a hybrid structure to sustain its research and development. Translation note: this historical GPT-4 response is translated from the Spanish article; it is not an independently verified description or a quotation checked against an English original. OpenAI's origins as a research organisation with an entirely non-profit model are crucial to understanding the events of the past few days. OpenAI's website provides a diagram of the organisation's extremely complex current structure : its controlling board of directors, non-profit entities, holding company and capped-profit company, in which Microsoft holds 49%… Diagram text and relationships: the board controls OpenAI, Inc., a 501(c)(3) public charity labelled “OpenAI Nonprofit”. This entity wholly owns and controls OpenAI GP LLC and owns a holding company together with employees and other investors. OpenAI GP LLC controls the holding company and OpenAI Global, LLC. The holding company is the majority owner of OpenAI Global, LLC, labelled “capped profit company”; Microsoft is its minority owner. The original diagram is already in English. This complex and unusual structure underlies the events of these days. But the external board overseeing OpenAI, which dismissed Sam Altman, has also played a decisive role . Last week, its members included: Ilya Sutskever : OpenAI co-founder and chief scientist, recognised for his work in deep learning and natural language processing. Adam D'Angelo : CEO of Quora and formerly CTO of Facebook. Tasha McCauley : technology entrepreneur, co-founder and CEO of Fellow Robots, a robotics company serving the retail sector. Helen Toner : director of strategy at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, and an expert in AI policy and national security. Alongside them were the dismissed Sam Altman and Greg Brockman, who was removed from his role on the board he chaired — and apparently was not even informed beforehand of Altman's dismissal — before also resigning as the company's president. A chronology of the dismissal and return In very brief terms — you can read a more detailed chronology at Xataka, for example — events unfolded as follows: Friday, 17 November : OpenAI announces the dismissal of CEO Sam Altman . The board cites a lack of transparency in his communication as the reason. Mira Murati is appointed interim CEO. OpenAI president Greg Brockman resigns in solidarity, as do three senior researchers. Saturday, 18 November : the news surprises major investors, including Microsoft, which says it learned of the dismissal only one minute before it became public. OpenAI chief operating officer Brad Lightcap rules out misconduct as the reason for the dismissal. The possibility of reinstating Altman and Brockman emerges. There are rumours that both are exploring a new AI project. Sunday, 19 November : negotiations over Altman's return fail, despite his visiting the company and taking a photograph with his visitor pass. Reports emerge that Emmett Shear, the former Twitch CEO, will replace Murati as interim CEO. OpenAI's board members reaffirm their decision to dismiss Altman. Before the stock market reopens on Monday, Microsoft announces that it has hired Altman and Brockman to lead a new advanced AI research team. Monday, 20 November : the possibility of a partnership between Microsoft and OpenAI is floated, which could stabilise the situation. Several OpenAI employees express support for Altman on social media through heart emojis. Ilya Sutskever, a board member and critic of Altman, expresses regret over the dismissal and a desire to reunify the company. OpenAI employees threaten to resign and join Altman at Microsoft unless the board reverses its decision and steps down. At the time of writing, more than 740 of the company's 770 employees have signed the letter against the board. Altman reaffirms his commitment to OpenAI's mission and to continuing its partnership with Microsoft. Tuesday, 21 November : late in the day in California, as we are closing this newsletter on Wednesday morning in Spain, an agreement in principle is reached for Sam Altman's return: OpenAI's announcement, transcribed from the original English screenshot: We have reached an agreement in principle for Sam Altman to return to OpenAI as CEO with a new initial board of Bret Taylor (Chair), Larry Summers, and Adam D'Angelo. We are collaborating to figure out the details. Thank you so much for your patience through this. Under this agreement, Bret Taylor, formerly co-CEO of Salesforce, and Larry Summers, US Treasury Secretary during Bill Clinton's presidency, join the new initial board. These are the facts of a crisis at what Musk has called the start-up with the greatest potential in history: with fewer than 800 employees, it was already valued at close to US$90 billion. Microsoft's “move” has not yet been completed. It could allow the company to acquire virtually all OpenAI's talent and its models at no cost and without regulatory interference. Simply announcing the hiring of Altman and Brockman sent Microsoft's shares to an all-time high, adding more than US$115 billion in value in the first hour of trading on Monday. It also prompted Elon Musk to tweet a subtitled video of “El Risitas”, which we include in our meme of the week section, capturing this extraordinary situation. With the latest news and Sam Altman's return to OpenAI, it appears that Microsoft will not absorb the entire OpenAI team directly, but will very probably secure closer integration and a greater say in decisions. How this ultimately ends will undoubtedly shape the coming years of AI development. Until now, Microsoft has had access to OpenAI's talent and technological advances, but in a fairly limited way. For example, a clause states that if AGI — artificial general intelligence, which experts increasingly see as approaching — is achieved, those OpenAI models would not pass directly to Microsoft but would be for the public good. That arrangement could now break down if virtually all OpenAI employees move directly to Microsoft, or could change if Sam Altman ultimately returns to lead OpenAI with Nadella's support. Competitors such as Salesforce and Nvidia have publicly made substantial multimillion-dollar offers, even on X, formerly Twitter, to try to lure away talent seeking to leave OpenAI amid the upheaval. But behind this Hollywood-style drama of the past few days, the various rumours and leaked internal accounts — the only information currently available about the deeper reasons — appear to point to two underlying issues. Both, particularly the second, are highly relevant to political approaches to AI and its regulation. Non-profit purpose versus commercial deployment: research versus business One possible major disagreement, as The Algorithmic Bridge discusses, for example , appears to concern the imbalance that Altman was supposedly creating within a company whose foundations are non-profit. More and more resources were being devoted to commercialising ChatGPT and raising round after round of funding to launch new products, including the announcement at the developers' event in early November of a kind of app store for ChatGPTs. Altman's approach, which seemed aimed at placing OpenAI among the world's four or five largest technology companies, could clash sharply with the position defended by chief scientist Ilya Sutskever. He sought to prioritise the company's resources for research into new large models and, especially in recent months, the superalignment of AI systems to ensure their long-term safety. Those who want to move faster and those who want to slow down AI development and deployment Connected to the previous issue, several analysts — Tomás Pueyo explores it at length in his newsletter, for example — point to a degree of conflict, reinforced by these tensions, despite all OpenAI employees' commitment to safe AI. On one side are those seeking a slower, safer deployment of new AI foundation models . On Tuesday, The New York Times reported a dispute between Sam Altman and Helen Toner over an academic article by Toner that raised doubts about OpenAI's safety work . This could also help explain the appointment of Emmett Shear as interim CEO. Although he describes himself as a techno-optimist, he has said in recent interviews that AI's pace should drop from 10 to 1 or 2, because the risks of AGI are too great to get it wrong. On the other side are those who believe new AI models must be developed safely but also very rapidly: the capabilities they would give humanity to address many of its greatest challenges — climate change, curing diseases, energy — would far outweigh the possible risks, and every additional day before these advances are achieved is another day of suffering for humanity. Ilya Sutskever may favour a slower, safer deployment of models, in contrast to Sam Altman's commercial appetite. This could stem from his work in OpenAI's laboratory, where several tweets by him and Altman in recent months point to significant, even unexpected, advances in new models' capabilities, and from his work on AI superalignment : the aim is for future AGIs to feel positive emotions towards humans, rather than being mere “intelligences”. This also connects with the previous issue. It remains to be seen how all this will develop, depending on whether OpenAI retains control of its models — impossible if 95% of its employees leave — or whether the situation is reversed, as now appears likely with Altman's return. The possible de facto acquisition of OpenAI by Microsoft — which now seems unlikely to happen, at least in that form — would be a business masterstroke, but also raises many questions about the world's most powerful AI being monopolised by its largest companies. Microsoft had already announced annual investment of more than US$50 billion in AI server infrastructure from 2024. With OpenAI, Microsoft would now clearly move ahead of Google, which previously absorbed DeepMind, then the leading AI company, to turn it into its AI laboratory. These corporations may be slower and more careful in deploying large AI models, although there is fierce competition between them and with perhaps slightly smaller but still well-resourced players such as Amazon, Tesla, Salesforce and Nvidia. Yet their size and capabilities also make them quite capable of establishing virtual monopolies, as we have already seen with computer and mobile operating systems, business applications, browsers and app stores. From a political perspective, the moves of recent days should prompt close attention to the underlying issues and to how political action can respond effectively to the challenges posed by the very structure of AI development and deployment, while continuing to encourage the rapid, responsible development of a technology that, used well, could usher in a golden age for humanity. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

AI agents: a new way of interacting with technology Bill Gates’s vision of personal AI agents prompts an exploration of hypothetical applications in public services, participation, policy analysis and scrutiny. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Government & Public Services 007 Analysis AI agents: a new way of interacting with technology Last Thursday, 9 November, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates published an interesting article on his blog about how artificial intelligence will completely redefine human interaction with technology . The change will be at least as significant as the shift from typing commands to interacting with icons on a touchscreen. In his reflection, Gates introduces the concept of an “agent”: advanced software that responds to natural language and can perform a range of tasks based on a deep understanding of the user . The article is particularly relevant because it appeared in the same week that OpenAI , the company behind ChatGPT, introduced a concept that represents the first clear step towards agents: custom GPTs . AI agents , as Gates describes them, are more than simple tools: they are personal assistants that understand and anticipate users' needs . Instead of using different apps for different tasks, we will simply tell our device what we want to do in everyday language . Depending on how much information we are willing to share, the software will be able to respond in a personalised way because of its deep understanding of our lives. These agents will not be limited to simple tasks. They will be proactive, able to carry out tasks across applications and improve over time by remembering activities and recognising intentions and patterns in users' behaviour. Gates gives several examples, including this one: if you say you would like to catch up with an old university friend, the agent will work with your friend's agent to find a time to meet. Just before you arrive, it will remind you that his eldest son has just started at the local university. AI agents will have a considerable impact in areas such as healthcare, education, productivity and entertainment. In healthcare, they will help both patients and professionals, facilitating diagnosis and the management of treatment. In education, they will personalise learning, adapting to each student's interests and needs. At work, these agents will optimise productivity by helping with a range of tasks and processes. In entertainment and shopping, they will offer personalised recommendations and help with decisions. Gates also highlights that agents will be the next major platform in the computing industry, changing not only how we use software but also how it is written. He expects agents to replace search websites, e-commerce sites and traditional productivity applications, and to be accessible even to people without programming skills. We will be able to create any program or app we need simply by asking our agent for it. AI agents in politics and government Although Gates does not specifically address this field in his article, there is no doubt that AI agents have the potential to transform politics and government significantly. These agents could be used to improve efficiency in public administration, support data-driven decision-making and optimise government services. For example, an AI agent could help public officials analyse large volumes of information to formulate more effective policies, identify emerging social trends or even predict and manage crises. One specific application could be emergency management. An AI agent could monitor real-time data from sensors and social media to detect early signs of natural disasters or humanitarian crises. Using this information, the agent could coordinate the emergency response, optimise resource allocation and provide crucial information to decision-makers. This system would not only make emergency responses more efficient and effective, but would also save lives by acting more quickly and accurately. We asked GPT-4 to imagine specific agents for politics and government. Its suggestions included the following : Agents for citizen participation: Example: an AI agent designed to facilitate citizen participation in legislative processes. This agent could inform citizens about bills under consideration, collect and analyse public opinion, and provide legislators with a summary of those views. Impact: it would improve participatory democracy by enabling more citizens' voices to be heard and considered in the legislative process. Agents for policy analysis and forecasting: Example: an AI agent able to analyse large volumes of data to anticipate the consequences of different public policies. It could simulate the effects of policies in areas such as the economy, public health or education. Impact: it would enable policymakers to make better-informed, data-driven decisions, potentially reducing unintended outcomes. Agents for transparency and combating corruption: Example: an AI system dedicated to monitoring and analysing government transactions and public tenders to detect suspicious patterns or anomalies. Impact: these agents could be powerful tools in the fight against corruption, increasing transparency and trust in government institutions. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

The first major international AI safety summit: seeking harmony between progress and precaution The 2023 Bletchley Park summit brought agreements on AI safety, while leaving difficult questions about regulation, openness and international cooperation. Fernando Nieto Lobato Futures, Safety & Human Agency Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 006 Analysis The first major international AI safety summit: seeking harmony between progress and precaution Last week, on 1 and 2 November, the United Kingdom hosted a highly significant gathering on artificial intelligence: the UK AI Safety Summit . It took place at Bletchley Park, a site rich in symbolism as one of the birthplaces of modern computing during the Second World War, and brought together representatives of 28 countries and leading technology companies. Its main achievement was the signing of the Bletchley Declaration on AI Safety, a commitment intended to manage and mitigate AI risks and ensure its safe and responsible development and deployment. The AI Safety Summit's main objective was to address the risks of artificial intelligence at the frontier of development and discuss how a united global effort could mitigate them. The first day featured talks by business leaders and academics aimed at deepening understanding of the most advanced AI. Participants included renowned institutions such as the Alan Turing Institute, Stanford University and the Ada Lovelace Institute. Technology leaders from companies including Google, Microsoft, IBM and SpaceX also attended, with Elon Musk himself present, alongside OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and prominent political figures such as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and US Vice President Kamala Harris. The meeting's main achievement was the signing of the Bletchley Declaration, which states that developers of advanced AI technologies bear a significant responsibility for ensuring the safety of their systems. This commitment emphasises the need for a shared understanding of AI risks and promotes collaboration on safety research. British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak described the declaration's signing as a historic achievement and highlighted the UK's leading role in this field. Opinions on the declaration were divided, however. For example, Martha Bennett , a vice president at Forrester, suggested that, although symbolically important, it lacked substantive detail on how to regulate AI effectively. One of the most notable outcomes was agreement on a new framework for safety testing of advanced AI models. The framework aims to give governments a greater role in evaluations before and after deployment, moving away from the idea that technology companies alone should be responsible for these tests. In the UK, a new AI Safety Institute will conduct these evaluations, working with the Alan Turing Institute to assess new forms of frontier AI carefully. In addition, the distinguished computer scientist Yoshua Bengio will lead the preparation of a report on the current state of the science in advanced AI. The UK government appears to have sought a balance between the importance of AI safety and the business opportunity it offers the country. The remarks of Science and Technology Secretary Michelle Donelan highlighted the extraordinary opportunities AI could offer in areas such as the NHS (National Health Service), transport and the fight against climate change. In contrast to the British position, the United States announced several measures , notably the creation of an AI Safety Institute and an executive order requiring AI companies to notify the federal government when training potentially dangerous models . Biden approved an executive order on AI a few hours before the summit began, as we reported in last week's newsletter. Although the possibility that AI might displace or even threaten humanity remains a matter of debate, there is a palpable consensus about the danger of disinformation amplified by AI. The concern is that malicious use of generative AI could seriously manipulate elections in different countries. Alongside discussion of AI's short- and long-term risks, the summit revealed a marked difference of opinion between open-source and closed-source approaches to AI research . While some argue that the code for advanced AI models should not be freely distributed because of its dangers, the open-source community counters that a monopoly on AI research by profit-driven companies could produce harmful outcomes, and argues that opening up models can accelerate safety research . Jess Whittlestone, head of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, said that the debate remained complex. Although there was agreement on the need to seek more nuanced solutions beyond the open/closed-source divide, differences persisted over how to put those solutions into practice and prioritise them. Reactions to the summit varied. Praise from figures such as Darktrace CEO Poppy Gustafsson contrasted with warnings that perceptions of AI could be distorted, with suggestions that vested interests might be fuelling alarm about catastrophic scenarios. Moreover, despite the call for cooperation, it seems clear that each nation is pursuing leadership in AI. Perhaps the most vivid illustration of this was the cartoon Elon Musk himself shared during the summit : Text in the original English-language cartoon, reproduced in the Spanish article: the figures labelled UK, EU, China and US jointly say, “We declare that AI… poses a potentially… catastrophic… risk to humankind”, while their thought bubbles read, “And I… cannot wait… to develop it… first…”. They stand behind a sign reading “AI Safety Summit”. Musk's accompanying post reads “Sigh”. The UK AI Safety Summit has been a significant milestone in the global AI landscape. Although it produced concrete achievements, such as the signing of the Bletchley Declaration and the establishment of a testing framework, it remains to be seen how these initiatives will translate into practical, collaborative action internationally . Managing the risks associated with AI is essential, and it is encouraging to see world leaders and technology companies taking this responsibility seriously. The willingness is there; effective implementation and cooperation, however, are the next major challenge in this new era of artificial intelligence. — Text of the declaration — Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

AI innovations transforming public safety and the environment: Time's chosen inventions of 2023 Three inventions selected by Time in 2023 show how AI can support wildfire detection, wildlife protection and urban drone security. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services AI in Practice 005 Analysis AI innovations transforming public safety and the environment: Time's chosen inventions of 2023 Continuing an annual tradition stretching back more than two decades, Time magazine has selected and published its list of the best inventions of 2023 . Among this year's choices, a series of inventions in artificial intelligence capture the imagination and offer fresh perspectives on how AI could shape our shared future in the near term. Below, we focus on three inventions of particular direct relevance to politics and, especially, government, highlighting their potential to tackle critical problems facing our societies. We leave aside other AI projects on the list that we have already discussed, such as GPT-4 and DALL-E 3, and those whose applications lie well beyond this newsletter's main focus. Detecting wildfires: ALERTCalifornia One of the most critical challenges of climate change is the increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires. The University of California, together with the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) and industry partner Digital Path, has developed ALERTCalifornia, an AI system that significantly improves wildfire detection and response . Using a network of more than 1,050 cameras, the system can identify fires in their early stages with very high accuracy, thereby optimising resource allocation and evacuation procedures. Since its deployment in September 2023, the tool has proved particularly effective at detecting fires early in remote locations and at night. In its first two months, the system correctly identified 77 fires before anyone called the emergency services. Protecting wildlife: TrailGuard AI Poaching is a chronic problem affecting biodiversity in many parts of the world. TrailGuard AI is an AI system created by the US environmental organisation Resolve in collaboration with Intel. Designed to combat poaching in protected areas of India and Africa, the system uses compact cameras and machine learning algorithms to detect illegal activity and notify the authorities in real time. During testing, the system contributed to the arrest of more than 30 poachers. As well as facilitating arrests, TrailGuard AI improves intelligence on illicit poaching networks, helping to combat the illegal wildlife trade. The technology is compact enough to be easily concealed along trails, and work is under way to make it as affordable as possible so that it can be used widely in wildlife reserves. Urban security: drone detection with Dedrone As drones proliferate in urban airspace, the need for an effective detection and mitigation system has grown significantly. Dedrone has launched “City-Wide Drone Detection”, a system that acts as a virtual shield around designated areas , such as cities or critical facilities. In one concrete example, the Catalan police in Barcelona have already deployed this technology , demonstrating its applicability in a European setting. The system has been compared to air traffic control for drones, something that did not previously exist. The product is designed to neutralise threats and keep airspace safe, providing critical information such as the drone's altitude, flight path and pilot's location. It is presented as a comprehensive solution for detecting and mitigating drones in urban and business environments. Illustration reproduced from the Spanish article: monitoring drones and their routes in an urban setting. As these notable AI inventions selected by Time suggest, 2023 is shaping up to be a turning point in the application of artificial intelligence to critical public safety and environmental challenges. From early wildfire detection to combating poaching and regulating drone traffic in cities, AI innovations are providing tangible, effective solutions. These initiatives demonstrate not only the maturity of machine learning algorithms, but also how interdisciplinary collaboration between academia, industry and government institutions can produce significant results. However, as we continue to integrate these tools into our social and environmental infrastructure, it is essential, as we have discussed in previous newsletters, to maintain a critical approach that considers the ethical and political implications of their use, so that applying technology always serves collective well-being and long-term sustainability. Fernando Nieto Lobato Director of Digital Innovation, Institución Educativa ALEPH

The silent battle: China, the United States and the race for AI supremacy Pablo Martín Diez examines Kai-Fu Lee's account of China's AI advantages and the social contract needed in a world reshaped by automation. Pablo Martín Diez Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics Work, Welfare & the Social Contract 004 Analysis The silent battle: China, the United States and the race for AI supremacy “Entrepreneurship and mass innovation.” These words, spoken by Chinese Premier Li Keqiang at the Davos Forum in 2014, sum up the strategy China has pursued over the past decade . The result: the Asian giant leads in the number of artificial intelligence patents, leads the world in 5G connectivity and, it seems, may also have achieved quantum supremacy. Translation note: the quotation above is translated from the Spanish article. Its original wording has not been independently verified. Despite this technological momentum, Chinese artificial intelligence companies had yet to launch practical commercial applications on a par with their American counterparts. Last week, however, Baidu , “China's Google”, unveiled ERNIE 4.0, a chatbot capable of rivalling ChatGPT 4 . At the launch event , the company's CEO, Robin Li, demonstrated how ERNIE 4.0 could generate the plot for a novel and even a video advertisement for a car in a matter of minutes. Aware of China's technological strength, the United States is trying to curb its momentum through trade restrictions , such as those imposed on Huawei a few years ago or, more recently, the ban on exporting to China chips needed for artificial intelligence development, including the H800 and A800 from Nvidia, the sector's leading producer. The contest to lead the next wave is probably the most consequential in history . Artificial intelligence amplifies the winner-takes-all economy and will therefore bring an unprecedented concentration of wealth into the hands of very few companies and countries. Created with DALL·E 3 through ChatGPT. Original caption, translated from Spanish: An artistic image of a relay race, with runners representing China and the United States. They carry a baton symbolising artificial intelligence as they run along a digital track. From a Western perspective, the strength of the United States and Silicon Valley's giants is clear. Since the launch of ChatGPT, news of advances linked to artificial intelligence has appeared daily, while its possible applications across all kinds of sectors have multiplied. But what do we know about what is happening in China? Is China really capable of leading the AI wave? In this issue, we want to explore a Chinese perspective through Kai-Fu Lee , one of the world's foremost experts on artificial intelligence. Lee has worked for Apple and Microsoft, and was even president of Google China. He now runs his own venture capital fund to finance Chinese high-technology companies. In his book AI Superpowers , published in Spanish as Superpotencias de la Inteligencia Artificial , Lee argues that China is better equipped than other countries to lead the AI wave for the following reasons: Vast quantities of data : China has a huge population and a growing middle class that actively uses technology, particularly through WeChat, an all-in-one app combining chat, multimedia, payments, healthcare and more. This enormous volume of data is essential for training artificial intelligence models and improving their accuracy. Government investment : the Chinese government has demonstrated a strong commitment to AI by investing significantly in research, development and practical applications. Programmes such as the New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan underpin this investment. Leading technology companies : China is home to some of the world's largest and most advanced technology companies, including Alibaba, Tencent and Baidu, which are at the forefront of AI research and development. These companies compete fiercely to lead in areas such as facial recognition, natural language processing and robotics. A culture of rapid development : China's combative entrepreneurial mindset favours rapid experimentation and constant iteration. Companies can test new ideas and adapt quickly in response to the results, driving innovation in AI. Lee also argues that the talent of exceptional geniuses will matter less than the work of large numbers of well-trained engineers assisted by artificial intelligence itself. Despite the excessively competitive, almost warlike tone of the opening chapters, the end of the book , influenced by the author's experience of lymphoma, offers a universal, humanistic message, with concrete proposals for a new social contract as artificial intelligence's influence grows exponentially: Ethics in AI : the author stresses the importance of developing ethical and responsible AI, with guidelines and regulations to ensure that the technology is used fairly and safely. This means transparency in data use, privacy protection and consideration of the ethical implications of AI in decision-making. International collaboration : Lee advocates international cooperation in AI regulation and development. AI is a global technology, and nations must work together to address its challenges and share its benefits fairly. Career reorientation and lifelong learning : Lee argues that people must be willing to adapt and acquire new skills as AI transforms the economy and labour market. This requires greater investment in education and in developing skills that are difficult to automate and have a strong creative and strategic component. Cultural change : in any event, AI will eventually perform a large share of jobs. The writer therefore calls for a cultural shift in how societies perceive work and success, encouraging a focus on personal fulfilment and wellbeing instead of measuring a person's worth solely through their productivity at work. Professions exist today that would have been entirely undervalued a hundred years ago. Perhaps keeping older people company will become one of society's most highly valued occupations. Universal basic income or a social investment stipend : voices in Silicon Valley have advocated introducing a universal basic income as AI generates substantial economic gains while also affecting the labour market. Lee, however, believes it is important to give people a purpose so that they feel fulfilled. He therefore promotes a “social investment stipend”: “a living wage provided by the government for those who invest their time and energy in activities that promote a kind, compassionate and creative society. It would encompass three broad categories: care work, community service and education.” Translation note: the quotation defining the social investment stipend is translated from the Spanish article; its precise wording in the original English book has not been independently verified. Ultimately, the coming years will be marked by intense competition between the United States and China. But the impact of advances in artificial intelligence will affect all of humanity, and politics must be ready to offer citizens solutions that avert dystopian outcomes. P.S. Did you miss the words “Europe” or “European Union”? It seems that the Old Continent has been relegated to the role of legislator in this struggle to ride the AI wave. But that is a story for another issue… Pablo Martín Diez Academic Director, Institución Educativa ALEPH

AI's new frontier: multimodality and its applications in politics — GPT-4 V(ision) Three historical GPT-4 Vision experiments from October 2023: election posters, a campaign website and the appearance of a fictional candidate. Fernando Nieto Lobato AI in Practice Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 003 Practical experiment AI's new frontier: multimodality and its applications in politics — GPT-4 V(ision) Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved rapidly over the past decade , moving from simple data-processing tasks to sophisticated deep-learning capabilities. A crucial development along this path is the emergence of multimodal systems , which combine several types of data — text, images, audio and video — to provide more robust and versatile solutions. This advance is more than technological window dressing: it represents a qualitative leap towards emulating human cognition in machines . In this essentially practical article, we want to explore , through some concrete examples, what is probably the most powerful multimodal tool currently available to the general public : GPT-4 V(ision) . This advanced version of the GPT-4 language model adds the ability to “see” and interpret images . Here, we will explore practical examples of how GPT-4 Vision can be applied in politics , offering new perspectives and tools for political communication and marketing, just as it is being used in highly creative and surprising ways in many other contexts . Bear in mind that we are looking at the “six-month-old baby” version of this multimodal technology, which will undoubtedly advance rapidly and powerfully over the coming years. Yet what is already here — the way GPT-4 can now “see” , interpret and work with images, even though its novelty means we do not yet know how to give it the most precise instructions, or prompts — is already very interesting. Our own examples of GPT-4 V in political practice What follows reproduces the requests to the AI and its unedited responses . We have included the responses as text rather than images to make them easier to read. English edition note: the prompts and model responses below are historical examples recorded in the Spanish article published on 18 October 2023. They are translated in full here, including prompts transcribed from the screenshots. The quoted responses reproduce the model's assessments and recommendations at that time; they are not new advice or independently verified findings. Example 1: analysing election posters In this case, the posters are from Spain's July 2023 general election. Original screenshot, retained in Spanish. The four main slogans are translated in the response below. Additional poster text reads “Spain moves forward”, “Vote PSOE”, “Vote VOX”, and “Yolanda Díaz — candidate for prime minister”. Historical prompt — translated from the screenshot: Hello, I want you to act as a leading academic expert in political consulting, non-verbal communication and political marketing, and analyse in detail the image I am sharing with you, which shows the election posters of the main Spanish parties for the elections held in July 2023. After analysing it, I would like you to suggest — although I know that, because of your training, you have no direct knowledge of the electoral context or recent information about the parties — why they chose each of the posters, and their possible meanings or intentions. Then I want you to give a general analysis, highlighting similarities and differences above all. Finally, I want you to make recommendations to each party on how to improve its poster. Historical GPT-4 Vision response — translated from the Spanish article: To begin, let us remember that analysing election posters involves various components, from visual design, colour choices and the candidate's body language and non-verbal communication to the use of keywords and slogans. These elements are not chosen at random: they seek to convey a specific message to the electorate. Below is a detailed analysis of each poster: 1. PSOE — “ADELANTE” (“FORWARD”) Visual design : an image of the candidate surrounded by a group of people, smiling and looking ahead. Colours : predominantly red, traditionally associated with PSOE. Non-verbal communication : the candidate is smiling, conveying optimism and closeness to citizens. Slogan : “FORWARD” suggests progress and movement towards the future. Analysis : the message appears to be one of continuity and progress, with a focus on unity and inclusion. 2. PP — “ES EL MOMENTO” (“NOW IS THE TIME”) Visual design : a close-up of the candidate with a serious, determined expression. Colours : blue, PP's traditional colour. Non-verbal communication : looking directly at the viewer, which can be interpreted as confidence and determination. Slogan : “NOW IS THE TIME” conveys urgency and the idea of a necessary change. Analysis : the poster projects a message of strong leadership, reliability and the need for change. 3. VOX — “LO QUE IMPORTA” (“WHAT MATTERS”) Visual design : a close-up image of the candidate with a serious, thoughtful expression. Colours : green, VOX's identifying colour. Non-verbal communication : a reflective, profound expression. Slogan : “WHAT MATTERS” suggests focusing on essential or urgent issues. Analysis : it conveys a message about priorities, probably related to the central issues of VOX's campaign. 4. Yolanda Díaz — “Es por ti” (“It's for you”) Visual design : an image of the candidate smiling, with a friendly, approachable expression. Colours : pink and white, conveying femininity and purity. Non-verbal communication : an upward gaze, which may suggest hope or vision. Slogan : “It's for you” suggests an approach centred on the citizen. Analysis : the focus is on closeness to the electorate, suggesting that proposals and actions are directed towards citizens' wellbeing. Similarities and differences Similarities : all the posters use close-ups of the candidates, suggesting a focus on personal leadership. Differences : while some posters opt for more serious expressions (PP and VOX), others convey optimism and closeness (PSOE and Yolanda Díaz). The slogans also differ in emphasis, from progress (PSOE) to urgency (PP) and priorities (VOX). Recommendations PSOE : maintain the focus on unity and inclusion, but consider adding elements that highlight concrete proposals. PP : humanise the candidate further, perhaps by showing interactions with citizens or presenting proposals visually. VOX : clarify which issues are “WHAT MATTERS”, offering a more detailed view of its priorities. Yolanda Díaz : focus on specific proposals that support the slogan “It's for you”, showing how they will affect the electorate's everyday lives. In conclusion, election posters seek not only to inform but also to stir emotions and connect with the electorate. Every design element must align with the central message the party wishes to convey. Example 2: analysing an image of a website We chose Obama's website from 2012 because it is particularly iconic in digital political marketing. Original screenshot. This immediately identifies the main candidates. Imagery : the main photograph shows Barack Obama, smiling and energetic, in front of a series of American flags. It is a powerful image intended to evoke patriotism and leadership. Calls to action (CTAs) : there is a clear CTA to watch the “STATE of the UNION” and another to “DONATE”. The aim is to mobilise the audience both to engage with information and to contribute financially. Tone and messages : “KEEPING HIS WORD” and “Putting Americans back to work” are central messages, emphasising Obama's reliability and commitment to employment. Strengths Patriotic imagery : the combination of Obama's image and the flags evokes strong patriotic feelings. Clear CTAs : the calls to action are clear and prominent. Consistent messages : the emphasis is on Obama's reliability and commitment to central issues such as employment. Weaknesses Information overload : the page appears to contain a great deal of content in a small space. This may overwhelm some visitors. Lack of multimedia : although there is a CTA to watch a speech, embedding videos directly on the homepage could be more engaging. Suggestions for improvement Simplify and optimise : consider a cleaner, mobile-friendly layout, given that many users might access it on mobile devices. In conclusion, while the website effectively captures the spirit and key messages of Barack Obama's campaign, there are opportunities to improve the user experience, accessibility and integration of modern media. The city and its audience : a city of 200,000 inhabitants with high per capita income and a high level of education suggests an informed population with high expectations of its political representation. The candidate's image should convey confidence and professionalism, and align with this electorate's values and aspirations. 2. Initial analysis of the candidate's appearance : at first glance, the person in the image looks friendly and approachable. His smile is genuine, and his casual appearance suggests closeness to people. However, for a political campaign in the city described, he must also convey seriousness and professionalism. 3. Clothing suggestions Suit : a modern, fitted suit in neutral tones such as grey or navy blue would be ideal. These colours convey professionalism and confidence. The suit must fit well to create a polished appearance. Shirt : a white shirt is a classic choice that always works well in formal settings. To incorporate the party's colour, however, you could opt for a pale pink shirt, which would be subtle and stylish.
