AI at a political crossroads: Mustafa Suleyman on the containment problem Mustafa Suleyman's ten steps for containing advanced technologies, and what they demand of governments and international cooperation. Fernando Nieto Lobato Government & Public Services Power, Sovereignty & Geopolitics 002 Review & commentary AI at a political crossroads: Mustafa Suleyman on the containment problem Today, 11 October , as this newsletter goes out, the Spanish edition of The Coming Wave goes on sale . This bestselling book on artificial intelligence is co-authored by Mustafa Suleyman, one of the world's leading AI experts and a co-founder of DeepMind, the company that currently forms the core of Google's artificial intelligence operations. The Coming Wave , published in Spanish as La ola que viene: Tecnología, poder y el gran dilema del siglo XXI , offers a critical view of the implications of a range of developing technologies, led by AI, and raises significant questions about their impact on the global order . Last week, as you may recall, we brought some of these reflections to this newsletter in our article on disinformation. According to Suleyman and his co-author Michael Bhaskar, we stand on the threshold of a transformation that could propel humanity towards unprecedented technological and social progress. Yet this transition also carries the risk of disruption on a scale inconceivable in human history. Probably the book's most significant contribution is its focus on the “containment problem” . The authors warn of the emerging challenge of retaining control over increasingly powerful technologies, such as the convergence of AI and synthetic biology. These developments threaten to destabilise the “great bargain of the nation-state”, a pillar of the modern international order. Faced with this, Suleyman believes that today's governments, generally ill-prepared for this new situation, face an existential problem . Translation note: the quoted terms above are translated from the Spanish article; their precise wording in the English book has not been independently checked. The proposed solution: ten steps towards containing advanced technologies In the final part of the book, the authors propose a ten-step roadmap for effectively containing these disruptive technologies . These guidelines are a call to action which, although it may seem utopian, Suleyman and Bhaskar argue is essential to humanity's survival: Technical safety : concrete technical measures to mitigate potential harm and maintain control. Audits : a means of ensuring technological transparency and accountability. Chokepoints : levers to slow development and give regulators and defensive technologies time. Makers : ensuring that responsible developers build appropriate controls into technology from the outset. Businesses : aligning the incentives of the organisations behind the technology with its containment. Government : supporting governments so that they can build technology, regulate it and implement measures to mitigate harm. Alliances : creating a system of international cooperation to harmonise laws and programmes. Culture : a culture of sharing lessons and failures so that ways of addressing them can spread quickly. Movements : all of this requires public participation at every level, including pressure to ensure that every component of these containment processes is fully accountable. Coherence : ensuring that each element works in harmony with the others. Containment must be a virtuous circle of mutually reinforcing measures, rather than a cacophony of competing programmes riddled with gaps. Given this newsletter's focus, we will naturally examine steps 6 and 7 in a little more detail: these bear directly on political and governmental action concerning AI . Image generated with DALL·E 3 through ChatGPT. Prompt, translated from Spanish: An artistic illustration with watercolour brushstrokes for the newsletter “estrategIA”. Silhouettes of robots debating in a parliament symbolise AI's influence on politics, in soft, fluid colours. The essential role of government In the sixth step, entitled “ Governments: survive, reform, regulate ”, the author sets out the urgent need for governments to take a more active and specialised role in technological regulation and development . He argues that nation-states, with their control over fundamentals such as law and the economy, must address technology's emerging complexities in order to create and maintain resilient, secure social systems. The central premise is that technology , although largely developed and operated by the private sector, requires a deep understanding and comprehensive regulation on the part of government institutions . A lack of technical competence within the public sector is not an option. The author maintains that government investment in research and development is fundamental . Such investment encourages a positive feedback loop in which government not only understands but also controls the implications and applications of emerging technology. To achieve effective control, the authors recommend that governments invest in talent and internal capabilities , rather than relying solely on external consultants or suppliers. This approach will enable greater responsibility for, and ownership of, technological and political decisions. They also advocate creating specialised government roles, such as a minister for emerging technology , to oversee and regulate technological development effectively. The government's role extends beyond regulation alone. It must include detailed monitoring of how technology is used and how it affects the population. This transparency will not only inform public policy but also educate the public about technology's risks and benefits. On regulation, the book addresses the need to reassess licensing regimes for technological development. It proposes a more differentiated system based on the size and capabilities of the technological model in question. This would entail paying particular attention to AI laboratories working on more fundamental and potentially dangerous capabilities . It also points to the need for a complete overhaul of the tax system to fund safety and social welfare in the age of automation . It proposes taxing capital more heavily than labour and suggests initiatives such as a universal basic income as possible solutions to the economic challenges accompanying technological development. Finally, the book stresses that no government can tackle these challenges in isolation . Technological regulation must be an international effort, particularly because technology knows no borders. This is the subject of step 7 , which addresses the need for international regulation and cooperation to manage technological advances, especially in areas such as artificial intelligence and biotechnology. The book cites historical examples of successful cooperation, such as the 1995 Protocol on Blinding Laser Weapons, to argue that international cooperation is possible even on sensitive issues. Suleyman suggests that the most effective way to address the risks associated with emerging technologies is through strong, committed international alliances, rather than reliance on self-regulation or national rules . In this context, the book discusses the need to create a global institution devoted to technology, similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency, which could act as an AI auditing authority . This body would focus on global transparency and monitoring based on objective criteria, and would provide a foundation for government regulatory efforts. The industrialisation of disinformation: a new era on the horizon Generative AI could make convincing political disinformation cheap and widely available, with particular risks for local democracy. Fernando Nieto Lobato Democracy, Elections & Public Trust 001 Analysis The industrialisation of disinformation: a new era on the horizon “ Please remain. You furnish the pictures, and I'll furnish the war. ” Whenever disinformation comes up, those supposed words (which may well themselves be apocryphal) almost immediately spring to mind: the telegram from newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst (so magnificently brought to us by Welles in Citizen Kane ) to his illustrator in Havana , after the artist had asked to return to the United States because nothing was really happening in Cuba. Yet days later, just as Hearst himself had asserted, the United States entered the war in 1898. For although disinformation and the manipulation of information, including their political use, have been with us since time immemorial , technology has caused the number of cases to soar over recent decades, and particularly in recent years. Examples include Cambridge Analytica , especially its significance for Trump's 2016 campaign, and what happened around Brexit. The point is that, as generative artificial intelligence becomes widely available, disinformation will very probably become far more pervasive still, to the point where we may soon be unable to believe anything we see or hear unless we witness it in person. In his very recent book The Coming Wave , due to be published in Spain in a week's time, Mustafa Suleyman , founder of DeepMind, Google's artificial intelligence laboratory, devotes an interesting chapter to these issues and coins a term that particularly caught my attention: “the industrialisation of disinformation”. Until now, producing highly convincing manipulated information required professional work and advanced tools that were not generally available to everyone; or, as in Hearst's case, control of a mass-circulation newspaper and very little regard for the truth. We can now see how anyone with a simple mobile app will be able to create deepfakes that look entirely real to a non-specialist , whether already today or in the months or years ahead. Following a distressing case in Spain a few days ago, in which fake nude images of minors were circulated, one expert warned about the danger of “one-button apps”, which allow anyone with almost no knowledge to create fakes that cause enormous harm to others. In the coming years, we will very probably see even candidates for mayor in small towns, or their advisers, able to generate fake statements by other candidates , with barely any technical knowledge, by cloning their voices. They will be able to create fabricated news stories on fake versions of respected websites replicated with AI, or even fake but entirely convincing videos showing their rivals committing illegal acts , simply by typing a few lines of text. These technologies are already available to anyone in an early form and will become more widespread and sophisticated in the years ahead. Combined with mass, anonymous distribution through social media, this could have terrible effects, particularly in local politics, where public scrutiny is much more limited. This past week, for example, an AI video inpainting tool was presented that directly removes watermarks from any video . Watermarking is one of the precautions used by some AI video generators to identify their output. In response, companies such as Google are trying to develop their own systems for mandatory marking of everything generated with artificial intelligence . But these systems would need worldwide adoption, which does not look easy. As with text generated by GPT-4, which the company itself admits cannot be reliably distinguished from something written by a human, it will be very difficult to prevent these special safeguards from being easily defeated simply by combining several AIs and manipulating the output again . Indeed, given how hard it may be to establish that safeguard, some are already advocating the reverse approach: marking real photographs and videos produced by cameras , so that they can be distinguished from synthetic output. We therefore seem to face a very complicated future for political disinformation. AI itself has been, and continues to be, used to detect and combat deepfakes and disinformation campaigns, on many social networks, for example. Yet its new generative capabilities may bring an unstoppable flood of disinformation in the coming years that looks highly “authentic” to human eyes. As Suleyman points out in his book, this will make it much easier to sow instability : Translation note: the Spanish article identified the following book passages as translations from English made with GPT-4. They are translated back from that Spanish text here; they have not been checked against the original English edition. Anyone motivated to sow instability now has an easier task. Suppose that, three days before an election, the president is caught on camera using a racist slur. The campaign's press office vehemently denies it, but everyone knows what they have seen. Outrage spreads across the country. Poll ratings plummet. Swing states suddenly shift towards the opponent, who wins against all expectations. A new administration takes office. But the video is a deepfake, one so sophisticated that it evades even the best neural networks for detecting fakes. The threat here lies less in extreme cases than in subtle, nuanced and highly plausible scenarios that are exaggerated and distorted. It is not the president storming into a school, shouting nonsense and throwing grenades; it is the president saying resignedly that there is no choice but to introduce a set of emergency laws or bring back conscription. It is not Hollywood pyrotechnics; it is supposed CCTV footage showing a group of white police officers beating a Black man to death. But the threat could become far more damaging in the near future, when AI takes another step forward. In the book, Suleyman discusses the harm that could be caused by a radicalised terrorist seeking to recruit followers for his organisation through personalised videos. Soon these videos will be fully interactive and believable. You will be speaking directly to him. He knows you and adapts to your dialect and style, playing on your history, your personal grievances, the bullying you suffered at school, your terrible, immoral, Westernised parents. This is not disinformation as carpet bombing; it is disinformation as a surgical strike. With all these dangers already on the horizon, we are very probably entering a new era of political disinformation . Perhaps the only bleak consolation is the point made by The Economist's editor-in-chief, Zanny Minton-Beddoes, in this interesting discussion with Yuval Noah Harari and Mustafa Suleyman : “ In the analyses we have carried out [at The Economist], we think AI may have less impact on elections and the political system in the short term because trust in politicians is already at rock bottom **.” Translation note: this final quotation is translated from the Spanish article's rendering of the discussion; its precise English wording has not been verified against a transcript.
